sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The Hebrew title, following the ancient custom of naming books by their first word(s), is bereshit, “in the beginning.” The Greek title, based on the book’s content, is genesis , “origin.” Both titles are appropriate since the book is about the origin of our world as God’s good creation, marred by human sinfulness.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Because this anonymous book is part of the unified Pentateuch, establishing its authorship and date cannot be separated from the composition of the Pentateuch as a whole (see Introduction to the Pentateuch). Evidence relating to Genesis itself, however, suggests that, like the remainder of the Pentateuch, Moses gave the book its essential substance, and later editors supplemented it, all by the Holy Spirit’s inspiration. The New Testament gives specific testimony that Moses authored the Pentateuch, and within it Genesis. Jesus said that “Moses gave you circumcision” (John 7:22; Acts 15:1), which is uniquely given in Gen. 17. It is not surprising that the founder of Israel’s theocracy may have shaped this masterful introduction to the grand narrative that ultimately runs from Genesis to Kings. Importantly, the historical narrative of Genesis furnishes the theological explanation for God’s activity in the world.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Moses likely drew upon already existing oral and written sources as he wrote the book of Genesis. Readers should also be aware that although words known only from the middle of the second millennium occasionally appear in the text, the grammar of the Pentateuch was updated at some point, as were some place names (14:14 note). Also, the list of kings in 36:31–43 was apparently added after the monarchy was first established in Israel at the time of Saul. The date of the writing of Genesis, along with the rest of the Pentateuch, hangs on dating when Moses was active, likely around the fifteenth century B.C. This date for Moses is also tied to the dating of the Exodus. See the introduction to Exodus for more detail. Like its authorship and date, the purpose of Genesis cannot be considered apart from its place within the Pentateuch as a whole (see Introduction to the Pentateuch. As the opening part of this Old Testament grand narrative, Genesis sets the scene, beginning with the creation of the world.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Genesis forms part of a continuous narrative (Genesis–Kings) that selectively recounts events from the creation of the world to the downfall of the city of Jerusalem in 587/86 B.C. This is no ordinary history, however, because it includes within its scope the actions of God. Accordingly, this historical narrative is set apart from modern histories, which focus only on the activities of people. Although the book of Genesis is unique, it has interesting points of similarity with other ancient Near Eastern writings. The first eleven chapters of Genesis share many parallels, as well as conscious dissimilarities with ancient Near Eastern myths that preceded the time of Moses (Mesopotamian creation accounts such as the Enuma Elish; flood accounts such as those included in the Atrahasis Epic ; and the eleventh tablet of the Gilgamesh Epic ). Names and customs in the narratives about the patriarchs (chs. 12–50) accurately reflect that era, suggesting an early author with reliable documents. The Ebla texts (twenty-fourth century B.C. ) mention Ebrium, possibly the Eber of Gen. 10:21, and the Mari texts (eighteenth century B.C. ) attest to names such as “Abraham,” “Jacob,” and “Amo­rite.” The practice of granting a birthright (i.e., additional privileges to the eldest son, 25:5–6, 32–34; 43:33; 49:3) was widespread in the ancient Near East, and the sale of an inheritance (25:29–34) is documented at different periods in this area. The adoption of one’s slave (15:1–3) is found in a Larsa letter from Old Babylonia, and the adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh by their grandfather (48:5) may be compared to a similar adoption of a grandson at Ugarit (fourteenth century B.C. ). The gift of a female slave as part of a dowry and her presentation to her husband by an infertile wife (16:1–6; 30:1–3 and notes) are attested in the laws of Hammurabi (c. 1750 B.C. ). These and similar facts support the historical nature of the narrative. Direct proof of the historical reliability of the Genesis narrative has not been discovered, but this is not surprising given the age and nature of the events described in Genesis. Unfortunately, the lack of such evidence is often cited as a reason for questioning its historicity. However, such argumentation is flawed, and it makes no allowance for the antiquity of the materials being considered. Much of Genesis focuses on the experiences of a semi-nomadic family that lived about 2000 B.C. Ultimately, the reader is invited to accept the claims of Genesis and evaluate them in light of the rest of Scripture.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The literary structure of Genesis is marked by a series of headings that shape the overall account. After the prologue (1:1–2:3), Genesis is divided into ten parts marked out by the formula “These are the generations of ...” Each heading is followed by a genealogy of those descended from the person named (or objects, in 2:4) or by stories involving his notable descendants. To some extent, accounts one through three and accounts four through six parallel one another: (a) stories about the developments of humankind universally at the creation and at the re-creation after the flood (accounts one and four, respectively); (b) the genealogy of the redemptive lines through Seth and Shem (accounts two and five); and (c) the stories of the epochal covenant transactions with Noah and Abraham (accounts three and six). The final two pairs of accounts extend the Abrahamic line, contrasting his rejected offspring, Ishmael and Esau (accounts seven and nine), with stories about the elect, Isaac and Jacob respectively (accounts eight and ten). The headings in Genesis draw attention to a unique line of descendants that begins with Adam and concludes with the family of Jacob. Members of this family line include significant individuals such as Noah and Abraham. Beginning with Adam, his unique family line is destined to play a vital role in the fulfillment of God’s redemptive plan for the world, anticipating later the establishment of the Davidic dynasty and eventually the coming of Jesus Christ. Genesis reveals God’s plan both to overthrow Satan through a future member of this line descended from Eve (3:15) and to bless all the nations of the earth (12:3; 22:18). By the end of Genesis, two potential royal lines are highlighted. The first is associated with Joseph and his younger son Ephraim. The other potential royal line focuses on Judah and his younger son Perez. Genesis 49:8–10 anticipates that the line of Joseph/Ephraim will eventually be rejected by God and replaced by that of Judah, but this state of affairs will not come about until the time of David (Ps. 78:66–72). Genesis is a more difficult book to read than most suppose. The modern tendency is to read a short section of Genesis with little consideration given to the overall content of the book. Such an approach fails to recognize that Hebrew narrative writing often communicates important ideas through recurring motifs, word plays, and subtle changes between similar scenes. The depth of Genesis is often missed, with many readers failing to grasp the important truths contained in the text.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: As the opening part of the grand narrative that runs through the books of Genesis to Kings, and then on through the entire Bible, the book of Genesis sets the scene for all that is to follow. The initial chapters of Genesis are exceptionally important, for they explain how the relationship between God and humanity is broken and how God mercifully sets in place plans for the redemption of the whole world from the power of Satan. Although the opening chapters leave some questions unanswered (e.g., the origin of evil in the world), chs. 1–3 are fundamental for understanding the whole Bible. At the start of Genesis, human beings are created to be God’s vice-regents, extending His rule over the earth as they are fruitful and multiply. Given authority by God to rule over other creatures, human beings are privileged by God in a special way. Yet, through an act of betrayal, Adam and Eve are persuaded by a mysterious serpent to disobey God. They do so with tragic consequences for the whole world. Against this background, the book of Genesis narrates how God, in punishing the human couple, promises to send a descendant of the woman who will overcome the serpent, later revealed to be Satan. As Genesis traces the offspring of Eve, Abel’s murder by his brother Cain is the first indication that evil’s grip on the world will not be easily loosened. Humans proved their depravity by token religion, fratricide, and unrestrained vengeance (ch. 4); by tyranny, violence, and thinking evil continually (6:1–8); and by erecting an anti-kingdom against God (Nimrod and the infamous city with its high tower, 10:8–12; 11:1–9 note). God’s verdict about humankind stands: “The intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (8:21). With the exception of Noah and his family, humanity is destroyed. Just as miraculously and surely as God sovereignly transformed the dark empty void at earth’s origin (1:2) into a glorious habitat for humankind and brought it to rest (1:3–2:3), so also God sovereignly chose the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, promising to send through them a future descendant who would mediate God’s blessing to the nations of the world (12:1–3, 7; 13:14–17; 17:1–8; 26:2–6; 28:10–15). Before Jacob was born and had done either good or evil, God revealed that Jacob would rule over Esau, his older twin brother (25:21–23). God chose Jacob, even though he cheated his brother, deceived his father, and blasphemed God (ch. 27). God even used Judah’s scandalous wrongs against Tamar, and her daring ruse as well, to advance the messianic line (ch. 38). The heavenly King displayed His glorious rule by miraculously preserving the matriarchs in pagan harems (12:10–20; ch. 20) and opening their barren wombs (17:15–22; 18:1–15; 21:1–7; 25:21; 29:31; 30:22). He overrode human ways and customs by repeatedly choosing the younger, not the older, to inherit the birthright of the firstborn and with this the power to mediate blessing to others (25:23 note). God inclined the heart of His elect to trust His promises and to obey His commands. Against all hope, Abraham counted on God to give him innumerable offspring, and God credited that to him as righteousness (15:6). Confident of God’s sure promises, Abraham gave up his rights to the land (ch. 13); and Jacob, renamed “Israel” and clinging only to God (ch. 32), symbolically gave back the birthright to Esau (ch. 33). At the beginning of the Joseph story, Judah sold Joseph as a slave (37:26, 27), but later the former slave trader was willing to become a slave in the place of his brother (44:33, 34). Secure in the truth that God’s gracious design had brought good out of sins as heinous as murder and slave trading, Joseph forgave his brothers without recrimination (45:4–8; 50:24).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The opening chapters of Genesis portray God in two complementary but complex ways. On the one hand, Gen. 1:1–2:3 presents Him as a transcendent being who exists apart from and outside of the universe He creates. His authority and power are demonstrated by His ability to order the world merely by speaking. He is both a God of order who establishes boundaries and the source of moral judgment who declares what is good. On the other hand, Genesis 2:4–3:24 pictures God as immanent, a deity who sculpts the first man from the ground and later fashions from one of his ribs a suitable companion for him. This God walks in the garden and communicates face-to-face with those He has created. Set side by side, both portraits of God bring out distinctive aspects of His nature. As the rest of Genesis unfolds, we witness in a variety of ways the transcendence and immanence of God as He both judges human wrongdoing and graciously establishes the means by which humanity may once again know His favor and blessing. Through the covenants that He establishes with Noah and Abraham, God reveals Himself as one who will be faithful to what He promises. In the outworking of His plan of salvation, God displays both His sovereignty and His graciousness, working patiently in the face of human rebellion and corruption.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The book of Genesis provides the foundation upon which the whole of Scripture rests. Opening the grand story of the Bible, it sets the scene, introduces the characters and their relationship to one another, and reports certain events that prove decisive for understanding the world in which we now live. In particular, the opening chapters of Genesis not only explain how humanity has become alienated from God, living under His curse rather than His blessing, but also reveal that God will not allow evil to win the final victory. Through a process that begins in Genesis, God will eventually overcome the serpent/Satan through the offspring of the woman, the new Adam, Jesus Christ (3:15).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: What starts in Genesis is fulfilled in Christ. The paradise lost by the first Adam is restored forever by the last Adam. God Himself proclaimed that the woman’s offspring would destroy Satan (3:15). The genealogy begun in ch. 5 and advanced in ch. 11 is completed with the birth of Jesus Christ (Matt. 1; Luke 3:23–27). He is the ultimate offspring promised to Abraham (22:18; Gal. 3:16). The elect are blessed in Him because He alone, by His active and passive obedience, satisfied the law’s demands and died in their stead. All who are united to Christ by faith are Abraham’s descendants (Gal. 3:26–29). The bold prophecies and subtle types in Genesis show that God is writing a history leading to eternal rest in Christ. On the threshold of biblical prophecy Noah predicted that the Japhethites would find salvation through the Semites, a prophecy fulfilled in the New Testament (9:27 and note). The gift of the bride to Adam provides an image for understanding the gift of the church to Christ (2:18–25; Eph. 5:22–32). Melchizedek’s priesthood is like that of the Son of God’s (14:18–20; Heb. 7). This marvelously unified sacred history certifies that the focus of Genesis is Christ.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The interpretation of Genesis has been profoundly distorted in the past two centuries by methodologies that have dismissed the book’s obvious unity, preferring rather to focus on hypothetical literary sources or numerous independent oral compositions. Scholarly attempts to reconstruct a complex process of transmission stray well beyond what may be known with certainty, often driven by misguided presuppositions about how Israelite religion developed. As a result, the message of Genesis as a unified work has largely been ignored or replaced by ideas that fail to do justice to what the text of Genesis says in its received form. Against such a negative background, recent studies in Hebrew narrative writing have helped scholars better appreciate how ancient writers constructed literary works. This has led to a greater understanding of the message of Genesis.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The tension between Genesis and modern science about the origins of the universe and of living species is largely resolved when it is recognized that they are speaking from different perspectives. The questions of who created and why are more central to the book’s overall message than are specific details about how and when the universe was created. Science cannot answer the former questions, and Genesis says little about the latter (1:2, 5, 6, 11 and notes). Though this topic is important, of far greater significance is the redemptive narrative that begins with the creation of the first Adam and culminates in the new creation achieved by the last Adam. Throughout most of the twentieth century, scholars holding to the “documentary hypothesis” have contended that Genesis is composed of conflicting documents: J (for Jahweh/Yahweh, “the L ORD ”), E (for Elohim, “God”), D (for Deuteronomist—although rare in Genesis), and P (for Priestly writer). While this scheme is still accepted by some, many scholars today question the criteria used for identifying these alleged sources, with some emphasizing instead the unity of the text as we have it. For example, the flood story, once thought to be a classic example of the documentary hypothesis, is now conceded to demonstrate remarkable unity (6:9–9:29 note). See Introduction to the Pentateuch.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The title of the book, “Exodus,” is derived from the Greek word exodos (Luke 9:31), which means “exit” or “departure.” The book takes its name from the central event of Israel’s departure from Egypt, recorded in the book’s first fifteen chapters.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: It is not possible to separate the authorship of Exodus from the authorship of the Pentateuch as a whole (see Introduction to the Pentateuch). Both the Jewish and Christian tradition ascribes authorship to Moses. Within the book, there are explicit references to Moses writing down the materials (Ex. 24:4, 34:28) or to demands that Moses write (Ex. 17:14). Further, Jesus, referring to Exodus, calls it “the book of Moses” (Mark 12:26; Mark 7:10). While the book itself is anonymous and while there appears to be reference to an event shortly after the time of Moses (Ex. 16:35–36), there are no compelling reasons to deny the essential Mosaic authorship of the book.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Exodus carries forward the story of God’s fulfillment of His promise to Abraham to bless him and make of him a great nation (Gen. 12:2). It begins by referring to the descent of Jacob’s family into Egypt (1:1–7), linking with Genesis, especially Gen. 46:8–27. The book concludes with Israel at Sinai where the tabernacle is completed. While multiple views of the date of the exodus have been proposed (see Special Issues below), the events covered in the book may be credibly placed against the following historical background. Joseph’s rise to power (1:5) probably precedes the rule over Lower Egypt of the Semitic Hyksos (c. 1700–1550 B.C. ). The reference at 1:8 to a new king “who did not know Joseph” likely refers to the expulsion of the Hyksos by the eighteenth dynasty founder Ahmose I (1550–1525 B.C. ). If the exodus is dated c. 1447 B.C. (see Special Issues), the Pharaoh of the initial oppression was probably Ahmose I (1550–1525 B.C. ), while the Pharaoh of the exodus was Thutmose III (1479–1425 B.C. ). Moses’s birth would have fallen within the reign of Ahmoses I (1550–1525 B.C. ). Given Moses’s authorship of Exodus, we should date the book after the exodus event (c. 1447 B.C. ) and before his death, about 1406 B.C.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Exodus forms an integral part of the continuous narrative that runs from Genesis to Kings, recounting events from the creation of the world to the downfall of the city of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. Unlike modern histories, which focus only on the activities of people, this narrative focuses on God’s actions and words. Exodus has within it a variety of literary forms that have been carefully integrated into the theological-historical narrative. The poetic victory song of ch. 15 forms the climax to the deliverance of the Israelites from Pharaoh’s army. The Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33) contains a mixture of materials: case laws (21:1–22:20); moral imperatives (22:21–23:9); cultic instructions (23:10–19). The instructions for the building of the tabernacle and the appointment of priests are set out in considerable detail (chs. 25–31), as is the report of the tent’s construction (chs. 35–40). The inclusion of such different types of material within Exodus enriches greatly the reader’s perception of what took place.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The narrative recorded in the book of Exodus may be viewed as falling into two halves with ch. 18 forming a hinge that links them together. Jeth­ro’s visit to Moses close to Mount Sinai provides an opportunity to review what has happened to Moses and the Israelites in the preceding chapters of Exodus. Jethro’s response provides a suitable summary for all that has occurred: “Blessed be the L ORD , who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and who has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians. Now I know that the L ORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people” (Ex. 18:10–11). After looking backwards, the rest of ch. 18 looks forward, anticipating how God will provide within the Book of the Covenant legal judgments to guide those involved in resolving disputes (Ex. 21:1–22:20). By establishing different levels of judges within Israel, the people will be helped to fulfill their calling to be a holy nation. The written preservation of the words of God’s covenant has central importance for the theology of the book of Exodus. God Himself not only speaks the Ten Commandments to His assembled people at Sinai, but He also later inscribes these on tablets of stone, “written with the finger of God” (31:18; cf. 32:15, 16; 34:1, 28). The terms of the covenant were further specified by the so-called “Book of the Covenant” (20:22–23:33), the words of God written down by Moses, the mediator of God’s covenant (24:4, 7; cf. 34:27). Elements of the Sinai covenant resemble in both form and content the state treaty form of the second millennium B.C. , particularly the Hittite state treaties. These treaties included a preamble (20:2), general obligations (20:3–17), specific obligations (21:1–23:33) and ratification (24:1–11). A copy of the treaty was often preserved at the sanctuaries of the parties (e.g., the two tablets of 31:18). Also, the similarity of the content of the case laws of chs. 21:1–22:20 to ancient Near Eastern codes (particularly the Code of Hammurabi of Babylon, c. 1750 B.C. ) has often been noted. The Exodus case laws, however, give greater prominence to the value of human life compared to property.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Several major themes are evident in the book of Exodus. First, it tells how the Lord liberated the people of Israel from Egypt to begin to fulfill His covenant with their fathers. A second major element of the book is the covenant ratification at Sinai, which specified the terms of relationship between the holy God and His people. The third theme issues from the first two and is their consummation: the reestablishment of God’s dwelling with people. Each of these themes involves a triumph of divine grace: God’s mighty rescue of His people from slavery in Egypt, His thunderous self-revelation at Sinai, and His gracious condescension to dwell among His erring people in the tabernacle. The unfolding of these themes also reveals the Lord’s holiness and grace in His cov­enant obligations and in His willingness to forgive His disobedient servants. Crucial to the narrative is Moses’s role as mediator between God and people. As God’s chosen servant, Moses is the mediator of judgment against Egypt and is the one through whom God delivers Israel. Through Moses God gives His revelation at Sinai. Moses also shepherds the people through the wilderness to the Promised Land. He pleads for the people, and he is the one through whom the Lord provides food and water. Moses’s role in the history of redemption prepares pointedly for Christ, the Mediator of the new covenant (Deut. 18:15). The revelation that Moses receives of God’s name “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (34:6) justifies the building of the tabernacle, but that description of the Lord will be revealed more fully in the incarnate Christ, the greater servant of the Lord, who will tabernacle among His people (John 1:14, 17; Heb. 3:1–6). God’s covenant obligations (the Ten Commandments as broad principals and the Book of the Covenant, containing case laws, moral imperatives and cultic regulations) reveal His holy nature and require holiness of the people among whom God will dwell. The instructions for building the tabernacle (chs. 25–31) and the report of how these were fulfilled (chs. 35–40) underline the importance of God coming to dwell among the Israelites. God’s presence in their midst distinguished them from every other nation.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Underlying the deliverance of the Israelites from slavery in Egypt is the motif of God making Himself known. He comes not merely to rescue His people, but more importantly to reveal something of His glorious nature to them. From beginning to end, Exodus describes how God reveals Himself through both powerful supernatural events and spoken words. In Exodus God moves from being perceived as a distant deity to becoming a God who dwells in the midst of His people. The experience of the Israelites is contrasted with that of Pharaoh who refuses to know the Lord: “Who is the L ORD , that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the L ORD and moreover, I will not let Israel go” (5:2). Yet, while the Israelites were given every reason to believe in God because of all that they witnessed in Egypt and in the wilderness, even they were rebellious. Having covenanted to worship God exclusively, they soon committed apostasy by fashioning a golden calf. While they fully deserved to be punished, God displayed grace, revealing to Moses something of His remarkable nature: “The L ORD , the L ORD , a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children’s children, to the third and the fourth generation” (34:6–7). God’s own description of Himself would form one of the central statements of His nature in the Old Testament. Having displayed His awesome power in rescuing the Israelites from the king of Egypt and later destroying his army, the book of Exodus underlines the majesty of God in the description of the tabernacle that is constructed for His use. Manufactured from the finest of materials, including considerable quantities of gold, the tabernacle was meant to honor the King of Kings.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In addition to its description of the historical events by which Israel is delivered from slavery to become God’s people, Exodus also provides an important illustration of God’s saving work. The savior God redeems His chosen people from the powers of evil, judges those powers, and claims His people as His firstborn son, a holy nation of priests and kings among whom He dwells. At the heart of this process is the Passover, an event by which the firstborn male Israelites are ransomed from death and set apart as holy to belong to God. Not only is God the Savior of His people, but He then invites them to accept Him as their King through the covenant at Mount Sinai. The pattern of divine victory over enemies, followed by the establishment of the divine dwelling place, is repeated in Christ’s first and second advents (e.g., Eph. 2:14–22; Rev. 20:11–22:5).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The sacrificial death of Jesus at the time of Passover provides the key to understanding how the book of Exodus prepares for the coming of Jesus Christ. God’s deliverance of the Israelites from oppressive slavery in Egypt anticipates a greater deliverance from slavery to sin that is accomplished through the death of Christ, the Lamb of God, our Passover sacrifice (John 1:29; 1 Cor. 5:7). As the “bread of life” (John 6:35, 48), Jesus is new manna from heaven. The sprinkled blood of animal sacrifice is now replaced by the blood of Christ (24:8; Matt. 26:27, 28; Heb. 12:24; 1 Pet. 1:2). His “exodus” at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31) accomplishes the salvation of the true people of God. God’s new covenant people are joined to Jesus Christ, in whom the Gentiles become the people of God, members of the commonwealth of Israel, and fellow citizens with the Old Testament saints (19:5, 6; Eph. 2:11–19). The full meaning of the description of Israel in Exodus may now therefore be applied to the churches of the Gentiles (1 Pet. 2:9, 10).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: In the past two centuries the interpretation of Exodus has been significantly influenced by methodologies that have focused attention on the hypothetical literary sources that were used to compose the present text. While Moses may have used various written and oral sources in writing Exodus (e.g. “the Book of the Covenant” in Exodus 21–24), scholarly attempts to deconstruct these sources usually rely on unfounded presuppositions about how Israelite religion developed, or they depend on unsatisfactory criteria for distinguishing one source from another. As a result, the message of Exodus as a unified work has largely been ignored or replaced by ideas that fail to do justice to what Exodus says in its received form. Additionally, debate over the historicity of the exodus event has significantly impacted the way that many scholars approach the text (see Special Issues below). Also of significance is the prominent role of the exodus event and Moses as the deliverer in African and African-American Christianity.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The date and route of the exodus have been subjects of considerable debate. Biblical chronology dates the exodus event at 480 years before the reign of Solomon (1 Kin. 6:1). This would place the event at about 1447 B.C. This early date is consistent with Judg. 11:26, which declares that three hundred years had elapsed since Israel entered Canaan. The c. 1447 B.C. date is also supported by 12:40, 41, where 430 years is the duration of Israel’s stay in Egypt (itself a reference to Gen. 15:13). The Pharaoh of the exodus would then be Thutmoses III (1479–1425). Moses’s death would have occurred sometime later, in 1406. B.C. Advocates of a much later date appeal to the name “Raamses” (or “Rameses” Gen. 47:11) as one of the store cities built with Israelite labor (1:11). Rameses II (1279–1213 B.C. ) is taken to be the Pharaoh of the exodus, and the approximate date is 1270 B.C. , with the death of Moses taking place around 1230 B.C. This was held to be more consistent with the archaeology of cities destroyed in Palestine and with the lack of earlier settlement in Transjordan (the region east of the Jordan River and the Dead Sea). However, more recent discoveries in Transjordan and a new evaluation of the destruction of Jericho have weakened the case for the late date. The route of the exodus began at Raamses (or Rameses). Its exact location is the subject of considerable debate, though modern Qantir is the site most favored (Tell el-Dab’a). From there the Hebrews journeyed south to Succoth (13:20). Here, apparently unable to move on, the Hebrews turned northward (14:2). Three sites are mentioned, Baalzephon, Migdol, and Pi-hahiroth, all of which seem to have been located west of Lake Ballah. There were three possible routes of Israelite escape. The “way of the land of the Philistines” (13:17) connected Egypt with Canaan by the heavily fortified coastal route. A second route, the way of Shur, began near the Wadi Tumilat in the Delta area, crossed to Kadesh-barnea, and branched off to Canaan. The Egyptian boundary wall of Shur may have been a major obstacle to this route. In leading the people south to southern Sinai, the Lord not only brought them to the mountain He had designated to Moses, but distanced them from further contact with the Egyptians. The deliverance through the sea may have been through one of the bitter lakes north of the Gulf of Suez. The Sinai peninsula is a triangle of land measuring approximately 150 miles (241 km) across at the top and 260 miles (420) along the sides. Two arms of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Suez and the Gulf of Aqaba, flank it. The Hebrews proceeded south along the west coast of the Sinai. The bitter waters of Marah (15:22–25) are possibly identified with Bir el-Mura or ‘Ayun Musa (“springs of Moses”). Elim with its many springs and trees has been tentatively identified as Wadi Gharandel, the encampment by the Red Sea (Num. 33:10). The wilderness of Sin lay along the western edge of the Sinai Plateau close to the Gulf of Suez. If the traditional location of Mount Sinai as Jebel Musa is correct, Israel would have then turned inland by a series of valleys to Jebel Musa, traveling through the desert of Rephidim, where they fought against the Amalekites (17:8–16). Rephidim was the last encampment in the wilderness of Sinai before the sacred mountain. Then they proceeded to Mount Sinai (ch. 19) where they were invited by God to enter into a special covenant relationship with Him, the result being that He graciously descended to dwell in their midst in the newly constructed and highly ornate tabernacle.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: Leviticus , the Latin form of the Greek title of the book, means “about Levites.” The Jews have traditionally called the book vayikra’ (“and He [the Lord] called”), after the opening words of the book. The Levites, who form much of the subject matter of this book, were the tribe of Israel from which the priests were drawn; they were responsible for maintaining Israel’s worship facilities and practices,band promoting holy living. The title is apt, because the book is primarily about the Israelites being a holy nation due to God’s presence among them. It is not addressed solely to priests or Levites, but to all Israelites, telling them how to offer sacrifices and maintain ritual and moral purity in light of God’s presence among them.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The conclusion that Moses wrote Leviticus derives from the internal character of Leviticus itself and of the Pentateuch as a whole, as well as from Old and New Testament references to Moses as an author. For a more complete discussion of the issues relating to Mosaic authorship, see “Introduction to the Pentateuch.”

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Much of Leviticus reports the words of God to Moses and his brother Aaron, but it never states when and how these words were written down. The precise date that Leviticus was committed to writing remains somewhat uncertain, though it likely occurred during the wilderness wanderings prior to Moses’s death (c. 1406 or 1230 B.C. ). The majority of critical scholars place the writing of Leviticus in the postexilic era (c. the fifth century B.C. ), many centuries after Moses. This view is improbable, however, because the content of Leviticus does not fit such a late period: the worship of the second temple differed significantly from that enjoined in Leviticus, and Leviticus is presupposed or quoted by earlier books such as Deuteronomy, Amos, and, most obviously, Ezekiel. The book reflects the ideals of worship and holiness that were accepted in Israel from the time of Moses to the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Leviticus records various instructions that were given by God in order for the people to be a holy nation. Most of Leviticus consists of speeches, with only a few events being narrated. However, these divine speeches form a manual of worship for the tabernacle with specific directions for sacrifices and offerings, laws about purification and purity, and specification of punishments for false worship. Apart from the numerous short introductions to the instructions given by God, the only reported events are the consecration of the priests and the associated deaths of Nadab and Abihu (8:1–10:20), as well as the punishment of a man who curses God (24:10–23).

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Leviticus is dominated by speeches, spoken by God usually to Moses (e.g., 1:1; 4:1), but sometimes to both Moses and Aaron (e.g., 11:1; 13:1). God’s instructions, however, are normally intended for the Israelites as a whole (e.g., 1:2; 4:2) or for the priests in particular (e.g., 6:9; 21:1). This reflects Moses’s role as mediator between God and the people, something which the people requested after God spoke the Ten Commandments directly to them (Ex. 20:18–21). An analysis of the vocabulary of Leviticus reveals that certain key words occur with considerable frequency. These terms underline the importance of the categories of holiness, cleanness/purity and uncleanness/impurity. Leviticus is particularly interested in how the Israelites were to be a holy nation so that the Holy One of Israel might reside in the tabernacle at the center of their camp.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: No book in the Old Testament presents a greater challenge to the modern reader than Leviticus, and imagination is required to picture the ceremonies and rites that form the bulk of the book. However, it is important to try to understand the rituals in Leviticus for two reasons. First, rituals enshrine, express, and teach those values and ideas that a society holds most dear. By analyzing the ceremonies described in Leviticus, we can learn about what was most important to the Old Testament Israelites. Second, these same ideas are foundational for the New Testament writers. The concepts of holiness, cleanness and uncleanness found in Leviticus shed important light on how New Testament writers interpret the death of Christ (see Christ in Leviticus below). While the rituals of Leviticus are often obscure to us, they were so central to Old Testament thinking that they required no explanation to the first readers of Leviticus. Every Israelite knew why a particular sacrifice was offered on a specific occasion and what a certain gesture meant. For readers today, every hint in the text must be grasped to understand these things, and a judicious reading between the lines is sometimes required. Leviticus is part of the covenant instructions given at Sinai. The ideas that inform the whole Sinaitic covenant, including God’s sovereign grace in choosing Israel and His moral demands, are presupposed here. Certain themes are especially prominent in Leviticus. First, God is present with His people, a direct result of the tabernacle having been constructed. Second, because God is holy, His people must also be holy (11:45). Third, since people are sinful and ritually unclean, they cannot expect to come close to or dwell near the holy God. Contact between a sinner and divine holiness will result in death. Hence, atonement for sin through the offering of sacrifice is of paramount importance. These themes may be elaborated as follows: 1. The Divine Presence. The book of Leviticus presupposes the concluding event of Exodus. God now dwells with His people in the tabernacle or tent of meeting. Nevertheless, access into God’s immediate presence is still restricted due to human sinfulness. Since God is present in the Most Holy Place, entry is barred to all but the high priest once a year on the Day of Atonement (16:17). Though God’s presence is usually unseen, He may manifest His glory on special occasions such as the ordination of the priests (9:23, 24). The greatest of God’s gifts is that He deigns to dwell with His people (26:12). 2. Holiness. The aims of Leviticus are summarized in 11:45: “You shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.” People are meant to be like God, which entails imitating God in daily life. The holiness of God involves His being the source of perfect life in its physical, spiritual, and moral dimensions. Animals offered to Him in sacrifice must be free of blemish (1:3), and priests who represent God to people and people to God must be free of physical handicaps (21:17–23). Those who suffer discharges, particularly of blood, or who have disfiguring skin diseases are barred from worship until they are cured and become ritually clean again (chs. 12–15). Physical wholeness is seen as symbolizing the perfection of divine life. Yet holiness is also an inward matter of attitudes issuing in wholesome moral behavior. The concept of holiness is especially emphasized in chs. 17–25, which are chiefly concerned with personal ethical conduct, epitomized in 19:18 by the statement, “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” 3. Atonement through Sacrifice. Since Israel failed to live up to God’s righteous requirements, a means of atonement was essential so that both moral lapses and shortcomings could be pardoned. To this end, Leviticus gives the most extensive descriptions found in the Old Testament of the sacrificial system (chs. 1–7), the role of the priests (chs. 8–10; 21–22), and the great national festivals (chs. 16; 23; 25). These great ceremonies were designed to make possible the coexistence of the holy God with His sinful people. Leviticus also shows clearly Israel’s sinfulness: no sooner are Aaron’s sons ordained than two of them profane their office and die in a fearful display of divine judgment (ch. 10). Those suffering from skin disease or bodily discharge, as well as those guilty of grave moral sins, are barred from the worshipping community because their imperfections are incompatible with a holy and perfect God (chs. 12–15). In showing the sinfulness of Israel, the nation God set apart from the unholy world and called to be holy, the symbols of Leviticus teach the universality of human sin, a doctrine endorsed by Jesus (Mark 10:18) and Paul (Rom. 3:23). Leviticus speaks to humanity in every age, reminding us of the depth of our sin, but also pointing us to the sacrifice of Christ, whose blood is far more effective than the blood of bulls and goats.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Through the symbols and rites it describes, Leviticus paints a picture of God’s character that is both presupposed and deepened in the New Testament. Leviticus teaches that God, as the Holy One of Israel, is the source of perfect life, that He loves His people, and that He desires to dwell among them. In this we see a foreshadowing of the incarnation, when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The symbolism that underlies the customs and rituals of Leviticus not only stresses that God is holy, but it also underlines that He is the source of life and wholeness. For this reason, any and every thing associated with death stands in opposition to God and His purposes. To come close to God is to find life in all its perfection; to move away from God is to enter the domain of death and evil.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Perhaps more than any other book of the Bible, Leviticus provides an important insight into the nature of divine holiness/wholeness. While the storyline in Leviticus involves little action, with the Israelites remaining at Mount Sinai, the content of the instructions they receive from God is exceptionally important, since it defines how they are to be a holy nation, distinct from all other nations. Importantly, much of Leviticus underlines the moral standards that God expects of His people in order for them to be holy as He is holy. While the coming of Jesus Christ and the creation of the church as a new dwelling-place for God impacts some of God’s instructions in Leviticus, the underlying moral expectations do not change. God still demands that His people should be holy as He is holy.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The book of Leviticus underlines how the concepts of holiness, cleanness, and uncleanness impact every aspect of life, reflecting the consequences of human sin which is associated with death. In the Gospels, Jesus frequently brings healing to people who have illnesses that make them ritually unclean and exclude them from the worshipping community of Israel (e.g., lepers). Jesus often heals those who are ritually unclean by touching them. He himself is never made unclean, but His power transforms those who are unclean. For the Gospel writers, this is further evidence of Jesus’ divine status, for only God can cleanse the unclean. Caught between divine holiness and human sinfulness, the people’s paramount need is for atonement and cleansing. It is here that Leviticus has the most to teach Christians, since its ideas help explain the New Testament description of the atoning work of Christ, which is based primarily on the Passover sacrifice. He is the perfect sacrificial Lamb who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). His death is the ransom for many (Mark 10:45). His blood cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). Additionally, Jesus is the perfect High Priest who enters not the earthly tabernacle once a year on the Day of Atonement (ch. 16), but has ascended to the heavenly tabernacle forever, because He has not offered merely a goat for the sins of His people, but His own life (Heb. 9; 10). The rending of the temple veil when Jesus was crucified was a visible demonstration that His death opened up the way to God for all believers (Matt. 27:51; Heb. 10:19, 20). Leviticus restricts salvation to the old covenant community of Israel. The food laws (ch. 11) and the prohibitions on mixtures (19:19) reminded Jews of their unique status. But the New Testament opens the kingdom to all nations and abrogates the food laws (Mark 7:14–23; Acts 10), while at the same time insisting on the separation of the church from the world (John 17:16; 2 Cor. 6:14–7:1). While the Old Testament sufferer had to wait for God to heal him (ch. 14), in the Gospels God in Christ draws near and heals both lepers and those with discharges (Luke 8:43–48; 17:12–19). The God of Leviticus, whose essential character is shown to be holy life, is shown in the Gospels to be present in Christ and His redemptive work.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Like the other books of the Pentateuch, the interpretation of Leviticus has been heavily influenced in the past two centuries by critical ideas regarding the process by which the Pentateuch was composed. Under the “Documentary Hypothesis” of the late nineteenth century, much of the material in Leviticus was assigned to the post-exilic period and viewed as reflecting a form of religion inferior to that found in other Pentateuchal sources. Such thinking has been rightly challenged, but it continues to be widely held. While the material in Leviticus is perhaps some of the most difficult for modern readers to appreciate, when correctly approached it complements well all that is said elsewhere in the Pentateuch.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The Christian appropriation of the book of Leviticus presents particular difficulties. Why is it that Christians ignore many of the instructions that are given by God for the people of Israel? Why, for example, did Jesus and the early church abandon the food regulations set out in ch. 11? For the Christian reader of the Bible, the book of Leviticus may initially seem to have little to say to those who live under the new covenant established by Christ. To be sure, Christians are not expected to offer the sacrifices listed in chs. 1–7, conform to the dietary rules of ch. 11, or adhere to the ritual regulations concerning uncleanness in chs. 12–15. All of these regulations, together with the instructions for the Levitical priesthood, are related directly to the creation of the tabernacle as God’s residence under the Sinai Covenant. Under the new covenant, with its organic temple, the church, instructions for holy living take a different form. Yet although the civil and ceremonial regulations of ancient Israel are no longer in force, they still have much to teach us about the nature of God, especially His holiness. For this reason, the book of Leviticus continues to be of tremendous relevance for Christians.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: In the Hebrew Bible, it was customary to designate each of the five books of Moses by the word with which it began. For Numbers, this practice was modified by using the fifth Hebrew word as a title. This word, translated “in the wilderness,” (Hb. Bemidbar ) is an apt description of the book’s content, since it describes the nation’s experience during forty years in the wilderness. When the Bible was translated into Greek, its books were given Greek names. In the case of Numbers, the Greek translation abandoned the excellent Hebrew name and used a Greek word meaning “numbers” ( arithmoi ) that actually describes only a few of its chapters. This somewhat inappropriate Greek title was carried over by translation into the English Bible tradition.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Together with the rest of the Pentateuch, Numbers has traditionally been ascribed to Moses. This conclusion is based upon the unitary character of the Pentateuch and upon the clear witness of both the Old and New Testaments associating these books with Moses and noting his role in writing sections within them (Introduction to the Pentateuch: Author and Date). It is further supported by the obvious antiquity of the materi­als contained in the Pentateuch. The Book of Numbers itself refers to Moses’s activity chronicling the events described in the book (33:2). That much of the book comes from Moses’s hand does not rule out the possibility of later editorial activity and the likelihood that some portions were added after Moses’s death (e.g., 12:3).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Since Moses was the primary author of Numbers, we may reasonably date the composition of the book to the period after the wilderness wandering (which followed the exodus) and before the death of Moses in about 1406 or 1230 B.C. (See Introduction to Exodus: Special Issues). The book begins with the preparations for the march across the wilderness, tells of experiences along the way, describes the failure of faith that led the exodus generation of Israelites to refuse to undertake the conquest of the Promised Land, tells of the forty years of waiting until an entire adult generation would die, and ends with the preparation for entering Canaan. Given its content, Numbers was likely written as a warning to the generation of Israelites born in the wilderness that they should persevere in faith and obedience where their parents had not. For future generations of God’s people, the book would speak a similar message.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Numbers forms an integral part of the “five books of Moses,” the Pentateuch, as well as in the larger theological-historical narrative that runs from Genesis to Kings. It presupposes what has already been told and anticipates events that will be described in later books. As in other books of the Pentateuch, the overall narrative incorporates different types of material that enrich the description of what occurs. In Numbers these include census lists (chs. 1, 26) and various passages that outline regulations concerning different areas of religious life (e.g., duties of Levites; Nazirite vow; offerings and special festivals).

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Numbers may be viewed as falling into four main sections (see Outline of Numbers below), the first and last focusing on preparations for entering the land of Canaan. Both of these sections are introduced by a census numbering the men who are eligible to fight in the army. The second census, however, confirms that of all those counted on the first occasion, only two remain alive to enter the land of Canaan (Joshua and Caleb; see 26:64–65). The explanation for the death of the first generation comes in the middle two sections of Numbers. The first of these, which is the longer (chs. 10–21), describes how the Israelites rebel against God when confronted by the challenge of taking the land of Canaan and how they fail to trust God fully to provide for them in the wilderness. For these failures the adult generation is condemned by God to die in the wilderness, and the whole nation must spend forty years in the wilderness. The second of the middle two sections (chs. 22–25), which prepares for a new generation of adult Israelites entering the Promised Land, focuses on a series of blessings pronounced by a foreign prophet, Balaam. These blessings echo the divine promises given to the patriarchs in Genesis, indicating that, in spite of punishing the Israelites in the wilderness, God has not abandoned His plans for the nation. Several episodes in Numbers form a striking parallel to episodes in Exodus that recount how the Israelites complained to God regarding a lack of food or water in the wilderness. Interestingly, whereas in Exodus the people go unpunished for their failure to trust God, in Numbers, God punishes them in differing ways (compare, for example, Ex. 16 with Num. 11). Having committed themselves to be God’s holy nation at Mount Sinai, the Israelites are judged and punished according to the terms of the covenant.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The events of Numbers vividly portray the faithfulness of the covenant God despite the failures of an erring humanity. God directs His people as they prepare for their journey through the wilderness, comforts them in difficulties, deals with their fears and failures, and rebukes or punishes them when necessary. This portrayal of God’s faithfulness stands in sharp contrast to the book’s repeated depiction of human faithlessness, the utter failure of humanity to meet God’s standards by its own strength. Human failures are clearly portrayed and contrasted with the wise measures of the ever-faithful God. Even Moses, their great leader, sinned and was not permitted to enter the Promised Land, although he saw it from a distance (20:6–13 and notes; 27:12–14). This shows that even the best of persons are still sinners and are saved only through the merits of Christ—salvation comes only by the grace of God through faith in Christ.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: In general terms, the book of Numbers portrays God consistently with how the preceding books have presented Him. Numbers underlines the sovereign power of God in history. Despite imposing obstacles, great dangers, and the failures of His people, God brings them safely through the wilderness. His sovereign power is sufficient for every eventuality.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Numbers contributes to the grand narrative that begins in Genesis by describing the forty years that Israel spends in the wilderness. This period of time between the ratification of the Sinai covenant and entering into the land of Canaan is presented as a period of testing, when God exposes the people’s lack of true commitment to Him. The Apostle Paul later recalls in 1 Cor. 10:1–13 how these things were written in order to be a warning to others. Although the adult generation of Israelites that Moses led out of Egypt witnessed God’s power in saving them and entering willingly into a covenant relationship with Him, they were still exceptionally prone to sin. All of their spiritual experiences did not prevent them from being idolaters, indulging in sexual immorality, testing God, and grumbling against God. Like the ancient Israelites in the wilderness, Christians may also be tempted to sin despite God’s steadfast faithfulness.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Whereas Genesis anticipates the coming of a future king through whom the nations will be blessed, and Exodus presents the Passover as a paradigm for divine salvation, anticipating Christ’s death as the supreme Passover sacrifice, Numbers provides no comparable link with Christ. Nevertheless, the New Testament connects Jesus with the book of Numbers in other ways. In particular, whereas the Israelites fail when tested in the wilderness, Jesus demonstrates His complete faith in God when tempted and tested by the Devil (Matt. 4:1–11; Luke 4:–13). The work of Christ is foreshadowed by the typology of the red heifer (19:2–10; Heb. 9:13), the rock that provided water (20:11; 1 Cor. 10:4), and the raised serpent that brought life out of death (21:4–9; John 3:14, 15). The specific prophecy of the conquests of David, the coming one who would defeat Israel’s enemies (24:15–19), foreshadows the time when Christ, who is the consummate fulfillment of the Davidic covenant, will universally be recognized as the greatest King of all.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Like the other books of the Pentateuch, the interpretation of Numbers has been heavily influenced in the past two centuries by critical ideas regarding the process by which the Pentateuch was composed. Under the “Documentary Hypothesis” of the late nineteenth century, much of the materi­al in Numbers was assigned to the exilic or early post-exilic period and viewed as reflecting an inferior form of religion to that found in other Pentateuchal sources. Such thinking has been rightly challenged, but it continues to be widely held by critical scholars.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Some commentators question the reliability and feasibility of the census figures that appear in chs. 1, 2, and 26 because they are unexpectedly high for the ancient world. For example, if the number 603,550 represents only the males who were eligible for military service (1:3), the total number of Israelites in the wilderness was more than two million once we account for women and children as well. Given that it would have been quite difficult to support the needs of such a large group of people for the many years Israel wandered in the desert, and since other ancient kingdoms rarely report armies of that size, some scholars doubt that the census totals reported in the book of Numbers are accurate. Consequently, a variety of suggestions have been made to address the issue of these apparently inflated numbers. It has been argued that perhaps the figures are not merely a military census, but that they also include women and children. Thus, the number 603,550 is inclusive of the entire nation. Others have suggested that the word for “thousand” actually refers in these chapters to a military unit or group. So, for example, the numbers for the tribe of Reuben (1:21) would actually be “forty-six units (totaling) 500 soldiers.” The entire enrollment of Israel, then, would be 598 units totaling 5,550 soldiers. Others suggest that the census figures derive from a later period in Israel’s history and were then projected back into this earlier episode, but this can be safely rejected given the proven reliability of the biblical account. None of the aforementioned solutions entirely solves the proposed difficulty. The one solution that is rarely heard today from critics of the census figures is that the numbers are reliable and that the author is reporting them accurately. We should not miss the irony here, for the primary purpose of a census is numerical accuracy. Furthermore, if almighty God was with the Israelites in the wilderness, there is no good reason to deny that He could have met the needs of millions of people even in the harshest of conditions. In any case, we can be sure that Moses is reporting true numbers even if we are not sure whether they represent all the Israelites in the wilderness, all of Israel’s enlisted soldiers, the total number of military units, or something else. No matter the explanation, the dramatic expansion of the Israelite nation represents a clear fulfillment of the promises of God to Abraham (Gen. 15:5; 22:17; 26:4) and to the other patriarchs (Gen. 28:14; 32:12).

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book of Deuteronomy, the fifth book of Moses, receives its title from the Septuagint, which called it Deuteronomion , meaning the “Second Law,” or the “Repetition of the Law.”

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: By its own testimony (1:1, 5; 31:22), Deuteronomy is the work of Moses. Mosaic authorship is affirmed many times elsewhere in the Old Testament (e.g. 2 Kin. 14:6), in ancient Jewish sources (e.g., Josephus), and in the New Testament. This view was almost universally held until the rise of rationalistic criticism in modern times (See Introduction to the Pentateuch: Author and Date). Scholars correctly point out that the last chapter could not have been written by Moses, and it is widely agreed that ch. 34 was written by another hand. It is possible that Joshua added the description of Moses’s death and Israel’s acceptance of Joshua in order to link his own book to Moses’s great production. In light of vv. 10–12, others suggest that a later scribe added this chapter in order to demonstrate the unity between the Law and the Prophets. Such obvious additions do not, however, negate the essential authorship of Moses. More controversially, some critics have alleged that the language of 1:1, 5 indicates that the writer of the book must have been located on the west side of the Jordan River, i.e., in Canaan (the Hebrew phrase here translated “beyond the Jordan” is often translated “the other side of the Jordan” or “this side of the Jordan”). Such a description, they argue, belies the credibility of Deuteronomy as a work of Moses, since Moses never crossed the Jordan. This argument assumes that the Hebrew phrase in question must always refer to the region east of the Jordan. It is evident, however, that the precise meaning of the phrase must be determined by the context, and that it can refer either to Transjordan (the region to the east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea; see 1:1–5; 3:8; 4:41, 47, 49) or to Canaan itself (3:20, 25; 11:30; Josh. 9:1, 10) without requiring the speaker to be on the other side of the Jordan. Here it clearly means the region east of the Jordan, as the geographical descriptions indicate (1:1, 5).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: In the nineteenth century, biblical critics contended that Deuteronomy was written about 620 B.C. as part of the religious reform of King Josiah, in which he insisted that worship be centered in Jerusalem. These critics said that the regulation of the central sanctuary (ch. 12) was invented by a writer who supported Josiah’s reform. In more recent years, however, this view has received less favor. Some have dated Deuteronomy as early as Samuel, others as late as the exile. Many critics still date the book in the seventh century B.C. , to the period of Josiah. But these scholars also question the unity of the book. If some parts seem “early” (from Moses’s time), they ascribe those parts to an old tradition that has conveniently been preserved. If other parts seem “late” (during or after the time of Josiah), they are said to be “later editions” or to result from “late editing.” However, there is no textual support for these elastic, subjective, and speculative conclusions. No concrete evidence rules out the composition of Deuteronomy at the time of Moses, making reasonable allowances for additions by someone who appended Moses’s obituary to the book, and for some later updating of Hebrew grammar and place names. The background and setting of the book reflect conditions prior to the conquest of Canaan under Joshua. There is no mention of a king in Judah or of the city of Jerusalem, which is named over one hundred times by the prophet Jeremiah (who wrote in Josiah’s day). It is unlikely that a sixth-century author would make no allusion whatever to that capital city or its temple. The twelve tribes are represented as one nation (instead of, as in Josiah’s period, the kingdoms of Judah and Israel). The Transjordan cities of refuge are named, while those in Canaan (which are named later by Joshua) are not. The Babylonian names of months are not used, and there are no Persian loan words in the vocabulary, even though such words would be expected to appear in a work supposedly written during a period when these empires were dominant. Moses, Aaron, and Joshua are named, but no later persons or later historical incidents are mentioned. It is unlikely that a later author, even one well-versed in the lore of the past, could so completely avoid the use of later terms and the mention of persons and events of his own period. Some scholars have noted the general conformity of Deuteronomy’s structure to the covenant or treaty form of the mid-second millennium B.C. (the approximate time of Moses). They find the following treaty elements in Deuteronomy: (a) a preamble identifying the covenant mediator (1:1–5); (b) a historical prologue reviewing previous covenant history (1:6–4:40); (c) stipulations expounding the covenant way of life (4:44–11:32; 12–26); (d) a declaration of sanctions stating the blessings for obedience and curses for disobedience of the covenant (chs. 27–30); and (e) a provision for the administration of the covenant after the death of the inaugural mediator (chs. 31–34). Though aspects of this approach have much merit, the present layout of Deuteronomy is shaped by two lengthy exhortatory speeches by Moses. While these speeches possibly mirror in part the original form of the covenant initiated at Mount Sinai, the present text of Deuteronomy incorporates that form within the overall narrative of the Pentateuch. This evidence leads to the conclusion that Moses, Israel’s lawgiver, wrote Deuteronomy (excluding the record of his death in ch. 34) before his death in 1406 B.C.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Deuteronomy narrates the events that took place between the events recorded in Numbers Numbers and the events recorded in Joshua. Moses spoke to the Israelites while they were encamped on the plains of Moab, just before Joshua took command and led them into the land of Canaan. The content of the speeches is in keeping with their context; Moses was close to death, and these were his parting words to the people he had led for the past forty years.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Much of Deuteronomy consists of two substantial speeches given by Moses, exhorting the Israelites to love and obey God (chs. 1–4; 5–26). With the conquest of Transjordan successfully concluded, Moses challenged the Israelites in these farewell addresses. Deuteronomy combines exhortation and instructions, and it serves as an example of how the covenant obligations should be taught. The opening address (1:5–4:40) recounts the experiences of Israel under Moses’s leadership. Deuteronomy does not speak of how Moses confronted Pharaoh and how the miraculous signs and wonders forced Pharaoh to let the people go, but it alludes to the exodus repeatedly (five times in the first address: 1:20, 34; 4:20, 34, 37). Moses recounts God’s providential and miraculous care for the people during the journey from Egypt to Sinai. Then he details their defeat both spiritually and militarily at Kadesh-barnea. There are references here to events recorded in Numbers, but like the record in Numbers, almost nothing is said about events during the forty years of wilderness wandering. The journey around Edom toward Transjordan is mentioned, and the defeat of the kings Sihon and Og is recorded in fuller detail than in Numbers. Then comes the allocation of land in Transjordan for the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh (as in Num. 32), and the narrative ends with reference to Moses’s plea for himself to enter Canaan, which God disallows (as in Num. 27:12–23). Moses concludes the first speech with exhortations to be loyal to the Lord. The second speech begins with exhortations (5:1–11:32). The address continues to 26:19, with Moses’s expounding the statutes and judgments linked to the Sinai covenant (chs. 12–26). The speech begins with the Ten Commandments, almost exactly like the wording in Ex. 20, aside from the fourth commandment (5:12–15 note). The terror of the theophany (a visible self-revelation of God) at Mount Sinai is recalled, with a summons by Moses to obedience. At Mount Sinai, only the Ten Commandments were given directly by the voice of God; the rest of the covenant obligations were mediated through Moses (5:22 note). The famous Shema , “Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one,” is given in 6:4, with the exhortation to teach, remember, and obey. Chapters 6–11 are sprinkled with examples of God’s care and judgments since leaving Egypt—all allusions to material in Exodus and Numbers. These examples serve to warn Israel to trust the Lord and not themselves. This leads to a promise of success in the coming conflict in Canaan. The statutes and judgments in chs. 12–26 include regulations for worship, clean foods, slaves and debts, annual feasts, judges, cities of refuge, and various matters of conduct. Most of these have some parallel to material found in the previous books of the Pentateuch, which parallels are noted at the appropriate places. The final chapters of Deuteronomy contain a mixture of shorter speeches by Moses and narrative reporting. In chs. 27–30 Moses exhorts the Israelites yet again to obey the instructions or Torah that he has given them. Moses gives instructions for a solemn ceremony to be held in the valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, near Shechem, after Israel has secured a foothold in Canaan—a ceremony reminiscent of the covenant ceremony of Ex. 20:1–24:8, and that Joshua later carries out (Josh. 8:30–35). These instructions and exhortations are given by Moses with emphasis on Israel’s obligation before God to hear and obey the Lord’s commands. The final sections of the book are equally important and powerful (31:1–34:2). They include the installation of Joshua as Moses’s successor; the great Song of Moses celebrating the greatness of God and His care for His covenant people, but warning the people of their proneness to disobedience (ch. 32); Moses’s song of blessing, directed to the twelve tribes after the fashion of Jacob’s blessing of his twelve sons in Gen. 49 (ch. 33); and finally, the addendum describing the death of Moses (ch. 34).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: As already noted, Deuteronomy records Moses’s final speeches to the Israelites. The people stand on the threshold of a new future in the land of Canaan, and Moses exhorts them to love and obey the Lord in order to experience life in all its fullness. With good reason, Moses underlines the need for exclusive loyalty to God, warning of the danger imposed by the idolatrous practices of the nations already living in Canaan. Additionally, Moses sets out afresh the obligations of the Sinai covenant, reminding the people of how obedience will bring blessing and disobedience will bring cursing. Deuteronomy concludes with the expectation that the Israelites will fail to keep their covenant obligations.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: By recalling what God has already done for the Israelites in delivering them from bondage in Egypt, Moses portrays God as both all-powerful and compassionate. Moreover, the Lord has been faithful to the promises made to the patriarchs, in spite of the wavering faithfulness of the Israelites. As in Exodus and Leviticus, the covenant obligations underscore God’s moral nature, emphasizing His holiness and purity.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: As an exposition of the covenant obligations placed upon the Israelites, the book of Deuteronomy is exceptionally important. As the subsequent books of the OT reveal, the persistent inability of the Israelites to uphold their side of the covenant resulted finally in divine judgment and punishment. The OT prophets returned to the covenant stipulations in Deuteronomy as they called Israel to repentance. As Moses anticipated and God warned, the Israelites eventually experience the full force of the curses set out in Deuteronomy 27, 28. Their failure underlines the inadequacy of the Mosaic covenant and explains why a new covenant was initiated by Jesus Christ. While Christians are not directly bound by the obligations of the Mosaic covenant, the moral values underlying these obligations remain instructive and provide guidance for everyday living.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: According to Deut. 17:14–20, the Israelite king was to meditate daily on the teaching set out in Deuteronomy 5–26 and live by it. As the divinely chosen heir to the Davidic dynasty, Jesus undoubtedly knew well the contents of the book of Deuteronomy and quoted it when tempted by Satan (Matt. 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13). Through types and prophecy, Deuteronomy also points to Christ. He is the Passover Lamb (16:1 note) and the coming Prophet (18:15–19 note). Moses, the founder of Israel’s theocracy, mediated the old covenant, but Jesus Christ, the Son of God, mediated the new covenant (Jer. 31:31–34; Heb. 3:1–6). Whereas the old covenant was written on tablets of stone, Christ writes the new covenant through the Spirit of the living God on the tablets of human hearts (2 Cor. 3:3). The old covenant called for shedding the blood of animals; the everlasting new covenant was instituted once and for all by the blood of Christ (Jer. 32:40; Heb. 9:11–28). The old covenant calls for a heart religion, but it failed through human weakness and became obsolete after its fulfillment at Calvary (Rom. 8:3; Heb. 7:12; 8:13).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Deuteronomy is quoted in the New Testament over fifty times, a number exceeded only by Psalms and Isaiah. Since the early nineteenth century, critical scholarship has significantly influenced how the book of Deuteronomy has been approached, denying its Mosaic origin and arguing that it was the invention of a later period. Naturally, such an approach undermines the authority of Scripture and distorts the biblical picture of how Israelite religion developed from the time of Moses onwards. The evidence for the late composition of Deuteronomy is not compelling, and it relies largely on questionable presuppositions (see Date and Occasion above).
