sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book derives its title from the name of its central character, Joshua. As the successor to Moses, Joshua was from the tribe of Ephraim, which from the time of Joseph until the prophet Samuel was the tribe associated with the overall leadership of the nation of Israel.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The author of the book of Joshua is unknown, and our knowledge of when this book was written depends on the interpretation of certain clues within it. Theories range from the view that the book was largely composed by Joshua himself (the tradition of the Jewish Talmud) to the modern critical hypothesis that it was written by someone long after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. From the standpoint of the final form of the book, it is probable that a man or group committed to the theological outlook of Deuteronomy gave Joshua its canonical form. See Date and Occasion below and Introduction to the Historical Books.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: It is not clear when Joshua was composed. Comments within the book itself, such as notices that something is true “to this day,” suggest that many of its sources came from a time between the death of Joshua (24:29–31) and the time of Samuel and Saul (c. 1050 B.C. ). Because Sidon is still reckoned as Phoenicia’s leading city (11:8; 19:28), some date the book no later than 1200 B.C. ; after that time Tyre gained the ascendancy. Jerusalem is as yet unconquered (15:63), a feat accomplished by David (2 Sam. 5:6–10), and Gezer is not as yet under Solomon’s rule (16:10; 1 Kin. 9:16). On balance it appears that the book was written after Joshua’s death but before Saul (c. 1050 B.C. ) and his successors. The author wrote doubtless to recount the astounding fulfillment of the Lord’s promises under Joshua. At the same time, recognizing the need to consolidate the Israelite conquest of the land, the author wrote in hope of the rise of another faithful servant who, like Joshua, could lead the Israelites to victory over every enemy still in the land.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: In the English Bible, Joshua is grouped with the historical books, reflective of its primary genre, historical narrative. As a history of conquest, the book also reflects features of military history or military reports, such as the lists in chapter 13.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The theme of land—or, perhaps more accurately, taking possession of land—dominates the book. The vivid account of the Israelites’ crossing the River Jordan under the leadership of Joshua and capturing the walled city of Jericho dominates the opening chapters and casts a long shadow over everything else that is recorded. This emphasis upon possessing land is further underlined when we look at the overall structure of the book, which falls largely into two parts. Chapters 1–12 describe the process by which opposition to the Israelite conquest of the land is overcome. This climaxes in chapter 12 with a list of the thirty-one kings defeated by Joshua. Thereafter, in chapters 13–21, details are given as to how the land is to be allocated among the nine and a half tribes that have crossed the Jordan. The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh were already settled on the eastern side of the Jordan prior to the conquest.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The main theological idea in Joshua is the promise of God to give the land of Canaan to the descendants of Abraham, the people of Israel (Gen. 12:7). This aspect of the various divine promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Gen. 12:1–3) dominates from Genesis through Deuteronomy. Joshua testifies to God’s faithfulness to this promise by recounting the successful entry of the Israelites into the land (2:1–5:12), the dispossession of some of the land’s inhabitants (5:13–12:24; cf. Gen. 15:13–16 and notes), and the allocation of the territory to the twelve tribes, with some of it already taken in Joshua’s lifetime and other portions remaining to be possessed (chs. 13–21). The closing sentence of the main body of the book (21:45) summarizes the overall theme: “Not one word of all the good promises that the Lord had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (21:45; see 23:14). This bold assertion of God’s complete faithfulness is accompanied by the recognition that much of what was promised was still unrealized (e.g., 13:1; 23:5) and that the complete enjoyment of the fulfilled promise remains conditional upon the people’s obedience (e.g., 23:12, 13, 15, 16). The Promised Land would not be fully occupied until the reigns of David and Solomon, for God recognized in the time of Moses that the Israelites would not take possession of the whole land in a short period of time (cf. Deut. 7:22). Of particular note is the distinction drawn between those tribes that had already occupied territory in Canaan and those whose allocated land is still to be taken. Attention is given first to the tribe of Judah (chs. 14–15), which is portrayed as the most active and successful in possessing territory in Canaan. Observe in particular the very detailed list of locations mentioned in connection with Judah. This anticipates the special role that Judah later plays in the history of Israel as the tribe from which the Davidic monarchy comes. The tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh are listed next (chs. 16–17), suggesting that they take second place in occupying the Promised Land. Significantly, although Joshua is from the tribe of Ephraim and leadership is clearly linked to this tribe, the Ephraimites are somewhat fearful about attempting to drive out the powerful Canaanites, who are equipped with chariots (17:15–18). As for the remaining tribes, they are apportioned land by lots (chs. 18–19). This is territory that has yet to be seized, which implies that these tribes have been less active in settling within the land of Canaan. Interestingly, the territory allocated to the tribe of Simeon falls within the boundaries of the land already taken by the tribe of Judah. While some tribes are quick to seize land, God ensures that every tribe is given an appropriate allocation of land.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Apart from stressing the faithfulness of God to His promises and the power of God in overcoming Israel’s enemies, the book also highlights the importance of faith in God and the need to live by the moral standards He demands (Deut. 28). Through obedience to God, Joshua enjoys success as the leader of Israel. While the inhabitants of Jericho who stand in defiance of God are punished, the Canaanite family of Rahab survives because of her faith; her willingness to help the Israelite spies escape from the city is testimony to her belief that Israel’s God is the one true God. While Rahab survives, as do the people of Gibeon (ch. 9), Achan the Judahite comes under God’s severe judgment for taking from the plunder of Jericho that which was devoted to God. These contrasting experiences underline the importance of trusting and obeying the Lord—faith, not ethnicity, finally determines one’s place among God’s people.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Joshua should be understood in relation to the Pentateuch, the content of which is summarized in 24:2–10. These verses recount the history of the descendants of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob from the time the promise was first given to Abraham (Gen. 12:1–3) to the death of Moses (Deut. 34), who led the Israelites from Egypt to the land promised to them by God. But the Pentateuch ends with the people still outside the Promised Land. Furthermore, the generation of Israelites who came out of Egypt did not make it to the edge of Canaan but had fallen under God’s judgment because of their rebellion in the wilderness (Num. 13; 14; Deut. 1:26–36), and even the death of Moses is understood in those terms (Deut. 1:37; 32:48–52). In this context, Joshua speaks of the Lord’s faithfulness to His promises made to the patriarchs, despite the rebellion of the earlier generation of Israelites and God’s subsequent judgment. Joshua should also be understood in relation to the history of Israel in the land, recorded in the books of Joshua through 2 Kings. The story is a tragic one as far as Israel is concerned. The nation failed to follow the Lord wholeheartedly, and it was all but destroyed by God’s judgment in the form of the successive assaults by the Assyrians in the eighth century B.C. (2 Kin. 17) and the Babylonians in the sixth century (2 Kin. 25). The book of Joshua confirms from the outset that the demise of Israel cannot be blamed on a failure of God’s power or faithfulness, for under Joshua the Israelites enjoyed success during the first phase of conquering the Promised Land. The New Testament provides a third perspective from which the book should be understood. The promise of God, to which the book of Joshua points, is the gospel preached to Abraham beforehand (Gal. 3:8; Gen. 12:1–3). This promise was kept by God through the time of Joshua and is ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ (Acts 13:32, 33; Heb. 4:8–11). The faithfulness of God proclaimed in Joshua is His faithfulness to the gospel of Christ. Israel’s entrance into and occupation of the land prefigures the Christian’s life in Christ, to be consummated with the entrance and life of God’s people in the new heaven and earth (Rev. 21).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Joshua is one of the few Old Testament leaders portrayed positively. As the one who led Israel into the Promised Land, obeying God faithfully, Joshua provides an Old Testament model of what might be expected from the Messiah. With good reason, the Greek name “Jesus” is equivalent to the Hebrew name “Joshua,” which means, “the Lord is salvation.” Like Joshua, Jesus battles against forces opposed to God (e.g., Matt. 12:24–29), and those who follow Him continue in this struggle against the powers of evil (e.g., Eph. 6:10–18). As Israel’s warrior, Joshua is a type of Christ as the Lord’s warrior. Further, chapter 5 records a preincarnate appearance of Christ as “the commander of the army of the Lord” (v. 14).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: With the rise of critical scholarship, two issues have dominated the study of Joshua. First, doubts have been expressed about the historicity of the account of Israel’s conquest of Canaan (see Special Issues below). Second, questions have been raised about the morality of what occurred when the Israelites dispossessed those already living in the land of Canaan. Importantly, the gift of the land of Canaan to Abraham’s descendants is associated with the divine punishment of its present inhabitants. As Gen. 15:16 reveals, the Israelites were only to take possession of the land when the sin of the Amorites had reached its full measure. In a similar fashion, Lev. 18:25 states that the expulsion of Canaan’s descendants is due to their defiling of the land. Interestingly, Leviticus uses the image of the land vomiting out its inhabitants, a motif that associates possession of the land with righteous behavior and loss of land with immoral behavior. In light of this, Israel’s seizure of Canaan is a vivid reminder of the reality of divine judgment upon those who by their unrighteous actions forfeit their land.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Any attempt to relate the accounts of the book of Joshua to data gained from archaeological investigations must reckon with the nature of both the biblical record and the archaeological evidence. All historical writing is selective in what it records and interpretive in the manner in which it pre­sents its material. Biblical history has a particular interest in the purposes of God. Archaeological evidence is often ambiguous and illustrative rather than specific in the information it yields. The task of correlating archaeological data and the biblical record is well illustrated by the debate over Joshua. Among those who accept the biblical representation of the Israelites entering the land of Canaan from outside and settling within it, there are basically two schools of thought. One believes there is persuasive archaeological evidence (such as the destruction of Canaanite cities and occupation patterns) for a successful Israelite conquest of Canaan in c. 1250 B.C. The other argues that archaeological evidence (such as that at Jericho) together with texts such as 1 Kin. 6:1, Judg. 11:26, and Ex. 12:40 indicates that the conquest should be dated earlier (c. 1400 B.C. ). The difficulties arise from uncertainties about the identification of modern sites with biblical locations, disputes over the dating of materials, biblical chronology, and how certain data should be interpreted. Ongoing research continues to bring to light new evidence. As the case for a late thirteenth-century conquest of Canaan has become weaker, new discoveries at Tell el-Dab’a (biblical Rameses) in Egypt lend support to a fifteenth-century date. The Israelite conquest of Canaan and the associated destruction of those already occupying the land raise serious questions regarding the morality of what occurred. Was this a process of ethnic cleansing sanctioned by God? While this criticism is often raised by those who wish to undermine the authority of the Bible, the biblical accounts of large numbers of people being put to death cannot be easily overlooked. In considering the significance of such events, various factors need to be taken into account. First, such events are inevitably associated with human sinfulness and presented as acts of judgment sanctioned by God. As the “Judge of all the earth” (Gen. 18:25), God alone has the authority to determine the fate of people. When punishment comes, we must believe that it is due to the seriousness of human sin. While God may display considerable tolerance toward the wrongdoing of people, such behavior will ultimately be punished. God alludes to this regarding the inhabitants of Canaan in Gen. 15:16. Second, God’s punishment of the Canaanites and other groups is not motivated by racial or ethnic concerns but by universal moral considerations. God’s actions are not one-sided. Num. 25:9 records how 24,000 Israelites died in the plague that God sent because they worshiped Baal of Peor. Earlier, 23,000 Israelites were struck dead at Mount Sinai for committing sexual immorality while worshiping the golden calf (1 Cor. 10:8; cf. Ex. 32:6, 35). Indeed, of the entire adult generation that God delivered out of slavery in Egypt, only Joshua and Caleb survived to enter into the land of Canaan (Num. 26:65). Throughout the history of the Israelite nation, God raised up nations to bring destruction upon His own people when they promoted injustice and immorality. Although modern readers may balk at the severity of the divine punishments reflected in the early books of the Bible, these are entirely consistent with God’s warnings to the people of Israel (see Lev. 18:24–29).

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The name of the book of Judges derives from the title given to twelve Israelite leaders who delivered their people from oppression during the period after the conquest under Joshua up to the establishment of the monarchy under Samuel. The term “judge” in this book principally refers to a leader with multiple roles: in foreign affairs the judge was a military deliverer; in national affairs the judge was an administrator of justice; and in religious affairs the judge was a model covenant keeper.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The author’s name is not given in the book itself or anywhere else in the Bible; the writer is anonymous. It is likely that the final author collected various historical episodes and then put them together into a historical account. This author clearly affirmed God’s final choice of the tribe of Judah (David and his sons), and not the tribe of Benjamin (Saul and his sons), to rule over Israel (20:18). The author’s loyalty to David and the tribe of Judah indicate that he lived and wrote during the early period of David’s reign at Hebron. The writer of Judges addressed the Israelites of his day from the same theological point of view as that of Deuteronomy, specifically in regard to covenant keeping and the consequences of covenant breaking (Deut. 26–28).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The book records events that occurred between the death of Joshua in the mid-fourteenth century or late thirteenth century B.C. (Josh. 24:29) and the appearance of Samuel, the last judge in the middle of the eleventh century (1 Sam. 1). The first of the judges in the book, Othniel, appeared during the generation following Joshua. Samson, the last judge in the book, was a contemporary of Samuel. During this period, Israel was oppressed from within by the Canaanites and from without by the Arameans, Moabites, Midianites, Ammonites, Amalekites, Amorites, and Philistines. The earliest the book would have been composed is after its last recorded event, namely, the civil war between Benjamin and the rest of the tribes of Israel (Judg. 19–21), which presumably took place in the first half of the eleventh century B.C. Judges may have been written in the early part of David’s kingship because the book says the Jebusites controlled the city of Jerusalem “to this day.” David captured the city and made it his capital c. 1000 B.C. , and the Jebusites did not inhabit the city after that time. Judges amplifies the picture of the conquest already recorded in Joshua. The latter portrays an initial conquest of the Land of Promise, but its capture was unfinished and incomplete (see Josh. 13:1). Judges furnishes the same viewpoint (see Judg. 1:3–8). In other words, the allotted territory of the Land of Promise was generally captured under Joshua, but the Canaanites were not dislodged completely. The character of the period may be defined by the book’s thematic statement: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). This thematic statement is, on the one hand, clearly political; that is, there existed no centralized government in the land. The twelve tribes were a loosely tied confederation, and at times anarchy prevailed in the land. On the other hand, this theme sentence is also an ethical critique. During this time, moral relativism reigned. It was a period of confusion, degradation, and apostasy. The threat of religious assimilation was real. Because Israel had not fully conquered the land, Canaanites and Israelites lived side by side. That contact led to religious syncretism in which Baalism was assimilated into Israelite worship. In the final analysis, the period of the judges was generally a dark, grim one for the people of God.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The dominant literary format of Judges is historical narrative. The biblical author, however, employed various other genres in the writing of it. For example, he included poetry (5:1–31), riddle (14:14, 18), prayer (13:8), and conquest itineraries (1:1–36). The core of the book is a series of heroic stories that demonstrate the ever-increasing apostasy of the Israelites and God’s repeated deliverance of the people from oppression.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Judges can be divided into three distinct sections (see Outline below). Each section has its own internal style and consistency, containing lively narration of God’s people and leaders in action. Occasionally humorous, sometimes tragic, but never dull, the individual stories within each section, while complete in themselves, invite the reader to compare one judge with another. The introduction (1:1–3:6) contains two balanced sections that show how Israel moved from conquest to apostasy through failure in foreign wars (1:1–2:5) and failure with foreign idols (2:6–3:6). The body (3:7–16:31) contains the stories of the judges arranged in a concentric pattern with Gideon in the center; this structure underscores the downward spiral toward apostasy. Othniel (3:7–11), who is married to the godly Achsah, contrasts with Samson (13:1–16:31), who is always chasing foreign women; the seizing of the fords of the Jordan in the days of Ehud (3:28), which results in the conquest of Canaanites, contrasts with the seizing of the fords of the Jordan in the days of Jephthah (12:5), which results in the conquest of Israelites; the driving of a tent peg by a woman into the head of a Canaanite leader in Deborah’s day (4:21) contrasts with the dropping of a millstone by a woman on the head of an Israelite leader in Abim­elech’s day (9:53). The conclusion (17:1–21:25) contains two sections that show the results of apostasy in terms of the cult (i.e., worship) and in terms of morality. These failures mirror the introduction with a focus on failure through domestic idols (17:1–18:31; cf. 2:6–3:6) and failure in domestic wars (19:1–21:25; cf. 1:1–2:5). Each episode and section in 1:1–2:5 employs verbal repetition, historical comparison, and quotations from the book of Joshua to emphasize the connections between people, places, and events. The reader is invited to search for the pattern and moral framework of the history. Compared to the largely positive picture presented in Joshua, the portrayal of Israel in Judges is largely negative. Judges 2:11–19 outlines a pattern that recurs throughout Israel’s history during the bulk of the period of the judges (3:7–16:31). This provides the macrostructure for each of the judgeship stories that take place in the book. The opening part of the cycle is the apostasy of the people of God (vv. 11–13). Repeatedly the Israelites commit idolatry (e.g., 3:7, 12; 4:1; 6:1; 8:33; 10:6; 13:1). The second element of the pattern is God’s response to the defection of His people: He becomes angry and sells them into the hands of their enemies (vv. 14–15). In the majority of the stories, God chastises and disciplines His people in this way (e.g., 3:8, 12–14; 4:2; 6:1–2; 10:7). Because of the oppression, the people cry out to the Lord for deliverance (e.g., 3:9, 15; 4:3; 6:7; 10:10). Then God raises up a judge to deliver the people for a season from their oppressors (v. 16). The bulk of material in the book focuses on this aspect of the cycle (e.g., 3:9–11, 15–29; 4:4–24; 6:8–8:27; 13:2–16:30). The cycle normally ends with the statement “and the land had rest [x] years” (e.g., 3:11, 30; 5:31; 8:28). Subtle changes are evident in the cycle, and these changes underscore the downward spiral in the stories. The pattern of crying out, the Lord raising up a judge, and the land having rest starts to break down with Deborah, when the text says Deborah “summoned Barak” (4:6) instead of stating that the Lord raised up a judge. After the people cry out in the days of Gideon, the text says, “The Lord sent a prophet” (6:8). Further breakdown is evident in the days of Jephthah when instead of crying out to the Lord, “the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob” (11:5). The breakdown in the pattern culminates in the days of Samson when there is no cry and no rest. Judges 2:11–19 underscores the repetition of the cycle. Even though the individual judges succeed for a short time, the nation quickly returns to its ways of idolatry (v. 17) and becomes more corrupt in each subsequent cycle of the pattern (vv. 18–19). By the close of the book, the reader is confronted with a tragic story in which the tribe of Benjamin acts similarly to the Sodomites in Gen. 19:1–13 (Judg. 19:14–20:48). The cycle of the period of the judges forms a downward spiral into religious and moral disaster. The full cycle appears in Judges seven times (3:7–11, 12–30; 4:1–5:31; 6:1–8:28; 8:33–10:5; 10:6–12:7; 13:1–16:31). The number seven in Hebrew culture often symbolized completion and fulfillment (e.g., Gen. 1:1–2:3). By the end of Judges, therefore, the reader witnesses an almost full-blown anarchy in Israel: “everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” In addition, the reader ought to be struck by how highly structured and well-composed this book is.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The Lord promised Abraham and his descendants that they would have a land of their own (Gen. 12:7; 13:15; 17:8), and in the book of Joshua Israel began to take possession of it. During the subsequent period of the judges, however, the existence of Israel was deeply threatened by two things: (1) the danger of military invasion, especially at the hands of the Philistines; and (2) the recurrent apostasy of the Israelites. The former was a strong threat because Israel had no standing army for mutual tribal defense. The latter was even more dangerous because it involved a continual breaking of the covenant with the Lord, and it would eventually result in the exile and captivity of the people of God (18:30). The principal form of Israelite apostasy was idolatry. Time and again, Israel abandoned the Lord and went after the Canaanite deities Baal and Asherah (2:11–13; 3:7; 6:28–32; 8:33) and other foreign gods (10:6). The biblical author employs strong language to describe Israel’s idolatry: “They whored after other gods” (2:17; 8:27, 33). This explicit sexual language equates idolatry with spiritual adultery; that is, Israel was forsaking the Lord as husband by prostituting herself with other deities. Israel’s apostasy was in direct contrast to God’s faithfulness to the covenant relationship. Despite Israel’s recurrent sin, God delivered the people repeatedly. This continual deliverance was a tremendous testimony to God’s long-suffering, patient, and faithful character. He did not deliver Israel because of her righteousness, repentance, or upright disposition; rather, salvation came strictly from God’s mercy and compassion (2:18). The events of Judges are foundational to the establishment of a monarchy in Israel. From the setting apart of the Hebrew people in the time of Abraham, God promised that they would one day be ruled by a king (Gen. 17:6, 16; 35:11; 49:10). Deuteronomy confirms this promise when it describes in detail the type of king Israel ought to have when the monarchy is later formed (17:14–20). Judges demonstrates what life was like in Israel in the absence of a godly king: anarchic and chaotic.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The judges are often described as ones who “saved” Israel from oppression (2:16; 3:9, 31; 8:22; 13:5). The reality is that the biblical author often underscores the truth that it was the Lord who “saved” His people by means of the judges: “Whenever the Lord raised up judges for them, the Lord was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge” (2:18; cf. 10:11–12). The biblical doctrine highlighted here is later proclaimed by the psalmist: “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 3:8; cf., Pss. 37:39; 62:6–7). The Lord is the one and only true Savior of His people. Judges clearly teaches that sin brings God’s judgment and punishment. The apostasy of Israel resulted directly in the nation’s being given over by God into servitude to another people. Yet the book also presents the truth that repentance leads to deliverance and rest. When the people of God turned back to Him in sorrow and repentance, He saved them from the hand of their oppressors. This pattern is a standard biblical truth that has great spiritual application. The apostle Paul taught that “the wages of sin is death” (Rom. 6:23), and thus humankind is under God’s condemnation. But there is also hope, as the apostle Peter declared to the crowds gathered in Solomon’s portico: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3:19). At the heart of the book is the sovereignty of God. It was God who employed pagan nations as an instrument to punish Israel because of her apostasy. It was God who raised up deliverers for Israel when the people cried out to Him for salvation. It was God who empowered judges with the Spirit of the Lord to defeat those non-Israelite nations and to bring rest to the land of Israel. God was in total control of this seemingly chaotic period in the history of Israel.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In the book of Judges, the Lord commonly delivers His people through the use of a judge/deliverer/mediator. These recurrent accounts picture the salvation of the Israelites in a temporal, external, and physical manner through a flawed human set apart by God for this task. The stories prefigure the work of the Messiah, who is the only one who can mediate the true, final, and everlasting salvation of the people of God. As Peter taught in the temple precincts, “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Christ, then, is the final judge/deliverer who redeems the people of God. Judges also anticipates the coming of a righteous, faithful king. The establishment of the monarchy in Israel was the initial fulfillment of that need. However, the kings of Israel and Judah never attained the idealized royal position that God had established (Deut. 17:14–20). This set the stage for the coming messianic king, the final, absolute king who justly rules over the people of God forever.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: As the nation of Israel became increasingly immoral, this was reflected even in the judges. Each successive judge had more flaws and fell further short of the ideal picture of a leader than the judge before him. In addition, the deliverances they secured were short-lived periods of peace and rest for the land of Israel. These deficiencies encourage the reader to yearn and long for an ultimate deliverer to usher in a final rest for the people of God. In other words, the tenor of the entire period of the judges cries out for the promised Messiah (Gen. 3:15), one who will come and redeem His people forever. The angel of the Lord makes a number of appearances in the accounts of the judges (2:1–5; 5:23; 6:11–24; 13:1–25). Each of these is a theophany, that is, a visible, physical representation of the Lord. For example, after Manoah and his wife saw the angel of the Lord, Manoah said to his wife, “We shall surely die, for we have seen God” (13:22). The angel of the Lord spoke as if he were God: it is he who said to Israel, “I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers” (2:1). Some commentators believe that the angel of the Lord is the preincarnate Messiah. This conclusion, while not provable beyond all shadow of a doubt, is theologically sound, since “no one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: For well over a century, the commonly held view is that Judges evolved over time. In other words, it went through various stages of writing and editing. One widely held position among liberal scholars is that early in Israel’s monarchic history, there existed a number of narratives that purportedly came from the period of the judges. Some of these stories were then collected in the eighth century B.C. and incorporated into a larger collection of historical books in the next century. Finally, the entire collection was edited and updated after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. This position asserts that several editors worked on the book. Recently, however, studies have begun to recognize that, in fact, the book of Judges is a single literary unit. Given its structure and careful composition, there is every reason to believe that it records true history and is substantially the work of a single author.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The writer of the book of Ruth is anonymous. This, however, has not stopped speculation in regard to authorship. A widely held position is that Solomon wrote the book after the death of his father, David. The Babylonian Talmud considers the prophet Samuel to be the author: “Samuel wrote his book, Judges, and Ruth.” Some commentators argue that this makes sense because they believe that Judges and Ruth were originally one book. Others argue that Ruth was composed during the fifth century B.C. The title of the book does not help to identify the author. It simply refers to one of the main characters of the story and not to its writer.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The earliest date the book of Ruth could have been written is during the time of David because the genealogy at the close of the book ends by listing his name. David’s rise to the throne of Judah occurred around 1010 B.C. , and he ruled over Judah, and later over all Israel, until about 970 B.C. The author thus wrote the book during David’s reign or later. The writer may have employed both written rec­ords and oral history that were related to David. The setting of the story is provided in v. 1 of the opening chapter: “In the days when the judges ruled.” The period of the judges is the backdrop for the story of Ruth, and that period is encapsulated in the last verse of Judges: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (21:25). That statement reflects a political anarchy in which there was no central authority in Israel. It also demonstrates a lack of spiritual focus; the land was dominated by relativism. God’s Word was no longer the standard of living. The people were trusting in themselves and ignoring their covenant obligations to God. The story takes place during a time of famine in the land (1:1). Agricultural adversity struck the people of Israel in the Land of Promise. In the Old Testament, famine is often understood as a sign of God’s displeasure with an unfaithful Israel (Lev. 26:18–20). This reflects the period of the judges, a time of disobedience and unfaithfulness. This was also a time of moral collapse, great apostasy, and physical hardship. The looming question at the outset of the book is, how will the people of Israel respond to such adversity?

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The genre of the book of Ruth is historical narrative in the form of a short story. The book contains a simple plot that revolves around three main characters: Naomi, Ruth, and Boaz. Its literary style stands between a short tale like the brief account of Ehud (Judg. 3:12–30) and a long novella like the extended record of the life of Joseph (Gen. 37–50). The purpose of short stories in Scripture is to teach and encourage the people of God in an entertaining way.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The book is written in highly artistic prose narrative. The writer employs various literary forms in order to present his message in a dramatic manner. For instance, the author uses leading words that appear repeatedly throughout a passage. In 1:6–22 the verb “to return” appears twelve times. While this verb can simply indicate one’s physical return to a particular place, it is often used in Scripture to refer to spiritual renewal (e.g., Hos. 3:5; 6:1; 7:10). So, the repetition of the verb in Ruth likely signifies that the characters were returning not only to the Land of Promise but also to the Lord. The meaning of the names of the characters is also important for the development of the story. For example, “Naomi” derives from a Hebrew word that means “sweet, pleasant, delightful” (1:2), but by the close of chapter 1, Naomi wants to be called “Mara” instead, which means “bitter” and not “sweet.” These names thus echo Naomi’s radically altered circumstances. Another interesting feature regards the women of Bethlehem. They appear in 2:19 and again in 4:17. As secondary characters they serve to move the narrative along at these two crucial junctures.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: 1) Emptiness to fullness. An overarching theme is how God fills people who find themselves empty. Though titled “Ruth” because Ruth is the heroine, the story is largely about Naomi’s being brought from emptiness to fullness. Having lost all of the males in her life, which means losing all forms of temporal security and provision, Naomi begins to be filled as Boaz, through Ruth, provides her with grain (2:18; 3:17), and she experiences poetic fullness when Ruth and Boaz provide her with a son (4:13–17). 2) Cost of disobedience. The people of God need to understand that there are consequences to their sin. Although believers have been delivered from sin by the work of Christ, there are yet temporal results from disobedience to God and His Word. Elimelech and his family are God’s covenantal people, yet when hardship strikes, they move to Moab. They place themselves under Moabite authority, and even the two sons of the family marry foreign women. This activity results in poverty, death, and widowhood. 3) God’s sovereignty. God’s providence shines forth even in the midst of sin and disobedience. Though Elimelech’s family moves to Moab, a land of unbelievers, this book highlights God’s sovereign, unconditional election of Ruth the Moabite as a believer. She is made an heir of salvation. This story, then, is a picture of the engrafting of the Gentiles into the people of God. The fact that Ruth is included in the genealogy of Jesus confirms this truth (Matt. 1:5). God’s sovereignty is further revealed throughout the book in many ways. He providentially preserves the line of the Messiah; behind the scenes, God is working, guiding, and directing the events of the story. 4) Faithful living. Boaz and Ruth are characters of faith and people of integrity, industry, and honor. They exhibit their faith in how they live and act. Their conduct is a true reflection of their faith as followers of the Lord. 5) Redemption. The biblical concept of redemption is the heart of the story. Redemption was a Hebrew cultural practice in which something alienated might be restored to a family by a kinsman-redeemer or next of kin. Thus, if someone had to sell himself or his land to pay a debt, the kinsman-redeemer had the duty to step in and act upon the situation. He was to redeem and restore. As one can imagine, there were varied circumstances in regard to these laws, and the book of Ruth presents customs applicable to the period of the judges. More importantly, the Hebrew customs of redemption are a picture of God’s relationship to and activity on behalf of His covenant people.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Although the human relationships in the story ought to be encouraging to the reader (and in some ways the characters are worthy of emulation, especially Ruth and Boaz), this is hardly the main point of the book. More important is that the book of Ruth anticipates the coming of a king to the throne of Israel. The book records the ancestry of David, the most beloved king in the history of Israel. The book thus finds its climax in the coming David, whose ancestors are Ruth and Boaz. Moreover, by describing both Boaz and Obed as redeemers (4:14–15), the book of Ruth suggests that David will also be a redeemer. Therefore, the book serves the higher purpose of pointing to the future reality of David and his line.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The eventual arrival of David, however, is not the ultimate climax of the book. In reality, the book has its final fulfillment in the coming of the last and consummate king—Jesus Christ, the son of David. Indeed, many of the main characters are listed in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt. 1:1–17). The reader needs to keep Christ’s genealogy in mind continually when studying the book, for the provision of a son for Naomi is a key part of the story of Israel and God’s salvation, the glorious end of which is the great coming of the Messiah, our redeemer. The women of Bethlehem declare to Ruth that a son, the redeemer, has been born to her (4:17). The angels declare to the shepherds the birth of the “Savior, who is Christ the Lord.” (Luke 2:10).

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The books of Samuel have had various titles. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) treats Samuel and Kings as parts of a unified work called “the book of the Kingdoms.” It was probably the first to divide Samuel into two separate books because of its length, a practice followed by most subsequent translations. The title “Samuel” derives from the fact that the prophet Samuel is a transitional and pivotal character in the books. It was Samuel who anointed the first kings of Israel, Saul and David (1 Sam. 10:1; 16:13), and thus helped in Israel’s transition from a tribal confederacy to a united monarchy.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The author of 1 and 2 Samuel is anonymous. Jewish tradition, at least as early as the Babylonian Talmud in the sixth century A.D. , believed that Samuel wrote these books. The major difficulties with this view are that Samuel and his name appear nowhere in 2 Samuel and that his death is recorded in 1 Sam. 25:1 and 28:3. He certainly could not have recorded the events that took place after his death. Some have suggested that he wrote much of the material of 1 Samuel, and then others took over the writing. They refer to 1 Chr. 29:29 as confirmation: “Now the acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the Chronicles of Samuel the seer, and in the Chronicles of Nathan the prophet, and in the Chronicles of Gad the seer.”

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The final form of the books of Samuel dates from a time after the occurrence of the events recorded. The books do contain information from sources contemporary with the events narrated in them, such as David’s eulogies for Saul and his sons (2 Sam. 1:17–27) and his lament for Abner (2 Sam. 3:33–34). They rely to some degree on stories, chronicles, and poems that came from an earlier period. The text itself gives evidence that demonstrates that its final composition was later than the recorded events. For example, 1 Sam. 27:6 says, “Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.” That statement denotes that a number of kings have ruled over Judah since the death of Solomon and the division of the monarchy. Found also in that verse is an expression common in the books of Samuel: “to this day” (1 Sam. 5:5; 6:18; 27:6; 30:25; 2 Sam. 4:3; 6:8; 18:18), which indicates that the writer is narrating events that had taken place prior to his time. It is reasonable to believe that the final editing and composition of the books occurred in the ninth or eighth centuries B.C. , that is, sometime after David’s reign. It is likely that an official court historian wrote 1 and 2 Samuel within one to three centuries of the events. There is little compelling reason to think that the books were given a final form in either the exilic or the postexilic period. Although the exact dates of the events recorded in Samuel are elusive, the general chronology of the period can be defined. Definite figures are given for the duration of David’s reign over Judah and Israel (2 Sam. 5:4–5), but there is no clear indication of how long Saul reigned (1 Sam. 13:1 note). The specific years of David’s and Saul’s reigns have been established by working back from the dates of events recorded in Kings, which have their own chronological difficulties (see Introduction to 1 Kings). There is broad consensus that David began his rule in Hebron around 1010 B.C. and died around 970 B.C. Samuel may have been born about 1100 B.C. Thus, the books of Samuel cover a period that includes most of the eleventh century B.C. and the first quarter of the tenth century B.C. In the latter half of the eleventh century B.C. , a time when international powers of the ancient Near East were preoccupied with internal conflicts, Israel was transformed from a loosely knit tribal confederation into a united monarchy. The institution of the monarchy was a new stage in the political and religious history of Israel, although the idea of kingship itself would have been known to Israel from the practice of its neighbors (Judg. 3:12; 4:2; 8:5). It is remarkable not that Israel eventually installed a king but that it resisted doing so for so long. One cause of Israel’s reluctance is revealed in the words of Gideon: “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you” (Judg. 8:23). A fundamental tenet of Israel’s faith was that the Lord Himself (Yahweh) was Israel’s sovereign, their great King (1 Sam. 8:7; 12:12; Num. 23:21; Ps. 5:2; Mal. 1:14). Nevertheless, the opening books of the Bible contain indications that Israel, in accordance with the divine will, would one day have a human monarch (Gen. 49:10; Num. 24:7, 17–19; cf. Gen. 17:6, 16; 35:11). Moses anticipated a time when Israel would be settled in the Promised Land and would desire a king, and he gave instructions to regulate kingship when it came (Deut. 17:14–20; cf. 28:36). As 1 Samuel opens, that time has almost arrived. The two books of Samuel are not a formal, comprehensive history of Israel during the monarchic period. Rather, the biblical writer focuses primarily on the three most prominent Israelite leaders of the time: Samuel, Saul, and David. 1 Samuel 1–8 describes Samuel’s birth, call to ministry, and judgeship. Samuel is often considered the last judge of Israel, and he was a pivotal figure between the era of the judges and the monarchic period. The next section, 1 Samuel 9–31, recounts the failed kingship of Saul, the first ruler of Israel. It relates his being chosen as king, his anointing to the office by the prophet Samuel, his early military victories, his repeated disobedience to the commands of God, his final rejection as king, and his death at the hands of the Philistines during the battle at Mount Gilboa. Second Samuel is a narration of the kingship of David. It details the rise of David to the kingship over all Israel, his early military conquests, his fall into sin, and the constant internal rebellion that took place within his kingdom.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The prevailing literary style of the books of Sam­uel is historical narrative. The biblical author, however, weaves various other literary forms with the narrative: prayer (1 Sam. 2:1–10), poetry (1 Sam. 15:22–23), short story (1 Sam. 17:1–58), obituary (1 Sam. 25:1), song (1 Sam. 29:5), lament (2 Sam. 1:17–27; 3:33–34), covenant (2 Sam. 7:1–17), and others. The heart of the books is a pair of court histories: one recounting the kingship of Saul and the other the kingship of David.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The narratives of 1 and 2 Samuel are written in an economical style using a variety of narrative techniques: keywords (e.g., 1 Sam. 2:29 note); comparative characterizations (Saul and Jonathan, David and Uriah; see 1 Sam. 13:22; 14:6 notes; 2 Sam. 11); repetition and variation (Saul’s two confessions in 1 Sam. 15:24, 25, 30); and analogy (Nabal compared with Saul in 1 Sam. 25; cf. vv. 14, 36 notes). Sensitivity to such literary features can open the door to theological and historical understanding and to a sense of the unity of the text. The overall literary structure of the two books is a deliberate comparison and contrast between the lives and kingships of Saul and David. In a general way, the narratives of the two kings run parallel: after ascending to the throne, both characters had early military successes. However, these were soon followed by grievous sins committed by both rulers. The similarity ends at that point because of the divergent ways in which the two kings dealt with their sin. sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: At the very heart of 1 and 2 Samuel is the establishment of the institution of kingship. The founding of a monarchy for Israel was not bad in itself; in fact, its very roots go back to the book of Genesis. Contained in the divine revelations to the patriarchs was a promise of kings coming through their posterity (Gen. 17:6, 16; 35:11). Jacob prophesied that the scepter, the symbol of kingly authority, would not depart from the tribe of Judah until the ultimate, final king would appear (Gen. 49:10). The institution of a monarchy in Israel was clearly in accord with the eternal plan of God, and He declared that truth in the Scriptures prior to Israel’s settlement in Canaan (Deut. 17:14–20). This kingship, however, was to be different from the monarchies of the nations surrounding Israel. The human ruler of Israel was not to be autonomous; rather, he was to be subject to God and fully dependent on God’s word as the rule and authority of the kingdom. Thus, the foundation of biblical kingship is that ultimately God is king and will always be king. As the psalmist proclaims, “The Lord is king forever and ever” (Ps. 10:16). Under this structure, a theocratic monarchy , Israel was to have a human king who served as deputy under the Lord, the ultimate king. When Israel sought a king (1 Sam. 8), the elders, moved by a sense of military insecurity, advocated for a king similar to the kings of the nations around them. They wanted a human king who would deliver them from their enemies, which amounted to a rejection of the theocratic monarchy. The Lord Himself assessed Israel’s choice: “They have rejected me from being king over them” (v. 7). In response, the prophet Samuel warned Israel that their desire for such a king would have dire consequences, such as oppression of the people (1 Sam. 8:10–18), but the people dismissed his argument and demanded a king similar to the other ancient Near Eastern monarchs. In response God selected Saul to be the first king of Israel. The choice of Saul reflects one of the important themes of the books of Samuel: God raises up and brings down (see 1 Sam. 2:7–8). Unfortunately, Israel’s first king, Saul, turned out to be exactly what Samuel had warned against. Saul’s kingship began well, but it soon became dark and dysfunctional. He was followed on the throne by David, who was the greatest king in the history of old covenant Israel. He was a ruler after God’s own heart, and his kingship started out quite well. However, David soon fell into deep sin, particularly seen in his relationship with Bathsheba, and throughout the second half of 2 Samuel, David’s kingdom was in disarray. By the close of the book, the reader is struck by the flawed and broken nature of David’s kingship. David’s kingship is properly understood as a pointer to the coming of a greater king, that is, the messianic monarch (2 Sam. 7:12–16). In other words, David himself was not the messianic ruler; he was a forerunner of him. This is evident by the close of 2 Samuel, when David’s kingdom is shown in turmoil and disorder. The reader thus longs for the arrival of the promised king who would live according to God’s word (Deut. 17:14–20). The messianic king eventually came in the person of Jesus Christ, “the son of David” (e.g., Matt. 9:27; 12:23; 21:9). In 1 and 2 Samuel, Israel is in the process of becoming a kingdom, which can be defined as “a land or realm over which a monarch rules.” Earlier, at Mount Sinai, God vowed that His people would one day be a “kingdom” and a “nation” (Ex. 19:6). From Sinai, God led Israel through the wilderness to the Land of Promise, and they then conquered Canaan under the leadership of Joshua. The subsequent period of the judges was one of anarchy. All of that led to the events recorded in 1 and 2 Samuel. Despite the initially promising reigns of Saul, David, and Solomon, each of these rulers demonstrated an inability to exercise the righteous kingship that God’s people needed. After the death of Solomon, the monarchy divided into the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Both of those kingdoms were eventually destroyed and their populations sent into exile. The failures of the kings of Israel and Judah illustrate the need for a greater ruler. When the messianic King appeared, His message was that “the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3:2). The final, ultimate King came to usher in the final, ultimate kingdom—an eternal kingdom that will never perish (1 Pet. 2:9). THEOLOGY OF 1 AND 2 SAMUEL Although the books of 1 and 2 Samuel describe the attempt by Israel to establish a human monarchy, in the final analysis, God was king over Israel. As the sovereign over Israel, he governed the people as well as all the other events that occurred which affected them. Whatever took place in Israel during those days, it was God who ordained it (1 Sam. 2:6–7). The Lord was the one who orchestrated Saul’s search for his father’s lost donkeys, which then led to his anointing at the hands of Samuel (1 Sam. 9:15–16). God also predetermined the choice of David to succeed Saul on the throne of Israel (1 Sam. 16:7). It was the Lord who sat enthroned as king over Israel in those days. Indeed, it is the Lord who sits enthroned as king over all creation yesterday, today, and forever. 1 AND 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The books of 1 and 2 Samuel play a key role in the unfolding of God’s redemptive plan throughout history. In many ways, David’s career typifies that of his greater Son, Jesus Christ. Both were sanctioned by a prophet—David by Samuel (1 Sam. 16:13) and Jesus by John the Baptist (Matt. 14:5; John 1:29–31; 5:31–35). The Spirit of the Lord came upon both (1 Sam. 16:13; Mark 1:9–11). Both were rejected by jealous kings (1 Sam. 18:9; Matt. 2:16) and warned to flee for their lives (1 Sam. 20; Matt. 2:13–15). Rejected by their own people without cause (1 Sam. 23:12; John 19:15), both learned to depend upon God in exile. Hannah’s giving birth to Samuel and her subsequent song of praise (1 Sam. 1–2) serve as paradigms for Mary’s birthing of Jesus and her magnif­icat (Luke 1:46–55). In addition, God’s choice of David’s line to sit upon the throne of Israel forever (2 Sam. 7:16) found its fulfillment in the coming of the messianic king.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: For the last 150 years or so, critical scholarship has attempted to unravel the compositional history of 1 and 2 Samuel. There are a myriad of interpretations of that process. Today, some scholars believe that the two books are part of the so-called “Deuteronomistic History,” in which the final stages of the composition did not occur until the period of the exile. Thus, over the span of many centuries, various authors, editors, and redactors had input into the compositional structure of the two books. However, it is presently impossible to reconstruct the compositional history of 1 and 2 Samuel, and it is likely that it was written in an essentially final form at a much earlier date than supposed by some scholars.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: 1 and 2 Samuel originally formed a single book. For discussions of most topics related to 1 and 2 Samuel, see Introduction to 1 Samuel.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The entire account of 2 Samuel centers on the kingship of David; it is, in a sense, his court history. The book may be divided into four sections in regard to his kingship: David’s ascendancy to the throne, first over Judah and then over all Israel (1:1–5:5); David’s glorious kingship (5:6–10:19); the failure of his kingship (11:1–20:26); and then some final reflections on his kingship (21:1–24:25), including his last words (23:1–7). In addition to the themes covered in the introduction to 1 Samuel, additional features of 2 Samuel require highlighting. Importantly, 2 Sam. 7 describes the covenant that God established with David. Although God denied David’s request to build a temple for him (vv. 4–7), He promised, through the prophet Nathan, that one of David’s “offspring” would be established on the throne of Israel (v. 12). This descendant would one day build a house, or temple, for the Lord (v. 13a). Additionally, the eternal nature of the descendant’s kingship is underscored as God vowed that it would last “forever” (vv. 13b, 16). God would discipline David’s offspring for iniquity but would not abandon him (vv. 15–16). This prophecy found its initial fulfillment in David’s son Solomon: Solomon was David’s direct descendant, he was established as king over Israel, and he built the temple of the Lord. The prophecy of the Davidic covenant, however, has greater expectations than what occurred in the time of Solomon, especially in regard to the kingship’s eternality. Indeed, there appeared a greater fulfillment of the prophecy in the coming of Jesus Christ: He is the son of David, He is the true king of Israel, He is building a greater temple (Heb. 3:1–4), and His throne is eternal. The pivot of the book of 2 Samuel is David’s sin with Bathsheba and against Uriah in chapters 11–12. When confronted by Nathan, David’s repentance was genuine, and God’s forgiveness was immediate. Yet sin still had its consequences for David and his reign. In his later years, David witnessed his own sins replicated in the lives of his sons. God further promised that “the sword shall never depart” from David’s house (12:10). The king lived to see four of his sons die, three of them—Absalom, Amnon, and Adonijah—by the sword. Not until David survived two rebellions, first by his son Absalom and then by Sheba, son of Bichri (ch. 20), did David’s reign regain a measure of equilibrium. Thematic closure is provided for the books of 1 and 2 Samuel by a kind of epilogue in 2 Sam. 21–24. These chapters are symmetrical in outline, and at the center are two poems celebrating the two fundamental reasons for David’s blessedness. First, the Lord was his deliverer (22:2–51); and, second, the Lord made an “everlasting covenant” with him (23:1–7). This ending demonstrates the fervor of David’s heart and the way that he valued his relationship with God above all else.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The name of the books of 1 and 2 Kings is derived from its title in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) identifies the books as “3 and 4 Kingdoms,” which follow the books of 1 and 2 Kingdoms (the Septuagint’s name for 1 and 2 Samuel). It is evident that 1 Kings originally belonged with 2 Samuel because the court history of David, which dominates 2 Samuel, is not brought to conclusion until 1 Kings 1:1–2:12. In addition, it is also clear that the two books of Kings were originally one book, and they were later divided right in the middle of the reign of the Israelite monarch Azariah.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The author of the books of 1 and 2 Kings is unknown. Jewish tradition assigns the composition to the prophet Jeremiah. The Talmud concludes that “Jeremiah wrote his own book, the book of Kings, and Lamentations” ( Baba’ Bathra 15a). Although it appears as if Jeremiah probably makes reference to 2 Kings in his prophecy, there is no evidence that he is the central author of that book. Many scholars today believe that the points of view of the books of Joshua, Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel, and 1 and 2 Kings are similar, and, in fact, they all develop the theological ideas expressed in the book of Deuteronomy.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The books of 1 and 2 Kings record the history of Israel starting with the transition of the monarchy from David to Solomon (1 Kin. 1:1–2:12) and concluding with the release of King Jehoiachin from a Babylonian prison in 561 B.C. (2 Kin. 25:27–30). All indications are that the final compilation of the books occurred during the Babylonian exile. Since there is no mention of the return of the people in 538 B.C. , it is likely that the final edition of the work was completed by the mid-point of the Babylonian exile (c. 550 B.C. ). The compilers obviously employed earlier materi­als, and some of these were perhaps contemporary with the events recorded. The earlier sources included a variety of genres, such as prophetic, administrative, and historic writings. A few of these sources are named in 1 and 2 Kings: “the Book of the Acts of Solomon” (1 Kin. 11:41), “the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel” (1 Kin. 14:19), and “the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah” (1 Kin. 14:29). In addition, a number of statements in 1 and 2 Kings describe conditions that prevailed before the time of the exile and comment on them by saying that they continue “to this day” (1 Kin. 8:8; 9:21; 12:19; 2 Kin. 8:22). These statements point to the existence of preexilic material that was included in the very first edition of the books of Kings and then commented on by later editors or compilers. Finally, 2 Kings closes with a specific and detailed chronology of the days, months, and years of the events surrounding the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. This material could have been written only during the subsequent exilic period. Some scholars argue for a double redaction or editing. They believe that the main writing of the two books occurred during the reign of the Judean King Josiah (late seventh century B.C. ). According to this view, a later historian of the exilic period updated this history, adding a brief record of Judah’s final years. Whether one holds to a one-edition hypothesis (exilic) or a two-edition hypothesis, the books demonstrate a unified perspective.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The dominant literary style of 1 and 2 Kings is historical prose narrative. As with the other Historical Books of the Bible, however, the books of Kings interweave various other literary styles of composition within the overall framework of historical narrative. For instance, the author employs short story (1 Kin. 3:16–28), prayer (1 Kin. 8:22–53; 2 Kin. 19:14–19), benediction (1 Kin. 8:54–61), court intrigue (1 Kin. 11:14–40), prophecy (1 Kin. 13:1–3; 2 Kin. 19:20–28), eulogy (1 Kin. 14:19–20), and miracle account (1 Kin. 17:17–24). The heart of the books is a history of the monarchy of Israel and Judah that demonstrates that God is the true king over all things.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: After his recording of the reign of Solomon (1 Kin. 1:28–11:43), the biblical author provides a detailed description of the division of the monarchy (1 Kin. 12:1–14:31). From that point on, the bulk of the material in the two books is devoted to the history of the two kingdoms of Israel (north) and Judah (south). The writer alternates between the two kingdoms in order to underscore that, in reality, he is presenting the history of one people—God’s people. This cycle between the reigns in the north and the south continues until the northern kingdom is captured and sent into exile by the Assyrians in 721 B.C. (2 Kin. 17:6–41). The author then traces the history of the kingship in Judah until the fall of that nation in 586 B.C. (2 Kin. 18:1–25:30). The reporting of the reigns of individual kings appears in a fairly consistent structure or framework in the books. Normatively, a reign has an introductory section that begins with the date a king ascended to the throne, based upon the year of the contemporary king in the other kingdom. So, for example, we read, “Now in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah” (1 Kin. 15:1). This is sometimes followed by the age of the king when he came to the throne, such as, “Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign” (1 Kin. 22:42). The length of the king’s reign is then included. His ancestry appears next: for the Judean kings the mother’s name is usually provided, and for the Israelite kings it is normally the father’s name. Finally, the introductory section provides a theological summary of the nature of the king’s reign. This theological assessment is formulaic: for the kings of the northern kingdom the moral evaluation normally reads, he “did what was evil in the sight of the Lord.” And, often, the king in question is compared to the standard of monarchic wickedness in Israel, that is, Jeroboam 1. The author says of the king that “he walked in the way of Jeroboam” (e.g., 1 Kin. 15:26, 34; 16:19, 26; 22:52; 2 Kin. 10:29; 13:2, 11). All kings in the northern kingdom receive a negative evaluation. Likewise, some southern kings receive a negative evaluation (e.g., 1 Kin. 15:3). Some kings receive qualified approval, doing what was right in the eyes of the Lord but not removing the high places (e.g., 1 Kin. 15:11–14). Only two kings received unqualified approval, Hezekiah (2 Kin. 18:3–4) and Josiah (2 Kin. 22:2). The paradigm for the goodness of the southern kings is David (1 Kin. 15:11; 2 Kin. 18:3; 22:2). The reigns of particular kings also contain formulaic concluding remarks. Normally an obituary is provided in which the king’s death is reported. For the Judean kings, often more information is given, such as the place of burial, which is often “in the city of David” (1 Kin. 15:24; 2 Kin. 14:20; 15:7, 38; 16:20). In addition, a notice of succession appears, designating the particular royal son who ascended to the throne or, if applicable, the name of the usurper who seized the throne (e.g., 1 Kin. 15:8, 24; 16:28; 2 Kin. 10:35; 12:21; 13:9). The introductory and concluding formulae bracket events and incidents that the biblical writer reports about each king. Every monarch is remembered for at least one major episode during his reign, although certain kings receive extended treatments.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: 1. Like king, like nation . Rulers have a powerful influence upon a nation for good or bad. Prov. 14:34 states, “Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.” In 1 and 2 Kings, there is a clear correlation between the spiritual state of a king and that of the people he leads. Normally, when a godly king rules, the people fear the Lord; however, when an evil king reigns, the people tend to fall into greater immorality and idolatry. There are exceptions to the adage “like king, like nation,” such as the kingship of Jotham (2 Kin. 15:34–35; cf. 2 Chron. 27:2). However, a common refrain for the kings of Israel is that they did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam, by “which he made Israel to sin” (e.g., 2 Kin. 13:11; 14:24; 15:9). 2. Prophets. Because of the wicked leadership of many of the kings of the two nations, God raised up prophets to serve as a check and balance against them. The prophets passionately insisted on undivided allegiance to the Lord and His law, opposing any alliance or political posture that might jeopardize the distinctiveness of Israelite religion. Not surprisingly, this strict adherence to the covenant often pits the prophets against kings and queens who were willing to compromise in politics and religion with Israel’s neighbors. Although the writer gives most of his attention to Elijah and Elisha, he mentions many other prophets: Nathan (1 Kin. 1:22), Ahijah (1 Kin. 11:29–39; 14:1–18), Shemaiah (1 Kin. 12:21–24), Micaiah (1 Kin. 22:8–28), Jonah (2 Kin. 14:25), Isaiah (2 Kin. 19:1–7; 20:14), and Huldah (2 Kin. 22:14–20). 3. The division. The roots of the division between the northern and southern kingdoms were long-standing and deep-seated. This history is important to trace, for it provides one of the important reasons for the division. In Gen. 49, Jacob blessed his sons and the tribes that would descend from them. Judah received a special blessing: he would rule over his brothers, and the great king would descend from him (vv. 8–12). Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, also were given a privileged position among the tribes of Israel (vv. 22–26). During the period of the conquest, Judah received the first land allotment (Josh. 15:1), and Ephraim received the second (16:5). During the settlement, Ephraim twice attempted to establish a kingship in Israel in its allotment (Judg. 8:22ff.; 9:7–16, 22). These were unsuccessful because God had other plans: “He rejected the tent of Joseph; he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loves. He chose David his servant ... to shepherd Jacob his people, Israel his inheritance” (Ps. 78:67–71 passim). The rivalry between Ephraim in the north and Judah in the south continued through the reigns of Saul (1 Sam. 11:8; 18:16), David (2 Sam. 2:4; 5:5; 20:1–22), and Solomon. When Jeroboam, an Ephraimite, led the revolt that resulted in the division, he said the following to the northern tribes: “What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David” (1 Kin. 12:16). THEOLOGY OF 1 AND 2 KINGS At the very heart of the books of 1 and 2 Kings is the reality of monotheism. Yahweh is the only Lord of the cosmos and ruler over the kingdoms of the earth (2 Kin. 19:15). God leads His people into battle, answers their prayers, honors their sacrifices, and displays a special concern for the poor and oppressed. Undivided devotion to God is a hallmark of the covenant (1 Kin. 18:21, 39). Related to the existence of the one supreme God is the author’s contention that there can be only one, central sanctuary (Deut. 12). The construction of the temple by Solomon is a major event in Israelite history. Accordingly, great attention is given in 1 Kings to the preparations for and construction of this edifice, including detailed descriptions of its dimensions and furnishings. In addition, worship at other cultic sites was prohibited. As the books of Kings chart the deteriorating devotion of Israel’s kings, the problem is not so much a wholesale abandonment of Yahweh for other gods, but combining the worship of Yahweh with the worship of other deities in unauthorized worship sites. The writer cites the worship of other gods as a major reason for the defeat and exile of both Israel and Judah (2 Kin. 17:7, 16, 19; 21:3–5). At the center of the relationship between God and Israel is the covenant. Although the monarchy has been established and ordained by God, the power of the king is not absolute. Everyone, king and people alike, are responsible for remaining faithful to their covenant with God. Each king is evaluated based on whether he kept the Torah—the law of the covenant. Because God is faithful to keep the covenant He made with David (2 Sam. 7:14–16), He preserves the Davidic dynasty as the rulers of Judah in spite of the grievous sins committed by certain kings. 1 AND 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In general, a proper assessment of the period recorded in 1 and 2 Kings is that it was a failure. The people repeatedly break the covenant with the Lord, and they constantly fall into idol worship. Overall, the monarchy is ineffectual, and a majority of the kings are wicked. At the close of 2 Kings, both kingdoms have been destroyed by foreign powers, and the people, for the most part, have been exiled. The end of the book portrays despair and hopelessness for the people of God. Such troubling circumstances ought to cause the reader to yearn for something more and different. They ought to cause one to hope and long for a new and final covenant, a new and final kingdom, and a new and final king. These are all realized in the coming of Jesus Christ. Jesus is the Son of David and the King of kings (Matt. 21:9; 1 Tim. 6:15). He has established a new covenant with His people (Luke 22:20; Heb. 8:13; 12:24), and He has ushered in the “kingdom of God” (Mark 1:15).

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The books of Kings are filled with chronological data. The author dates the building of the temple 480 years after the exodus (1 Kin. 6:1). He provides figures for the length of David’s and Solomon’s reigns, and he gives explicit information on the reigns of all of Judah’s and Israel’s kings. Coordinating this data with Assyrian, Babylonian, and other extrabiblical records is a challenging task, since knowing how long a given king reigned does not establish precisely when he reigned. Furthermore, it is possible that the manner in which the northern kingdom dated the reigns of its kings was different than the manner in which the southern kingdom dated the reigns of its kings. If so, this could alter our understanding of the overlapping reigns and dates of the kings in Israel and the kings in Judah. Additionally, the possibility of co-regencies in which two successive kings of Judah or two successive kings of Israel ruled at the same time for portions of their reigns may mean that what we might think is the beginning of a reign is actually the beginning of a co-regency. This would mean that the total reign of two co-regents is actually shorter than if we were to add the total number of years given for each king’s reign in 1 and 2 Kings. For example, a co-regency between Asa and Hezekiah would indicate that a total of approximately thirty-three years passed between the ascension of Asa to the throne and the death of Hezekiah instead of the forty-five years that we get if we simply add the given lengths of their reigns together (2 Kin. 16:2; 18:2). In fact, dating the reigns of Asa, Hezekiah, and Manasseh is notoriously difficult, which means that we must be content at the present with approximate dates for the beginning and ending of each of their reigns. In any case, there are some dates that can be established with relatively little doubt. The dates of the fall of Israel and the fall of Judah are known with some certainty, and other major dates can be calculated from them. These dates are widely accepted: 970 B.C. End of David’s Reign 970–930 B.C. Solomon’s Reign 930 B.C. Division of the Kingdom 722 B.C. Fall of Israel 586 B.C. Fall of Judah

sections.content: 1 and 2 Kings originally formed a single book. For discussions of most topics related to 1 and 2 Kings, see Introduction to 1 Kings.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: 2 Kings begins with the reigns of Ahaziah in Israel (853–852 B.C. ) and Jehoshaphat in Judah (870–848 B.C. ). It traces the history of the northern kingdom to its destruction at the hands of the Assyrians in 722 B.C. (2 Kings 17:6). After this conquest, Hezekiah of Judah (715–686 B.C. ) established a great religious reform in the southern kingdom (18:1–4). His reformation is a high point in the book; however, it did not continue after his death. One of the final eras of hope for Judah was the reign of Josiah (640–609 B.C. ). He attempted to free Judah from Assyrian control, to bring about a religious reform in Judah, and to integrate the territory of the former northern kingdom into his own land. After Josiah was killed at Megiddo in 609 B.C. , Judah was, for all intents and purposes, finished as a nation. In 586 B.C. the Babylonian army delivered the final blow as it captured Judah and Jerusalem, destroyed many Judean cities, and then sent many of the Judeans into exile. However, the last recorded event in this book is the release of Jehoiachin from prison. His exaltation above all the other exiled kings in Babylon offers a glimmer of hope that God has not abandoned His commitment to establish David’s dynasty forever. Eventually, this is fulfilled through Jesus Christ (Matt. 1:1).
