sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book of Chronicles, now in two parts as 1 and 2 Chronicles, was originally a single work, known in Hebrew tradition as “words [or events] of the days,” an expression that often appears in the books of Kings as part of longer phrases (e.g., 1 Kin. 14:29), and in other places by itself (Neh. 12:23; Esth. 2:23; 6:1). The Septuagint entitled the book “Paraleipomenon” (“of the things left out”), but Jerome in the fourth century, and Luther in the sixteenth, called the book the “Chronicle of the Entire Sacred History.” The modern English title is derived from Luther’s title.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Jewish tradition regards Ezra as the primary author of Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah. At least two reasons make this identification plausible: the book was written following the Babylonian exile of the Jews, near the time of Ezra’s ministry (see Date and Occasion below), and many passages in Chronicles sympathize with the priestly concerns of Ezra. Other considerations cast doubt on the traditional view of authorship. The date of composition for Chronicles cannot be limited to Ezra’s lifetime (see Date and Occasion); the focus on kingship characteristic of Chronicles is not present in Ezra’s teaching; and Ezra’s distress over the apostasy associated with intermarriage is not a prominent theme in Chronicles. In other words, historical and scriptural evidence does not point decisively to Ezra, and most scholars do not now think that all three books came from a single author, although they share similar interests. By convention, the anonymous author is known as “the Chronicler.” It is often argued that his interest in the temple and its personnel indicates that he himself was from a priestly or Levitical family.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The final verses of 2 Chronicles indicate that it was written after the release of the exiles from Babylon in 538 B.C. The absence of Hellenistic influences suggests that the history was composed before the Alexandrian period (that is, before 331 B.C. ). Nevertheless, opinions vary over the precise date of composition. Some interpreters have proposed that the Chronicler wrote as early as the reconstruction of the temple under Zerubbabel (c. 520–515 B.C. ). At least three pieces of evidence support this view. First, the Chronicler consistently presents the temple and its personnel in close partnership with the royal line of David. This emphasis suggests a date near the time of Zerubbabel, when expectations of royal and priestly partnership were high (Zech. 4). Second, there is close attention to the details of priestly and Levitical duties (1 Chr. 6:1–81 note). This suggests a connection with the time when the new temple order was being established. Third, the writer’s omission of Solomon’s downfall due to intermarriage with pagan women (1 Kin. 11:1–40; Neh. 13:26) suggests that Chronicles may have been written before intermarriage became a major issue in the community following the exile in Babylon. The majority of interpreters have dated Chronicles during or shortly after the ministries of Ezra and Nehemiah, in the latter half of the fifth century or the early decades of the fourth century B.C. It is reasonable to locate the book during the period from about the time of Zerubbabel to soon after the ministries of Ezra and Nehemiah. The major themes of the book fit well within these boundaries (between 515 and 400 B.C. ). Since 1 Chr. 3:17–24 lists at least two generations beyond Zerubbabel, a date somewhat after 460 B.C. is more probable. The Chronicler wrote to encourage those who had returned from the exile because they were facing serious difficulties. The restoration had not brought about the dramatic changes for which many hoped. Instead, they had to endure discouraging economic hardship, foreign opposition, and internal conflict. These problems raised many questions. Who are the legitimate heirs to the promises God gave His people? What political and religious institutions should be embraced? Is there hope for a new Davidic king? The historian who wrote Chronicles addressed these and similar questions.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The primary genre of Chronicles is historical narrative, with generous use of genealogy. While a history, Chronicles was composed for both historical and theological reasons. The Chronicler’s extensive use of historical documents and his devotion to numerical and chronological details (e.g., 1 Chr. 5:18; 2 Chr. 14:1, 9; 16:1, 12, 13) indicate that he intends to give his readers an accurate historical record. He does not merely offer information about the past, however; he also writes to convey a relevant theological message. Comparing Chronicles with Samuel and Kings reveals that this account of Israel’s past is shaped to address the needs of the community recently returned from Babylonian exile.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The Chronicler combines information from more than one source. He depends on a number of biblical texts, especially Samuel and Kings (or possibly the sources from which they were compiled), but also the Pentateuch, Judges, Ruth, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Zechariah. There are specific citations of several royal sources not otherwise known, such as “the chronicles of King David” (1 Chr. 27:24), “the Book of the Kings” (2 Chr. 24:27), “the Book of the Kings of Israel” (1 Chr. 9:1; 2 Chr. 20:34), “the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel” (2 Chr. 16:11; 25:26; 28:26; 32:32), and “the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah” (2 Chr. 27:7; 35:27; 36:8). The Chronicler uses prophetic sources, including the writings of Samuel (1 Chr. 29:29), Nathan (29:29; 2 Chr. 9:29), Gad (1 Chr. 29:29), and others (2 Chr. 9:29; 12:15; 13:22; 26:22; 32:32). Variations of style and content in the work suggest that there may be still other unspecified sources that the Chronicler has skillfully compressed and amalgamated into a coherent account. Because a major theme of his work is the significance of the Davidic dynasty, he omits extensive documentation regarding the kings of the northern kingdom of Israel. Description of the reign of the first king, Saul, is largely confined to an account of his death, thereby setting the scene for David to succeed him. Even in describing Davidic kings, the Chronicler condenses his account so that it focuses on the particular themes he wishes to examine.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The primary themes of Chronicles may be summarized in many ways, but three concerns are prominent: the people of God, the king and the temple, and divine blessing and judgment. 1. The people of God. The writer identifies the people who should be counted as heirs of God’s covenant promises. The prominence of this theme appears in his frequent use of the expression “all Israel” (1 Chr. 11:1; 2 Chr. 10:1; 29:24). On the one hand, the author considers returnees from Babylonian exile to be the people of God. Representatives of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh who have returned to the land are the chosen people (1 Chr. 9:3 note). On the other hand, the author considers the restoration of Israel to be incomplete as long as any of the tribes remain outside the land, separated from the Davidic king and the Jerusalem temple. As a result, the Chronicler is careful to include both the northern and southern tribes in his genealogies (1 Chr. 2:3–9:1), to present the picture of the united monarchy under David and Solomon extending to all the people (1 Chr. 11:1 note), and to depict the reunification of the northern and southern kingdoms in the days of Hezekiah. Thus, the Chronicler teaches that the returned exiles are the remnant of God’s people, but they look forward to the restoration of all the people of God. As Hezekiah put it, “For if you return to the L ORD , your brothers and your children will find compassion with their captors and return to this land. For the L ORD your God is gracious and merciful” (2 Chr. 30:9). 2. The king and the temple. Chronicles presents the people of God as organized around two central institutions: the Davidic throne and the Jerusalem temple. The genealogies give special attention to David’s lineage (1 Chr. 2:10–17; ch. 3) and to the organization of priests and Levites (1 Chr. 6). David’s line was chosen by God as the permanent dynasty over the nation (1 Chr. 17; 2 Chr. 13:5; 21:7; 23:3), and the establishment of David’s throne demonstrates divine love and blessing for Israel (1 Chr. 14:2; 2 Chr. 2:11). The historian also focuses on the temple as the place where God’s name resides (2 Chr. 7:12, 16; 33:7). The joy and splendor of music in temple worship is revealed (1 Chr. 6:31–47; 9: 33; 13:8; 15:16–24, 28; 23:5; ch. 25; 2 Chr. 5:1–13; 7:6; 23:13; 29:25–30; 34:12; and notes). According to the Chronicler, the full restoration of the kingdom cannot take place apart from the Davidic king and the Jerusalem temple. As the L ORD said to David, “I will raise up your offspring after you, one of your own sons, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for me, and I will establish his throne forever” (1 Chr. 17:11, 12). 3. Divine blessing and judgment. The author shows his readers how to receive God’s blessings in their day. He stresses the close connection between fidelity and blessing, infidelity and judgment (1 Chr. 28:9; 2 Chr. 6:14; 7:2–22; 15:2; 16:7–9; 21:12–15; 24:20; 28:9; 34:24–28). The king and the temple cannot in themselves secure God’s blessing for Israel; there must be obedience to the Mosaic law and to prophetic and priestly instruction. The L ORD blesses those who uphold the purity of temple worship and rely on Him alone (1 Chr. 5:20; 2 Chr. 13:18; 14:7; 32:20, 21). When the people or the kings turn to sin, an immediate retribution of illness and military defeat often follows (1 Chr. 10; 2 Chr. 13:1–16; 16:12; 28:1–5; 33:1–11). Even so, the people can be restored to blessing by seeking God in repentance and prayer (1 Chr. 21:1–22:1; 2 Chr. 7:13–15; 12:1–12; 33:10–13). The Chronicler shows that the full restoration of God’s people will come only as they live in fidelity to the L ORD . Azariah says it well: “If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you” (2 Chr. 15:2). THEOLOGY OF 1 CHRONICLES Chronicles is primarily an exercise in applied covenant theology. Starting as it does with Adam, it emphasizes the overarching sovereignty of the God who has a purpose that runs throughout human history, and it implies that this purpose will surely be accomplished. The genealogies of chapters 1–9 reminded the postexilic community, who were suffering a loss of identity and purpose as they existed on the fringes of the vast Persian Empire, that they were central to God’s purpose, which spans the ages. More particularly, the Chronicler views the community as those for whom God was the L ORD (Yahweh), who graciously entered into covenant with them and bestowed on them immense spiritual privileges. The Chronicler focuses on the Davidic covenant (ch. 17) and its implications, especially the privilege accorded by the temple and God’s presence there in their midst. 1

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: A book that stretches from Adam (1:1) to the return from the exile in 538 B.C. —and indeed beyond that in some of the genealogies (e.g. 3:21)— inevitably covers much of the larger story of the Bible. However, the significance of the storyline is not so much that these things happened but that they are part of God’s structuring of human history to achieve His redemptive purpose. There is a momentum throughout Chronicles that guides the perceptive reader to scan the horizon for greater things yet to come. In 1 Chronicles the emphasis is primarily on how the basis for the future is set in the Davidic covenant with its provision of a dynasty and a place of worship for God’s people. CHRIST IN 1 CHRONICLES In selecting and structuring his material, the Chronicler adopts the framework found in Samuel and Kings, which is based on the reigns and actions of kings. Though he appears to adopt a more priestly perspective, the Davidic covenant and dynasty are nevertheless a formative influence in his perception. Consequently, throughout Chronicles there is an underlying messianic foundation that culminates in Christ, the promised Son of David. The book’s concept of the people of God becomes a reality in Christ. Like the community of the restoration, those who follow Christ are the heirs of Israel’s promises (Gal. 3:14, 29; 4:28; Eph. 2:11–22; 3:6). However, the church also extends beyond Israel to include the Gentiles (Luke 2:32; Acts 9:15; 11:1, 18); and in the end all of God’s elect, “the Israel of God” (Gal. 6:16), will be united under the lordship of Christ. The hope for David’s throne to be restored is fulfilled in Christ. He was born the Son of David, the heir to the Davidic covenant (Luke 1:32; Rom. 1:3; Rev. 22:16). Christ met all the conditions of obedience placed on David’s line (Rom. 5:19; Phil. 2:8; Heb. 5:7–10). In the resurrection, Christ took His throne in heaven (Acts 2:33–35; Eph. 1:20–23; Phil. 2:9; Rev. 3:21), from which He leads His people into blessing and victory (Rom. 8:37; Eph. 4:7–13). He will reign until all His enemies are defeated (1 Cor. 15:24–26). The purposes of the temple are fulfilled in Christ. Christ was Himself the perfect sacrifice for sin (Heb. 9:11–28; 1 Pet. 3:18; 1 John 2:2). He mediates our prayers and intercedes on our behalf in heaven (Heb. 3:1; 4:14–16; 6:20; 7:26; 8:1). As our high priest and captain, He will bring all His people into the presence of God (John 14:1–4; 1 Thess. 4:16–17). Finally, the book’s revelation of divine blessing and judgment is realized in Christ. Jesus bore the judgment of God on sin, and He sets His people free to follow the path of obedience (Rom. 3:21–26). He gives His people new life and makes them citizens of God’s kingdom (John 3:16; Phil. 3:20).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Treating Chronicles as a supplement to Samuel and Kings, rather than as a work in its own right, has led over the centuries to the work being misunderstood and undervalued. The extensive treatment of the temple and priestly offices further diminished Reformed interest in the work until quite recently. Many critical discussions of Chronicles have characterized material not found in Samuel or Kings as distorted or fanciful. However, recent archaeological work has substantiated the Chronicler’s information, and his work is now appraised more positively.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: As noted above, it is clear that the Chronicler used Samuel and Kings (or sources that Samuel and Kings also used) in the writing of his account of the history of Israel and Judah. In comparing Chronicles, Samuel, and Kings, readers will find a few discrepancies between the different accounts, particularly when it comes to the use of numbers. Often, but not always, the numbers that the Chronicler reports in his telling of events are higher than the numbers used in Samuel and Kings. For example, 2 Sam. 8:3, 4 and 1 Chron. 18:3, 4 both report David’s defeat of King Hadadezer of Zobah. However, whereas the account in 2 Samuel states that David captured 1,700 of Hadadezer’s horsemen, 1 Chronicles asserts that David captured 7,000 horsemen. Scholars continue to investigate the reasons for these differences, and no universally satisfying solution has yet been found. Evidence from the Dead Sea Scrolls suggests that the Hebrew text of Kings and Samuel that the Chronicler used may differ in slight ways from the Masoretic Text upon which most modern translations of Samuel and Kings are based (see theological article “Old Testament Textual Criticism”). It is also possible that some accidental scribal mistakes were made in copying the numbers used in these texts, since many of them look very similar to one another in the original Hebrew, making it relatively simple for the scribal eye to confuse one number for another. Other scholars suggest that we do not know enough about how the ancient Hebrews used numbers to say definitively that there are differences between Chronicles and the books of Samuel and Kings. We await more textual and archaeological evidence to come to a firm conclusion about this matter. At this point, we note that the appearance of these minor discrepancies, which do not affect any doctrine of the faith, actually provide further evidence that the Bible is the best preserved text from antiquity. Other ancient texts exist in such a poor state of preservation that large and vitally important sections are in question. Where textual questions exist with respect to the Bible, they concern only peripheral issues that do not affect the actual meaning of the text in any significant way. We can therefore be confident that God has preserved His Word for His people. RSB_13

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: Although the break between 1 and 2 Chronicles has been inserted sensitively into the narrative, it is merely a later scribal convenience for easier handling of Greek scrolls, which contained vowels as well as consonants and so were longer than the corresponding Hebrew manuscripts. The original work was conceived of as a unity. See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Title.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Date and Occasion.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The Chronicler continues the approach he employed for the reign of David, and he structures his narrative as a court history in which the fortunes of the nation are determined by the actions of its kings. The account, however, does not give primary emphasis to military or economic affairs but to the religious health of the people. This is a presentation of covenant history to encourage the restored community in Judah to greater faithfulness in the conduct of their individual and national life.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The Davidic covenant (1 Chr. 17) and Solomon’s prayer (2 Chr. 6) are used by the Chronicler to help his audience integrate their understanding of events in their national history as later events conform to the structures set out earlier. When the covenant king and his people faced danger, prayer to the Lord, as envisaged by Solomon (e.g. 6:21, 25), gave access to divine forgiveness and assistance (12:6; 13:14; 14:11; 18:31), even for as abandoned a character as Manasseh (33:12, 13). The Chronicler assumes his audience is familiar with the accounts in Kings to such an extent that what he says would not be understood properly without it (e.g., 32:24–33). However, the Chronicler develops his source material from Kings to bring out his primary message that covenant obedience brings divine blessing, and covenant unfaithfulness entails divine chastisement. The latter outcome was tragically evident throughout the lives of some kings, and for Jehoram (21:4–20), Ahaziah (22:1–9), Ahaz (28:1–27), Amon (33:21–25), Jehoahaz (36:2–4), Jehoiakim (36:5–8), Jehoiachin (36:9, 10), and Zedekiah (36:11–14) the Chronicler is content to maintain the adverse characterization of Kings. While he retains the mixed assessments given earlier of Asa (14:2–16:14) and Jehoshaphat (17:1–21:3), he presents other monarchs more positively than Kings: Rehoboam (10:1–12:16), Joash (22:10–24:27), Amaziah (25:1–28), Uzziah (26:1–33), Josiah (34:1–36:1), and Manasseh (33:1–20). By passing over their failures and providing other examples of success not mentioned in Kings, he depicts Abijah (13:1–14:1), Jotham (27:1–9), and Hezekiah (29:1–32:33) in a very favorable fashion, in part to create within the audience a hope for the coming of the King who realizes the ideal presented in his positive portrayal of these kings.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The Chronicler retells the history of Israel and Judah in order to provide theological answers to three fundamental questions that arose after the Jews returned from exile in Babylonia. First, how can the heirs to God’s covenant promises be known after the dislocation of exile and return? Second, what is to become of their central political and religious institutions, the Davidic throne and the Jerusalem temple, and how should they be related to one another in the restored community? Third, how are the people to understand the experience of exile and restoration in the light of God’s law and grace, His judgment and forgiveness? The discussion of these themes, begun in the Introduction to 1 Chronicles, is continued here with respect to 2 Chronicles. The Chronicler is concerned to emphasize the privilege extended to the nation through the covenant the Lord instituted and maintained with them. It is their responsibility to perpetuate a true relationship with Him by means of worship at the temple, which is under the care of its priestly and Levitical guardians. What was sound and proven from the past provides the key to moving forward in harmony with God and being accepted by Him. 1. The United Monarchy under Solomon (1:1–9:31). The opening section of 2 Chronicles depicts Solomon as the divinely blessed successor of David. The Chronicler passes over Solomon’s struggle for power (1 Chr. 23:1 note) and his later downfall due to intermarriage (1 Kin. 11:1–40). He shows Solomon as the king of “all Israel” (1 Chr. 11:1 note), and as the prime instrument for constructing the temple in Jerusalem (2 Chr. 2:1–8:16). There is a brief notice of his death (9:29–31). Solomon’s reign is narrated in a topical and symmetrical form, opening and closing with passages describing the king’s wisdom and wealth (ch. 1; 9:13–28). Just inside these passages are sections about his international relations (ch. 2; 8:17–9:12). Inserted between these passages are sections about the building of the temple and Solomon’s other projects throughout Israel (3:1–5:1; 8:1–16), and in the center is the description of the temple dedication (5:2–7:10) and the divine response to it (7:12–22). A concentric outline of this kind emphasizes the topics in the middle, in this case the dedication of the temple. 2. The Divided Kingdom (10:1–28:26). The record of Israel’s history from Rehoboam to Ahaz focuses on events in the southern kingdom of Judah. Although Kings is the source of much of the information, Chronicles omits large blocks of material dealing with the northern kingdom of Israel. The focus of Chronicles is on Judah and its capital, Jerusalem, the place of the Davidic king and the temple of God. The kings of the period are measured by the ideal of the united monarchy. The king must be faithful to the law of Moses; he must support the temple order established by David and Solomon; and he must listen to prophetic and priestly instruction. Some kings are evaluated negatively (Jehoram, 21:4–20; Ahaziah, 22:1–9; Ahaz, 28:1–27), others positively (Abijah, 13:1–14:1; Jotham, 27:1–9). For the most part the records are mixed (Rehoboam, 10:1–12:16; Asa, 14:2–16:14; Jehoshaphat, 17:1–21:3; Joash, 22:10–24:27; Amaziah, 25:1–28; Uzziah, 26:1–23). See Literary Features above for a comparison with the assessments found in Kings. From his inspired history of Israel and Judah, the Chronicler shows that God blesses His people when they are faithful, and He chastises them when they turn away from Him. Victory, security, and prosperity come to those who seek the Lord. Defeat, trouble, and illness come upon those who forget Him. 3. The reunited kingdom (29:1–36:23). Beginning with Hezekiah, Israel enters a new phase of her history. Like David and Solomon, Hezekiah is able to unite the faithful of Israel and Judah around the Davidic throne through worship and celebration at the temple (29:1 note and 29:24 note). This reunited people experience periods of failure: Manasseh’s apostasy (33:1–10); the reign of Amon (33:21–25); and the kings of Judah just before the Babylonian exile (36:2–14). But each failure is followed by God’s gracious renewal of the people: Manasseh’s restoration (33:11–17); Josiah’s reforms (34:3–35:19); and the return from exile in Babylonia (36:22–23). Despite the failures of the reunited kingdom, God continues to grant blessings to His repentant people. He extends His mercy to them, offering them His blessing. At the same time, the events of the period demonstrate the requirements placed on those who long for the full restoration of the kingdom. The nation must turn to the Lord in humility and live faithfully before Him. THEOLOGY OF 2 CHRONICLES To the themes of the covenant people of God, the king and the temple, and divine blessing and judgment (see Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Characteristics and Primary Themes), 2 Chronicles adds repeated references to the disobedience of representatives of the dynasty and its tragic consequences for the people as a whole. Even so, the royal house is preserved, and it is possible through repentance to reverse its downward progression (see Manasseh, 33:11–17). The temple continues as an important instance of the principle of God with us, typifying the incarnation of the Messiah. The Chronicler’s description of divine providence is often presented as a theology of immediate retribution. In Samuel and Kings, divine retribution comes on the northern kingdom (2 Kin. 17:7–20) and on Judah (2 Kin. 23:26, 27) as the culmination of a process over many generations. On the other hand, many scholars argue that in Chronicles the successes or failures of a king are rewarded or punished within his own lifetime. However, the Chronicler’s approach is much more subtle. He does not lose sight of the long-term impact of the conduct of the nation (2 Chr. 7:19–22; 36:15, 16). Even so, his major concern is to commend covenant obedience to his contemporaries, and he therefore chooses historical examples that make his point as forcibly as possible. “Whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Gal. 6:7). But the Chronicler does not simply equate reverses experienced in life with prior disobedience. The aggression Asa encounters from Baasha in chapter 16 comes after a chapter extolling Asa’s religious reforms. More significantly, Hezekiah’s extensive reforming activity in chapters 29–31 is followed by Sennacherib’s invasion, as the Chronicler himself notes in 32:1. His is not a naive approach to events but an urgent call to repentance. Because of the enduring commitment of the Lord, the covenant people are never totally without a way back to blessing if only they will repent (7:13, 14). It is also argued that the Chronicler focuses unduly on external aspects of religion. Starting with Jabez’s prayer in 1 Chr. 4:10, land/territory is used as an index of spiritual favor, as are large families. Some commentators also consider the temple and its material adornment to be too prominent in the Chronicler’s presentation of true piety. Here also, significant qualification is required. The temple was the focus of divine presence on earth in the Chronicler’s day, and due respect for it was indicative of heart allegiance to the Lord. Moreover, the Chronicler does not tire of mentioning that what is required is not a mechanical performance of religious rituals but a wholehearted commitment to the Lord (2 Chr. 6:14, 38; 15:12, 15; 19:9; 22:9; 25:2; 31:21; 34:31; and similar expressions in 16:9; 29:31). 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Whereas 1 Chronicles presents the whole sweep of human history from Adam down to the Chronicler’s day, 2 Chronicles covers a more abbreviated time span. Its focus is on the need for ongoing faithfulness in living out the demands of the covenant so as to enjoy the favor and blessing of the Lord. The temple with its sacrificial rituals continues to play a vital role in the progress of salvation history. The complementary focus on the Davidic dynasty promotes hope for the eventual realization of the messianic promise. CHRIST IN 2 CHRONICLES When those holding a God-appointed office in Israel live up to the demands of that office, they became types of Christ, foreshadowing the corresponding aspects of His work. The Chronicler’s positive portrait of kings such as David, Solomon, and Hezekiah enhance their likeness to Christ and so serve to foster expectations of the perfect king who completely fulfills the task of establishing God’s kingdom and providing for His people.

sections.content: See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: History of Interpretation.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: See Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Special Issues.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book is named after its major character, who does not appear until the second section (chs. 7–10), and also in chapters 8 and 12 of Nehemiah. Ezra was a priest and scribe who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with a number of other exiles in 458 B.C. He was authorized by the Persian king to inquire about the religious situation in Jerusalem and to undertake any necessary reforms.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: It is not known who wove together all the documents included in Ezra and Nehemiah to produce the finished canonical books (see Literary Features). Despite an earlier view that a single author wrote the books of Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah, the current scholarly consensus views it as improbable that the historian who wrote Chronicles was also the author of Ezra and Nehemiah (see Introduction to 1 Chronicles: Author). Ezra kept a journal or “memoirs” (7:28 note), as did Nehemiah. Given his literary skills (7:6 and note), Ezra may well have been the compiler of the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, as is held by Jewish tradition.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Ezra’s return has traditionally been dated to 458 B.C. , understanding “the seventh year of Artaxer­xes” (7:7) to be that of the Persian king Artaxer­xes I (465–424 B.C. ). However, there were two later kings with the same name, and there were also many popular Jewish names held by different people in the community over the years. In particular, high priests were often named after their grandfather. Some have argued that the evidence favors Ezra’s arrival in Jerusalem as occurring in 398 B.C. under Artaxerxes II (405–359). This and other proposals have to satisfy the requirement that Ezra and Nehemiah are mentioned together in Neh. 8:9; 12:26. Although there are unresolved aspects to the chronology of the period, the traditional dating remains preferable. The primary sources incorporated into Ezra and Nehemiah, such as their respective memoirs and the various documents sent to or issued by the Persian authorities, were contemporaneous with the events they described. It is probable that Ezra 7–10 and Nehemiah can be dated in the period 430–400 B.C. , though it is less certain whether Ezra 1–6 was written then or somewhat later. The work was composed to encourage the Jews who had returned from exile by revealing to them that though they were still under Persian rule, their sovereign God was continuing His redemptive work and reestablishing true worship among them.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Ezra-Nehemiah is a historical narrative composed of numerous originally separate documents, woven together to form a beautiful and powerful whole. Lists play a significant role in both books. There are lists regarding (a) the temple articles (1:9–11); (b) those who initially returned from exile (2:3–70, repeated in Neh. 7:8–73); (c) the leaders who returned with Ezra (8:2–14); (d) those involved in mixed marriages (10:18–43); (e) those who rebuilt the wall (Neh. 3); (f) those who sealed the covenant (Neh. 10:1–27); (g) new residents in Jerusalem and those in the villages (Neh. 11); and (h) the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:1–26). Much official correspondence has also been included. These letters were written in Aramaic, the language of international diplomacy at that time. There is (a) the letter of Rehum to Artaxerxes (4:11–16); (b) the reply of Artaxerxes (4:17–22); (c) the letter of Tattenai to Darius (5:7–17); (d) the memorandum regarding the decree of Cyrus (6:2–5); (e) the reply of Darius to Tattenai (6:6–12); and (f) the letter of Artaxerxes on behalf of Ezra (7:12–26). Inclusion of the Aramaic material indicates the extent to which the language was known in Jerusalem and also incorporates an implicit claim that the material cited is authentic and accurately represents the history of the period. In addition, the decree of Cyrus (1:2–4) and materi­als from Ezra and Nehemiah themselves have been included (7:27–9:15; Neh. 1:1–7:5; 12:27–43; 13:14–31). The latter may have been developed from reports of their activities prepared for submission to the Persian king.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Although modern Bibles present Ezra and Nehemiah as two separate books, they are treated as one composition in Hebrew manuscripts, the Talmud, Josephus (c. A.D. 37–100), and the oldest manuscripts of the Septuagint. Origen ( A.D. 185–253) was the first to separate Ezra and Nehemiah into two books. Some scholars consider the repetition of the virtually identical lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 as evidence that the two book were initially independent compositions, though combined at a very early date. As befits what is primarily a historical account, the main literary structure of Ezra-Nehemiah is chronological. However, it is also possible to detect other structural patterns. For instance, Ezra-Nehemiah may be considered as tripartite, corresponding to the threefold return of the Jews from exile in Babylon, first under Zerubbabel shortly after 538 B.C. (chs. 1–6), then under Ezra in 458 (chs. 7–10), and finally under Nehemiah in 445 (Neh. 1:1–7:3). These sections share a common structure that begins with an account of who returned and is followed by a description of what they achieved, despite intense opposition, because God was with them and blessed their efforts. The books as a whole then conclude with an account of the reforms needed to secure the well-being of the returned community (Neh. 7:4–13:31).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Three themes of Ezra and Nehemiah can be found in the decree of Cyrus (1:2–4). First, rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem is God’s objective in the history of redemption immediately following the return from exile. Second, the people of God as a whole, and not merely the great leaders, are vital for accomplishing this purpose. Third, the written word is a powerful tool used by God to accomplish His objective. Cyrus commissioned the return from exile for the express purpose of rebuilding “the house of the Lord, the God of Israel” (1:3). Cyrus’s commission was directed toward the entire people of God, not toward specific leaders. The long lists of otherwise unknown individuals testify that the people of God as a whole were responsible for the rebuilding of God’s house. Cyrus’s written decree was the human instrument generating the action in Ezra and Nehemiah. Written documents play a major role in the subordinate actions as well. Letters stop and start the work on the temple (4:23, 24; 6:6–7). A letter gives Ezra authority to carry out reforms (7:25, 26). The written Word of God is a moving force in the narrative (3:2; 10:3; Neh. 8:1; 9:13). This theme is significant, since the era involved is that of the last Old Testament prophets (Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi). There would be a period of silence after them, during which the people of God would be informed exclusively by the written Word. The silence was broken by John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ. The overall purpose of Ezra and Nehemiah is to affirm that God works sovereignly through responsible human agents to accomplish His redemptive objective. Cyrus issued his decree because the Lord had moved his spirit (1:1). Those who returned came back because the Lord had moved their spirits (1:5). Ezra succeeded because the good hand of God was upon him (7:9). Artaxerxes supported the work of rebuilding because the Lord had put it in his spirit (7:27). Human beings acted freely and responsibly under the providence of the sovereign God to bring His plans to fruition.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Ezra-Nehemiah was written to encourage the small Jewish community in Jerusalem and its immediate surroundings in the Persian province of Yehud as they sought to remain faithful to their covenant commitment to the Lord. The narrative makes clear that past generations of returnees had to struggle against opposition as they attempted to live lives pleasing to God. They would have been unable to achieve what they did without divine assistance, sought through prayer. Furthermore, the community was called on to organize around the worship of God in the temple and in obedience to his covenant requirements. By separating from inappropriate interaction with those around them, the community would avoid jeopardizing its witness. The way forward for the original readers of the history was to emulate past prayerful dependence on God and adherence to His requirements. In that way they would enjoy cohesion and stability despite outward pressures to compromise their faith. Two further features of Ezra are worthy of mention. One is the role played by prayer in furthering the purposes of God (9:6–15; see also Neh. 9). This is based on a mature understanding of God’s dealings with his people over the centuries. It is also the case that Ezra accords to the inscripturated Word of God a comprehensive and central role in directing the life of the community (7:6). The Scriptures have a profound impact on the spiritual sensitivity of the people (9:4; 10:3).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The covenant community, first in the northern kingdom of Israel, and then later in the southern kingdom of Judah, had persistently been disloyal to the Lord and breached the terms of the cov­enant. Their rebellion brought on them the curse of the broken covenant in the form of exile to Babylon. When the Babylonian Empire was conquered by the Persians in 539 B.C. , it was a mark of the Lord’s gracious commitment to His people that despite their treachery the exile did not end their national existence. God’s purposes would prevail despite human sin, and He intervened to inspire in the new Persian rulers of the Jews a favorable disposition to God’s people so as to permit them to return to Jerusalem. The exiles who returned from Babylon anticipated an immediate fulfillment of the prophetic promises regarding God’s restoration of their community. They had to cope with the tension that arose from the gap between their expectations and the gradual realization of the divine promise (9:8–9). Ezra points to the need for ongoing covenant faithfulness and also to the good that can be achieved by individuals raised up by God to strengthen and reform His people. Despite the fact that the returned exiles achieved much, there remained a sense of incompleteness. However, it was clear that the God of heaven, who controls human history, would ensure that his promises would come to consummation. The message for both Ezra’s original readers and for us is that the Lord’s covenant blessing will be enjoyed by those who remain faithful to Him. As God’s people anticipate the completion of His purpose, they are to strive after holiness as individuals and as a community.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: There are no direct messianic prophecies in Ezra. However, the leaders of the community who are presented in a positive light foreshadow the awaited leader of God’s people. Ezra and others were prepared to confront those who were going astray and to persist in their activities despite opposition. So, too, would the Messiah (Matt. 23). The narrative focuses on the temple, and the significance accorded it also anticipates the person and work of Christ, who becomes “this temple” (John 2:19–22), the one through whom God dwells among His people, and who supersedes the physical structure of an earthly temple. The second temple also foreshadows the spiritual reality of the church as the temple of God (1 Cor. 3:16–17; 2 Cor. 6:16). This theme reaches its consummation in the holy city of God, the new Jerusalem, which has no specific temple building because the divine presence wholly pervades it (Rev. 21:22).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Although the New Testament presupposes the events related in Ezra-Nehemiah, there is no direct quotation from either book. Many traditions, however, arose regarding Ezra that accord him a greatly enhanced status as a scholar and, mistakenly, as a seer. On the contrary, Ezra was a priest and interpreter of God’s revealed Word rather than a channel for further divine disclosures. While the status and achievements of Ezra and Nehemiah have been widely acknowledged, the books named after them have not often been intensively studied until recent years.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book is named after its central figure, Nehemiah. Nothing is known about his background apart from what is found in the book itself. His family seems to have been part of the Jewish diaspora, and he himself rose to a position of prominence in the Persian court. He was sent as governor to Jerusalem with a mandate to rebuild the city walls. The book is a record of his achievement in this regard and also of the problems he encountered in a second period of governorship (ch. 13).

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The earliest extant evidence presents Ezra and Nehemiah as originally a single book composed from a variety of historical sources, including the personal memoirs of Ezra and Nehemiah. However, Nehemiah shares with Ezra a list of returnees (Ezra 2 parallels Neh. 7). Since it seems improbable that an author would have incorporated the same list into his work twice, this suggests to some commentators that Nehemiah was composed separately and initially stood alone. According to Jewish tradition, Ezra was the individual responsible for compiling these sources into their current form (see Introduction to Ezra: Author).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Assuming that Ezra (or a younger contemporary) compiled Ezra-Nehemiah into its final form, these narratives were written during the period 430–400 B.C. to encourage the Judeans who had returned from exile in Babylon and were reestablishing their community in and around Jerusalem (see Introduction to Ezra: Date and Occasion).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: See Introduction to Ezra: Genre.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Nehemiah has many features similar to those found in Ezra. It is a mixture of narrative and source material (lists and genealogies). However, the story line in Nehemiah is stronger, partly because of the shorter length of time covered (about thirteen years) and partly because a greater part of the book is a first-person account of Nehemiah’s activities as civil leader in Jerusalem (chs. 1–7; 12:27–13:31). There are a number of memorable episodes in the book, particularly the narratives about the rebuilding of the wall (chs. 2–7) and the covenant renewal ceremony (chs. 8–10). Throughout there is a continuing focus on Nehemiah, who is presented as a dominating, heroic figure but one whose motives and actions are determined by his zeal for the Lord and the Lord’s cause. Particularly striking are his various asides and prayers, asking God to remember his deeds and letting the reader know his thoughts. These asides and prayers serve to draw readers into Nehemiah’s narrative, enabling them to identify with him (1:5–11; 2:4; 2:11–12; 4:6–7; 4:19; etc.).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The major theme of Ezra and Nehemiah is that God works sovereignly through responsible human agents to accomplish His redemptive purposes. The author develops this theme in Nehemiah with particular attention to the rebuilding and dedication of the defensive walls of Jerusalem (1:1–7:3; 12:27–43) and the reconstitution of the whole people called “Israel” in their covenant relationship with God (7:4–13:31). See Introduction to Ezra: Characteristics and Themes for further discussion of the themes of Ezra and Nehemiah as a whole. The activities of Ezra and Nehemiah were both authorized by the Persian king. Unlike Ezra, whose focus was on rebuilding the community spiritually by commending adherence to the written law of God, Nehemiah’s concerns were of a more practical and administrative nature: rebuilding the city walls, rectifying anomalies and injustices in the life of the community, and securing sufficient population for Jerusalem to make the city viable. These steps enabled the community to survive and so fulfill its function in God’s purpose of being the people through whom the Messiah would come. However, all Nehemiah’s initial reforms were thrown into question, and in large measure they had to be repeated (ch. 13). Neither Ezra nor Nehemiah themselves were able to bring about the lasting changes needed in the hearts of God’s people–that would await the coming of the Messiah.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Nehemiah lived with an awareness of the transcendence of the God of heaven (1:4, 5; 2:4, 20). He recognized that He is creator and also the God of covenant faithfulness, “great and awesome” (1:5). The extent to which these attributes were generally acknowledged may be seen in the prayer of chapter 9. Both leader and people had a faith that was grounded in acceptance of the revelation of the Pentateuch (1:7, 8; 9:14). Nehemiah is personally an outstanding example of a life in which prayer is the platform for effective action. He fasted and prayed for days before making his concerns known to the Persian king (1:4–11), but based on that habit of extended prayer he was equally ready to engage in momentary prayer at critical junctures in his mission (2:4; 4:4, 5; 6:9). The book of Nehemiah also brings out the importance of formal renewal of covenant commitment as a means of strengthening the community. It is not the people who dictate the terms of the covenant. Rather, in gratitude they rededicate themselves to the Lord and pledge anew to obey His commands. In light of this, there arose in the Judah of Nehemiah’s day a genuine desire to eradicate all false worship from the community. In encouraging and leading the people in the process of rededicating themselves and their nation to God, Nehemiah illustrates the importance of theology for those in leadership.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The events recorded in Nehemiah follow closely those found in Ezra—indeed Ezra himself reappears in 8:1. Though the temple had been rebuilt earlier, Jerusalem remained in ruins, which was out of accord with God’s covenant commitment. But it was not just a matter of restoring city walls; that was only part of the restoration of the cov­enant people through whom God would fulfill His purposes. There also had to be a renewal of their worship (chs. 8–10), repopulation of Jerusalem (chs. 11; 12), and repeated reforms when their conduct deteriorated (ch. 13). Nehemiah, though of a different character from Ezra, was similarly raised up by God to provide faithful leadership for the community in order to guide and motivate the efforts needed to provide for its continuance. Nehemiah is portrayed as a decisive and effective leader. Chapters 8–10 show the people responding in covenant renewal, confessing their past failure, and acknowledging their continuing dependence on God so that they may realize the promises He had made to them. However, the final note of Nehemiah is one of incompleteness. Whatever had been achieved, more needed to be done. The narrative of the past is recounted to stimulate continuing faithfulness.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: In addition to the themes already mentioned in Introduction to Ezra: Christ in Ezra, it is important to consider how Nehemiah ends on a note of anticipation. As the book ends, the temple, priesthood, and sacrifices are all restored, awaiting the High Priest who is to come and offer the final, effectual atonement for sin. This ending inspires the reader to look for the Messiah who perfectly fulfills God’s plan for Israel.

sections.content: See Introduction to Ezra: History of Interpretation.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: Named after its principal character, the book has always been known as “Esther.” A member of the Jewish diaspora community in the Persian capital of Susa around 480 B.C. , Esther was swept up in events beyond her control to become the wife of the emperor. Her royal status enabled her, under God, to intervene and reverse the threatened annihilation of her people. The book is not mentioned or quoted explicitly in the New Testament, but in rabbinic tradition it was, not surprisingly, read at the feast of Purim (see Date and Occasion).

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Although the author of the book of Esther is unknown, his interest in the origin and observance of the festival of Purim, his intense nationalism, and his intimate knowledge of the Persian court, customs, and geography suggest that he was a Persian Jew living in Susa. Mordecai has been suggested as the author, but this cannot be established. Modern suggestions of female authorship are at variance with normal practices of the culture from which the book comes.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The earliest possible date for the book is shortly after the events described in it, that is, the mid-fifth century B.C. The latest possible date is during the first century B.C. A late fifth- or fourth-century dating is now generally preferred by scholars, who point to linguistic evidence as well as the author’s favorable attitude toward the Persian king and Gentiles in general as evidence for an early date. The writer of Esther wrote his book to explain the origin of the celebration of Purim, to establish Purim as a festival celebrated by each new generation of Jews, and to regulate its observance (9:20–32). He also conveyed the message that it was possible for Jews to work within the governmental structures of a heathen empire in such a way that the antagonism of their enemies could, with divine assistance, be thwarted. Moreover, he conveyed that God is able to deliver and protect His people through the providential ordering of circumstances, not just through dramatic miracles.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Is this an historical narrative, skillfully written to bring out certain truths? Or is it pious fiction, intended to set out the same truths? The vast majority of modern scholars favor the latter option even though the book contains no obviously supernatural intervention such as miracles, which is so often used to designate a work as fanciful. There are, however, significant features that point to the historical accuracy of the narrative. For instance, the banquet in Ahasuerus’s (Xerxes’s) third year (1:3) corresponds with the great council in 483 B.C. to plan for the invasion of Greece, as is related by the Greek historian Herodotus. The four-year gap between the banquet of 1:3 and the seventh year of Ahasuerus’s reign when Esther was brought into the royal presence (2:16) corresponds to the time Ahasuerus was off fighting the Greeks (see 2:1 note). The author also reveals an impressive knowledge of the layout of Susa and especially of the palace. Many Persian terms for objects and Persian names are found in the book, and almost all of them are also attested in ancient Persian texts. Difficulties over matters such as the number of provinces in the Persian Empire (1:1) and the lack of external attestation for the existence of Vashti (1:9), Esther, and Mordecai (2:5) are not as significant or insurmountable as they appear to some scholars.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Esther is renowned for the high quality of its literary artistry, which functions as the principal vehicle for its religious meaning. The author skillfully uses narrative tensions created by reversals or sharp contrasts of fortunes and expectations, as well as by roles that are often highly ironic in nature. Notice the two descriptions of banquets held by Ahasuerus and his wife, the first described in full detail and the second presented tersely (1:1–9); the striking contrast between the initial portrait of the king as powerful and pompous (1:1–8) and the subsequent revelation of his incompetence and weakness; the effective contrast between the king’s response when Vashti fails to appear before him and when Esther appears unannounced (1:11–21; 5:1–3); the ironic reversal of Haman’s career (6:4–12); the pathetic scene in which Haman pleads for Esther’s mercy, only to be accused of attempted rape (7:7–9); and the poetic justice of hanging Haman on his own gallows. The last is an example of the ironic reversals in the fortunes and position of Haman and Mordecai (7:9, 10; 8:1, 2; 9:25). Such reversals, when compared with those of the exodus, the Babylonian exile, and even the crucifixion and resurrection, subtly reveal God’s hand in the salvation history of His people. The writer also uses repetition or duplication to weave the various parts of the story together. For example, notice the three references to official records (“chronicles”) located at significant turning points in the narrative (2:23; 6:1; 10:2). There are three sets of paired banquets marking the beginning, middle, and end of the book: the banquets of Ahasuerus (1:3, 4, 5–8), Esther (5:4–8; 7:1–10), and the two celebrations of Purim (9:18–32). See also the banquet theme in 1:9; 2:18; 3:15; 8:17; 9:17; the threefold mention of the size of Ahasuerus’s empire (1:1; 8:9; 9:30); the repeated promise to Esther of “even to the half of my kingdom” (5:3, 6; 7:2; see 9:12); the repeated insistence that the Hebrews did not plunder their enemies (9:10, 15, 16); the two accounts of Esther’s hidden identity (2:10, 20); the double assembling of virgins (2:8, 19); Haman’s two interchanges with his wife and friends (5:10–14; 6:13, 14); the two veilings of Haman’s head (6:12; 7:8); the two references to the subsiding of Ahasuerus’s anger (2:1; 7:10); and the two reminders that the laws of the Medes and Persians cannot be altered (1:19; 8:8). The use of the number seven is noteworthy (1:5, 10, 14), as is Esther’s repeated request and reception of favor (2:9, 15, 17; 5:2, 8; 7:3; 8:9). The literary technique of foreshadowing is also employed in the book. Most striking is the prediction of Haman’s wife that he would “surely fall” because Mordecai was a Jew (6:13). The author is a master of suspense and paces the speed of the narrative well. The constant references to time not only present the events as history (1:1, 2) and underscore the theme of God’s providential working in history but also keep the story moving (e.g., 2:1, 15, 19, 21; 3:1). The writer of Esther creatively builds upon the symbolic or typical aspects of the names of two of the main characters to show how the personal antagonism between Haman, the archenemy of the Jews, and Mordecai, the faithful Jew, was part of the historic conflict between Israel and the Amalekites. This conflict provides the foundation for the plot against all the Jews (2:5 note; 3:1 note). Similarities in phrasing, setting, story line, and emphasis also suggest that the Joseph story was an important model for the writer of Esther (note the similarities between 2:2–4 and Gen. 41:34–37; 3:10; Gen. 41:42; 8:6; and Gen. 44:34).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: A number of important themes are intertwined in the book. The theme of feasting or banquets establishes the setting of the main action of the narrative, culminating with the celebration of Purim and contrasting with the theme of fasting (4:3, 16; 9:31). A contrast of obedience and disobedience also runs through the book. The initial disobedience of Vashti in chapter 1 sets the stage for the challenges facing Esther about obeying Mordecai (2:10, 20; 4:8–16) and standing up against the king’s law (4:11, 16; 5:1, 2). The stage is also set for Mordecai’s refusal to obey Haman’s command and his contrary willingness to carry out Esther’s instructions (4:17) and to serve both the Persian king and the best interests of the Jews (10:3). The theme of providential protection of the Jews, as indicated in 4:14, is basic to the narrative and is a reason for the book’s continuing significance among the community of faith. Related to this theme is that of rest and relief from enemies, which the feast of Purim commemorates (9:16, 22, see Deut. 25:19).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The theology of a book that does not explicitly mention God may seem to be an elusive concept. It is to the credit of the writer that in a low-key fashion, he conveys through the narrative that God is always present with His people, even when His presence is not obvious or acknowledged. The pattern of events he describes can only be explained by the unseen hand of God at work. Most analyses of the literary structure of the book identify chapter 6 as the fulcrum of the story, and that chapter does not focus on either Esther or Mordecai but on a king who, for some reason, cannot get to sleep. If sleep is a gift given by God (Ps. 127:2), is not insomnia a sign that He is at work? Furthermore, in 4:14 Mordecai sets out his belief that there are no coincidences in life. “From another place” points obliquely to God as the source of help and as the one who has brought Esther to the royal position she occupies. The acts of mourning, fasting, and wearing sackcloth in 4:3, 16 are not merely conventional expressions of grief; they embody a belief in God and would be accompanied by prayer. Similarly the indirect passive “had been turned” (9:22) invites the question as to the instrumental agency effecting this change. In these ways and others, the author repeatedly hints at God’s presence behind the incidents described. The narrative also raises the question of how God can be providentially in control of events on earth while individuals such as Haman, intent on genocide, are able to attain a powerful position of influence. The answer has to lie in the fact that our world remains in rebellion against God while He works out His purposes of blessing and judgment in it. “The Lord has made everything for its purpose, even the wicked for the day of trouble” (Prov. 16:4). God may withdraw His restraining hand both to make clear the virulent hostility of evil men and to induce a deeper dependence on Himself among those whose trust is in Him. The need for cultivating such increased reliance and stronger faith is apparent in the compromised stance of Mordecai and Esther at the beginning of the narrative. Unlike Daniel, who adhered to Jewish dietary practices (Dan. 1:8) and made no secret of his allegiance (Dan. 2:28; 6:16), Mordecai and Esther initially concealed their nationality and beliefs because of pressure to assimilate to the surrounding culture. Only the events in which they were caught led them to reveal their background. Finally, the book is a fitting illustration of the ambiguities of divine providence in an era when the Lord is not speaking through his prophets. Israel, in exile, lived in an era of ambiguity. Mordecai and Esther, members of the exilic community, did not enjoy an explicit revelation of the way forward. They and their fellow Jews needed to trust God, and God does meet them in surprising ways as the narrative unfolds. Today, God’s people must often deal with a similar ambiguity. As we wait for the return of Christ, we do not always know the clear way forward when we must make decisions and deal with the unexpected in our lives. We must trust the Lord and follow His revealed will as He works out events in our lives in ways that we do not often anticipate.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The seeming absence of God in Esther does not detract from its contribution to the development of the ongoing message of Scripture. The narrative exemplifies the divinely ordained structure of human history set out in the protoevangelium, the enmity between the two seeds (Gen. 3:15). It focuses on the survival of the people of God at a time when the political power of this world’s empire has the ascendancy, and they themselves are weak and helpless. Furthermore, although God is not named, He is far from absent. Though His people are not to expect visible, overwhelming, miraculous displays of divine power to transform their situation, God remains firmly in control through His providential intervention. He truly governs “all his creatures and all their actions.” In grace, He protects even their faltering witness.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: There are no direct prophecies of Christ in Esther. However, the account of the intervention to protect the community in Esther’s day does serve to stir up a desire for the greatest intervention of all, the coming of the Messiah.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The question of whether the book of Esther belongs in the canon of Scripture was raised early on by both Jews and Christians, though the book’s commendation of the popular festival of Purim argued strongly in favor of its inclusion in the Jewish canon. Objections voiced by some Christians to Esther’s canonicity included its absence from some of the earliest lists of canonical books, its lack of citation in the New Testament, its dearth of overt references to God and to religious practices, its excessive Jewish nationalism, and its spirit of vengeance. Some of these objections were alleviated by the expanded version of the book of Esther found in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament). This Septuagint text contains over one hundred verses not found in the Hebrew text, which made the book more religiously acceptable to some. These additions include a dream of Mordecai about the coming destruction of the Jews and prayers of Mordecai and Esther for deliverance. However, when the Protestant churches judged the shorter Hebrew version of Esther to be the authoritative version, objections to the book’s canonicity resurfaced. The violence in book is a kind of civil war, which Cicero called the worst of all calamities. The author of Esther shows the relief of the people when justice triumphs and does not criticize the means employed, such as the hanging of Haman’s sons. But it would be a mistake to consider these events as models for behavior. The extreme situation and threat under which they happened limits what can be concluded from them. The author does not engage in moral reflection about the massive killing and the motives of the avengers. The reader struggling with some of the questions that arise needs to go to other places such as the prophets, Job, or Revelation, where the discussion includes such questions and answers may be found. Positively, the book of Esther testifies clearly to the invisible hand of providence that will not allow the covenant people to be utterly destroyed.
