sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book is named after its principal character. The linguistic etymology of Job’s name (originally a two-syllable word, i-yob ; Ger. Hiob ) is uncertain (see 1:1), but it is a well-attested form in the second millennium B.C. There seems to be a play on Job’s name; twice he says that God counts him as an enemy ( oyeb ), so the folk etymology would be something like “enemy” or “hostile.”

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The relationship between the opening narrative of the book (the prologue, chs. 1; 2) and the content of Job’s discussions with his friends (the dialogue, chs. 3–27) make clear that Job was not the author. Had Job known what took place in the divine council, there would have been no point to the debate over whether he brought on his sufferings by sinful conduct. Rather, God used a skillful poet from the covenant community to write this remarkable book. The language presents many challenges to the translator because of its poetic grammar and its rich vocabulary. We know that the author was an Israelite since he refers to God by the covenant name Yahweh, while Job and his companions (see 1:1) use such terms as “God” and “the Almighty” (12:9 is the only exception). The probability is that the poet used sources from patriarchal times, including some from Job himself, in composing the book.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: There are two considerations: when the incidents recorded took place, and when the current record was made. There is no precise answer to either. The events date from the patriarchal period and occur in a non-Israelite setting. We cannot specify when the author of Job lived and wrote, but the classical Hebrew of the prologue places him after 1500 B.C. The final form of the book may not have appeared until the era of Solomon or somewhat later, when Hebrew wisdom literature reached its zenith. The references to Job in Ezek. 14:14, 20 and the discovery of fragments from Job among the Dead Sea Scrolls have ruled out attempts to date Job as late as the second century B.C.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Among the wisdom writings of the Old Testament, the book of Job stands with Ecclesiastes as a demonstration of the complexity of both wisdom and living skillfully. It provides another perspective to complement traditional wisdom as it wrestles with the suffering of a righteous individual alongside the affirmation that God is just and good. Sometimes called “retribution theology,” the simplistic version of this traditional or folk wisdom holds that good behavior is always rewarded and bad or immoral behavior is always punished, that the good succeed and the evil do not. Throughout the Wisdom Literature, we see the biblical authors wrestling with the temporal outworking of God’s justice and the question of suffering. Job, in particular, treats the subject with a frankness that is often baffling. The book does not suggest that there is an evil deity or that God’s power is limited. Instead it praises the Creator’s sovereignty, wisdom, and glory. That the God of Job is neither evil nor limited is seen in two portrayals of Job’s relationship with God. The first is taken from the book’s prologue and epilogue. The prologue depicts Job’s submission to the divine will in the midst of suffering. There Job appears as a good man who trusts the goodness of his God. Finally, in the epilogue (42:7–17), God honors his trust by restoring him. The second portrait in the poetic core of the book (chs. 3–42:6) shows Job’s indignation over his plight. He thinks that God has become his enemy and is unjustly afflicting him. Job comes to this conclusion because he knows that God is sovereign. If he believed in a limited deity, he would have no problem with God’s justice or goodness, since then he could not hold God responsible for every event, including his misfortune. The superb literary artistry with which the material in the book is presented is universally acknowledged. Three main classifications have been proposed for the genre of Job: lawsuit, lament, and disputation. Lawsuit is supported by the use of legal language (e.g. 5:8; 13:3; 23:6) and procedures (e.g. ch. 32; 40:7, 8). This analysis focuses on Job as instituting proceedings against God. Initially an informal resolution is sought (chs. 4–14), and when that fails, more formal action is taken (chs. 15–31). After Job’s friends, who have acted as self-appointed advocates for God, fall silent and thereby concede the case, Elihu appeals against their decision (chs. 32–37). However, it takes direct divine intervention before Job withdraws his suit (40:5). Lament analyzes the book on the analogy of the lament psalms (see Introduction to Psalms: Genre). The laments found in chs. 3 and 29–31 support this approach. In Job the lament is presented in dramatic form with the friends’ intervention interpreted as extending comfort to the one in distress. Disputation uses the controversy dialogues recorded in ancient Near Eastern literature to elucidate the framework of Job, which obviously consists of a series of controversial interchanges between wisdom speakers. Their speeches are not primarily dialogue in which opponents’ viewpoints are taken up and answered. That may happen, but the disputation is closer to the presentation of a series of position papers to argue a particular case. However, while each of these interpretations reflects aspects of the book of Job, none provides an exhaustive analysis. Job is a unique and powerful literary creation precisely because it is a skillful blend of various genres. The book’s impact transcends its components.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Compositions similar to the book of Job appear in Mesopotamian and Egyptian sources from Old Testament times. One (“A Dialogue about Human Misery”) is about a counselor who criticizes a sufferer for his impiety while the sufferer struggles over the character of the gods. Furthermore, the literary format of Job is not unique among documents from the ancient Near East, consisting of a prose prologue, a poetic dialogue, and finally a prose epilogue. But there is no other work dealing with the problem of human suffering in light of the transcendence and goodness of God that approaches the theological depth, literary sophistication, and practical application of the book of Job. The author of Job was a literary craftsman and employed many techniques to convey his message. Two features are of special significance: irony and mythological language. Irony occurs in various guises. Verbal irony is a figure of speech in which the intended meaning is the opposite of the literal sense conveyed by the words used (e.g., 12:2). It is also present in God’s questioning of Job (38:4, 5, 18, 21) where there is no doubt as to the answer that has to be given. Irony becomes sarcasm when it is uttered with the intention of distressing or hurting whoever is addressed. More significant in Job is the use of dramatic irony , which occurs when an audience (or readership) knows in advance the outcome of a play (or narrative) while the characters involved do not. There may then be tension between a character’s understanding of his situation and that of the audience/reader. This is achieved in Job by the way in which the poetic dialogues are embedded within a prose framework. The prologue makes clear that Job is innocent of heinous wrongdoing, but this information is not available to his so-called comforters. Such dramatic irony heightens the presentation in various places (e.g., 3:23; 7:12). Language borrowed from ancient Near Eastern mythology is found in various passages throughout the book (e.g., 3:8) but especially in the speeches of Job and of God. However, this use of images and idioms from the surrounding pagan cultural environment does not endorse their polytheistic beliefs regarding natural forces or superhuman entities any more than John Milton’s classical allusions in Paradise Lost indicate an acceptance of Greco-Roman mythology. The linguistic allusions are perhaps more than conventional figures of speech. They may in fact be employed to counter a mythological worldview and to emphasize the absolute supremacy of Yahweh, the covenant Lord of Israel and only true God.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The book’s exploration of the themes associated with God’s purpose in human suffering unfolds as follows. In the prologue we view the God-Job relationship from the divine perspective. God chooses Job to be one of His suffering servants, an instrument through whom to accomplish a spiritual triumph: “Have you considered my servant Job?” (1:8, 2:3). Satan falsely accuses Job of serving God for the sake of material blessings (1:9–11). Job is given the high calling of remaining true to God even when everything is taken away and grim suffering becomes his daily lot. Will Job do as the Adversary predicts and curse God to His face? This is the question that drives the moving drama of the book as Job loses his initial confidence and sinks into despair. If Job remains faithful, God will show through Job that the Adversary is a liar. While the prologue gives us the divine perspective, the central section of speeches presents the human perspective. As a human being Job is ignorant of what took place in the divine council. He struggles with a traditional view that all suffering is an immediate punishment of human sins, a simplistic retribution theology that is a perversion of Proverbs. Job’s counselors, like many others, consider the depth of Job’s suffering to be adequate evidence that his sin is great (see John 9:2). As Job confronts the heartless counselors used by Satan to accuse him falsely, he says things for which he must later repent (42:5, 6). He knows the counselors are wrong, but he cannot understand how a pious person should suffer so much when the godless enjoy prosperity and health (12:6). Like the psalmists, Job often complains to God in the language of legal disputes. Some of what Job says shocks his friends. While they say all the right things about God, they never say anything to Him. Job wrestles with God and tells Him every doubt and fear. His is a living relationship with God, while theirs consists of dead aphorisms. It is not so much what they say as how they apply it to Job that shows the arrogance of insisting that they know why Job is suffering. They are insensitive (13:4, 5; 16:2; 19:21) as well as shallow and presumptuous regarding divine things. Job has been falsely accused; he is not suffering for his sins, though he cannot avoid wondering about this. But even though he imagines God is angry with him, in his better moments he still believes God is just and will provide a redeemer (16:19–21; 19:23–27). This hope becomes a reality when Job finally has the face-to-face audience with God that he requested (13:15–18; 31:35–37). When God appears in the storm (chs. 38–41), Job is not rebuked as one suffering for his sins but is humbled before the Lord as one whose ill-advised speech had obscured God’s purpose (38:2; 42:2, 3). God reveals Himself as Job’s friend, bringing him before the astonishing works of creation to show him that the one he has reproached is sovereign in goodness and power. Job recognizes that God is and remains his friend. When his eyes have seen the Lord, and he has repented in dust and ashes, Job has come to understand that God on His throne is sovereign, and He rewards those who belong to Him despite times of pressure and pain. The reader learns that Job suffered, not because he was one of the worst of men but because he was one of the best, and that his ordeal glorified his God.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: From earliest times it has been evident that the Lord is “the Judge of all the earth” who does what is just (Gen. 18:25). God cannot condone human sin, and Job and his counselors agree that the wicked will receive punishment from on high. At its simplest, the retribution principle states the scriptural truth that God punishes the wicked and rewards the faithful (see Prov. 11:21; Gal. 6:7, 9). But an orthodox retribution principle does not specify when, or how speedily, God will act. Moreover, it is to go beyond the teaching of Scripture to employ the retribution principle in reverse and make the simplistic conclusion that those who at present experience great misfortune or affliction are thereby proven to be great sinners (see Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3). This, however, is the logic that Job’s counselors employ: they witness his intense agony, and their theology leads them to infer that Job greatly sinned. These wisdom teachers overextend the applicability of the retribution principle so as to have a theology with no loose ends. For them, suffering is punishment or chastisement. They see no place for innocent suffering, which would attribute unworthiness to God for allowing it to happen. They are determined to defend God, and they do utter many high sentiments regarding Him. What they say, however, is dismissive and condescending as regards Job. They cannot (or will not) grasp the nature of his predicament. Moreover, their approach binds God to their understanding of the world and leaves no room for grace. Against the conclusions of his friends, Job solemnly and repeatedly protests, but he can no more explain his situation than his friends can, for they all share the same basic presuppositions. Job never doubts the existence of God, and he remains convinced that God is just. But he cannot reconcile that with what was happening to him. Even so, Job differs from the counselors in that he has no doubts about his personal integrity. Consequently, he is led to question the adequacy of God’s administration of justice (see 9:21–24; 12:4–6; 24:12; 40:8). To ask why there is unmerited suffering is not wrong, but to demand that God provide an explanation for all that He does is. God’s ways are more complex than human understanding. Human beings must take care not to challenge God’s sovereignty or assume that their finite discernment is greater than it really is.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Job’s setting in the patriarchal world reminds us that the tensions and agonies of human existence stretch back to the earliest times. Though the world is still divinely controlled, it is no long­er the world it was originally intended to be. Anomalies and enigmas abound through the presence of sin and the (divinely limited) activities of Satan. The book does not seek to explain how these factors interact and contribute to the progress of the divine plan of redemption. Instead, it focuses on exploring how to live faithfully through dark hours of suffering, weakness, and trial. The advice and encouragement it gives in this regard remain a priceless legacy until the consummation.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: In the midst of Job’s struggle to understand God’s providence in his life, he becomes aware of his need of a mediatorial figure, a redeemer, to stand between God and himself (see 16:19–21; 19:25–27; 33:23). Even so, it does not appear that Job ever becomes aware of how his deeply felt longing will finally be realized. That realization, of course, is found only in Christ. In one aspect of his experience, however, Job does foreshadow Christ. He is an innocent sufferer caught up in the tension and enmity of the struggle between the forces of good and evil. He cries out to God in his desolation and is exposed to the bewildering dereliction of receiving no reply (see Ps. 22:1, 2). But through that darkness he comes to know God in a fuller and more intimate fashion. Might it not in measure be said of Job, as our Lord said of Abraham, that he rejoiced to see Christ’s day? “He saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The church has often emphasized only the message of the prologue and epilogue because it is easier to understand than the dialogues. The reference of James 5:11 to the “steadfastness” of Job is not based on a shallow interpretation that ignores the central section of dialogues. James does not stress Job’s passivity but his perseverance and, with it, God’s compassion and mercy in accomplishing His purposes. God’s purpose in Job’s suffering is the key to understanding the seeming discrepancy between the tranquil Job of the prologue (chs. 1; 2) and the raging Job of the central section. God’s purpose is complex, involving more than one question of faith. Over the centuries there has been ongoing fascination with the enigmas of human life and suffering as portrayed in Job. Many commentators have contributed significantly to our understanding of this complex work—none more so than John Calvin, who preached 159 sermons on the book. But none has exhausted the analysis of Job, and what is said often closely reflects the presuppositions that the generation represented by the expositor brings to this complex text.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The title “Psalms” comes from the Greek and Latin tradition. The Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses the word Psalmos, and the Latin Vulgate translation, which was the Bible the church used during the Middle Ages, uses the word Psalmus . Both of these terms mean “a song sung to the accompaniment of stringed instruments.” The New Testament uses psalmos as well (Luke 20:42; 24:44; Acts 1:20). The corresponding Hb. word mizmor occurs frequently in the title of various psalms (e.g., Ps. 3). The Hebrew title, however, is “Praises,” a translation of the Hb. word tehillah (“praise”), and this title captures the overarching movement in the book from lamentation and suffering at the beginning to praise and glory at the end.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Many of the psalms begin with a title linking the psalm with a particular individual or group, using a Hb. preposition that could possibly indicate dedication (“to David”), subject matter (“about David”), or authorship (“by David”). However, one of the few psalm titles with expanded content (Ps. 18) leaves little doubt that the title intends to identify the composer of the psalm. David is by far the most frequently cited author, most of his psalms being in the first two books (see Structure), though there is a small collection of psalms by him at the very end (Pss. 138–145). The tradition that associates David with singing and psalm composition is so strong (1 Sam. 16:14–23; 2 Sam. 1:17–27; 2 Sam. 22; 2 Sam. 23:1; 1 Chr. 6:31; 15:16; 16:7; Ps. 18; Amos 6:5; Matt. 22:43; Acts 1:16) that there is little doubt that David wrote many or all of the psalms that bear his name. Other authors appear in psalm titles: Moses (Ps. 90), Solomon (Pss. 72; 127), the sons of Korah (Pss. 42–49; 84; 85; 87; 88), Asaph (Pss. 50; 73–83), and Ethan the Ezrahite (Ps. 89). A number of psalms have no designated author (e.g., Pss. 1; 71).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The titles of the psalms show that they were composed by individuals in response to particular corporate or individual experiences. The dates and occasions of the psalms (see the introductory paragraphs to the psalms in the notes) range from the time of Moses (Ps. 90), to the experiences of David (Ps. 51), to the time after the Babylonian exile (Ps. 126), a span of approximately one thousand years. Still, the psalms that originated in specific situations and were collected for use in private devotion or public worship were never so time-bound that they could not be used in a variety of new situations. Forming the collection as a whole took several centuries, and was not completed until sometime after the exile in Babylon. The entire collection is also known as the Psalter.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The broadest genre consideration is that the book of Psalms is poetry, not prose. For additional discussion of the poetic character of Psalms, see the Introduction to Hebrew Poetry. Distinguishing characteristics allow the individual psalms to be assigned to literary categories for the purpose of study. These categories are not to be seen as mutually exclusive but as perspectives from which to gain insight into the various psalms. The following are the literary categories commonly used in the book of Psalms. 1. Hymns. Hymns were composed for times when all is well. Hymns are easily recognized by their exuberant praise of the Lord, and they typically praise the Lord for who He is as the Creator (e.g., Ps. 104) and Redeemer (e.g., Ps. 105). Hymns usually have three sections: a call to praise God, the praise proper, and a concluding affirmation of faith or renewed call to praise. Psalm 103 is a good example of this structure: Call to Praise (vv. 1, 2), Praise (vv. 3–19), and Call to Praise (vv. 20–22). For other examples of hymns, see Pss. 8; 19; 29; 33; 65; 67; 68; 93; 96; 98; 100; 111; 113; 114; 117; 135; 145; 146; 147; 148; 149; 150. 2. Laments. Laments were composed for when all is not well, and thus express emotions experienced in times of great sorrow or loss. In a lament, the psalmist opens his heart honestly to God, a heart filled with sadness, loneliness, perplexity, grief, abandonment, fear, or anger. With few exceptions (Pss. 44; 88) the laments turn to the Lord with confidence at the end. Laments usually have two sections: the plea for help followed by confidence or praise. Psalm 6 is a fine example: Plea for Help (vv. 1–7) and Confidence in Being Delivered (vv. 8, 9). For other examples, see Pss. 3; 5; 7; 13; 17; 22; 25; 26; 27; 28; 38; 39; 42; 43; 51; 54; 55; 56; 57; 59; 61; 63; 64; 69; 70; 71; 74; 79; 80; 83; 86; 89; 102; 109; 120; 130; 140; 141; 142; 143. 3. Thanksgiving Psalms. Psalms of thanksgiving are like hymns in that they focus on the praise of God. The difference is that the hymns focus on what God has done in the distant past, in creation or in redemptive history, while the psalms of thanksgiving focus on what God has done in the recent, personal history of the psalmist. In particular, psalms of thanksgiving were written to celebrate those times when the Lord answered a prayer of lament. Like the hymns, the thanksgiving psalms usually have three sections: an opening intention to give thanks, a recollection of trouble (often mirroring the structure and language of the lament), and a concluding renewal of thanksgiving. Psalm 116 is probably the most personal example: Thanksgiving and Love (vv. 1–3), Recollection of Trouble (vv. 3–11), and Thanksgiving and Praise (vv. 12–19). For other examples, see Pss. 18; 30; 34; 40; 41; 66; 92; 118; 124; 138. 4. Psalms of Confidence (or Trust). In between the laments and the psalms of thanksgiving are the psalms of confidence. There is typically some sort of trouble in view in these psalms, but the anguish is not as intense as in the laments, and the psalmist is not yet completely out of trouble. The dominant mood of these psalms is confidence that the Lord will deliver the psalmist. Unlike the first three genres, the psalms of confidence apparently have no common structure. For examples, see Pss. 16; 23; 27; 62; 73; 91; 115; 121; 125; 131. 5. Kingship Psalms. Since God, the King of the universe, is the subject of many psalms and since David, the human king, is the subject of many other psalms, kingship is an important concept in the Psalter (see Characteristics and Primary Themes). A few psalms, however, focus so intensely on divine kingship (Ps. 47) or on human kingship (Ps. 45) that they stand out as a separate genre. Lacking any formal structure, the kingship psalms are held together by themes such as creation, redemption, judgment, supremacy over idols, and universal care. For examples of divine kingship psalms, see Pss. 24; 29; 47; 48; 93; 95; 96; 97; 98; 99; 145; and for examples of human kingship psalms, see Pss. 2; 20; 21; 45; 61; 63; 72. 6. Wisdom Psalms. Some psalms are at home in the world of Proverbs, Job, and Ecclesiastes. There is a certain diction that these psalms share with the other wisdom books: pronouncements of blessing, numerical sayings, “better than” sayings, alphabetic structuring, and admonitions. The wisdom psalms also make use of themes found in the Wisdom Literature: the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked, the contrast between the wise and the foolish, practical advice, retribution, and the fear of the Lord. The convergence of wisdom’s diction and wisdom’s themes suffices to place certain psalms in this category. For examples, see Pss. 1; 19; 32; 34; 37; 49; 73; 112; 119; 128.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The psalms are arranged in five books. The end of each book is marked by doxology (Pss. 1–41; 42–72; 73–89; 90–106; 107–150). Jewish tradition holds that the number five was chosen to match the five books of Moses, and this is certainly the case. Both the five books of Moses and the five books of the Psalms are torah (instruction) from the Lord (Ps. 1:2). Book 1 begins with the inauguration of the Davidic covenant (Ps. 2) and ends with the promises of Ps. 2 coming to realization (Ps. 41). Book 2 ends with the covenant of kingship being transferred to Solomon (Ps. 72), who is a type of the blessed man of Ps. 1 (see the imagery in Ps. 72:5–7) and a type of the Messianic King of Ps. 2 (see the language in Ps. 72:8–11). Book 3 then ends on an ominous note. The first psalm of the section complains that the righteous suffer. The last psalm of the section laments that the Davidic covenant seems to have failed, with the king’s crown rolling in the dust (Ps. 89). Ps. 88 is the only psalm without praise. The remaining books answer the question burning in the hearts and minds of the postexilic community: “How do we live in the absence of the Davidic king?” Book 4 replies that we live by faith that the Lord is still King in spite of evidence to the contrary. Within this book, Pss. 93–99, called “enthronement psalms,” look to God’s reign on earth. Book 5 replies that we live with an obedience (Ps. 119) that focuses on the true worship of God (Ps. 145–150). It begins by thanking God for bringing Israel back from the exile, and includes psalms holding up David as a model for piety (138–145), as well as psalms predicting the reign of the Messiah (110).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Psalms 1 and 2 introduce us to the main themes of the book of Psalms: the life of holiness and happiness (Ps. 1) under the reign of the divine King and His Messiah (Ps. 2). Psalm 1 gives us the purpose of the book of Psalms: to provide a manual for meditating on the instruction of the Lord, so that we can experience the “blessed” life, a life of abundant holiness and happiness. Psalm 2 gives us the overarching message of the book of Psalms: the Divine King reigns through His Messiah, who comes from the line of David. In fact, concerns related to the Davidic king are so prevalent in the Psalter that the book of Psalms in many ways functions as the hymnbook of the king. In the ancient Near East, the king was a key figure in worship, leading the people in the praise and worship of their deities. The king of Israel, of course, stands out among the other kings in the region as a worshiper of the only true God, the representative of God’s people before the divine throne. Thus, the book of Psalms has special importance for the sons of David and, preeminently, David’s greatest son—the Messiah. It is no accident, therefore, that the New Testament authors extensively quote from the book of Psalms, even indicating that they belong on the lips of Jesus in a special way (e.g., Heb. 2:10–13; 10:5–7). Since the Davidic king had a key role in worship, we also see that the book of Psalms is designed specifically for liturgical use. Many of them, in fact, call on the people of God to worship the Lord (e.g., Pss. 95:6; 132:7). Consequently, the psalms have been treasured by God’s people for use in His worship down through the centuries.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Just as the Psalter was formed during the entire period of the Old Testament, so the theology of the psalms is as large as the Old Testament. Martin Luther called the Psalms “a little Bible, and the summary of the Old Testament.” The overarching presentation of God in the book of Psalms is God as King. Two corollaries to God as King in the Psalms are God as Creator and God as Redeemer. God’s transcendence and his immanence, along with virtually all of his other attributes, run like golden threads through the entire Psalter. Therefore, the book of Psalms gives us one of the most complete and comprehensive revelations of the character of God in the entire Bible. If we want to know who God is, what He has done, and how we should respond to Him, the book of Psalms is one of the best places to start.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The book of Psalms was in all likelihood completed during the postexilic era and was compiled among other reasons to answer the question: “How do we live in the absence of the Davidic King?” (see Literary Features). As such, the book of Psalms served to give hope to God’s people that the Messiah would one day come, a hope that is realized finally in Christ and the consummation of His reign, as revealed in the New Testament. As we await the return of Christ, believers today are somewhat like believers who are seeking to understand how we are to live in the physical absence of the Davidic king, though we know that even now, Christ rules as the King of kings by His Spirit in the church and over all creation as the Creator and Lord of all. Like the Jews before the incarnation, we await the coming of the Messiah, only this time we are looking for His second coming, and the book of Psalms still serves to encourage that hope.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Christian readers of the Psalms appreciate the relationship these ancient songs have to Jesus Christ. Jesus told His disciples after the resurrection that “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). The Old Testament, including the Psalms, looked forward to Christ’s coming, His suffering, and His glorification. Jesus and the New Testament writers use the Psalms to express His suffering (Matt. 27:46) and His glorification (Matt. 22:41–46), in keeping with the overarching movement of the Psalter (see Title). Often, individual psalms begin with the reflection of David on his life or on events in his life and them move to David’s greatest son, the Messiah to come, such as Pss. 2 and 110. Psalm 23 points the reader directly to Christ, the Good Shepherd who gave His life for His sheep (cf. John 10:11–18). In addition, since Jesus is Lord of the covenant, the Psalms are sung to Him, and since Jesus is Servant of the covenant, the psalms are sung by Him. Jesus is therefore above us as the One to whom we sing, and Jesus is beside us as the One who sings with us in all of life’s experiences (Heb. 2:12).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Traditionally, a psalm was interpreted in its presumed historical context from the books of Samuel and Kings. One problem with this approach is that only fourteen psalms contain historical information in the title. A second problem is that some of the historical information in the titles is problematic (see Special Issues). So this approach is only partially helpful. At the end of the nineteenth century, there was a move to study a given psalm in the context of other psalms from the same genre. This approach remains an integral part of interpreting the book of Psalms to this day. In the mid-1980s, the book of Psalms began to be studied not as a random collection of poems but as a purposely arranged collection. This means that a given psalm is to be interpreted in the context of the surrounding psalms as well as in the context of its genre.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The Curses of the Psalms. Some psalms, called imprecatory psalms, cry out not only for the righteous to be vindicated, but also for God to punish the wicked (e.g., Ps. 69:22–28). Such prayers reflect the calling of Israel to holy war as God’s instruments of judgment. With the coming of Christ to bear God’s judgment, the warfare of God’s people continues, now primarily directed against “spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12). In their warfare, Christians are commanded to bless their personal enemies, overcoming evil with good (Rom. 12:17–21). Theologians are divided over whether there might be circumstances under which Christians may pray the imprecatory psalms against the church’s enemies in the new covenant era. If there is a place for such prayers, two things must be kept in mind: First, as under the old covenant, the imprecatory psalms are not for use against just any enemy who causes problems for God’s people; rather, they are for enemies who are flagrantly and impenitently evil in their actions against Christ’s church. Second, in praying imprecatory psalms, space must always be allowed for the Lord to answer them by redeeming our enemies through judgment, just as He has done for us. Christ bore the imprecations that were rightly directed at us as the enemies of God, and so we passed through judgment in Him unto eternal life. God may do the same for our enemies, uniting them to Christ so that He bears the imprecations in their place, granting them the gift of eternal life (cf. Gal. 3:10–14). Titles. Scholars have long debated whether the titles of the various psalms were written by the authors of the psalms themselves or if they are later additions. The titles are either an original part of the psalms or they come from early tradition, and were added before the final canonical form of the book was completed before the Septuagint translation of 200 B.C. Although the debate continues, evidence such as the appearance of the same information in the title to Psalm 18 and in 2 Samuel 22:1 means that the titles should be taken as original to the psalms and thus contain critical information about their original setting. In other words, the life settings described in the psalm titles are accurate and reflect the historical circumstances under which they were written. The titles contain five types of information: 1. Authorship. See the discussion at Author above. 2. Historical Background. Fourteen psalms have historical information in the title (Pss. 3; 7; 18; 30; 34; 51; 52; 54; 56; 57; 59; 60; 63; 142). There are a some places where it is either hard to match the content of the title with the content of the psalm (e.g., Ps. 30) or to match the content of the title and the psalm with the historical narrative (e.g., Ps. 3 and 2 Sam. 18:5). While the historical titles may give us an indication of the origin of a psalm, they are of limited help in interpretation; see History of Interpretation above. 3. Genre. A number of the terms in the titles classify the psalms into ancient genres. Some are frequent, e.g, mizmor (“psalm”) and shir (“song”), while others are rare. It is difficult, however, to know the precise meaning of the terms used, and some psalms are both a mizmor and a shir (Pss. 30; 66; 67; 68; 75; 83; 87; 88). In contemporary discussions, genre is discerned from the structure and content of the psalms and not from the titles. 4. Musical Direction. Some musical notes refer to instruments, e.g., “flutes” (Ps. 5) and “stringed instruments” (Ps. 6). The meaning of other musical notes is obscure, which is why translators transcribe the Hebrew terms, e.g., “Sheminith” (Ps. 6) and “Shiggaion” (Ps. 7); the same holds true for the ubiquitous “ selah ” (Ps. 3:2). 5. Instructions. Occasionally, the titles indicate how the psalms were used in formal worship. Of these, the best known are the “Songs of Ascents.”

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: Very few books in the OT have their title included in the canonical text. Proverbs is one of them, as the first verse is the title to the book: “The Proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.” The title of the book in English, Proverbs, reflects just the first word of the Hebrew title. (For more details, see the notes at Prov. 1:1.)

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings from a number of authors. Solomon’s name appears in 1:1; 10:1; 25:1. Proverbs 22:17–24:22 and 24:23–34 are attributed to “the wise.” Chapter 30 is attributed to Agur. Proverbs 31:1–9 is attributed to Lem­uel, while Prov. 31:10–31 is anonymous. That Solomon was a key figure in the wisdom movement, and wrote and collected many proverbs, is clear from 1 Kin. 4:29–34. Solomon’s general influence on the book of Proverbs is considerable, and his direct authorship of much of the material need not be doubted. The statement in 1:1 (“The proverbs of Solomon”) cannot be taken to assert the Solomonic authorship of all of the content, as the above non-Solomonic collections make clear, nor even final the compilation of the whole, since 25:1–29:27 was not compiled until the reign of Hezekiah, some two hundred years after Solomon. The statement in 1:1 need not be taken to assert anything more than the quintessential role played by Solomon in the wisdom tradition. The Solomonic title may refer as much to the stamp of Solomon’s character on the OT Wisdom Literature as to its direct authorship of some of the material. While it is obvious that he did not write the whole book as we have it, 1:1–7 indicates that this is no haphazard collection but a purposeful construction with clear aims.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Given that Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings from various authors working at various times, one must distinguish the dating of particular sayings from the dating of the completed book. The earliest sayings would come from the tenth century B.C. (Solomon), while the book as a whole could not have been completed before the days of Hezekiah (c. 715–686 B.C. ; cf. Prov. 25:1) and could have been completed as late as the days of Ezra (c. 400 B.C. ), though they may reflect much earlier thought that was preserved through oral tradition. This general conclusion is supported by the fact that that there are similar ancient Near Eastern collections of wisdom that predate Solomon and by the fact that wisdom collections completed after Ezra, such as Sirach (second century B.C. ) and The Wisdom of Solomon (first century B.C. ), show some significant differences from the wisdom in Proverbs.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The broadest genre consideration is that Proverbs is poetry, not prose. For additional discussion of the poetic character of Proverbs, see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry and Introduction to Wisdom Literature. The Book of Proverbs displays several forms of wisdom writing. In chs. 1–9, there are a number of longer poems that are similar to the “instruction” form of some early Egyptian literature. Some relationship in form and content between Israelite and non-Israelite wisdom should not surprise us given the common concerns of wisdom in all cultures. Whether the instruction form was used in schools for the elite (as in Egypt) or in the home (as was probably the case in Israel), the content is wisdom for life as it was taught to young people by their elders. The instruction generally begins with an address (“my son”) coupled with an initial motivation, followed by a lesson and then a conclusion that may include the consequences of heeding or not heeding the lesson. Another major form in Proverbs is the short saying, found mainly in 10:1–22:16 and 25:1–29:27. These sayings are frequently given in a parallel form, in which the second line makes a direct contrast with the first, or in which the second line carries forward the idea contained in the first. The contrasting parallel is typically used to compare wisdom with folly and righteousness with wickedness. A third form is the numerical saying (6:16–19; 30:15, 16, 18, 19), which appears to promote the perception of order in the world in the face of complex issues and experiences of life. The numerical sequence also seems to provide a general framework for listing specific teachings and to add rhetorical power to the teachings. Proverbs 2 provides an example of a sophisticated acrostic poem. The first eleven verses are governed by aleph , the first letter of the first half of the Hebrew alphabet, while vv. 12–22 are governed by lamed, the first letter of the second half of the Hebrew alphabet (2:1–22 note).

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The literary structure of the book of Proverbs reveals its overall function and message. The prologue (Prov. 1:1–7) makes clear that the overall purpose of the book of Proverbs is the gaining of wisdom. Prov. 1:8–9:18 sets before the reader two journeys, with two different destinations (see also Ps. 1 and the contrast of the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked). These two ways of living are personified as Wisdom and Folly. Will the reader embrace Woman Wisdom or Woman Folly? Since Woman Wisdom is a metaphor for God’s own wisdom, the choice is ultimately between the true, living God and idols. Once one makes the choice for Woman Wisdom, one can move on to Prov. 10:1–31:9, chapters which give specific instruction on how to live out a life of faith with Woman Wisdom. The book comes to a conclusion by setting forth a portrait of Woman Wisdom in all of her exquisite beauty (Prov. 31:10–31).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The two primary themes of the book of Proverbs are wisdom and the fear of the Lord. In short, wisdom is the skill to survive and thrive by living in accordance with the order that God has established in his world. The fear of the Lord is living in accordance with the principles manifest in His Word and world because we stand in awe of Him and trust Him as our God. For more on these themes, see Introduction to the Wisdom Literature. There are many other themes in the book of Proverbs, including how to use speech in a way that benefits and does not harm, how to handle one’s sexual drive, how to be industrious and enjoy the benefits of labor, how to avoid sloth and poverty, how to relate well to both God and neighbor, how to love the right woman, and how to think about life and death. While some of these themes are addressed in more extended poems, many of them are addressed in short proverbs scattered throughout the book. So, while there is always benefit in reading the chapters in Proverbs sequentially, there is also benefit in collecting proverbs on a given theme that are scattered throughout the book, making it possible to study all that the book of Proverbs has to say on a particular topic. This is especially helpful in regard to chapters 10–31. As an example, consider a brief look at one theme: beneficial words. First, beneficial words benefit others. “The mouth of the righteous is a fountain of life, but the mouth of the wicked conceals violence” (10:11); well-spoken and timely words do no harm to others but enhance their quality of life. “A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it breaks the spirit” (15:4); well-spoken and timely words sustain the spirit of others in times of adversity. Second, beneficial words also benefit oneself. “From the fruit of his mouth a man is satisfied with good, and the work of a man’s hand comes back to him” (12:14); the words one speaks can bring one as much benefit as the work one does. These topical studies are beneficial to living skillfully, and are especially helpful when approached through the lens of the way of wisdom in chapters 1–9.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Because the book of Proverbs is often thought of as a practical manual for wise living, the work does not usually come to mind immediately when one thinks of where to turn in the OT for teaching about God. While the book is a practical manual, the practicality is rooted in rich biblical theology. The fact that God’s covenant name (Hb. YHWH ) occurs eighty-seven times in the book of Proverbs leads us to perceive that here we find a rich repository for teaching about God and our relationship with Him. At the heart of the book of Proverbs is the doctrine of God as Creator (3:19–20; 8:22–31; 20:12; 22:2). As Creator, God is in control of His creation (16:4, 9, 33; 19:21). While His holiness is not taught explicitly, the holiness of God is assumed as the foundation of the moral code contained in the book of Proverbs (3:7; 14:2; 16:6; 21:3). As a holy God, He is also just (11:1; 16:11; 29:26). The sovereign, holy, just Creator is knowable (2:5; 9:10), because He has chosen to reveal himself (2:6; see Job 28), and those who know Him find Him to be completely trustworthy (3:5; 16:20; 22:19; 28:5; 29:25). Far from being a distant God, the Lord is close enough to hear the prayers of those who trust Him (15:8, 29). Above all, the theology of Proverbs is practical theology. God has established His covenant with His people, and the book of Proverbs offers instruction on how to live in this world in light of the covenant. It teaches us how to live as the people of God

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In the Hebrew Bible, the book of Proverbs is preceded by the Law (Genesis–Deuteronomy) and the Prophets (the Former Prophets: Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings; the Latter Prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the Twelve Minor Prophets). The Law sets forth the foundational principles of the covenant and the ideal life to be experienced by following the principles of the covenant. The Former Prophets show the failure of the covenant people to experience this ideal in history. The Latter Prophets provide divine interpretation of this failure in history. The book of Proverbs is in the third and final section of the Hebrew Bible, the Writings. The overall function of this section is to teach the covenant community how to live out the ideals set forth in the Law but not experienced in the Prophets. One implication of reading the book of Proverbs in this context is to realize that while it does not contain explicit teaching on redemptive history, its position within that history is presumed. Among other things, this means that the principles taught in the book of Proverbs are to be lived out not as legalistic rules but as a response to God’s redemptive work in the past on behalf of the community. For new covenant believers, this means that we strive to live out the principles in the book of Proverbs as our response to God’s grace to us in the redemptive work of Jesus Christ. James is sometimes called the New Testament version of Proverbs. How believers should read James is a good model for how believers should read Proverbs and the other Wisdom Literature books. See Introduction to James.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The New Testament understands Jesus Christ to be the culmination of the Old Testament wisdom tradition in a number of ways. First, Jesus is the consummate wise person. In Luke 2:52 we read that “Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man,” which is a clear allusion to Proverbs 3:4, which promises that the wise person “will find favor and good success in the sight of God and man.” Second, Jesus is the consummate wisdom teacher. Mark 1:22 tells us that people “were astonished at his teaching, and Mark 6:2 indicates that “many who heard him were astonished, saying, ‘where did this man get these things? What is the wisdom given to him?’” Third, and much more radically, according to the New Testament, Jesus Christ is the incarnation of God’s wisdom (1 Cor. 1:24, 30; Col. 2:2, 3). The call of Prov. 1–9 to embrace wisdom is thus ultimately a call to embrace Jesus Christ. Meanwhile, the specific instructions on how to live out our life with wisdom in Prov. 10–31 are our instructions on how to live out our life of faith in Jesus Christ. Because we have embraced Christ and are in Christ, we possess the mind of Christ, and the Holy Spirit empowers us to become increasingly wise (1 Cor. 1:30; 2:16). The book of Proverbs must be read not as a series of legalistic principles but as a revelation of the grace of God in Christ and our response to that grace.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Though not traditionally emphasized as a significant source of Reformed doctrine, the book of Proverbs does have a certain pride of place in the Reformed tradition, especially that of the English Reformation. Matthew Poole (1624–1679), Matthew Henry (1662–1714), and Charles Bridges (1794–1869), for example, extolled the book of Proverbs as a practical guide to godly living and wrote commentaries on the book that are still in use today. Jonathan Edwards (1703–1758) not only used the book of Proverbs in his own meditation and self-examination, but he also preached from it extensively.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The title of Ecclesiastes in the Hebrew tradition is Qohelet , a transliteration of the second word in the Hebrew text. The Hb. word qohelet means “gatherer,” and can refer to the act of gathering proverbs (12:9) or gathering people to teach them (Ex. 35:1). Originally a title (like “the baker”; see the use with the definite article in 12:8), Qohelet became a name (like “Baker;” see the use without the definite article in 1:1, 2, 12; 12:9, 10). Qohelet is often translated into English as “Preacher” or “Teacher.” This tradition goes back to Martin Luther, whose title for the book in German is Prediger (“Preacher”). The use of “Ecclesiastes” goes back to Ecclesiastae in the Latin Vulgate, which is dependent upon Ecclesiastes (“a member of the assembly”) in the Greek Septuagint. The majority of the occurrences of qohelet in the book of Ecclesiastes use the word as a name, but the introduction and study notes will use “the Preacher” or “the Teacher.”

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: For many interpreters of Ecclesiastes, the lineage (1:1), kingship over Israel in Jerusalem (1:12), unsurpassed wisdom (1:16), and unrivaled wealth (2:4–9) of the author indicate that Solomon, calling himself “the Preacher” (1:12), is the author of Ecclesiastes. There is also a concluding tribute in the book (12:9–14) that praises the Preacher’s wisdom in a way that reminds the reader of Solomon’s wisdom. Other interpreters, however, believe that the style of the Hebrew used in the book, as well as what they see as the negative view of rulers that seems to show itself at times in Ecclesiastes (4:13; 7:19; 8:2–4; 10:4–7), indicate that the work was written after Solomon’s time as a legitimate voice of the wisdom tradition that has Solomon as its most famous exponent, and was, therefore, associated with his name. Since Solomon is never explicitly named as the author, it is difficult to be dogmatic on this issue. Good scholars have differed on this. Moreover, our understanding of the message of the book does not depend on knowing with certainty who wrote it.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Those who see the book as coming from a writer later than Solomon generally date Ecclesiastes after the Jewish exile in Babylon, which occurred in the sixth century B.C. If Solomon was the author, the book is to be dated from the tenth century B.C. Ecclesiastes has been understood as an apologetic work, an attempt to recommend faith in God to unbelievers by way of answering negative arguments. While the book’s teaching may be used in evangelism, most Jewish and Christian interpreters have understood Ecclesiastes to be addressed to God’s people, rather than to those who are ignorant of God or in rebellion against Him. The book is God’s wise counsel to those who know His ways but have found them at times to be frustrating and perplexing.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The majority of the book, the central monologue (1:12–12:7), is an autobiography by the Preacher. In this section, he repeatedly refers to himself in the first person (e.g., 1:12; 10:5). This central monologue is surrounded by a prologue (1:1–11) and an epilogue (12:8–14) in which the Preacher is repeatedly referred to in the third person (e.g., 1:1, 2; 12:8). The narrator, the author of the prologue and epilogue, introduces the Preacher’s thought in the prologue, illustrates the Preacher’s thought with the Preacher’s own words in the monologue, and then supplements the Preacher’s thought in the epilogue. So, we could refer to Ecclesiastes as narrated autobiography.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Ecclesiastes is a mixture of poetry and prose, but it is not always easy to determine where the poetry ends and where the prose begins, and vice versa. Some texts are clearly poetry. E.g., the ESV and many other translations concur in translating 8:1 in poetic style. At the same time, some texts are clearly prose. Many translations, including the ESV, render 2:1 in prose style. Other texts, however, appear as prose in some translations and poetry in others (e.g., 1:2; 2:10–16). Like several translations, the ESV on the whole lays out much of the text as prose, but other English versions render more of the text as poetry. At the end of the day, the varying opinions of translators show that Hebrew prose and poetry are different points on a literary continuum, and much of Ecclesiastes is on the border between prose and poetry. For more on interpreting the poetry of Ecclesiastes, see Introduction to Hebrew Poetry.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Ecclesiastes contains three overarching themes: (1) facing the frustrating/ perplexing side of life; (2) finding joy and satisfaction in life; and (3) fearing God throughout all of life. But before looking at these themes, it is important to understand two foundational concepts: (1) “vanity” and (2) “under the sun.” The Hb. word translated “vanity” ( hebel ) occurs thirty-eight times in the book of Ecclesiastes and is thus a key term for understanding the book. There is no single English term that captures the meaning of Hb. hebel . On the one hand, hebel refers to that which is frustrating. The frustration of life is articulated in the opening poem (1:3–11). The poem begins with a question, “What does a man gain by all his toil at which he toils under the sun?” The illustrations that follow answer the question with a resounding “nothing.” One labors to earn or accomplish something, not nothing; thus, to get nothing as a result of one’s labor is frustrating. The frustrating side of life is also articulated in the image of chasing after the wind, an image used frequently in the book (1:14, 17; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6, 16; 6:9; cf. 5:16). On the other hand, hebel also refers to that which is perplexing. The perplexing side of life is articulated in texts, such as 3:11; 7:14; and 8:17. There are experiences in life that humans simply cannot understand. Finally, the term hebel also carries the nuance of “fleeting.” A text such as 11:10 reminds us that youth is fleeting—here today and gone tomorrow. The Hb. phrase translated “under the sun” occurs twenty-eight times in the book of Ecclesiastes and is thus also a key phrase for understanding the book. “Under the sun” refers to life in this world, as is clear from the fact that “under the sun” covers the period while one is alive (6:12) and before one dies (9:3–16). But there is more to it than that. “Under the sun” does not simply refer to life in this world but to life in a world that has been adversely affected by the fall. From this perspective, the book of Ecclesiastes can be seen as a biblical commentary on Genesis 3:16–19. In addition to the specific allusions to Gen. 3:16–19 found in Eccl. 3:20 and 12:7 with reference to humanity’s return to the dust, there is also the convergence of the term “vanity” and the phrase “under the sun” (1:14; 2:11, 17, 19; 4:7). “Under the sun” is the sphere where “vanity” is experienced. “Under the sun” is the place where humans experience the frustrating/perplexing side of life. This brings us to our first theme, which is facing the frustrating/perplexing side of life. The book of Ecclesiastes will not allow a simplistic or unreasonably optimistic view of life. Knowing and trusting God does not automatically eliminate the frustrating/perplexing side of life. At times, in fact, knowing the Lord can seem to make life more perplexing (e.g., 6:1, 2). As with the other books of Wisdom Literature, Ecclesiastes rejects a naive approach to life. In spite of the fact that the language of the motto in 1:2 and 12:8 is absolute—“everything is vanity”—there is a second theme that brings balance to the first: enjoying and finding satisfaction in life. The Preacher routinely commends experiencing joy and satisfaction in life. He does so both with prosaic language (e.g. 3:12, 22; 7:14) and with poetic imagery. In particular, he adopts the image of eating and drinking, an image that combines both joy and satisfaction (2:24; 3:13; 5:18). Since there are joyful and satisfying days of prosperity as well as frustrating and perplexing days of adversity (7:14), we can conclude that when the narrator summarizes the Preacher’s teaching by saying, “All is vanity” (1:2; 12:8), he is using hyperbole to put in bold relief the need to face the frustrating/perplexing side of life along with finding joy and satisfaction in life. This brings us to the author’s third theme: fearing God throughout all of life. When the narrator concludes by saying that we should fear God (12:13), the narrator is simply drawing out the logical conclusion of the Preacher’s message throughout the book. Prior to the conclusion, Eccl. 5:1–7 draws our attention to the temple, the house of God, stressing the fear of God for the life of wisdom (cf. 7:15–18). This section is a clear indication that the Preacher is well aware that life under the sun is not finally without significance, for God sees it all. Furthermore, fearing God prevents us from making unfulfilled promises, pledges that can contribute to our feeling that life is empty because their fulfillment is empty (5:4–7). In sum, this key portion of the book is a key part of its apologetic. The only solution to the apparent emptiness and fleetingness of life in the fallen world is the fear of the Lord. Leading up to the conclusion, the Preacher also teaches that the purpose for everything God does is to lead His people to fear Him (3:14). This includes the things that we experience as frustrating/perplexing as well as those that we experience as joyful and satisfying. To fear God is to know Him, to stand in awe of Him with an abiding faith, and to demonstrate this faith by keeping His commandments (Introduction to the Wisdom Literature). Ecclesiastes teaches us that all of life’s experiences, including both the good times and the bad times, are designed by God as an arena in which we have the opportunity to grow in our knowledge and reverence, and to express a maturing, obedient faith in Him.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: While the book of Ecclesiastes is obviously not a systematic theology, it does communicate a profound theology that is key for understanding life and our relationship to God. One dimension of this theology calls for special comment: divine sovereignty and human responsibility. Like other books in the Old Testament, Ecclesiastes does not simply address the interface between divine sovereignty and human responsibility as a theological/philosophical question that must be pondered. Rather, Ecclesiastes sets forth the teaching that with regard to our experience of life, God is absolutely sovereign and human beings are absolutely responsible. A key text that focuses on divine sovereignty is 5:18–6:3. In the first part of this text (5:18–20), the Preacher sees what is “good and fitting” (v. 18) in the gift that God gives to some: the gift of wealth and possessions coupled with the ability to enjoy them (v. 19). The ability to enjoy life is after all a gift from a sovereign God (2:24, 25). In the second part of this text (6:1–3), the Preacher sees what is “an evil” (v. 1), namely, God gives someone wealth and possessions but not the ability to enjoy them. This is “vanity” (v. 2). Having possessions and enjoying them are two different things and whether or not one has the ability to find satisfaction in one’s possessions is determined by God. But the Preacher is not a fatalist. He also teaches that God gives joy and satisfaction “to the one who pleases” God (2:26) and to those who “do good” (3:12, 13). So the experience of joy and satisfaction in life is a gift from a sovereign God for those who take care of their human responsibilities. While there is a mystery here, it is a mystery that points us to Christ who, through His obedience, sufferings and death, has merited for us the joy (Heb. 12:2) and the satisfaction (Is. 53:11) that we experience in part in this life even as we anticipate the fullness of these in the life to come. Indeed, even our present sufferings are “slight momentary afflictions” when compared to the glory that is stored up for us in Christ (2 Cor. 4:17).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The Bible’s storyline starts with a creation that is “very good.” In the beginning, “under the sun” was the sphere of perfect joy and perfect satisfaction for humanity; nothing was frustrating and nothing was perplexing. All of that changed when Adam and Eve sinned against God. “Under the sun” became the sphere of the frustrating and perplexing, though joy and satisfaction are still to be found. The book of Ecclesiastes is a commentary on life “under the sun” after the fall and before the final redemption. Ecclesiastes teaches us to face the frustrating/perplexing aspects of life, to find joy and satisfaction with thankfulness when possible, and to fear God regardless. But how can this be done? On what resources can we draw to face, to find, and to fear? The ultimate answer is not provided in the book of Ecclesiastes but in the pages of the New Testament as they reveal to us God’s final redemption in Christ.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The New Testament does not directly quote the book of Ecclesiastes, but it does allude to the book in two key texts. The first is Rom. 8:18–25, where the apostle Paul is describing life as it has been adversely affected by the fall. In verse 20, Paul says that “the creation was subjected to futility,” and the Greek word that Paul uses for “futility” ( mataiotēs ) is the same Greek word that the first translators of the Hebrew Bible used to translate the key term in the book of Ecclesiastes, hebel (“vanity”). Paul is in effect describing life “under the sun.” As Paul describes life under the sun, he does so without despair by pointing us to “the glory that is to be revealed in us” (v. 18) and the “hope” (v. 20) of being “set free” (v. 21) from the vanity of life. He says of this redemption that “we wait for it with patience” (v. 25). In this text, Paul does not tell us precisely what it is that we are waiting for, but he does in the second text, which alludes to the book of Ecclesiastes. This second text is 2 Corinthians 5:1–11. In verses 1–9, Paul describes life in a way that is quite similar to the description in the book of Ecclesiastes. We groan and are burdened (vv. 2, 3; Eccl. 1:13 in the NIV), we must live by faith and not by sight (v. 7; Eccl. 8:11, 12), and our goal is to please God (v. 9; Eccl. 2:26). Our lives are much like the life of the Preacher, but there is a difference: we have “the Spirit as a guarantee” (v. 5; see Rom. 8:23) of our deliverance through resurrection from the dead (vv. 2–5), a teaching not found in Ecclesiastes. Paul concludes this text in a way strikingly reminiscent of the conclusion to the book of Ecclesiastes by reminding us that we will all be judged for what we have done “whether good or evil” (v. 10; Eccl. 12:14). In light of our “fear of the Lord” (v. 11; Eccl. 12:13), we seek to persuade others of the hope that we have in Christ. Because of Christ’s resurrection from the dead, which guarantees our resurrection from the dead, we know that even those experiences which are frustrating and perplexing are ultimately not in vain (1 Cor. 15:58).

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The title of the book in Hebrew is best translated “Song of Songs,” a construction that expresses the superlative (cf. “Lord of lords”). In other words, this is “The Very Best Song.” In the English tradition, the book goes by a few different names. One is “Canticles,” a shortened, anglicized form of the Latin title, Canticum Canticorum , which is an exact translation of the Hebrew title. Another is “The Song of Solomon,” based on a presumed Solomonic connection.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: According to Song 1:1, the Song of Songs “is Solomon’s.” The phrase “is Solomon’s” can be translated as “by Solomon” (as its author), “for Solomon” (as the person to whom it is dedicated), or “associated with Solomon” (as one of Israel’s renowned composers; see 1 Kin. 4:32). The traditional view of both Jews and Christians is that Solomon authored this book.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: If the Song was written “by Solomon,” it was composed in the mid-tenth century B.C. If the Song was “dedicated to Solomon,” this might also favor a very early date. Some have taken the reference to Tirzah in Song 6:4 to indicate an early date, either when Tirzah was the capital of the northern ten tribes (c. 900 B.C. ) or even earlier during Solomon’s reign and before hostility arose between Israel and Judah (c. 950 B.C. ). Certainty is not possible on this issue, since Tirzah probably means something like “pleasant” or “beautiful,” thus explaining the reference to this particular city. If the Song is “associated with Solomon,” no insight is gained for dating the book. While all of Scripture was written for all times and all places, some books have a more timeless feel than others, and the Song is one such book. Unlike the books of Kings, which were originally written to the exilic community in Babylon, or the books of Chronicles, which were originally written to the postexilic community in Judea, the Song gives no evidence of a narrow occasion for its composition. No specific audience seems to be in view.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Except for the opening verse, the Song is poetry. In a sense, the entire book is one poem, hence the title “The Song [singular] of Songs [plural].” But the Song is also a collection of smaller poems. The boundaries of these individual poems are not always clear, as is obvious from consulting different translations or contemporary commentaries. There are several questions that must be answered with regard to the genre of the Song. The first question: Is the Song an allegory or is it love poetry? In both Jewish and Christian history, the allegorical approach to interpreting the Song has predominated. The majority of contemporary commentators, however, both Jewish and Christian, favor a literal reading of the book as love poetry, and this is the position taken here. See History of Interpretation. The second question: Is the Song to be read as a drama or simply as an anthology of love poems? Some read the Song as a drama with two characters, the Shulammite woman and the king/shepherd. Others read the Song as a drama with at least three characters—the Shulammite woman, the shepherd, and the king—and a plot centering on the question as to whether the Shulammite woman will end up with her true love, the shepherd, or with the man in power, the king. (In this view, the Song has a similar plot to other stories both ancient and modern.) While the dramatic reading is possible, commentators who take that position have been unable to reach unanimity regarding the number of characters or the flow of the plot. Thus, it seems we are on safer ground in reading the Song as an anthology. The third question: Is the anthology a loose connection of poems or one that is highly structured? On one end of the spectrum of opinion, the Song is seen as a loose connection of poems held together by common themes and images. On the other end, the Song is seen as a concentric structure of twenty-eight parts. The evidence in the text seems to lead us away from both extremes and to the conclusion that the Song is a moderately structured anthology of love poetry with some movement from the beginning to the end, movement that falls short of full plot development.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: There is a key repetition that seems to play a role in the macro-structure of the book: “I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem” (2:7; 3:5; 5:8; 8:4). This repetition is similar to the repetition of “these are the generations of” in the book of Genesis, a repetition that plays a key role in the structure of Genesis. Of interest is the fact that in both books, the repetitions are exact except for one modified text in each book (Gen. 5:1; Song 5:8). Given this fourfold repetition in the Song, it seems that the book can be divided into six sections: Introduction (1:1); Group One (1:2–2:7); Group Two (2:8–3:5); Group Three (3:6–5:8); Group Four (5:9–8:4); and Conclusion (8:5–14). Further evidence for this macro-structure is found in the repetition of the line, “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me!” This line occurs twice, in 2:6 and 8:3, immediately preceding the first and fourth occurrences of the refrain. While the flow of thought may fall short of full plot development, there does appear to be some movement in the groups of poems. After the superscription (1:1), there is an emphasis in the first group on the woman’s desire for her lover (1:2–2:7). This is followed by the second group, which has an emphasis on the approach of her lover (2:8–3:5). The poems in the third group focus on her loss of her lover (3:6–5:8), while the fourth group brings us to the return of her lover (5:9–8:4). This quasi-story line comes to its consummation in 8:5–14.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The overarching theme of the Song is human love and sex. There are, however, three subthemes. The first is delight, and this subtheme is highlighted in 1:2–2:7 and 3:6–5:8. Both the man and the woman express unabashed delight in each other: “Behold, you are beautiful, my love” (1:15); “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved” (1:16). The Song contains many images that articulate this delight, so any study of the Song must include the unpacking of these images. The second subtheme is disappointment, and this is the focus of 3:6–5:8. The woman realizes that there are risks in love, but she is willing to take those risks. Regrettably, taking these risks sometimes results in disappointment. Such disappointment is expressed most poignantly in 5:6: “I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone.” In spite of the disappointments experienced in love, there is a third subtheme—desire—that finds special articulation in the final group of poems (8:5–14). “Love is strong as death” (8:6); “Many waters cannot quench love” (8:7). So, the Song ends with an expression of deep desire that overcomes the disappointments, “Make haste, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or young stag on the mountains of spices” (8:14).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The Song is about more than love and sex—it is about love and sex redeemed. The paradisiacal imagery reminds us of the beginning, before the fall, when human love was everything God intended it to be and nothing God did not intend it to be. The themes of delight and desire in this book show us that human love and sex are not inherently evil, but still contain a great deal of the beauty intended by God in the beginning. This contributes to a full-orbed biblical sexual ethic that embraces the goodness of the sexual relationship between man and woman when it is expressed in the appropriate context—the biblical covenant of marriage wherein husband and wife become one flesh (Gen. 2:18–25). Historically, many interpreters have been somewhat embarrassed by the sensual imagery of the Song, largely due to assumptions left over from the Greek philosophers who viewed the body and physical pleasure as evils, things to be escaped or avoided for the good of the soul. But Scripture does not teach that the spirit is good and the body is bad; rather, both the physical and the spiritual are part of the Lord’s good creation. God made a world that was originally “very good,” commanding human beings to procreate and fill it (Gen. 1:26–31). Sex within the context of marriage is therefore good and holy, a gift of God for spousal enjoyment and the furthering of physical, spiritual, and emotional intimacy between husband and wife. Originally, the Song was written to convey these themes, and although it does point us ultimately to Christ, we need not be afraid to read the Song as an expression and affirmation of the goodness of love and sex within marriage.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The garden imagery in the Song (see explicit references in 4:12, 15, 16; 5:1; 6:2; 8:3) is intended to remind us of the garden of Eden, where the first man and woman “were both naked and were not ashamed” (Gen. 2:25). In that way, the Song points us back to the beginning, when human beings were in perfect relationship with God and with one another. It reminds us that love, sex, and marriage were originally good gifts and in many ways remain good gifts; therefore, they can be redeemed from the negativity that so often surrounds them as we live in harmony with the Lord’s design for them. The redemption and restoration of these relationships can be realized more and more in this life as we anticipate the consummation of all things in which everything will be fully restored. This consummation has been guaranteed by the perfect Husband, the One who has redeemed His bride by loving her and giving Himself for her (Eph. 5:22–33). The theme of disappointment in the Song confronts us with the fact that human love, like every other dimension of life, has been adversely affected by the fall (cf. Gen. 3:16–19). In a fallen world, human love is no longer everything that God intended it to be. This points us forward to the hope of redemption, eliciting in us a longing for the restoration of all of our relationships and the renewal of creation that the Prophets reveal as the consummation of the Lord’s plan for the cosmos (Is. 65:17–25; Dan. 12:1, 2; cf. Rom. 8:18–25). This restoration and consummation, the Prophets explain, will occur only through the work of the Messiah (Is. 53; Amos 9:11, 12).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: As noted, the Song creates within the reader a hope for the fullness of relationship that God intended for men and women in the garden. Ultimately, then, Christian interpreters throughout history have not been entirely wrong in reading the work as a revelation of Christ. Only Christ can fully satisfy the longings of human beings for intimacy, for He alone is the One who provides rivers of living water that make it so we are never thirsty again (John 4:13, 14; 7:37, 38). Even the best marriages provide occasions for disappointment, as the Song recognizes (3:6–5:8). In that way, the Song reminds us that Christ is the only perfect Spouse. Only He can meet all of our needs. While the allegorical interpretation of the Song is off target, it is nonetheless the case that the Song is illustrative of the love of Christ for His church. Given the consistent use in both Testaments of marriage as an image for God’s relationship with His people (cf. Ezek. 16; Hos. 1–3; Eph. 5:21–33), it would seem odd for the Song not to give us a glimpse of that bond. God designed marriage to mirror His relationship with us, so it seems natural that God inspired the Song to mirror that relationship as well. While avoiding the excesses of the allegorical approach to the Song, the reader is certainly invited to reflect on the Song’s themes as windows into our relationship with God.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: As early as A.D. 100, we have evidence that Jewish interpreters felt discomfort with reading the Song literally. At that time, Rabbi Akiba stated that anyone who uses the book in such a literal fashion has no share in the life to come. Judaism has traditionally read the text as an allegory of redemptive history from Adam to the Messiah or as an allegory of God and the individual believer. Historically, Christian interpreters have followed suit, as exemplified in the writings of Hippolytus (c. 200), Origen (c. 250), Jerome (c. 400), and Bernard of Clairvaux (c. 1135). Many of the Protestant Reformers and the Puritans read the Song in this way as well. A shift in interpretation began to take place in the nineteenth century, and Jewish and Christian interpreters since the twentieth century have almost unanimously agreed that the Song is to be read not as an allegory but as love poetry. There are no doubt numerous reasons for this shift in interpretation, but two are particularly clear. One is rooted in the Protestant Reformation’s return to studying the Bible in the original languages and with an essentially historical-grammatical hermeneutic. There is nothing in the text itself that would lead one to read it allegorically; the difference in this regard between the Song and The Pilgrim’s Progress , for example, is obvious. The other reason for this change in interpretation is rooted in the rise of modern archaeology in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and discoveries of love poetry akin to the Song from the ancient Near East.
