sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book is named after the prophet whose oracles and ministry it records. The name “Isaiah” means “the Lord saves,” which fits the central emphasis of the prophet’s message.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Isaiah was a well-educated aristocrat by birth, with access to the king and the royal court. He was God’s appointed instrument to bring a message of judgment and ultimate restoration to Jerusalem. Isaiah was married, and two of his children are named in the book: Shear-jashub and Maher-shalal-hash-baz (7:3; 8:3). According to tradition, Isaiah was martyred by being sawed in two at the beginning of Manasseh’s reign.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Isaiah ministered for more than forty years, from 740 until well after 701 B.C. , through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (The complexity of dating Hezekiah’s reign makes it difficult to determine a precise end point for Isaiah’s ministry; cf. 36:1; 38:5 notes.) King Uzziah presided over a lengthy period of peace and stability. During his reign, Egypt was racked with internal strife and Assyria was preoccupied with securing its northern frontier. These conditions left Uzziah free to pursue his affairs largely in peace, allowing both the northern and southern kingdoms to recapture lost territory. By the end of Uzziah’s reign, both kingdoms had virtually reclaimed the boundaries established at the height of the Solomonic empire. However, by the time of Uzziah’s death and Isaiah’s calling as a prophet, the storm clouds were already gathering in the North with the rise of Tiglath-pileser III as king of Assyria. During Jotham’s reign, a war raged between Judah and the united kingdoms of Israel and Syria (the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734–732 B.C. ; cf. Isaiah 7–9). In this war Ahaz, the king of Judah, was opposed by a coalition of forces led by Pekah, king of Israel, and Rezin, king of Aram (Syria). Ahaz responded with fear and unbelief. He refused God’s sign (7:12) and tried to find a political solution by seeking help from the Assyrians. During the reign of Hezekiah, Judah and several other nations fought against Assyria when it was under the rule of Sennacherib (705–681 B.C. ). Sennacherib’s response was to devastate the countryside of Judah and lay siege to Jerusalem itself. But unlike Ahaz, Hezekiah trusted in the Lord and was delivered (37:14–35). Problems within Judah compounded these external dangers. Isaiah railed against the leaders for their hypocrisy (1:10–15), greed (5:8), self-indulgence (5:11), and cynicism (5:19). While the rich prospered, the poor were increasingly oppressed. Prosperity had eaten away at religious observances such that even while the people confessed the Lord as their king with their lips, their hearts were far from Him and their temple sacrifices were a mere sham. God raised up Isaiah to announce their fate (6:11–13). As Isaiah predicted, Israel was exiled in 722 B.C. , and Hezekiah barely escaped the Assyrian destruction (36:1–37:37). But his deliverance would be merely temporary, a stay of execution rather than a pardon. The stump would be burned again, though a remnant would survive this catastrophe too (6:13). Isaiah’s ministry of encouragement in his later years of service focused on the remnant who would survive the exile of Judah to Babylon. In a series of wide-ranging prophecies, Isaiah predicted the fall of pagan Babylon (46:1–47:15) and the ultimate salvation of Israel’s remnant. More than a century before Cyrus the Persian came to power, Isaiah named him as God’s anointed agent to restore the remnant to the land (44:24–45:13). The prophet urged the remnant to flee from Babylon when the opportunity becomes available to them (48:20, 21). He challenged the people to renew their loyalty to the Lord after they finally return to the land (56:1–8) and to avoid again engaging in acts of treachery (57:3–13). Beyond this future act of salvation Isaiah predicted the coming of a Servant and Savior much greater than Cyrus. This anonymous Servant would fulfill Israel’s original destiny by bringing justice to the nations (42:1–4) and becoming a light to the Gentiles (49:1–7). The Servant would suffer willingly to take away the sins of His people (52:13– 53:12) and thus establish a new covenant between the Lord and the new Israel (42:5–7). Because of these victories, God would reward and vindicate Him (50:4–11). The NT identifies the Servant as Jesus Christ, the true Israel and the incarnate Lord (Matt. 12:15–21).

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Isaiah’s composition is similar to that of the other writing prophets, with a mixture of oracles, sign-acts, and episodes from the prophet’s life woven together to bring a message of judgment and salvation for God’s people. Like several of the other prophets, Isaiah has a prominent call narrative (ch. 6), which authenticates and validates his ministry. It shares many features with the call of Moses in Exodus 3, demonstrating that Isaiah too is one of the “prophets like Moses” promised in Deut. 18:18. The first part of the book, chapters 1–35, focuses on God’s judgment on Israel and Judah by Assyria. The second, chapters 40–66, focuses on the remnant’s return from Babylon and their ultimate deliverance in the remote future (see note on 36:1–39:8 as a bridge transitioning Isaiah’s focus from Assyria to Babylon). The second part, like the first, begins with a vision of the heavenly court. Isaiah overhears God sending messengers to announce that the punishment of Israel and Judah has been satisfied and will come to an end (40:1–8). In contrast to the gods of the nations, which are idols of wood and stone that do not see or speak and cannot affect history, the Lord is sovereign even over distant future events. Isaiah’s vision of the coming of God’s kingdom encompasses the exile, the return of the Jews from exile, the mission, ministry, and kingdom of Jesus Christ, the mission and hope of the church, Jesus’ present rule over this world, and the restoration of all things in holiness and righteousness. Isaiah is a gifted preacher. Through his poetic imagination and rhetorical style he exposes the folly of relying on human structures by contrasting it with the wisdom of trusting in God’s kingdom. He uses satire and sarcasm to reveal the ridiculous nature of trusting in idols made of wood and stone that cannot move, speak, or act. Although the ungodly harden themselves against the Lord (6:10), becoming as blind and deaf as the idols that they worship, Isaiah’s prophetic oracles move the godly to respond with awe and worship of God.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Isaiah served God in the role of covenant prosecutor. His message consists of charges, condemnation, and judgments as he declares God’s curse on Israel, Judah, and the nations (1:2–31; 13–23; 56; 57; 65). Isaiah’s autobiographical account of his call to become a messenger from the Lord’s heavenly court is recounted in chapter 6, a vision that makes clear God’s utter holiness and transcendence. This God must demand justice and righteousness from His people. When Isaiah was summoned to represent the heavenly court in Jerusalem’s earthly court, he discovered to his dismay that God was sending him not to save Israel and Judah but to harden their impenitent hearts (6:9, 10). Isaiah was to present to the people the Lord’s complaint that they were faithless and rebellious (1:2, 3; 31:1–3; 57:3–10). God’s people had become like the nations in their pride, sarcasm, and selfishness. They had lost the vision of God’s kingdom of justice, righteousness, love, and peace, and they had tried to establish their own kingdom, for which they would inevitably face judgment. The Lord, however, was still committed to establishing a kingdom of justice and righteousness. The promise of a messianic king in the opening chapters focuses primarily on His role in bringing in this new kingdom (9:6–7; 11:1–9). The coming Servant in chapters 40–55 will extend the promised light not only to the remnant of Judah and Israel but to the nations as well (49:6). This kingdom cannot be brought in by human effort, but only by the Lord’s own redemptive acts. Ultimately, the Lord will establish a new heavens and a new earth where His kingdom of justice and righteousness will reign (65:17–25). The prophet also serves as an advocate for faith in the midst of a lost generation. He calls on the godly to seek the Lord, to hope for God’s kingdom, to experience God’s peace within, and to respond with faith to God’s forthcoming new acts of redemption. The Lord’s covenant ends ultimately with blessings on Israel, not curses (Deut. 30:1–14; Rom. 10:5–21). In the end, a godly remnant will survive the judgment. In the meantime, the faithful must pursue righteousness in their own actions even when they are surrounded by others who ignore the Lord’s commandments.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: From his call vision, Isaiah derived his characteristic understanding of God as majestic, holy, and glorious. Isaiah saw the Lord majestically towering over him, seated on a lofty throne, so that the skirts of His robe filled the temple. The Lord was surrounded by the seraphim, angelic attendants whose name means “burning ones.” Their cries of praise shook the doorposts of the temple, and smoke filled the building. This God is also holy and not like human beings with their sinful compromises. Isaiah’s favorite title for God is “the Holy One of Israel” (1:4; 5:19, 24; etc.). His ways are not like ours, nor are His thoughts (55:8, 9). For sinful Israel to find themselves in the hands of such a holy God is not good news. He is also the glorious God, before whom the nations are as a drop in a bucket and their idols even less significant (40:15). He created all things and rules over all (45:5–12). In the end, all nations will come to acknowledge this truth and bow down before the one true God, so that the earth will be as filled with His glory as the divine throne room in heaven (6:3; 40:5; 66:18).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The eighth-century prophets like Isaiah called God’s people to repentance on the basis of the covenant God made with Moses. They declared that the curses listed in that covenant would inevitably come upon the people if they failed to repent. But if the people responded, they would find the Lord waiting with open arms to receive them (1:18). At that point, there seems to have been more hope of a genuine turning back to the Lord than in the sixth-century prophets, by whose time the exile was inevitable. Yet the Lord nonetheless warned Isaiah that the people would not listen to him; they were blind and deaf and would remain so (6:9–13). The royal line would be cut off so that only a stump of Jesse would remain (11:1). Yet, the Lord would be faithful to fulfill His promises to Abraham and Sarah (51:2). He would bring the remnant back and restore them to Himself in a new covenant (42:5–7). The temple, which would be destroyed along with Jerusalem, would in the last days once again be lifted up as the focal point for the universe (2:2–4).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The book of Isaiah is one of the most frequently quoted OT books in the NT. Jesus was born of a virgin in fulfillment of Is. 7:14 (Matt. 1:23), and He declared that Is. 61:1 was fulfilled in His coming (Luke 4:18–21). Jesus is the promised Son of David and the triumphant King who ushers in a new kingdom of peace and justice (9:6, 7; 11:1, 2). His body is the new temple whose exaltation brings the nations to glorify God (John 2:19–21). Jesus is the Servant who is a light to the Gentiles (49:6). Isaiah 52:13–53:12, of course, is well known for its detailed description of the work of the Suffering Servant, the One who offers a perfect atonement for the sins of His people and provides for them the righteousness by which they are declared righteous in the sight of God. Philip preached the gospel to the Ethiopian eunuch from this passage (Acts 8:28–35).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: For most of the church’s history, the book of Isaiah has been treasured as the words of the eighth-century prophet who spoke not only to confront and encourage God’s people in his own day but also to speak clearly ahead of time of the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow (1 Pet. 1:11). However, for the past two centuries, many higher-critical scholars have disputed the unity of Isaiah, arguing that the book is the result of a complex transmission through many hands. They generally divide the book into three sections, assigning these to Isaiah of Jerusalem (chs. 1–39); to a prophet living at the time of the exile (second, or “Deutero-Isaiah,” chs. 40–55); and to a postexilic prophet (the “Third Isaiah,” chs. 56–66). One of the main evidences that these higher-critical scholars point to as evidence of at least three authors for the book of Isaiah are differences in language (e.g., different vocabulary) between the three sections of the work. However, while there are some linguistic differences between the three sections, the linguistic unity between them is often downplayed. In fact the use of the same terms throughout the three sections but almost nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible is key counterevidence to the claims of these scholars. Furthermore, any variations in language between the proposed divisions of the book are easily explainable as resulting from differences in subject matter, changed perspectives, or the prophet’s personal growth. Nevertheless, despite their best attempts, the aforementioned scholars have been unable to completely ignore the similarities among the three sections. Instead of positing a single author, however, many of these critics have concluded that a final (late) editorial hand unified the work. Indeed, there are unifying features of the book of Isaiah that cannot be honestly overlooked. These include the repetition of theological themes (Zion, the coming of God, the Davidic representative, and the outworking of the Lord’s sovereign plan), the names for God (“the Holy One of Israel”; cf. 1:4 and note), and the unified message of judgment and salvation. Based on this reality and many other evidences, conservative scholars defend the traditional understanding that the book is all the work of one prophet, Isaiah. The book was published under his name (1:1), and he is frequently mentioned in it (2:1; 7:3; 13:1; etc.). The NT names Isaiah as the author of passages from all parts of the book (Matt. 3:3; 8:17; 12:17; note esp. the combined references in John 12:37–41). Another reason why certain higher-critical scholars question Isaiah’s unity of authorship is their assumption that a prophet addresses only his contemporaries. This comes from their belief that only Isaiah’s contemporaries would have found his message relevant, and so Isaiah would have only spoken of things that immediately concerned them. They argue that since chapters 1–39 are addressed to the nation during the Assyrian invasions (c. 740–700 B.C. ), chapters 40–55 to the exiles in Babylon (c. 600–539 B.C. ), and chapters 56–66 to the community after its return to the land (c. 539–500 B.C. ), more than one prophet must have spoken, each making a fresh application of the themes of Isaiah of Jerusalem to his own generation. But this ignores that prophets often ask one generation to participate by faith in a salvation that lies in the distant future. Even though many people were unfaithful during Isaiah’s own day, a core group of faithful disciples (8:16–18) needed the encouragement of knowing that God’s promises to Israel were still in effect and that after the coming darkness of which Isaiah spoke, light would dawn (9:2–7). Furthermore, Moses anticipated the inevitability of Israel’s exile and return (Deut. 30:1–3), as did Solomon (1 Kin. 8:46–51). It is not far-fetched to imagine that, under the Lord’s inspiration, Isaiah also addressed similar future concerns, which had vital immediate ramifications in summoning the people of his own day to repentance and faith in the Lord who governs their future. Finally, a distinct anti-supernaturalistic bias on the part of many higher-critical scholars explains why many of them divide the book of Isaiah among at least three different authors. Critics often assume that miraculous prophecy, such as naming Cyrus more than a century beforehand and predicting the birth of Jesus from the Virgin Mary, is impossible. This unargued-for presupposition then drives their conclusions that the prophecy of Cyrus must have been written after his appearance and that Isa. 7 has nothing to do with the birth of Jesus. However, Isaiah reproaches Ahaz for precisely this kind of unbelief when the king refuses to recognize the Lord’s ability to demonstrate His power through signs (7:10–13). The Lord gave Hezekiah just such a sign as an assurance of his recovery (38:7, 8). In chapters 40–55, the Lord validates His sovereign rule over the nations precisely by the power of His prophets to speak the future before it happens. Pagan prophets could not show that their past prophecies had been fulfilled, nor could they give reliable prophecies of what was to come (41:21–29). By contrast, Israel’s God fulfilled Isaiah’s former prophecies about Assyria. The prophet also predicts the future, mentioning Cyrus by name. Isaiah delivers these supernatural prophecies (41:21–29; 44:24–45:8) to leave unbelievers without excuse (48:3–5). Isaiah’s remarkable prophecies about Christ’s suffering and death also present a strong case for supernatural prophecy.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book is named after the exilic prophet whose ministry it records. “Jeremiah” means “the Lord exalts,” and part of the prophet’s message is that the Lord plants and uproots peoples and nations according to His own purposes (1:10).

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Jeremiah prophesied during the reigns of the last kings of Judah: Josiah (640–609 B.C. ), Jehoahaz (609 B.C. ), Jehoiakim (609–598 B.C. ), Jehoiachin (598–597 B.C. ), and Zedekiah (597–586 B.C. ). The kingdom of Judah ended in the exile of most of its people to Babylon, chiefly as a result of two invasions by King Nebuchadnezzar (597 and 586 B.C. ), though the first deportations occurred as early as 605 (Dan. 1:1 note). The northern kingdom, Israel, was conquered by the Assyrians a century before Jeremiah began his ministry, but Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, fell to Babylon in 612 B.C. It was Jeremiah’s task to announce that God’s judgment would subsequently come upon the southern kingdom of Judah by means of the resurgent superpower Babylon. Jeremiah lived to see his prophecy fulfilled. This prophet was also a priest, from the priestly town of Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin (1:1 note). A lonely figure because of his unpopular message (15:17), he was divinely forbidden to marry as a sign of the imminent cessation of normal life (16:2). He also found himself opposed to the authorities in the land and to all classes of people (26:8). As a result, Jeremiah’s life was in serious danger more than once (11:18–23; 18:18; 26:8; 36:19; 38:6). His message placed him in the thick of political events, and he was sought out especially by King Zedekiah for counsel regarding the approaching Babylonian armies (37:3, 17). Politically, it was a turbulent time, as Egypt and Babylon contested the region. Jeremiah repeatedly prophesied a Babylonian victory, proclaiming that the Lord would use the Babylonian king, Nebuchadnezzar, as His scourge. When Jerusalem fell, the Babylonian commander had a special commission from Nebuchadnezzar himself for the care of the prophet, whose fame had spread to the heart of the empire (39:11–14). Jeremiah was not deported with those taken to exile in Babylon, but initially remained in Judah, only to be taken down to Egypt against his will by those who fled there after the murder of the Babylonian-appointed governor, Gedaliah (chs. 42–44). Jeremiah presumably died in Egypt.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The background to the book is the long struggle in Judah between the idolatrous worship of foreign gods, deeply embedded since the reign of Manasseh (696–642 B.C. ), and the worship of the Lord, which Josiah attempted to restore in his reforms (see 2 Kin. 22; 23). The reforms began in 628 B.C. (2 Chr. 34:3 note) and were given fresh impetus by the discovery of the “Book of the Law” in 621 B.C. (2 Kin. 22:8). Jeremiah’s call came in 626 B.C. (1:2 note), and his early ministry coincides with Josiah’s reforms. Jeremiah testifies, however, to the reforms’ failure to have a significant impact on the people’s lives, as the religious abuses of Manasseh reemerged under Josiah’s successors. The book itself was probably written in several editions. Jeremiah prepared the first edition in 605 B.C. , using Baruch as his scribe, in order to confront King Jehoiakim (36:1–19). Jehoiakim responded by burning the scroll (36:20–26); however, it was rewritten (36:27–32). This early version must have been expanded at a later date (cf. 51:60), perhaps by Jeremiah himself or by Bar­uch, to include many of Jeremiah’s later prophecies along with accounts of incidents from his life. This lengthy process may account for the existence of a much shorter version from which the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the OT) was created. The last event recorded in the book is Jehoiachin’s release from a Babylonian prison, which took place in 562–560 B.C. (Jer. 52:31–34). This last chapter of the book of Jeremiah, summarizing the events surrounding the fall of Jerusalem, seems to have been added as a postscript, since the close of ch. 51 marks “the end of the words of Jeremiah” (51:64).

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Jeremiah consists of a combination of oracles and prophetic sign-acts, along with experiences from the prophet’s life and reflections on the prophet’s own responses to God. Like other prophets, Jeremiah spoke oracles of judgment, identifying the sins of God’s people and pleading with them to repent, as well as oracles of hope assuring them of God’s unshakable commitment to preserve a remnant through the coming judgment. Jeremiah also delivered a number of oracles against foreign nations (chs. 46–51). He did not visit these nations to deliver them—the purpose of these oracles was to encourage God’s people that His standards of justice are universal, and that those who harmed His people would in due course pay for their sins, as God promised in the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 12:1–3). Even those nations that the Lord brought against Judah as His instruments of judgment were not exempt from such punishment; Babylon’s proud trust in her own gods would eventually be humbled. Because of the resistant nature of his audience, Jeremiah delivered a number of sign-acts in which he illustrated his message with striking or memorable actions. These sign-acts functioned as acted parables, reinforcing the unpalatable message. The prophecies of Jeremiah are not ordered chronologically; as a result, descriptions of the same events can be widely separated (e.g., chs. 7 and 26). It is not always easy to see why particular oracles have been grouped together, though sometimes there is a keyword or common theme that links otherwise diverse passages. For example, chs. 21–24 are framed by prophecies concerning each of Josiah’s successors up to (but excluding) Zedekiah. Similarly, chs. 35; 36 refer back to the reign of Jehoiakim after several scenes that involved Zedekiah.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Jeremiah’s message moved through a number of phases, though these do not correspond exactly to the structure of the book. (1) He called Judah to repent and avoid judgment that would otherwise come (e.g., 7:1–15). (2) He announced that the time for repentance was past, since judgment had finally been determined against the people (19:10, 11 notes). Judgment is the dominant note in the book and is understood as the invocation of the final curse of the covenant, namely, loss of the Promised Land (Lev. 26:31–33; Deut. 28:49–68). (3) The Lord would save His people, or a remnant of them, through the exile (24:4–7 notes). Though the Babylonians would prevail over Judah at the Lord’s command, this would be for a limited time. In turn, Babylon would also fall (25:9, 11, 12). This prophecy was fulfilled when Babylon was defeated by an alliance of Persians and Medes under Cyrus in 539 B.C. , clearing the way for the exiles of Judah to return (50:3; 51:1, 27, 28; 2 Chr. 36:20–23). This promise of eventual deliverance was Jeremiah’s answer to the false prophets who had constantly challenged his message of judgment (28:1–4). Jeremiah also had a message of salvation, but only on the other side of judgment (29:11–14). That message is crystallized in the prophecy of the new covenant (31:31–34). The new covenant prophecy is built around the main ingredients of the Mosaic covenant at Sinai: it spoke of God’s desire to have a relationship with His chosen people, and of the requirement upon them to return His love with obedience (Ex. 19:3–6; Deut. 7:6–11). The new covenant speaks of the empowerment of God’s people to obey Him (31:33 note; 32:40 note). Although it is promised in national terms (31:31 and note), it is something new, which the NT shows to be fulfilled in the greater “Israel of God” (Gal. 6:16) through Christ (22:30 note; 23:5 note; 30:9; 31:33 note; 33:18 note). Jeremiah faced great opposition from false prophets, who did not stand in the Lord’s council (23:21–26) and who preached much more popular messages of a peaceful and prosperous future. They anticipated a swift return from exile rather than a lengthy sojourn in Babylon (27:16). As a result, the people often resisted or resented Jeremiah’s messages. Jeremiah reveals his personal involvement with his message more fully than the other prophets (but cf. Is. 22:4; Mic. 1:8, 9), and he feels the agony of the people at the approach of the Babylonian armies even before they feel it themselves (4:19–21; 10:19–22; 14:19–22). He also feels the passion of the Lord concerning the sin he witnesses (8:21–9:3 notes). His role is mediatorial in nature. This role is most poignant in the series of passages often referred to as the prophet’s “confessions” (11:18–20; 12:1–4; 15:10–18; 17:14–18; 18:19–23; 20:7–18). In these passages, he expresses his anguish at the great burden of his prophetic calling, prays for vengeance on his personal enemies, and even accuses the Lord of having forced or deceived him (15:18; 20:7). Some of these prayers elicit answers from the Lord containing rebuke and reassurance (11:21–23; 12:5, 6; 15:19–21). The reassurance to Jeremiah in 15:19–21 is later echoed in a prayer of Ephraim, which receives its own answer (31:18–20). The Lord’s good intentions toward Jeremiah, therefore, became a foretaste of His intended faithfulness to the whole people, through and beyond the imminent judgment. If Jeremiah’s work was completed during the time of the exile (the latest historical point reached in the book), the purpose would be to chasten the exiles by encouraging them to ponder the meaning of their exile. At the same time, the purpose would also be to engender hope, since the prophet who had pronounced judgment—and had been proven right—had also preached a message of Judah’s eventual restoration to the land and the nation’s privileged relationship with God.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The central focus of the book of Jeremiah is the Lord’s troubled relationship with His rebellious people, Israel. Jeremiah clearly depicts God as the sovereign Lord who governs all of human history. Having created the universe, He directs all of its events according to His will and purpose (32:17). He rules the future as well as the past and protects those who are truly His people, including those who are far away from the land in exile in Bab­ylon (29:11). At the same time, those who presume on His protection while living in ways that are a functional denial of His lordship will perish (ch. 28). Though He called Israel to be His people and gave her the temple as the symbol of His enduring presence, these external signs cannot be relied upon in the absence of true faith (ch. 7). Not even the covenant with David will protect their kings who persist generation after generation in doing evil (22:18–30). God’s wrath is poured out on those who ignore His holy law and who turn to idols instead of to the true living water that flows from Him (2:13). Though it became increasingly clear in Jeremiah’s prophecy that the Babylonians would destroy Jerusalem, it was equally clear that God was not finished with His people. The Lord would raise up a righteous Branch for David to replace Jehoiachin (23:1–6). Through the Branch, the Lord would again shepherd and gather His people, reuniting the house of Israel with the house of Judah (33:14). In place of the old covenant that brought death and destruction through the people’s sin, the Lord would bring a new covenant through which His people would come to know Him and to serve Him in spirit and in truth (31:31–34). The result of this new covenant would be enduring peace and blessing for God’s people (32:37–41).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Jeremiah began his ministry during a time of national revival under King Josiah of Judah. It must have seemed as if the nation was finally turning back to God. After Josiah’s untimely death in battle, however, the forces of reformation were driven back, and the nation plunged into its old ways of apostasy once more. The judgment of exile threatened in Deuteronomy became a terrible reality. Yet as Jeremiah himself prophesied, that exile would not last forever but only for seventy years, the lifespan of an individual (Jer. 25:11, 12). After that, the Lord would return His people to His land, which He did in the days of Cyrus (Ezra 1:1). This restoration of the Jewish people did not bring about the fullness of the promise immediately, however. Instead, the seventy-year period of judgment extended further into a period of seventy “sevens” (Dan. 9) until the promised Christ came. It is through the coming of Jesus that the gospel brought true peace and unity to Jews and Samaritans, as well as Gentiles, uniting them as one new people under the true King, Jesus Christ. The new covenant that Jesus ushered in fulfilled the prophecy of Jeremiah, as the book of Hebrews makes clear (Heb. 8; 9).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Jesus inaugurated in His own blood the new covenant that Jeremiah promised (Luke 22:20). Jesus, the Good Shepherd of whom Jeremiah prophesied (31:10), laid down His life for His sheep (John 10:11). As the mediator of this new covenant, Jesus enables His people to receive the inheritance promised to Jeremiah (Heb. 9:15). He does so as the righteous Branch, the new shoot from David’s broken line, who is Himself “the Lord ... our righteousness” (Jer. 23:6; 33:15, 16). Through His own perfect obedience, Jesus not only brought salvation to the house of Israel and the house of Judah but to all nations. Like Jeremiah, Jesus pronounced judgment on those who had turned the Jerusalem temple into a den of thieves (Matt. 21:12, 13), and He wept over those whose stubborn rebellion would lead to their condemnation (Luke 19:41; Jer. 9:1)

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Jeremiah’s discussion of a new covenant that would replace the old, failed covenant was swiftly recognized by the church fathers as a pivotal passage in their early interactions with Jewish apologists. Following the lead of the book of Hebrews, the new covenant was identified as Christianity, while the old covenant was Judaism. Martin Luther picked up this approach and took it further in his own negative interactions with the Jewish community of his day, seeing in Jeremiah’s denunciation of the people of Jerusalem a wholesale rejection of the Jewish people. John Calvin, however, focused more positively on Jeremiah as a preacher of righteousness and the grace that would come in Christ. The power of Jeremiah’s prophecies to inspire the imagination may be seen in famous portraits by Michelangelo and Rembrandt. Both depict the prophet in a mood of somber, sorrowful reflection, underlining his role as “the weeping prophet.”

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: In the earliest days, when books were rare and had to be committed to memory, it was customary to refer to books of the Hebrew Bible by their first word, which in this case, fittingly, is ekah , an exclamation that introduces a cry of woe. Later rabbis referred to the book as qinot (“Laments”). This title was preserved in the Septuagint, followed by the Vulgate ( Lamentationes ), and appears in English translations today.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Although the book of Lamentations contains no explicit claim of authorship, it is traditionally attributed to the prophet Jeremiah. This has been true at least since the time of the Septuagint (c. 250 B.C. ), in which a note about the prophet’s authorship of the book appears as a heading before the first verse. The idea of Jeremiah as the author may have been encouraged by 2 Chr. 35:25, which states that the prophet composed laments for King Josiah. The book itself contains no explicit evidence that Jeremiah is its author, although passages distinctly recall his character and language, especially ch. 3 (cf. 3:48–51 with Jer. 14:17). Thus, it is not impossible that Jeremiah wrote some, if not most, of the book of Lamentations. However, since the book consists of five different poems that vary somewhat in style and sometimes seem to be spoken by an individual (ch. 3) and sometimes by a community (ch. 5), it is possible that the poems come from different pens. This study Bible will refer to the author as “the poet” in the study notes.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The link between Lamentations and Jeremiah is plausible not only because of similar expressions, but also because of the poems’ setting and theme. The setting is Jerusalem, during the period after the fall of the kingdom of Judah to the Babylonians in 586 B.C. and before the restoration of the exiles in 538 B.C. The lament concerning the loss of Judah’s king (2:2, 9), in distinction from other devastations of Jerusalem, fixes this occasion for the laments. A setting during the period of the Bab­ylonian exile makes Lamentations a fitting sequel to the book of Jeremiah. As Jeremiah foretold the fall of Jerusalem, Lamentations expresses the pain of the event itself. The Septuagint places Lamentations after Jeremiah, and the Christian tradition has followed that practice. In the Hebrew Bible, the book of Lamentations is found in the section of the Scriptures known as the “Writings.”

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The five chapters of the book are five poems. The most common approach to questions of genre sees these poems as laments that are like those appearing in other books of the OT, principally the book of Psalms. A unique aspect of these particular laments is that the context of distress in Lamentations is clearly that of the fallen city, whereas the context of the laments in the Psalter is often less discernible. Laments (both of the community and the individual) have certain typical characteristics, of which the most common are: (1) complaint about adversity, which the Lord either tolerated or even caused; (2) confession of trust; (3) appeal for deliverance on the grounds of the Lord’s character and His covenant; and (4) certainty of a hearing, often with an assurance that the enemies and persecutors will in turn experience the wrath of God (Ps. 74). The book of Lamentations has these typical marks, though it represents a unique set of variations upon them. Lamentations is sometimes compared with a particular kind of lament, the funeral lament (e.g., Amos 5:1–3), but it does not quite fit this category, because Jerusalem is not uniformly portrayed as “dead.” The clearest evidence for meter in Hebrew poetry is the book of Lamentations, which seems to use a line of five beats divided three-two. This meter is called Qinah (“elegiac”), after the Hebrew name for a lament. It is most often found in poetry of this sorrowful kind. A second poetic form found in Lamentations is the acrostic , in which lines or sets of lines are arranged according to the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Each line or group of lines begins with the succeeding letter. This method may indicate that the poet is giving a complete treatment of the subject matter. The acrostic also provides a form for the literary expression of grief, allowing the writer to impose a kind of order on the chaos that such a terrible tragedy brings.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The purpose of Lamentations cannot be stated in a single word. The book was composed as a way of coming to terms with the destruction of Zion. The center of gravity is the wrath of God against His people: Judah had sinned, and the prophets had pronounced God’s warning; therefore, God’s wrath is just. Long before Jerusalem’s fall, Amos had spoken of a day of the Lord against His people (Amos 5:18), a day that finally came (Lam. 1:12). Lamentations does not express total perplexity, as the book Job may appear to do at times. Instead, it justifies God’s punishment of Judah and offers a vindication of the prophets who predicted it. Lamentations is not a work of passive resignation. God’s wrath is accepted, but not without great emotional resistance. Could God behave like the enemy of His own people, and drive them to terrors that are painful even to describe (2:4, 5, 20–22)? Although the poet understands the justice of God, the agony and bewilderment of the event can be freely expressed. The book retains its power in times of anguish and sorrow. Yet in his anguish, the poet is able to affirm that God is still merciful and faithful (3:22–36). There is a way out of the crisis of the exile—the covenant Lord of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whose faithfulness to the patriarchs is a continuing foundation throughout the Prophets for new appeals to Israel and Judah to put their trust in Him (e.g., Mic. 7:20). The writer of Lamentations may perhaps be counted, with Abraham, as one of the supreme examples in the OT of faith in God. Jeremiah prophesied that there would be a definite end to the Babylonian exile (Jer. 25:11). The poet looks for such an end, and even hopes that Judah’s enemies will be judged for their crimes against her. In this hope, there is an understanding of the sovereignty of God over all the nations, the sovereignty that embraces all mysteries (3:37–39).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The central passage in the book affirms God’s covenant faithfulness ( hesed ) in the midst of the surrounding devastation (3:22–24). God is not distant from His people in their suffering, nor has He completely abandoned them, even though their sins are great and might merit such a fate. As the poet publicly confesses the sins of his people, he hopes that through such confession and repentance the people will be restored to God’s favor and thus to a new future (ch. 5). This is his only hope: there is no salvation to be sought or found in any other source, for the Lord alone is his portion (3:24). There is thus a movement within the book, as there is in most biblical laments, from the expression of terrible loss and pain to restored hope and prayer for renewal.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The book of Lamentations echoes the form and the terminology of the psalms of lament. Like the writers of those psalms, this poet is experiencing a time of judgment: the Lord has turned His face away from His people because of their sins. Yet Lamentations is the longest, deepest, and most profound lament in the Bible because it is a response to the deepest and most profound act of judgment by the Lord on His own people—the destruction of Jerusalem. This terrible disaster also helped shape the book of Psalms (e.g., Pss. 74; 137) as well as the writings of the prophets of the time (such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel), but the book of Lamentations is perhaps the fullest and most significant response to this pivotal event in biblical history.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Jesus voiced His own lament over Jerusalem during the days leading up to His rejection by His own people (Matt. 23:37–39; Luke 13:34, 35). He foresaw terrible consequences for Jerusalem because of that rejection (Matt. 24). Yet He Himself also uttered His own cry of abandonment as He endured the mystery of His redemptive suffering in our place (Matt. 27:46). His death on the cross is the ultimate expression of the covenant faithfulness of God that is new every morning and enables lost sinners to be restored to God’s favor. The solemnity and compassion of Christ’s words express the goodness and severity of God that undergirds the gospel (Rom. 11:22, 23). The book of Lamentations thus points beyond the humiliation and restoration of Jerusalem to the humiliation and exaltation of Christ. In beholding the life and work of Christ, the world can know that God is good and that He will do good in His time “to the soul who seeks him” (3:25).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: In Jewish tradition, portions of Lamentations are read annually on the ninth of Av (July–August), when Jews recall the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. as well as that of the second temple in A.D. 70. It marks an annual reminder of God’s justice and compassion: He is determined to punish sin, but He offers assurance that His covenant mercy remains new each day. Christian tradition, by contrast, has often neglected the book, along with the broader practice of lament. There is no surviving commentary on the book from before the ninth century A.D. , although the church fathers cited individual verses. Perhaps this is due to seeing the book primarily as a historical artifact rather than a vital piece of theological engagement. In more recent times, however, it has been valued for its significance in helping individuals and communities explore an appropriate response to deeply traumatic personal circumstances. The caveat, of course, is that our experiences of pain and loss may be significantly different from the poet’s pain over the fall of Jerusalem. Yet there are lessons to be learned, both individually and corporately, about how we should mourn over tragic events, especially when we connect the book with Jesus’ suffering and pain in our place.

content.text: JERUSALEM ONCE GREAT BUT NOW DEVASTATED

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book is named after the exilic prophet whose ministry it records. “Ezekiel” means “God makes strong,” a name that fits the task to which he was called (3:8 note).

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: We have no information about the prophet Ezek­iel beyond what his book tells us. Ezekiel was among the group of deportees that Nebuchadnez­zar carried away when he captured Jerusalem in 597 B.C. , and installed Zedekiah as king. These deportees also included King Jehoiachin, the royal family, and other leading citizens and craftsmen (2 Kin. 24:10–17). Ezekiel’s wife died shortly before the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 B.C. (24:15–18). If the prophet was thirty years old when he began his prophetic ministry (1:1), and this date corresponds to the fifth year of the exile of Jehoiachin (1:2, 3), then Ezekiel was about twenty-six when he was carried into exile. The last date recorded in the book (April 26, 571 B.C. ; 29:17) shows that Ezekiel’s ministry spanned at least twenty-three years, lasting until he was about fifty. The circumstances of his death are not known. Ezekiel was a priest (1:3). Priests ordinarily began their temple service at age thirty. However, in the year he would have ordinarily begun his temple service, Ezekiel was in Babylon, seven hundred miles (1,126 km) from Jerusalem. It was at this significant age in his life that God called Ezekiel to be a prophet, and his prophetic endowment was recognized by the leaders among the exiles (8:1; 20:1). In this book, God addresses Ezekiel many times by the phrase “son of man,” meaning “person” or “human being.” In this book, the phrase emphasizes human frailty and insignificance as compared with the transcendence of God (contrast its use as a messianic title in Dan. 7:13; Matt. 26:64; Mark 14:62; Rev. 14:14).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: In the late seventh century B.C. , the kings of Judah in Jerusalem were caught between the Babylonians and the armies of Pharaoh Neco of Egypt. King Jehoiakim was placed on the throne of Jerusalem by Pharaoh Neco (2 Kin. 23:34) in 609 B.C. After the Babylonians defeated the Egyptians at Carchemish in 605 B.C. , Jehoiakim switched his allegiance and became a vassal of Nebuchadnezzar. He remained a Babylonian vassal for three years and then transferred his allegiance back to Egypt (2 Kin. 24:1). Jehoiakim died in the same month that Nebuchadnezzar set out on an expedition to punish him. He was succeeded by his son Jehoiachin, who was left to face Nebuchadnezzar’s wrath. After a brief siege, Jehoiachin was taken into captivity with much of the population of Jerusalem, including Ezekiel, in 597 B.C. (2 Kin. 24:8–12). Ezekiel settled with a colony of Jewish captives, possibly near Tel-abib, on “the Chebar canal” (1:1), a canal flowing for sixty miles (97 km) from and back into the Euphrates, southeast of Babylon. This context of exile dominates the book. Nebuchadnezzar installed Zedekiah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, as ruler of Judah. He ruled until the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. Though Zedekiah became the last king of Judah, many people, including Ezekiel, considered Jehoiachin to be the last legitimate ruler from the Davidic line. Dates in the book of Ezekiel are therefore all recorded in terms of the years of Jehoiachin’s exile. Zedekiah’s reign was characterized by a similar vacillation between Egypt and Babylon (17:15–19), ending in the disaster of his failed rebellion against Babylon and the total destruction of Judah and Jerusalem. In that context, Ezekiel’s audience faced the temptation to give in to disillusionment and despair. They felt as if God had abandoned them, and they were cut off from His presence, spiritually dead (33:10; 37:1–11). How could they maintain their faith in the Lord when they were surrounded by symbols of the apparently all-conquering Babylonian deities? The answer lay in the Lord’s glorious power and sovereignty, His faithfulness to His promises, and His grace and mercy to those whom He had chosen and called to Himself. There is no reason to doubt the authorship of the book by the prophet himself, writing sometime during the early sixth century B.C. The completed book probably dates shortly after the last oracle, which was received in 571 B.C. It bears the hallmarks of the style of a priest, as one would expect given Ezekiel’s priestly background, and its unified structure and coherent worldview testify to the work of a single author.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Ezekiel, like the works of many of the writing prophets, is a combination of visions, oracles, riddles, and prophetic sign-acts. Oracles are straightforward pronouncements of judgment or hope for the people, outlining the sins for which judgment is coming upon them (especially in the first part of the book) or the attributes of God that will lead Him to deliver the remnant of His people (in the latter portion of the book). A subcategory of this genre consists of the oracles against foreign nations, which occur at the turning point of the book in ch. 24 as the news of the fall of Jerusalem comes to the exiles. A sequence of seven oracles against the nations (chs. 25–32) charges them with delighting in Jerusalem’s fall and assisting the Babylonians in their destructive acts. This was good news for Israel in exile, for it showed that at least part of the promise made to Abraham in Gen. 12:3—“him who dishonors you I will curse”—was still intact. Judgment would come on all those who delighted in the downfall of God’s people and profited from their demise. Sign-acts, in which the prophet accompanies his message with a striking or memorable action that illustrates his point, were particularly prevalent in Ezekiel’s ministry (3:22–26; 4:1–14; 5:1–4; 12:10–20; 21:6, 7, 18–24; 24:15–24; 37:15–28). These were useful means of revelation for resistant audiences who were reluctant to accept God’s word through the prophet. The sign-acts functioned as acted parables, reinforcing the unpalatable message. Ezekiel also used many parables (chs. 15–17; 19; 23) and proverbs (12:21, 22; 16:44; 18:2, 3). The visions that the prophet received lent authenticity to his message. He had personally encountered the God of whom he spoke, and in visions he had been shown the true state of those left behind in Jerusalem, as well as the future for God’s people after the exile. These visions added texture and memorability to the prophet’s words, and the glorious picture of the future that the visions depicted were an encouragement to God’s people to remain faithful in an often dismal and difficult present. The prophecy of Ezekiel had a profound influence on the book of Revelation, with Revelation incorporating many of Ezekiel’s themes.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The book of Ezekiel may be divided into three parts. In the first two, Ezekiel announces judgment on Jerusalem (chs. 1–24) and foreign nations (chs. 25–32). Many among the exiles and those remaining in Jerusalem hoped that the exile would be short, that those who had been deported would soon be returned to the city, and that Jerusalem would be spared further disaster. False prophets wrongly encouraged this belief. Since the Lord had chosen Jerusalem as His dwelling and had Himself defended the city in the past (see Is. 36; 37), many people believed Jerusalem was inviolable. Ezekiel had to warn the exiles that a worse fate was yet in store for Jerusalem because of the people’s long and continuing history of sin. The turning point in the book is the arrival of the news of the destruction of Jerusalem, which brackets the oracles against the nations (24:26, 27; 33:21, 22). After that, Ezekiel’s preaching became dominated by the promises of restoration and mercy for the future (chs. 33–48). This three-part structure (judgment against Israel, judgment against foreign nations, grace and mercy for Israel) can be found also in Isaiah and Zephaniah.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The book of Ezekiel contributes much to our understanding of God and His purposes. Among the prophet’s most significant theological emphases include: 1. The Holiness and Transcendence of God. The exiles were surrounded by emblems of the power of the Babylonian gods. In the face of this, Ezekiel proclaimed the still-greater power and glory of the Lord. Revelation to Ezekiel was therefore often mediated by an angelic guide (chs. 8; 40–48). When Ezekiel did see a vision of God, he could only describe it as “the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord” rather than provide precise details. God is judge, all-knowing and all-powerful, surrounded in splendor and ruling over the affairs of nations. God’s holiness is preeminent. Sin is an affront to His holiness and must be judged. Israel is a rebellious nation, fully deserving of judgment, but the exile is designed to produce a purged nation, a remnant ready to live in obedience before God (6:8; 9:8; 11:12, 13; 12:16; 14:22, 23). Perhaps no other prophet presents as Ezekiel does the history of Israel in such a comprehensive catalog of sin and failure. 2. The Grace and Mercy of God. God’s judgment of Judah and Jerusalem does not frustrate His purpose in electing Israel. God had promised to make Abraham into a mighty nation and bless his descendants (Gen. 12:1–3), and so He would show mercy to a remnant who would inherit His promises afresh and enjoy restoration to their land. Ezekiel’s message to the exiles was that God would again be in their midst (48:35; cf. 11:20; 14:11; 36:23, 27, 28). The nation would again live under a Davidic prince (37:24, 25; 45:7) who rules righteously (34:23). God would give to His people a new heart and a new spirit (36:24–28). Indeed, what the people could not accomplish in their own strength, God would initiate and accomplish on their behalf (cf. chs. 36; 37). 3. The Sovereignty of God. God rules over the affairs and destiny not only of Israel, but also of all other nations (chs. 25–32). The words God spoke through the prophet were certain to be fulfilled, as the destruction of Jerusalem during the prophet’s own ministry demonstrated. Yet the sovereign King had not abandoned His people forever. He would be with the remnant in exile (11:16) and would return to shepherd them (34:11–14) and to restore His sanctuary to their midst forever (37:28).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: When God called His people out of Egypt and made a covenant with them in the wilderness, He held before them life or death, peaceful existence in the land or exile, based on Israel’s obedience or disobedience (see Deut. 28; 29). Yet He announced ahead of time that given Israel’s stubborn attachment to sin, the nation would go into exile but that there in exile they would begin to grasp more fully the vastness of God’s grace (Deut. 30:1–3). Ezekiel was called to prophesy at the other end of that trajectory to people upon whom the covenant curses had descended and to hold out to them the hope of restoration. Yet the glorious vision of restoration in Ezekiel is incomplete. Though God would once again dwell with His people, access to His presence would be strictly limited to prevent the sanctuary from being profaned (chs. 40–44). God’s people would still need regular sacrifices of atonement for their sins (45:15, 17). The fullness of what Ezekiel anticipated does not arrive until the NT, when in Christ we are granted greater access than Ezekiel’s visions describe. In the book of Revelation, we see the New Jerusalem, which is itself an immense Most Holy Place. A perfect cube covered with pure gold, the city needs no temple because the Lord dwells there among His people (Rev. 21:22). In that city, all who are in Christ are freely able to approach the throne of grace and drink from the life-giving stream that flows from it (Rev. 22:1–3; cf. Ezek. 47:1–12).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The glory of God, which Ezekiel saw coming to the temple, arrived in the person of Jesus, of whom John testifies: “We have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). As the glory of God departed from Jerusalem and went to be with His people in exile, so Jesus left His Father’s side to identify with sinful man, suffering “outside the camp” on behalf of His people (Heb. 13:12, 13). The mediator who could not be found to turn aside judgment from Judah (Ezek. 14), is now found in Jesus, the Mediator of the new covenant, who offered His own blood for the sins of His people (Heb. 9:11–15). Jesus is the Good Shepherd promised by Ezekiel who restores justice for His sheep (John 10:11). All those who are in Him are new creatures, filled with the Spirit of God (2 Cor. 5:17; Eph. 5:18). But the salvation revealed in Jesus is far greater even than the salvation revealed to Ezekiel. In Christ, we have boldness to approach the throne of grace (Heb. 4:16). The city toward which we press needs no temple (Rev. 21:22), for the final sacrifice has been offered once and for all by Christ (Heb. 10:10). God has dealt the final blow to all those who would rise up against His city and His people (cf. chs. 38; 39 with Rev. 19; 20). In that city will be not only the full number of the tribes of Israel but a great multitude from all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues (Rev. 7:5–9). EZEKIEL IN THE

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The book of Ezekiel has always been difficult for interpreters. An ancient Jewish rabbi, Hananiah ben Hezekiah, is reported to have burned three hundred barrels of oil in his lamp before he was able to resolve all of the differences between Ezek­iel and the laws of Moses. Other rabbis considered the book too dangerous to be read by anyone under the age of thirty. Given its complex nature, early interpreters often adopted an allegorical approach to exegesis. In a homily on Ezek. 40:6–8, Gregory the Great identified the east gate of the temple as Jesus, the steps leading up to the gate as the merits of the virtues that lead to salvation, and the threshold of the gate as the ancestors of Jesus. For Thomas Aquinas, the closed gate in Ezek. 44:1–3 was the classic proof text for the perpetual virginity of Mary. From at least the time of the Reformation, chs. 38; 39 have often been read against the background of current events. For Martin Luther, Gog was personified in the Muslim Turks, while the seventeenth-century author Joseph Mede thought that the native inhabitants of the New World were descended from the Scythians and would invade Europe in the last days. More recently, dispensationalists have identified the “chief prince” (Hb. rosh ) of Ezek. 38:2 with Russia, Meshech with Moscow, and Tubal with Tobolsk, though these names are all of much more recent origin than the prophet’s time. In spite of the failure of many previous detailed timelines for the end, some continue to argue in the same vein. In the early part of the twentieth century, many scholars saw Ezekiel as advancing a new religious insight of “individual responsibility” that is radically distinct from older biblical texts that stress corporate responsibility (e.g., ch. 18). More recent scholarship has recognized that passages such as Ezek. 18 are more about generational responsibility than individual responsibility. And Ezekiel is clear that the history of any generation does not depend on the behavior of their father’s generation but on its own obedience. Some have also tried to psychoanalyze the prophet in view of his strange behavior. Ezekiel has been diagnosed as having suffered extreme problems in his relationship with his mother, as well as having suffered childhood sexual abuse. These attempts have not found much following, not least because psychoanalyzing a historical person based on his writings is always a highly speculative venture. Equally speculative have been attempts to identify the vision of the divine throne-chariot of ch. 1 as an interaction between the prophet and a spacecraft, a view popularized by author Erich von Däniken. Similar associations between Ezekiel’s vision and spacecraft have been identified in a variety of modern cults such as the Nation of Islam, whose founder, Elijah Muhammad, held such a view.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: The book is named after the person whose life story and prophecies it records. The name “Daniel” means “God is my Judge.”

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The authorship and date of the book of Daniel have been matters of considerable debate among biblical scholars. Traditionally, the prophet Daniel is assumed to be the author, but in recent decades this view has been questioned by many of the so-called “higher-critical” scholars of the Bible. The dispute centers on the way Daniel’s prophecies and visions look forward to a succession of four ancient empires, beginning with the Babylonian Empire (chs. 2; 7; 11). Daniel describes in great detail the historical relations between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms just before and during the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes (ch. 11). To account for this detailed knowledge, many scholars conclude that the book must have been written after the events of which it speaks. In this view, it was written by an unknown author around 170 B.C. , during the lifetime of Antiochus IV, and not during the time of Daniel, who was taken to Bab­ylon in 605 B.C. However, other factors favor the traditional view of authorship, not the least of which is the fact that those who deny that Daniel authored the book that bears his name generally do so because they presuppose that supernatural activities such as predictive prophecy are impossible. The book itself indicates that Daniel was its author (9:2; 10:2) and that it was written shortly after the capture of Babylon by Cyrus in 539 B.C. Also, Jesus quoted the prediction of “the abomination of desolation” found in this book as having been “spoken of by the prophet Daniel” (Matt. 24:15). There is no reason to assume that Daniel, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, could not have predicted in such great detail the events he describes. The Lord, after all, “declar[es] the end from the beginning” (Isa. 46:10) and “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph. 1:11). The book’s message of God’s precise control of future history was very relevant to Daniel himself and the hearers of his own day as they underwent the trials of the exilic period. In assuring his readers that God controls the future, he teaches that the Lord also controls the present, making the prophecies of the future meaningful for Daniel’s original readers and firmly establishing a purpose for Daniel to write his book in the era that he did.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The arguments that have been offered for dating the book of Daniel during the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes involve three issues: (1) the nature of Old Testament prophecy; (2) historical problems; and (3) the Aramaic language used in the book. Each of these topics will be considered in turn. Generally speaking, the prophets of Israel were primarily concerned with the religious and social circumstances confronting their contemporaries, rather than with predicting events in the distant future. When the prophets did predict future events, they often foresaw incidents in the near term, such as Jeremiah’s prophecies about the imminent fall of Jerusalem to the Babylonians. However, Daniel’s vision concerning the “king of the north” and the “king of the south” describes with amazing precision the history of relations between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic empires existing at the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes (11:2–39 and notes), though the description of the circumstances surrounding the death of the king (11:40–12:3) does not correspond to what is otherwise known about Antiochus’s death. On this basis, some scholars argue that the book of Daniel was written in Antiochus’s time, shortly before his death, more than four hundred years after the prophet’s lifetime. The reasoning here is somewhat circular, in that the idea that Israelite prophets did not predict events in the more distant future is based on the assumption that the prophecies in Daniel are late, as well as on a similar assumption regarding Isaiah’s prophecies concerning Cyrus (Is. 44:28; 45:1). A rejection of the possibility of predictive prophecy in general is what drives these conclusions, not actual textual and historical evidence. Interpreters of the book of Daniel who favor a late date of writing also propose that serious historical problems exist in the narratives about Daniel’s experiences in Babylon, particularly concerning Belshazzar’s relationship to Nebuchadnezzar (5:2 note) and the identity of “Darius the Mede” (6:1 note). Such interpreters typically identify the four kingdoms foreseen by Daniel (chs. 2; 7) as the Babylonians, the Medes, the Persians, and the Greeks (including the Seleucids and Ptolemies). This identification is difficult because there is no evidence for a Median kingdom in an interval between the Babylonian and Persian empires. The Persian king Cyrus (r. 550–530 B.C. ) conquered the Medes in 549 B.C. and the Babylonians in 539 B.C. (5:1, 31 notes). On the other hand, many scholars who date the book in the time of Daniel interpret the sequence of kingdoms as the Babylonian, Medo-Persian, Greek, and Roman empires. They point to the reference to “the Medes and Persians” in 5:28 as evidence that Daniel considered them as constituting one kingdom. Other scholars see the number “four” as a symbolic representation of completeness, as in the four winds of heaven (Dan. 7:2). They note the alternation between “kings” and “kingdoms” as if these were entirely interchangeable in Daniel’s mind (cf. 7:17 with 7:23). Concerning the date of the language used in Daniel, a large segment (2:4–7:28) is written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew. The reason for the change of language is not known. The Aramaic is probably of a later type, since the Aramaic of both Ezra and Daniel is closer to the later type of Aramaic found in the Dead Sea Scrolls copied by the community at Qumran than it is to the earlier type of Aramaic (official Aramaic) used in the Persian period (522–330 B.C. ). A strong argument can be made that these late forms entered the book through the work of editors who preserved the prophet’s writings for later generations, using recent Aramaic terms that readers would more easily understand. This practice of modernization of language in manuscript transmission was common in the ancient world, and if this practice is taken into account, there is no reason to suppose that this document could not have been written during Daniel’s years in exile. Finally, many other scholars have demonstrated that much of the Aramaic vocabulary in the book of Daniel was in use long before the period of the Qumran community (167 B.C. –70 A.D. ), pointing the composition of the book occurring in Daniel’s lifetime. Some have pointed to the use of several Greek loanwords for musical instruments (3:5 note) as another indication of a late date. However, there is abundant evidence of contact between the Greeks and the Near East long before the time of Alexander the Great, indeed, even before the fifth century B.C. Such contact is sufficient to explain the appearance of the Greek loanwords. In sum, the language of the book of Daniel does not present any compelling reason to doubt that the book was composed during the prophet’s lifetime.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Daniel falls into two distinct halves. The first portion (chs. 1–6) is a narrative of the challenges faced by Daniel and his three friends (commonly known by their Babylonian names, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego) at the Babylonian court. All four were exiled as young men but maintained a faithful witness to the Lord in spite of persecution. They were miraculously delivered from death in a fiery furnace (ch. 3) and in a lion’s den (ch. 6). In many respects, their behavior models Jeremiah’s counsel to the exiles in Jer. 29 to seek the peace of the city to which they had been exiled while waiting for the Lord to bring them home again. The latter part of the book (chs. 7–12) is apocalyptic; that is, it is a heavenly revelation of the end of the present age of conflict and its replacement with the final, eschatological age of peace, a transformation that is depicted in strange and mysterious imagery. Both parts of the book have the goal of comforting and exhorting the faithful, however, and the message of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream in ch. 2 is essentially the same as that of Daniel’s apocalyptic vision in ch. 7. Both portions speak to those undergoing trials and persecution and seek to give them hope that their present sufferings, however terrible, will not be in vain. God is the powerful sovereign ruler of all things, and He is able to rescue His saints from trials—or through trials—so human faithfulness to God will have its eventual reward.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The historical narratives in Daniel are not a connected historical discourse, but are independent units placed together for a specific purpose. The narratives do not give a history of Israel under Babylonian or Persian rule, nor do they give a biographical history of Daniel or his friends. The common thread is an emphasis on the way God’s absolute sovereignty operates in the affairs of all nations (2:47; 3:17, 18; 4:28–37; 5:18–31; 6:25–28). Nebuchadnezzar’s vision in chapter 2 shows that history is not under the control of other gods, nor can its mystery be discovered by human manipulation. History is under the control of the God who is utterly free to direct it and to reveal it as He pleases (Rev. 5:9). According to His sovereign pleasure, He will intervene among the kingdoms of this world and establish a universal kingdom that will endure forever. These truths are always of importance for God’s people in any era, especially when they suffer for their faith, but also when they suffer in various unexplained ways. The Jews may not have been subject to widespread and systematic persecution during the time of their subjection to Babylonian and Persian rulers, but sometimes they felt strong pressure applied, as Daniel and his friends could testify. Moreover, living in an empire where they were daily bombarded with pagan propaganda on the power of their gods must have challenged the faith of many. Systematic attempts to abolish the faith of the Jews did occurred during the reign of Antiochus IV, who named himself “Epiphanes,” meaning “God manifest.” Antiochus IV, who ruled the Seleucid Empire from 175 to 164 B.C. , tried to force the Jews to accept Greek culture and to abandon their religious practices. Many Jews submitted, but others refused and suffered severe persecution. They would have found great comfort in the book of Daniel, just as the early Christians suffering under the Roman authorities would also have found it intensely relevant in their own day. Daniel’s relevance, of course, has endured long past the era of the first Christians. Those who face the pressure of hostility today can learn from the model of Daniel and his friends, who refused to compromise with paganism at every turn. In addition to these overarching themes of Daniel, certain key concepts are relevant to discussion of the book. One of these is a “time of trouble” (12:1), commonly taken to be the “great tribulation” that is to precede the second coming of Christ (Matt. 24:21; Luke 21:23; Rev. 2:22; 7:14). Matthew links this trouble with “the abomination of desolation” (Matt. 24:15) predicted by Daniel (cf. Dan. 9:27; 12:11) and fulfilled by the Antichrist (the “man of lawlessness” in 2 Thess. 2:3, 4). The “Antichrist” may also be included in Daniel’s theology (Dan. 7:8, 20–22, 24–27; 11:36–45). The word does not occur outside the letters of John (1 John 2:18, 22; 4:3; 2 John 7), but both testaments contain references to a person of satanic hatred who appears in the final days of human history before Christ’s second coming. The Antichrist sets up the “abomination that makes desolate” (Dan. 11:31; cf. Matt. 24:15), exalts himself as a god (Dan. 11:36–39; 2 Thess. 2:3, 4), and is ultimately destroyed by Christ upon His return (Dan. 11:45; 2 Thess. 2:8 [cf. Is. 11:4]; Rev. 19:20).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The primary focus of the book of Daniel is the absolute sovereignty of God. Jerusalem may be destroyed with its temple in ruins, God’s people may be in exile, and wicked rulers may seem triumphant, but God remains supreme. God is greater than all circumstances, and His people should be true to Him in whatever situation they find themselves. The truth of God’s sovereignty should comfort His people during periods of persecution, and indeed, one of the primary purposes of Daniel is to encourage God’s people to trust in the Lord who directs history and whose will cannot be thwarted (4:35). Daniel also urges his readers to look beyond the horizon of their current circumstances, beyond Babylon, Antiochus IV Epiphanes, or Rome, to the coming of Christ, the One whose “dominion is an everlasting dominion.” It is Christ who, according to the purposes of God, will ultimately liberate His people, destroy all human kingdoms, and establish His eternal kingdom of righteousness and peace.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The book of Daniel tells the story of some of the Jews who were exiled by Nebuchadnezzar and testifies to God’s faithfulness to His promise to be with those who were in exile (Jer. 24; Ezek. 11). He sustained them in an often-hostile environment, as He would continue to sustain the remnant of His people after their return (see Ezra–Nehemiah). The promise that the kingdoms of this world will become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ (Rev. 11:15) is anticipated in Daniel’s visions (chs. 2; 7). The kingdom is inaugurated with the first coming of Christ (Matt. 10:7) and will be consummated at Christ’s return. In the meantime, His faithful people will often face the kind of persecution and even martyrdom that God’s people faced in Daniel’s day.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: One of Jesus’ favorite terms for Himself was “Son of Man,” a term that combines the idea of “mere humanity” (as is evident from its use in the book of Ezekiel) with the overtones of the divine and exalted “son of man” in Dan. 7:13. This human figure bears the marks of deity in that he comes on the clouds (a sign of deity throughout the ancient Near East), and receives the right to exercise judgment over all kingdoms and nations. In Dan. 7, the son of man is connected with the “saints” who suffer faithfully in the face of persecution, just as Jesus Himself suffered faithfully for His people. In Luke 20:18 (which combines Dan. 2:34, 35 with Is. 8:14, 15), Jesus is identified as the stone that crushes all previous world empires, replacing them with His own unending kingdom.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: There have been significant variations in overall approach to the book of Daniel, centering especially on its prophecies of the future. These variations fall into three main categories. The first approach is taken by those who conclude that the book was written in the time of Antiochus IV Epiphanes. According to this view, all references to events before the time of Antiochus are ordinary history, written after the events described. The only genuine prediction in the book is of the anticipated death of Antiochus and the expected intervention of God to establish His kingdom. However, Antiochus did not die in the manner depicted (11:36–12:3 note) and the kingdom did not materialize as apparently anticipated, so the interpreters who hold this view see Daniel as a failure in predicting the king’s end. See notes on 2:44; 7:14, 18. This view has largely been held by modern interpreters who have rejected the idea that biblical prophecy can have a predictive component. A second, more traditional view finds the primary emphasis of the book’s predictions to be on events beginning with the first coming of Christ. In this view, the focus is on the establishment of the “kingdom that shall never be destroyed” (2:44) at the coming of the “son of man” (7:13), who comes to “put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness” (9:24). In His obedient life and vicarious death, Christ accomplished salvation for His people and ushered in the kingdom of God, which now awaits consummation at His return. A third view sees a dual focus: one on Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the persecution of God’s people during his reign, and the other on the divine intervention in human affairs at the end of time when God’s kingdom is established. In this view, the emphasis is not on the first coming of Christ (chs. 2; 9 notes), but rather on Antiochus and the second coming of Christ. Within this approach, there are many differences in the interpretation of details by various commentators. Some forms of this view date back to the early church fathers, while others are distinctly more modern, rooted in nineteenth- and twentieth-century dispensationalism. One striking difference is that the early church fathers tended to see the book as a celebration of martyrdom and a call to it, whereas modern dispensationalism has often seen in the book a promise that Christians will be “raptured” before the end, thus avoiding suffering through the worst episodes of history.
