sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: Very little biographical data is provided in this book about its author, the prophet Hosea, the son of Beeri (1:1). The setting of the book is in the northern kingdom, and Hosea demonstrates a deep familiarity with the geography (4:15; 5:1, 8; 6:8, 9; 9:15; 10:5; 12:11), topography (2:22; 10:8), and history (5:13; 7:7, 11; 8:4, 8–14) of that land. Because of his detailed knowledge of Israel, it has been assumed that he was a native of the northern kingdom.

sections.heading: Date
sections.content: Some of the prophets date their ministries according to the reigns of particular kings. For example, Isaiah (1:1), Jeremiah (1:1–3), Daniel (1:1), Micah (1:1), and Zephaniah (1:1) all date their prophecies in conjunction with the rule of Judean kings. Haggai (1:1) and Zechariah (1:1) date their ministries according to the chronology of the kings of Persia. Hosea (1:1) and Amos (1:1) are the only writing prophets who include chronological references to both the kings of Judah and Israel. Hosea prophesied during the reigns of four Judean kings: Uzziah (767–740 B.C. ), Jotham (750–735 B.C. ), Ahaz (735–715 B.C. ), and Hezekiah (c. 727–c. 696 B.C. or 715–686 B.C. ; cf. 2 Kin. 20:1; Is. 36:1; 38:5 notes). The text also indicates that Hosea preached the words of God during the reign of the Israelite king Jeroboam II (793–753 B.C. ). Why the Israelite kings who followed Jeroboam II up until the destruction of the northern kingdom are not listed is unknown, although they are perhaps excluded because of their particular wickedness. In any event, Hosea ministered during the second half of the eighth century B.C. , which was a turbulent time that witnessed its low point with the destruction of the northern kingdom by the Assyrians in 722 B.C.

sections.heading: Occasion
sections.content: During its final years, the northern kingdom of Israel was in a state of political and social decline. The economic prosperity and political security that the nation experienced during the reign of Jeroboam II (c. 793–753 B.C. ) was followed by a period of political and social chaos and religious decline under the next six kings, who reigned for a combined period of twenty-five years (2 Kin. 15:8–17:41). Four of these kings were assassinated by those who usurped their thrones (Zechariah, Shallum, Pekahiah, and Pekah; cf. 2 Kin. 15:10, 14, 25, 30); one became a political prisoner (Hoshea; cf. 2 Kin. 17:3, 4); and only one was succeeded by his son (Menahem; cf. 2 Kin. 15:23). Hosea’s preaching reflects both the relative calm the kingdom experienced under Jeroboam II (2:5, 8, 13) and the later turmoil in domestic (7:3–7; 13:10, 11) and foreign affairs (7:8–12; 12:1). The Syro-Ephraimite war in particular (735–732 B.C. ; 2 Kin. 15:27–30; 16:5–9; Is. 7:1–9) seems to stand behind Hosea’s message in 5:8–10. Pekah of Israel formed an alliance with Rezin of Syria in order to resist the expanding Assyrian Empire ruled by Tiglath-pileser III. Pekah then attacked Judah when it refused to join the alliance with Syria. Assyria responded to Judah’s request for assistance by attacking Syria’s capital, Damascus, and systematically subjugating extensive territory in the northern kingdom of Israel. The northern kingdom’s political vacillation between Egypt and Assyria is also reflected in the text (5:13; 7:11; 8:9, 10; 9:3; 11:5; 12:1). This vacillation brought a further attack by the Assyrians, the arrest of King Hoshea, the siege of Samaria, and finally the end of the northern kingdom. Although this end is expected by Hosea, the fall of Samaria in 722 B.C. had not yet occurred at the time of his prophecy (13:16). In addition to political and social decline, the northern kingdom was also in a state of spiritual decline during the final phase of its history. The ancient faith of Israel, which Hosea describes so beautifully using analogies of marital and parental love (2:14–23; 11:1–4), had become polluted by elements of the Canaanite fertility religion. Such fertility cults focused especially on the worship of Baal, a god revered as the giver of rain and fertility. The Israelites incorporated elements of the Canaanite fertility religion into the orthodox faith, notably sexual rites that included ritual prostitution and drunken orgies (4:10–13). The worship of the Lord and the worship of Baal (whose name literally means “lord” or “master”) became intermingled and even seen as one (2:5–13). Religious corruption evidenced itself not only in this popular, syncretistic form of religion—sometimes called a “baalized” form of Yahweh worship—but also in the lives of the religious leaders. Through corruption, greed, and hardness of heart they not only neglected to instruct the people in the true faith, but also tolerated, and in some cases even sponsored, syncretistic religion (4:4–13; 5:1; 6:9).

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Determining the literary style of the book of Hosea is a complicated task. Because of the way that the text appears in the Hebrew Old Testament and in many English translations, one might suppose that it is entirely poetic. The reality is, however, that the poetic literary style is not uniform throughout the book. In particular, chapters 1–3 do not consistently employ line parallelism, which is a common mark of Hebrew poetry. On the other hand, this material is not normal Hebrew prose either. Although it employs certain markers of narrative, such as the sign of the direct object, the relative pronoun, and the Hebrew article, it is not consistent in using those features. Also, some parts of those chapters are written in the first person and some are not. The writing style seems to fit somewhere between the two genres of poetry and prose; perhaps a designation such as “exalted prose” might be an appropriate name for it. In contrast, chapters 4–14 of the book are more consistently poetic in nature. Hosea’s message is enhanced through his effective use of imagery. The strongest and most extended metaphors derive from the human experience of intimacy. Using the image of human marriage (chs. 1–3) and family life (11:1–4, 10), Hosea depicts God and His relationship with His people. In other figurative images, God is compared to moth and rot (5:12), winter and spring rains (6:3), a lion (5:14; 11:10; 13:7, 8), a leopard (13:7), a bear (13:8), and a cypress tree (14:8).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The central theme of the book of Hosea is Israel’s breaking of the covenant that God made with the people when He redeemed them from Egypt. That covenant was established at Mount Sinai in the desert, at which time the Lord found Israel “like grapes in the wilderness” and “like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season” (9:10). There God took Israel under His wing. There He “loved” Israel and called the people by the familial “my son” (11:1). However, Israel then departed from God, and the more He called after them, the farther they went from Him (11:2). The people fell into great sin and thus broke the covenant God had so graciously made with them. Hosea describes Israel’s sin in great detail. The people continually broke the commandments of the Decalogue (4:1, 2) and, in particular, they practiced idol worship (4:11–14). A forceful illustration of the broken covenant relationship was the unhappy marriage relationship between Hosea and his wife, Gomer (1:2). She proved unfaithful to her husband, and the prophecy teaches that this wandering paralleled Israel’s unfaithfulness to her husband, the Lord. Hosea ended up taking her back, and this act further paralleled God’s frequent activity of restoring Israel after her numerous unfaithful excursions. Hosea’s prophecy not only defines Israel’s sins, but it also warns of impending judgment because of them (5:9–14). The nature of the judgment is twofold: the land of Israel would be laid desolate, and its inhabitants would be thrown into exile (5:13; 8:8, 9). Although judgment would certainly come upon Israel, Hosea includes a note of joy and hope for the people of God in the future after judgment. Israel’s coming punishment would not be the end, but God would one day bring about a splendid time of restoration (1:10, 11; 2:14–23).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Hosea’s theology is rooted in the past acts of the Lord in behalf of His people. He called Israel out of Egypt (11:1), and He cared for the nation in the wilderness (11:3, 4). The Lord then settled and secured Israel in the land of Canaan. He served as the divine husband to His wife, Israel (2:16). Thus, at the very heart of God’s relationship with Israel was God’s fidelity, faithfulness, and keeping of the covenant. The Lord never wavered in His covenant loyalty to Israel. On the other hand, Israel had a history of infidelity to the covenant. She pursued “her lovers” (2:7) by going after other gods repeatedly. She went so far as to “hire lovers” (8:9), an act that compares Israel’s idolatry to an act of prostitution. Israel violated the terms of the covenant again and again (4:2; 8:1). This concept of idolatry as adultery is vividly symbolized in the primary imagery of the book, which concerns the infidelity of Hosea’s wife. Hosea’s final message is a call to Israel to repentance and covenant renewal (14:1–9). God takes the initiative again by wooing His wayward wife to return to Him. The long-suffering and patient character of God to His covenant promises is highlighted by this climactic summons. Israel’s unfaithfulness is ultimately overshadowed by God’s faithfulness.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In the New Testament, Hosea is prominently remembered as the prophet of hesed , which is a Hb. term meaning “steadfast love” or “covenant loyalty.” This concept takes center stage because Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,” twice in the gospel of Matthew (9:13; 12:7). In these two passages Jesus is teaching against the idea of mere external practice as fulfilling the true worship of God. Rather, Jesus quotes Hosea to demonstrate that true worship comes only from a heart that loves mercy. The book of Hosea is foundational to the New Testament teaching regarding the restoration of the people of God. The Apostle Paul quotes two restoration texts from the book of Hosea in his pivotal teaching in Romans 9:25, 26. Paul understands that judgment on Israel took place at her destruction and exile. Promises of restoration, found in Hosea 1:10 and 2:23, are fulfilled under the new covenant through Jesus Christ.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Within the book of Hosea, Christ is perhaps most evident in the much-discussed passage of 11:1, “Out of Egypt, I called my son.” Where Israel failed in her faithlessness to God, Christ prevails as the true son of Israel. He has not only paid the penalty for our constant spiritual whoredom, but He has also been the perfect law-keeper and therefore offers the positive righteousness demanded by God’s holy law. His work as Messiah brings about the final restoration of the people of God.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Hosea was often commented upon in the ancient church, the most significant interpreters being Jerome and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Some approached the text looking for the literal and plain sense while others, such as Cyril of Alexandria, employed a more allegorical method. In modern times, different approaches to this book have been proposed. Higher-critical scholarship has focused primarily on the marriage imagery of chapters 1–3. From 1900 through 1980, scholarship particularly attempted to write a biography on Hosea and his relationship with Gomer. Since then, feminist interpretation has also emerged in studies of chapters 1–3. Recent scholarship has provided a corrective to an exclusive focus on the first three chapters and is instead focusing on the whole book once again. Literary developments in biblical studies have begun to obtain a foothold, and they will not doubt continue to play a key role in interpreting the book for the foreseeable future.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The main problem in the interpretation of the book of Hosea is an ethical one. How could God have commanded Hosea to take “a wife of whoredom” and to bear “children of whoredom” (1:2)? At face value, it appears that the Lord commanded Hosea to marry a known prostitute. This moral dilemma has been dealt with in a variety of ways. Some argue that this text actually refers to later period, in which Gomer only became a prostitute after marrying Hosea and bearing him a son. Others believe that Gomer was not a common prostitute but rather a woman involved in cultic prostitution related to the fertility religion of Baal. Some have contended that perhaps Hosea never married Gomer, or perhaps that the entire story is mere allegory. The most obvious reading of the text is that the prophet actually married Gomer knowing that she would become unfaithful, and this circumstance was analogous to the Lord’s relationship to Israel, for He married her even though He knew she would prove unfaithful (Deut. 31:16). This human marriage thus gives clarity and vividness to the breaking of the covenant between Israel and God. The moral question deepens when one considers 3:1, 2. If the woman in question is not Gomer, then Hosea pays for a prostitute who is not his wife. Again, some would argue that this is mere metaphor or perhaps this is a second wife for Hosea. The dominant view, however, is that Gomer is the woman of chapter 3. Similarly, questions have been asked about Hosea’s children. Their names, like that of the child born to Isaiah and the prophetess in Is. 8:1–4, are intended to have symbolic significance (cf. Is. 7:3; Ezek. 23). The names given to Hosea’s children (Jezreel, Lo-ruhama, and Lo-ammi; 1:4, 6, 9 and notes) both illustrate Hosea’s message about God’s increasing displeasure with wayward Israel and also convey a message of hope, renewal, love, and restoration (2:21–23 notes). The fact that children’s names have meaning in the Old Testament does not signify that they were fabricated at a later time or that they were merely metaphorical. Rather, names were often bestowed on children that reflected the character of the child, a circumstance at the time of the child’s birth, or a prophecy concerning the child’s future.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: Joel is the prophetic speaker of the words of the text (1:1). His name is a compound in Hebrew that literally means “Yahweh is God.” Since he is unknown from any other texts in the Old Testament, what we do know of him derives solely from the book itself. Joel’s keen interest in Jerusalem, particularly in the temple and its functionaries (e.g., 1:9, 13, 14; 2:14–17, 32; 3:1, 6, 16, 17), suggests that he lived in Jerusalem and may have often ministered near the temple.

sections.heading: Date
sections.content: There are no specific chronological indicators within the book to help determine the date of its composition. Many scholars today date its writing to the time of the exile, after the destruction of Jerusalem at the hands of the Babylonians (586 B.C. ). Those who hold to this dating scheme often rely on arguments from silence, such as the fact that no king is mentioned nor is Israel, the northern kingdom, spoken of. However, the setting of the prophecy is in the land of Judah, and temple worship is spoken of throughout the book. This evidence points to the fact that the book of Joel is not exilic but was written before Judah fell to Babylon. With all that in mind, however, it is perhaps best to conclude with Calvin that the date of the book cannot be known with certainty.

sections.heading: Occasion
sections.content: The occasion of the book of Joel concerns a locust plague that descended upon Judah, one without parallel in the country’s history (1:2). The basic economy was ruined (1:11, 12). Even the sacrificial offerings in the temple were discontinued because of the vast agricultural devastation (1:13). Joel believed this plague to be God’s judgment on Judah because they were unrepentant (2:12, 13). It was, however, merely a temporal judgment but one that served as a warning or foretaste of a greater judgment that God will bring on impenitent people in the form of the eschatological “day of the Lord.”

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Joel is a work of prophecy that is relayed primarily in a poetic fashion. The use of line parallelism, an indicator of Hebrew poetry, is prominent in the prophecy. For example, Joel 1:11 says, Be ashamed, O tillers of the soil; wail, O vinedressers, for the wheat and the barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The prophet also employs numerous figures of speech, another indicator of Hebrew poetry, to provide vivid descriptions of his message. His use of symbolism, particularly in the locust plague, is a key feature of the book. Joel’s prophecy is highly structured around the themes of judgment, deliverance, and “the day of the Lord.” The writer uses this repetition to underscore and emphasize the certainty of judgment. Beginning at 2:28, the pivot or hinge of the book is the monumental description of God pouring out His Spirit on His people. By the close of the book, great hope is held out for a restored Judah, Jerusalem, and proper temple worship.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The principal theme of the book of Joel is “the day of the Lord,” a time of direct divine intervention in human history to reorder affairs on earth. This theme is associated with judgment upon Israel and Judah as well as the overthrow of their enemies. Such interventions in the flow of world history anticipated the final divine transformation of the day of judgment. Specifically the day of the Lord in Joel is focused on a future judgment against Judah and Jerusalem (2:32), and ultimately against all the nations of the world (3:1, 2). The day of the Lord also holds out a hope of restoration after judgment in which there will be a future deliverance for a repentant Israel (2:32). Repentance is another key theme in Joel’s prophetic message. The call to repentance is given not merely to a select number of the covenant community but rather to all the Lord’s people who are called to return to Him: young and old, men and women, leaders and followers, and even those who might otherwise be exempted from community responsibilities (nursing mothers and newlyweds, 1:13, 14; 2:15–17). The return to God that Joel calls for involves the whole person. Such repentance is to be manifested externally through actions such as mourning, weeping, crying out to the Lord, and fasting (1:13, 14; 2:15–17). Because merely external or ritual manifestations of repentance are not adequate, the Lord calls the people also to show the sincerity of repentance by returning to the Lord “with all” their hearts (2:12, 13). Joel also reminds God’s people that motivation for repentance lies firmly in the nature of God: “he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love” (2:13). Joel stresses that the hope of restoration lies ultimately in God, who exercises His sovereign freedom and grace in granting repentance and forgiveness to the people.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The book of Joel follows a pattern found in the majority of the prophetic books of the OT: oracles of judgment followed by oracles of salvation. Underpinning this common prophetic refrain is belief in the sovereignty of God. When, for example, Joel describes the locust plague that struck Judah (and symbolizes an invading army), he believes that it is the Lord who brought it (1:15; 2:11, 25). The ensuing repentance and salvation of the people also unfolds according to the providence of God (2:28, 29). Nature itself is at the beck and call of the Lord. Joel thus demonstrates that the Lord’s sovereign control extends to all things, including nature and human events. This complex vision of both the judgment and salvation of God leads to the declaration, “So you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who dwells in Zion, my holy mountain” (3:17). The stress on the day of the Lord in Joel is also a significant contribution to biblical eschatology (doctrine of last things). Joel reminds readers that they cannot take present peace or prosperity for granted, that there is a day of judgment coming for the whole world in which all will have to make an account before God (3:1, 2). On that day, all who have not turned to the one true Lord through His Son, Jesus Christ, will find themselves under divine wrath.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The book of Joel has had an important place in the life of the church. The New Testament indicates that Jesus and His followers were familiar with the writings of Joel. The book’s influence is most evident in the New Testament passages that speak of the end times. They use Joel’s vivid images to describe the day of the Lord and the plague of locusts (e.g., Mark 13:24; Luke 21:25; Rev. 6:12, 13; 9:2, 3). Also important are the promises in Joel 2:28–32, which Peter quotes at Pentecost, claiming they have reached their fulfillment in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the disciples in Jerusalem (Acts 2:16–21). Paul in Rom. 10:13 also refers to the prophecy, using Joel 2:32 to show that “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.” Salvation is offered to all peoples. As Joel states: “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved” (2:32). The church has continued to find the teaching in the book of Joel on the day of the Lord to be an important source of hope and comfort on the one hand, and a word of warning on the other. In times of distress and trouble, Christians have found the promises about the ultimate blessing, protection, and vindication of the Lord’s covenant community to be consoling and inspiring. At the same time, Joel’s graphic depiction of the dreadful aspects of the day of the Lord has served as a reminder of God’s holiness and judgment, and as a continuing call to wholehearted repentance and holiness of life.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: With the possible exception of 2:23 (see note), Joel does not directly mention a personal messiah or a royal deliverer. However, his prophecy frequently depicts general conditions of blessing associated with messianic times. Christ is evident in the text of Joel in the prophet’s climactic description of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit mentioned in (2:28–32), which was fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21). All those who repent and call on the name of the Lord will be saved (Acts 2:38–41; Rom. 10:13). Joel outlines the whole program of messianic intervention and deliverance, though he does so in general terms without chronological detail.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Over the centuries, interpreters have struggled with many questions connected to the book of Joel, notably its occasion and date, and also whether the locust plague is to be understood literally or figuratively. Most ancient interpreters of Scripture saw that the invasion of locusts in ch. 1 as referring to a literal event brought on by the faithlessness of the people. However, many of these same interpreters found in ch. 2 references to the locusts as also having symbolic significance of later military invasions of the land. Some ancient readers, such as Gregory the Great interpreted the locusts as a hierarchy of vices. Theodore of Mopsuestia concluded that the locust plague did not refer to any natural phenomenon, but to the Assyrian and Babylonian invasions, though not to those of later times. Though Jerome also adopted a figurative interpretation, he argued that the various types of locust in 1:4 anticipated a series of invasions culminating in that of the Romans.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The opening verse of the book identifies the speaker of the prophecy as “Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa” (1:1). Tekoa was a town in Judah some five miles (8 km) south of Bethlehem and nine miles (14 km) south of Jerusalem. Little else is known about the prophet apart from his own statement in 7:14 that he was “a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs.” He was therefore not a professional prophet, but God called him from the fields to bring the divine word especially to the people of the northern kingdom of Israel. Although his background was rural and apparently isolated from centers of learning, Amos clearly knew the surrounding nations and was acquainted with international history (1:3–2:3). He was also familiar with both the history of God’s covenant people and the covenant itself, as his references to the covenant obligations make clear.

sections.heading: Date
sections.content: According to Amos 1:1, the prophet’s ministry occurred during the reigns of Jeroboam II of Israel (793–753 B.C. ) and of Uzziah of Judah (792–740 B.C. ). Both of these reigns were long and, therefore, the timeframe for Amos’s prophecy is a broad one. The first verse of the book also dates Amos’s ministry beginning “two years before the earthquake.” We are not certain of the exact date of this earthquake, but it must have been a devastating one because the prophet Zechariah mentions it as well (Zech. 14:5). The reference to the earthquake, in addition to helping to date the ministry of Amos, may also be a symbolic harbinger of God’s judgment to come. In this regard, it may be similar to Joel’s use of a locust plague (Joel 1:1–3).

sections.heading: Occasion
sections.content: Under both kings, Uzziah and Jeroboam II, there was an economic, military, and cultural renaissance in the countries of Judah and Israel. It was a period of stability and prosperity. There was peace between Judah and Israel, and foreign threats were minimal. Jeroboam II, in particular, revived Israel by restoring the ancient borders of the kingdom extending from Lebo-hamath in central Syria to the north to the Dead Sea to the south. This territorial expansion had been predicted by the prophet Jonah son of Amittai (2 Kin. 14:25; Jon. 1:1). The reign of Jeroboam II was one of immense prosperity in the north, but this great wealth was accompanied by severe oppression of the poor. The prophet Amos entered that scene, prophesied primarily to the northern kingdom, and thundered against Israel’s persecution of the needy and downtrodden. Under Tiglath-pileser III (745–727 B.C.), Assyria gained strength and expanded to the north and west. Judah soon became an Assyrian vassal, and the state of Damascus, which had once stood between Israel and Assyria, became part of the Assyrian empire (2 Kin. 16:7–9). Tiglath-pileser III was succeeded by his son, Shalmaneser V (727–722 B.C.), who continued his father’s policy of westward expansion and forced Hoshea, king of Israel, to become his vassal. Hoshea rebelled, however, and mistakenly relied on Egypt for help that never came. Then Shalman­eser besieged Samaria, and after three years the Israelite capital fell (722 B.C.) and the northern kingdom of Israel came to an end (2 Kin. 17:3–6).

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Amos is a prophecy that is related almost entirely in Hebrew poetry. As with almost all poetical literature of the Bible, the written materi­al takes on a variety of forms: so in Amos we see oracles related poetically (1:3–2:16); hymns given poetically (4:13; 5:8, 9; 9:5, 6), and sermons presented poetically (3:1–6:14). The prophet is a master of striking imagery. Just consider 7:1–9:10, wherein Amos presents five pictures that demonstrate graphically the coming judgment of God. These symbols add a level of vividness to the prophet’s message that prose narrative cannot convey. The message of Amos may be divided into four major sections. The first two chapters are composed of proclamations of God’s judgment against Israel and seven of her neighbors: Damascus, Philistia, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and Judah (1:3–2:16). All the neighboring nations are accused of crimes against humanity, such as physical violence and oppression against other people. The prophet brings the longest accusation against Israel (2:6–16). The second section deals more specifically with the sins of the northern kingdom of Israel, and the divine judgment that will come upon that nation is expanded and elucidated (3:1–6:14). Amos confronts the rulers of Israel with their wicked and unjust ways, and he calls them to repentance. The coming judgment he proclaims includes the destruction of palaces and holy places, the overthrow of the kingdom, and exile for the people (5:27). The third section consists of five visions of the prophet (7:1–9:10). The first two visions (locusts and flood, 7:1–6) threaten divine judgment against Israel. The next two visions of a plumb line (7:7–9) and a basket of ripe fruit (8:1–14) point out the reality that Israel cannot avert God’s sentence. The final vision of God in the temple (9:1–10) pictures Him poised to strike in judgment. The last section of the prophecy promises a restoration of the fallen people of Israel (9:11–15). In a future time, God will raise up the Davidic dynasty, and Israel will be restored to a fertile land. Many commentators agree that this section refers to the Messiah, the coming king and son of David who will establish a final and eternal kingdom. This closing section is like a thunderclap. Up to this point the prophet has homed in on the certainty of judgment that is to come, but now he closes with great hope for a post-judgment restoration of the house of David. This promise of restoration is the great crescendo of the book.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Amos may have delivered the prophecies of this book at different places in the northern kingdom, such as Samaria and Bethel. It is certain only that he fulfilled some of his prophetic ministry at Bethel (7:12, 13). Unlike the messages of earlier prophets (with the possible exception of Joel), the words of Amos were preserved in writing as were those of his contemporaries Isaiah and Hosea. It was essential that these great covenant lawsuit messages be preserved both as reminders of Israel’s history and for the promises of restoration and redemption they contained. Amos attacks two major areas of sin commonly indicted by the prophets: idolatry and social injustice. Israel’s root problem was its false religion—“having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:5). Although Israel maintained the ritual formalities of the law, and even exceeded them (4:4, 5), idolatry was commonplace (2 Kin. 17:9–17; Amos 5:26), as were violence and injustice (2:6–8; 4:1). Amos’s boldness is worth noting. His speeches against the enemies of Israel would have been well received by the inhabitants of the northern tribes of Israel (1:3–2:3). These northern tribes constituting Israel also would have welcomed the judgment Amos pronounces on Judah (2:4, 5). Then Amos delivers his prophetic message of judgment to Israel, doing so without fear of an audience that would likely turn on him at that point (2:6ff.). The Lord sent warnings to Israel in the form of hunger, thirst, blight, locusts, plagues, and military defeat, but the people had refused to see His hand in these (4:6–11). Judgment must follow (4:12–5:20), and this punishment is portrayed in a series of verbal and visionary prophecies predicting wholesale destruction and exile. But the Lord chastises those He loves, and His judgment is really a sign of faithfulness to His covenant people. He promises to restore “the booth of David that is fallen” (9:11), and the ultimate future of His people is portrayed in a concluding description that resembles Eden in its fruitfulness and blessedness (9:13–15).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The God we encounter in Amos is the Creator who made human beings in His image. He is God, and there is no other. He does not tolerate idolatry, which in reality is the worship of demons (Deut. 32:16, 17; 1 Cor. 10:20). The Lord is sovereign and able to raise up one nation against another in judgment (1:3–2:3), a process that will continue until Christ’s return. God is also Judge, and He is even willing to raise up another nation to punish His people Israel (6:14). But for all this, He is a loving God who desires the life, not the death, of His people. Above all, He desires that they should “seek me and live” (5:4; 1 Tim. 2:3, 4).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Amos’s great restoration prophecy of 9:11, 12 is directly quoted in the book of Acts (15:16, 17), based on the Septuagint. The New Testament context is the Jerusalem Council in which the early church is considering whether or not Gentiles need to be circumcised in order to be saved (15:1). James, arguing against the Judaizers, quotes the Amos passage as confirmation that the restoration of the kingdom has begun. The raising up of the fallen hut of David (Amos 9:11) has already commenced with the appearance of the messianic son of David, Jesus Christ. The possession of all the nations upon whom the Lord reveals His name (Amos 9:12) has already begun to be fulfilled by the inclusion of the Gentiles into the kingdom of God inaugurated by the coming of the Messiah.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The restoration prophecies in Amos find ultimate fulfillment in the work of Jesus Christ. As noted above, the message of Amos 9:11, 12 is taken by Luke in the book of Acts and applied to the inclusion of the Gentiles under the missionary work of the apostles. As Amos foresaw that Edom would be brought under David’s kingship (9:12), so Gentiles are brought under the kingship of David’s greater son (Acts 15:16, 17).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: In Jewish tradition, interpretation centers on three different issues: the death of Amos, the date of Amos, and the consequences of the prophet’s confrontation with Amaziah. Though modern scholarship tends to date Amos as the oldest of the writing prophets, rabbinic exegesis placed Amos’s date after Hosea but before Isaiah. In the Christian tradition, many ancient writers commented on the destruction of the temple in A.D. 70 as a sign of the end of the old covenant and the beginning of the new covenant. The church fathers found many analogies to the crucifixion of Christ, the rending of the temple curtain, and the subsequent earthquake in their connections with the reference to the earthquake at the beginning of Amos. Several ancients attempted to find historical references to what they perceived to be the original horizon of the prophet. For example, Theodoret of Cyrus made reference to the Babylonians and Assyrians, noting how Hosea, Joel, and Amos were contemporaries. Theodore of Mopsuestia recognized that Amos spoke in almost all his prophecy of the future destruction of Israel.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: Like other prophetic books, this prophecy is named after its author. We know little of the prophet other than his name, which means “servant or worshiper of the L ORD .” The name itself appears to have been a common one, being used of twelve different people in the Old Testament. The value and authority of the message rests on the foundation that “the L ORD has spoken” (v. 18), and not on the fame or prominence of the messenger.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Since the book contains no evidence concerning the prophet’s family and provides no chronological information based on the reigns of kings, students of this prophecy have long debated the date of its composition. The prophet has in view a military assault on Jerusalem in which the Edomites gleefully took part (vv. 11–14), but he does not provide information that clearly dates the catastrophe. Some link the book to an invasion of Judah by Philistines and Arabs during King Jehoram’s reign (848–841 B.C. .), in which it is presumed that the Edomites participated (2 Kin. 8:20–22; 2 Chr. 21:8–10, 16, 17). Others relate the events prompting this prophecy to the Babylonian invasions of Judah, which resulted eventually in her collapse in 586 B.C. . Both Scripture (Ps. 137; Ezek. 35:1–15). Jewish tradition explicitly mentions the Edomites’ involvement in this final catastrophe, and the text of Obadiah seems to refer more naturally to the Bab­ylonian assaults. Furthermore, striking similarities between vv. 1–9 and Jer. 49:7–9, 14–16 suggest that Obadiah and Jeremiah were addressing Edom at roughly the same time. While we cannot date Obadiah precisely, we know that Jeremiah prophesied from about 626 B.C. . until after 586 B.C. . Furthermore, a date before the Babylonian campaign against Edom in 553 is suggested by the references to the future calamity to come on that land.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The title of the book describes it as a “vision,” a term used occasionally of messages communicated by God to prophets (e.g. Nah. 1:1; Hab. 2:3, 4). Apart from a short prose introduction, the vision is presented in poetic language.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Obadiah possessed exceptional literary skill, as is demonstrated in this brief but powerful composition of twenty-one verses. Irony, striking imagery, double entendre, and deliberate use of repetition are all employed to good effect. The divine message of the book begins by addressing the nations, who are called to execute God’s judgment upon Edom (v. 1). This is immediately followed by words addressed to Edom that set out God’s case against this nation and the nature of her punishment (vv. 2–18). In the final verses of the book, God describes the restoration of exiled Israel and the establishment of God’s kingdom (vv. 19–21). The announcement of Edom’s punishment for taking advantage of Judah is balanced by the promise of reinstatement for God’s people.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The prophecy is “concerning Edom” (v. 1) and is repeatedly addressed to that nation, but it was given to the covenant community as holy Scripture. The purpose, therefore, more than to warn Edom of imminent judgment, is to reassure God’s people of His triumphant justice at work for them. Edom prospered, Judah lay defeated, and the moral order of the world appeared to have been overthrown by lawless forces. But the prophet Obadiah was raised up with a message of God’s sovereign justice in order to strengthen His people’s weakened faith. The righteous purposes of God determine history, not the evil wills of men (Lam. 4:22).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The book of Obadiah highlights in particular the justice of God and His power to call nations to account for their actions against others. Edom did not believe it would ever have to answer for its cruelty against the people of Judah. But God summons the nations to punish Edom, ensuring that His covenantal commitment to the descendants of Abraham is not meaningless.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The relationship between Edom and Israel is unique because of their common ancestry as nations. Both are descended from Abraham’s son, Isaac, to whom Rebekah bore twin boys (Gen. 26:20–26). However, whereas Esau, also known as Edom, was the elder of the boys, God’s promises to Abraham were eventually confirmed in his younger brother, Jacob, later renamed Israel. The turbulent relationship between the two brothers is described in detail in Gen. 25–32. Of note is the fact that Esau/Edom despised his birthright as the firstborn son and sold it to Jacob for a bowl of stew (Gen. 25:29–34). When Jacob later deceived his father into giving him the blessing of the firstborn, Esau vowed to kill Jacob (Gen. 27). Eventually, after a period of exile in Paddan-aram, Jacob returned to Canaan and was reconciled with Esau (Gen. 32). However, the future relationship between the two nations was fraught with tension in spite of their kinship. Cf. Mal. 1:2–5.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: There are no specific references in Obadiah to the coming of a future messianic king. It is the Lord Himself who will intervene to reorder the affairs of “all the nations” (v. 15). The universal scope of the coming judgment is one aspect of the wider messianic deliverance foretold by the prophet. Despite Edom’s participation in the destruction of Jerusalem, God’s concern for His people will ensure that they are restored to enjoyment of divine blessing while their enemies are overthrown. There is a time coming when the land will be settled harmoniously by diverse groups (vv. 19, 20), a characteristic of the blessing to be enjoyed in the messianic age (Ps. 72:7, 8).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Throughout history, when the church has suffered at the hands of God’s enemies, the message of the prophecy of Obadiah has provided inspiration and support. It reminds us that God cares for His persecuted people, and behind their present circumstances He is always at work for them.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: This fifth book of the twelve Minor Prophets takes its name from its principal character, “Jonah the son of Amittai” (1:1). Of Amittai, nothing is known. Outside of this composition Jonah is mentioned only in 2 Kin. 14:25, as “Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher,” the proclaimer of God’s blessing to the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jer­oboam II (793–753 B.C. ). In accordance with that prophecy, Jeroboam extended the borders of his kingdom beyond the frontier of Syria. The divine message to Nineveh found in this book was spoken through this same Jonah; presumably, he or some other scribe wrote down this narrative after the events recounted.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Based on 2 Kin. 14:25, the events recorded in the book of Jonah should be assigned to the mid-eighth century B.C. Determining the date of the book’s composition is a difficult task, however, and the book has been dated between the eighth and late third centuries B.C. No compelling evidence precludes an eighth-century date for the composition of the narrative (3:3 note), and it seems likely that the book was written before the destruction of Nineveh in 612 B.C. The reign of Jeroboam II provides the setting for the Jonah story. This monarch was one of the strong military leaders in the history of the northern kingdom of Israel. According to 2 Kin. 14:25–28, he imposed his authority on the territories of Damascus and Hamath, thereby restoring Israel’s northern frontier to where it had been in the days of Solomon (1 Kin. 8:65). It is clear that Jeroboam’s reign, together with that of his Judean contemporary Azariah (also called Uzziah, 792–740 B.C. ), ushered in a period of remarkable peace and prosperity. As both Elisha and Jonah had prophesied (2 Kin. 13:19–25; 14:25), the northern kingdom enjoyed territorial expansion at the expense of Syria. By the outward appearances of population growth, territorial expansion, and commercial activity, Israel was indeed blessed by God. However, this was not the picture that was painted by the contemporary prophets Hosea and Amos as the kingdom fell into a state of social, moral, and religious decay. Their messages consisted, in part, of indictment and judgment of the nation for mixing the prescribed worship of the Lord with the idolatry of the surrounding peoples (religious syncretism) and for social injustice (Hos. 2:1–13; 4:1–5:14; Amos 2:6–16; 3:9–15). Eventually, because of their sin, God punished the people of Israel by sending the Assyrians, who under their king, Sargon II, captured Israel’s capital city, Samaria, in 722 B.C. According to Assyrian records, Sargon took into captivity more than 27,000 people. Since Hosea prophesied this punishment at the hands of the Assyrians (see Hos 9:3; 10:6; 11:5), Jonah probably realized that his actions in calling the people of Nineveh to repent would ultimately result in the destruction of his own nation.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of Jonah is a complex and highly artistic short story told in a compelling manner. As for the interpretation of the Jonah story proper, four distinct approaches have been suggested: allegory, midrash , parable, and historical narrative. Allegory is a method of teaching truths or principles by means of symbolic fictional narrative. A good example is John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress , an exciting fictional story that conveys the truth that the Christian life is a spiritual pilgrimage. However, the text of Jonah lacks any compelling indication that would call for such an allegorical understanding. Midrash is a type of commentary on Scripture classically carried on by Jewish scholars during the first thousand years of the Christian era. Jonah is treated by some as a type of early midrash , or commentary, on passages such as Ex. 34:6, 7 (cf. Jon. 4:2), a commentary in which the events depicted are not necessarily historical. Such an approach fails to reckon with credible defenses of the book’s historicity and appears to conflict with Christ’s witness regarding Jonah’s experiences (Matt. 12:39–42; Luke 11:29–32). The interpretation of the book of Jonah as a parable is perhaps the most common. A parable is a brief and usually fictitious story that conveys moral, religious, or spiritual truths. Parables are best illustrated by the teachings of Jesus (e.g., Matt. 13:45, 46; Luke 10:29–37; 15:11–32). Nathan’s parable in 2 Sam. 12:1–4 is a good Old Testament example. This view understands the Jonah narrative as a moral story with a teaching aim. There are a number of objections, however, to understanding the book of Jonah as a parable, such as the unusual complexity and length of the story. Also, and significantly, this interpretation also deprives the book of its historical foundation. In spite of its shocking surprises and sensational elements, Jonah should be understood as historical and prophetic narrative. The story centers on a specific figure and was written as a historical composition. Jewish tradition regards the narrative as history, and Christ’s references to the story (Matt. 12:38–41; Luke 11:29–32) lend further support to the historicity of the work. Jesus did not understand the Jonah story as a mere parable, but as a narrative firmly rooted in historical reality. Nevertheless, some scholars challenge the historical interpretation on several grounds, including the impossibility of the prophet’s survival inside the fish, the unlikelihood of the Ninevites’ dramatic repentance, the size of Nineveh at the time, and the fast rate of growth of the plant in chapter 4. Although some of these objections raise questions that must be considered and addressed, many of the criticisms spring from assumptions that deny God’s sovereignty in nature and history, including His ability to intervene supernaturally in the created order.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Although some scholars have challenged the literary unity of the book, suggesting theories of composite authorship or of substantial changes by a later editor, the present structure of the book suggests that it has been carefully composed. The book falls into two halves; the start of each is marked by God’s commanding Jonah to go to Nineveh. While some scholars have questioned the authenticity of Jonah’s thanksgiving psalm in 2:2–9 for his own rescue from death, it forms a striking contrast with his lack of gratitude in chapter 4 for the divine deliverance of the Ninevites. Unlike some stories whose plot structure demonstrates a kind of climax followed by a period of resolution, Jonah’s plot does not reach a climax until the end of chapter 4, which also concludes the book. It is one of only two books in the entire Hebrew Bible that end with a question (the other is Nahum).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Various themes have been suggested as summarizing the message of the book of Jonah. 1. Repentance. With good reason, Jews have traditionally read the book of Jonah on the Day of Atonement as part of their expression of repentance. Jews are to follow the example of the pagan sailors and wicked Ninevites who respond with repentance to prophetic preaching. 2. Unfulfilled prophecy. The nonfulfillment of Jonah’s pronouncement against the city of Nineveh draws attention to the conditional nature of divine prophecies. 3. Jewish attitudes towards Gentiles. The story of Jonah reveals that God’s salvation is not restricted to the Jews, but freely given to Gentiles. 4. Theodicy. The story examines the relationship between divine justice and mercy. Of these alternatives, the last has much to commend it, especially in the light of chapter 4, where a contrast is drawn between God’s pity for Nineveh and His destruction of the plant. Jonah, however, pities the plant, but calls for the destruction of Nineveh. Set against God, Jonah represents those who see divine justice and mercy as serving their own interests: mercy for themselves, but justice for their enemies. However, as the book of Jonah reveals, God is sovereign, His justice is impartial, and His forgiveness may extend to anyone. Despite the narrative’s focus on the prophet, the book of Jonah is a story about the mercy and love of God. The Lord was the God of Israel, and that nation had been the special recipient of His covenant mercy and salvation. But Jonah, along with many of his countrymen, had responded with a national pride and ethnic particularism that blinded him to the grand scope of God’s grace. Jonah was to learn, along with the nation, that Israel did not have a monopoly on the redemptive love of God (Acts 10:34, 35; Rom. 3:29). The story affirms the words of Ps. 145:8: “The Lord is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.” Additionally, the book emphasizes God’s willingness to forgive the Ninevites even while knowing that soon afterward they would decimate the northern kingdom of Israel. Jonah cannot reconcile God’s forgiveness of the wicked inhabitants of Nineveh with His willingness to punish His own people Israel.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: The theme of God’s universal sovereignty over humanity and creation is maintained throughout the book. God is presented as the Creator, the Maker of land and sea (1:9). Creation responds obediently to His every command (1:4, 15, 17; 2:10; 4:6–8). Like the Assyrians of Isaiah’s day did God’s bidding (though unwittingly; Is. 10:5–7), creation serves the will of the Creator.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In the New Testament, Jesus uses Jonah’s theme of God’s mercy on the nations as a rebuke to unrepentant Israel (Matt. 12:38–41; Luke 11:29–32). If the Ninevites repented at the preaching of the prophet Jonah, who was rescued from confinement in the huge fish, how much more should Israel repent at the preaching of Jesus, the Son of Man, who will be resurrected from the tomb? In a sense, then, Jesus magnifies God’s mercy on the Gentiles in order to rouse Israel to envy and repentance; the apostle Paul would do the same by his preaching to the Gentiles (Rom. 11:11–14).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: When some Pharisees and teachers of the law demanded a miraculous sign from Jesus, he told them that the only sign they would receive would be “the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matt. 12:39–42; cf. 16:4; Luke 11:29–32). Several comparisons exist between Jesus and Jonah. Both preached a message of repentance (Jon. 3:4, 5; Mark 1:14, 15). Both reappeared alive after three days. Both engaged in a mission that results in deliverance for repentant Gentiles but destruction for wicked Israelites/Jews (Jon. 3; Matt. 12:41, 42). Both offered their lives as a substitutionary sacrifice in order to save others (Jon. 1:11–16; Mark 10:45). Some or all of these factors may comprise “the sign of Jonah.” In short, the message of Jonah finds its culmination in the person and work of Jesus Christ. The kingdom of God that came at the advent of Jesus includes Jews and Gentiles and will stretch to the ends of the earth.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Throughout the centuries, Jonah has been interpreted in many different ways. Because of the connections with Christ in the NT, Jonah received considerable attention from the church fathers. Theodore of Mopsuestia, for example, emphasized the similar situations of the unbelieving Jews and the prophet Jonah. Augustine saw the book as pointing forward to Christ but also representing the immaturity of the nation of Israel. Calvin viewed the book principally within the framework of a work devoted to discipline: Jonah provides an example of how God treats errant and backsliding saints. The Enlightenment brought forward the theme of universalism: God extends His mercy beyond Israel to others. In the modern period, many scholars have speculated about the nature and size of the whale or fish and have expressed skepticism that the remarkable events of this book really took place.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Some scholars have argued that the story of Jonah contains historical inaccuracies that indicate it was written as a fictional account long after the destruction of Nineveh in 612 B.C. The issues raised concern the enormous size of the city and its population, the reference to the king of Nineveh rather than the king of Assyria, and practices that are known from the later Persian period but not eighth-century Assyria (e.g., the issuing of a decree by both the king and his nobles [3:7] and animals wearing sackcloth as a sign of mourning [3:8]). However, none of these supposed inaccuracies presents a compelling reason for doubting the veracity of what is recorded, and many of them are addressed in the study notes on the book that follow.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: As with other prophetic books, the prophecy is named after its author, Micah. He is identified by his hometown of Moresheth (1:1, 14), implying that he was an outsider to Jerusalem. Prophesying in the same period as Isaiah, he helped shape the character and policies of the southern kingdom of Judah. There is no record of Micah’s call, but there can be no doubt about his inspired preaching against injustice (3:8), which was one of the means by which God brought Hezekiah to repentance and so saved Jerusalem (Jer. 26:17–19).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Micah’s ministry extended for over twenty years during the reigns of Jotham (750–735 B.C. ), Ahaz (735–715 B.C. ), and Hezekiah (715–686 B.C. ), a time of Assyrian expansion and dominance in the ancient Near East. The northern kingdom of Israel was gradually overrun by the Assyrians, with the capital of Samaria finally falling in 722 B.C. to the Assyrian king Shalmaneser V (727–722 B.C. ). Ahaz of Judah allied himself with Assyria and modeled the worship at Jerusalem after Assyrian practices (2 Kin. 16:7–18). Ahaz’s son Hezekiah later revolted, and much of Judah was overrun by the Assyrian king Sennacherib, though Jerusalem itself was miraculously spared (2 Kin. 18:17–19:37). Although Micah predicted the destruction coming on Samaria and the northern kingdom of Israel (1:6, 7), his ministry was principally focused on the southern kingdom of Judah. At this time, a shocking contrast had developed between the extremely rich and the oppressed poor due to the exploitation of Israel’s middle class (2:8, 9) by greedy landholders (2:1–5). The oppressors were supported by Israel’s corrupt political and religious leaders (ch. 3). Because of this self-centered leadership, the whole nation became morally corrupt and ripe for judgment (6:9–16; 7:1–7). Consequently, God raised up Assyria as His wrathful rod against His sinful people (Is. 10:5–11). As Micah predicted (1:2–7), Samaria fell to the invading Assyrians. Judah subsequently felt the force of divine judgment when Sennacherib marched through the Shephelah (Judah’s western foothills) and up to the gate of Jerusalem, as Micah had also foretold (1:8–16).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Micah has drawn together a variety of oracles from throughout his lengthy ministry and incorporated them into a carefully designed overall structure. Most of his material is in poetic form, which imparted dignity and memorability to what he said. He makes extensive use of a variety of literary forms, such as lament (1:8–16; 7:1–7), disputation speech (2:6–11; 3:5–8), covenant lawsuit (6:1–8), prayer (7:14–17), and hymns of praise (7:18–20). His presentation is, however, dominated by scathing judgement speeches (2:1–5; 3:1–4, 9–12), designed to jolt his audience into recognition of their sin and to bring them to repentance. Even so, there are also salvation oracles that look forward to the coming of the Messiah and to the victory over evil that he will achieve (2:12, 13; 4:1–5, 6–8; 5:2–6, 7–9, 10–15).

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Micah arranges his nineteen prophecies into three cycles (see Outline below), each of which begins with prophecies of condemnation and impending judgment and ends with a prophecy or prophecies of salvation. Each cycle also begins with the same Hebrew word rendered “hear” (1:2; 3:1; 6:1). The middle cycle has three prophecies of judgment (ch. 3) and seven of salvation (chs. 4; 5). Micah uses many figures of speech (e.g., 1:4, 5, 7; 3:2, 3; 4:3, 4, 12, 13). He also employs wordplays to predict judgment (see notes, esp. on 1:10–15) and achieves vividness and immediacy by quoting his subjects, e.g., the false prophets trying to silence him (2:6, 7) and the converted Gentiles going up to Jerusalem to worship (4:2).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Micah is primarily a book proclaiming judgment and restoration for God’s people. The prophet declares that the holy and righteous God will no longer tolerate the persistent evil of His people (1:3). Many of the sins of the covenant community are mentioned, ranging from idolatry and sorcery (5:12–14) to deceit and fraudulent dealings (6:10, 11). But Micah heaps special condemnation on those who oppressed the poor by seizing lands that God intended as an inheritance for all His people (2:1–5; Num. 27:1–11 note). Judah’s leaders, both political and spiritual, are also condemned for their oppression of the people and for their disregard of justice and truth (ch. 3). Fundamental to Micah’s proclamation of both judgment and restoration are the terms of the covenant relationship between God and His people. While God faithfully fulfilled His responsibilities under the covenant (6:1–5), the people wallowed in disobedience. The people mistakenly assumed that outward ritual observances could replace true heart allegiance (6:7, 8); now the covenant curses were to be applied (6:13–16). Despite his prevailing tone of impending punishment, Micah did not fail to look beyond the judgment to future restoration and blessing. This, too, was rooted in God’s covenant relationship with His people (Gen. 17:2 note). Faithful to His covenant promises to the patriarchs (7:20), the Lord would preserve a remnant of His people (2:12; 4:7; 5:3, 7, 8; 7:18), and would raise up a ruler out of Bethlehem in Judah—the Messiah Himself (5:1–5). Micah’s prophecies of salvation reminded His original audience that their restoration would depend on the Lord’s merciful forgiveness and sovereign initiative, not on the works of their hands (7:18, 19).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Micah emphasizes the inevitability of divine reaction against sin, especially the transgression of God’s covenant people. This is balanced by a clear perception of the Lord’s inviolable commitment to His covenant. Though He would use both the Assyrians and the Babylonians as His instruments to punish the people, He would preserve a remnant through the impending calamity and through whom He would work out His divine purposes. Micah uses traditional language relating to a shepherd to describe the Lord’s relationship with His people (2:13; 4:6–8; 5:4; 7:14). He also emphasizes that God’s past intervention to deliver His people (6:4, 5; 7:14, 15) sets a pattern to be repeated in the future (7:19, 20).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The significant similarity between Mic. 4:1–3 and Is. 2:2–4 raises the question of the relationship between these two prophets. If one prophet uses revelation originally disclosed to the other, it is probably Isaiah who incorporated material from Micah. However, since their ministries overlapped, it is possible that God gave the same message to both prophets because it was especially relevant to their contemporary circumstances. Another Old Testament link is found in Jer. 26:18, which records an episode in which Mic. 3:12 is quoted more than a century after it was first revealed, helping to save Jeremiah’s life. In the New Testament, Mic. 5:2 is cited by chief priests and scribes to answer Herod’s inquiry as to the birthplace of the Messiah (Matt. 2:6; see also John 7:42). In Matt. 10:35, 36, Jesus applies the description of social disintegration found in Mic. 7:6 to the circumstances which will prevail because of His having appeared on earth.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Though the book of Micah is best known for its prediction of Bethlehem as the birthplace of the Messiah (5:2), significant information is also disclosed about His origin and mission. His birth in Bethlehem points to His having an obscure start in life (Is. 53:2) and designates Him as a royal descendant of Davidic lineage. Unlike other kings of David’s dynasty He will “come forth for me” (5:2). That is, He will act in accordance with all that God stipulates and so will completely fulfill the divine purpose. He will be able to achieve this because He will carry out his mission “in the strength of the Lord” (5:4). As ruler “in Israel” (5:2), that is, over the covenant people, His coming would be the basis for their return (5:3), and He would provide complete peace for His people (5:5). Micah also unveils a mysterious, superhuman origin for the Messiah in that He is “from of old, from ancient days” (5:2).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Apart from interest generated by his prediction of the birthplace of the Messiah (5:2), Micah’s prophecy was for centuries largely overshadowed by that of his contemporary, Isaiah, and commentaries on his work were combined with general treatments of the Minor Prophets. In the middle of the nineteenth century, however, Micah was not immune from the profoundly skeptical analyses of critical scholarship. Such scholarship identified as many as twenty-one distinct oracles within the book, which were assigned diverse origins—some as early as David; others as late as the first century B.C. In this scheme, only chapters 1–3 (with the exception of 2:12, 13) were assigned to the biblical prophet. More recent critical scholarship continues to see the book as the end product of an extensive process of editing and enlargement, though there is general acceptance that material original to Micah is contained in it, and there is greater interest in the unity of the book as a whole. In fact, more conservative scholars have pointed out that the unity of the work demonstrates that the book is from Micah himself and that much of the skepticism regarding Micah’s authorship is driven by ill-founded presuppositions about the impossibility of supernatural prophecy, not the actual evidence. In sum, there is no good reason to believe the book does not come from Micah’s hand.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The book is designated after its author, Nahum, whose name means “comfort,” possibly reflecting the comfort of his message to those suffering under Assyrian domination. His name is followed by “of Elkosh,” probably a reference to the location of his birth or the place where he prophesied. Attempts to identify Elkosh have been unsuccessful. Proposals have included locations near ancient Nineveh (with Nahum descended from the Israelites who were deported there earlier), in Galilee (the name “Capernaum” perhaps derives from the Hebrew for “village of Nahum”), and in Judah. The internal witness of the book supports Judah as the general vicinity of Nahum’s prophetic activity (1:15). However, as with most prophetic books, the message of the work, though rooted in the person and circumstances of the prophet, finally transcends the author and his ministry.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Nahum’s prophecy can be dated between the capture of Thebes by the Assyrian ruler Ashurbanipal in 663 B.C. , which Nahum reports as a past event (3:8), and the fall of Nineveh in 612 B.C. , which Nahum prophetically foretells (3:5–7). During this period of the seventh century B.C. , two major crises arose in the Assyrian empire. One came from the threat of the Medes and the advancing Scythians (642–638 B.C. ). The other, larger crisis was the Babylonian revolt (652–648 B.C. ) under the leadership of Ashurbanipal’s elder brother Shamash-shum-ukin, who was supported by the Elamites and peoples from the Iranian highlands. Ripple effects of this revolt were experienced as far away as Palestine and Syria. Eventually the revolt was suppressed by bitter warfare that shook the whole empire. A date for Nahum’s prophetic activities before or during this period of upheaval is attractive. Because the destruction of Thebes was apparently still fresh in the memory of his audience, a plausible date for Nahum’s prophecy therefore falls between 660 and 650 B.C. , in the days of King Manasseh of Judah, who was a loyal vassal of Assyria. Another possibility is the early part of Josiah’s reign, before the death of Ashurban­ipal in 627 B.C.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Nahum has been incorrectly regarded as a narrow nationalist who, inspired by feelings of hatred and vengeance, proclaimed a message of judgment against Nineveh, and at the same time extended the promise of unconditional salvation to his own people, Judah. But this view overlooks the fact that this book reflects the usual literary form of prophecies against foreign nations and is to be compared with similar proclamations in Is. 13–23; Jer. 46–51; Amos 1; 2; and Obadiah. A number of literary genres are evident in Nahum, such as a hymn (1:2–8) and the salvation oracle of 1:12–15, which yields a brief glimpse of a brighter future for Judah. However, the book is dominated by oracles of judgment. Taunt songs, ostensibly addressed to Nineveh (2:11–13; 3:14–17), mock it as the “bloody city” (3:1), soon to meet its doom at the hands of unnamed foes. These oracles were in fact designed for the ears of Judah as it suffered under Assyrian oppression.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The prophecy has a simple structure. In chapter 1 there is a build-up to the ensuing conflict that is described in chapters 2 and 3. Nahum describes the destruction divinely disclosed to him with a vivid, staccato rhythm that rivals an account of a war reporter. He pursues his theme of the impending doom of Nineveh with unrelenting tenacity, using poetic language and imagery of the highest order. Implicitly, Nahum voices the universal relief and joy of all who suffered under the merciless tyrant.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The book of Nahum has a double title (1:1). It is called an “oracle concerning Nineveh” and the “book of the vision of Nahum.” “Oracle” often indicates a divine message of judgment against a foreign nation (Is. 13:1; Mal. 1:1 note). “Vision” refers to a supernatural revelation to the prophet’s inner sight or hearing. At times a prophet was instructed to write down a specific message (Is. 8:1, 2; 30:8) or even “all the words” that the Lord required him to speak (Jer. 36). The written form then provided a strong additional witness to the certainty of the fulfillment of those divine pronouncements. The prophecy’s double title is solid confirmation of the authenticity of this oracle of doom against Nineveh and the inescapability of God’s imminent judgment on the Assyrian kingdom. As a true prophet of Yahweh, Nahum was profoundly aware that the Lord, the incomparable and all-powerful God, held universal dominion over the kingdoms of this world. This often neglected and disparaged book provides us with an important key for understanding past, present, and future history. Events do not occur as mere happenstance, but every particular of history is divinely determined. In the opening hymn (1:2–8) and especially in 1:2, 3 (the “text” of Nahum’s sermon), we learn that the Lord’s government of history is in accordance with His character as the covenant God. He demands undivided submission everywhere and from everyone. Rejection of Him and of His law leads not only to the necessary consequences of chaos in society and in nature, but inevitably evokes His personal displeasure, resulting in just retribution.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: God’s patience (1:3) must never be misunderstood as weakness. Corporate or individual sin will not be left unpunished. God ultimately ordains all the events of history, and He is sovereign over all nations. Nahum proclaimed the impending destruction of Nineveh as God’s righteous judgment, and he invited his people to a joyful celebration of this event long before it took place. Nineveh was a wicked, imperialistic, and deceitful metropolis with an arrogant and unscrupulous lust for power and domination manifested in merciless warmongering (3:1–4). In addition to its military exploits, Nineveh was condemned for its ruthless trade practices and insatiable materialism (3:16). Against this evil city, Nahum delivered the message that no earthly power that defied God’s law would finally escape His judgment (1:14; 3:5–7). For his original audience and all subsequent readers, Nahum vividly portrayed the wrath of God, whose way is in the “whirlwind and storm” (1:3). This same book declares the goodness of God (1:7). Judgment, however, is not the Lord’s final word through Nahum. God’s retributive judgment is also redemptive; it furthers His loving purposes for His people and His covenant promises to them (1:15; 2:2). He destroys the forces of evil with the purpose of creating a new world of freedom (1:13), peace, and lasting comfort. “He knows those who take refuge in Him” and cares for them (1:7).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In many respects, Nahum provides a sequel to the prophecy of Jonah, which Nahum immediately follows in the ordering of the Minor Prophets in the Septuagint (Eastern Orthodox churches follow this ordering as well). When Jonah prophesied more than a century earlier, the Lord extended mercy to the repentant city of Nineveh, much to the prophet’s chagrin. But it was not long until Assyria again adopted an expansionist policy characterized by ruthless cruelty, attested to both by subject nations and by Assyrian records of the torture and mutilation the Assyrians inflicted. Consequently, the city again fell under divine condemnation. God had used the Assyrians to punish Israel and Judah (Is. 10:5), but His aim was not to annihilate Judah. The Assyrians went too far, and their arrogance would lead to their just reward (Is. 10:12). The predicted downfall of Nineveh provides the scenario for the preservation of a remnant of God’s people until the coming of the Messiah. Although the impending judgment of God is a major theme of New Testament theology, Nahum is not quoted explicitly. The reference in Rom. 10:15 is more probably to Is. 52:7 than to Nah. 1:15.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: There are no direct messianic references in Nahum. However, the exhortation to “keep your feasts” (1:15) encouraged the faithful in the land of Judah to look forward to the One who would fulfill all that was symbolized in the festivals. Those familiar with the message in the “book of the vision of Nahum” will better understand the necessity of the cross of Jesus Christ, the Son of the jealous and avenging God. They will be able to proclaim from this book the glorified Christ, to whom all authority in heaven and on earth has been given (Matt. 28:18) and who is now guiding history toward that great day when He will hand over the kingdom to His Father, after He has destroyed all opposing powers, so “that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:24–28).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Among the Dead Sea Scrolls that were the possession of the Qumran community, there is a commentary that identifies parallels between the overthrow of oppression anticipated by Nahum and that which the community anticipated for their contemporary circumstances (first century B.C. ). Early Christian commentators generally followed the lead of the Septuagint and interpreted Nahum in the light of Jonah. At the time of the Reformation, both Martin Luther and John Calvin discussed the shallowness of Nineveh’s earlier repentance and the justice of God’s penalty imposed on the city. Many modern commentators argue that Nahum portrays a narrow, nationalistic spirit that ignores the deficiencies of his own nation and which depicts God as unworthily sanctioning and approving unbridled violence. This, however, is to ignore God’s triumph over tyranny and unbridled wickedness, as well as the repeated warnings to Israel throughout the Old Testament of God’s willingness to judge His own people. Nahum conveys an enduring warning to all earthly regimes that ignore their accountability to the Judge of all the earth.
