sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: This prophetic book takes its title from its author, Habakkuk. Our only reliable information about him and his prophetic activity comes from the book itself. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The reference in 1:1 to Habakkuk as “the prophet” may imply that he was well known. His use of the cultic and wisdom traditions of Israel in his preaching have given rise to the doubtful notion that he was a prophet attached to the temple in Jerusalem, though the suggestion that he worked in Jerusalem is attractive. We can be sure, however, that in this book we meet a true prophet with a burning zeal for the glory of the Lord. His “oracle” (1:1 and note) is remarkable in that it is not, in the first place, a word directed to the people, but an answer to his own painful questions.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Dates proposed for Habakkuk derive from two considerations: the period of Judah’s history described in 1:2–4 and the stage in the rise of the Chaldeans referred to in 1:6. The latter verse strongly suggests that while the Chaldeans, or Neo-Babylonians, were not yet the dominant power in the Near East when Habakkuk wrote, they had already begun to make their presence felt. This indicates a time after 626 B.C. , when the Chaldeans under Nabopolassar seized control of Babylon from the Assyrians, which rules out the references in 1:2–4 as being to Judah during Manasseh’s reign. Since 1:2–4 do not cohere with the reforming character of Josiah’s reign, a date after his death in 609 B.C. —a period when the evil reign of Jehoiakim formed a sad contrast to that of his father, the good king Josiah (Jer. 22:13–19; 26:20–23)—becomes probable. Moral and spiritual deterioration in Judah accelerated as king and people alike insolently flouted the covenant laws. Meanwhile, the Chaldeans had successfully combined with the Medes to overthrow Nineveh in 612 B.C. , but the dominance of Babylon was not clearly established until the battle of Carche­mish in 605 B.C. , when Pharaoh Neco II and his Egyptian army, who had come to assist the Assyrians against Babylon, were soundly defeated by Nebuchadnezzar II. Most of Habakkuk’s ministry probably occurred during Jehoiakim’s reign (609–598 B.C. ), with chapter 1 coming from before 605 B.C. and chapters 2 and 3 originating after that.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Habakkuk is an unusual prophecy in that there is no direct public address to the people. The book is rather a record of the prophet’s own struggles with questions of faith. In chapters 1 and 2, a dialogue, in the form of a question-and-answer session, takes place between the prophet and God. Habakkuk’s prayers or complaints to God have a structure similar to lament psalms (such as Pss. 10; 12) in which a complaint is followed by a divine response. The oracles of chapters 1 and 2 are followed by a psalm in chapter 3, with dedication and directions for performance (3:1, 19). This triumphant song is occasioned by a theophanic vision (3:3–15), which culminates in the complete trust expressed in the personal testimony of the prophet (3:17–19). Throughout this book, Habakkuk’s writing style reflects the depth and intensity of his feelings, especially the perplexity with which he wrestles and the assurance that his faith gains.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Prophets were not only inspired preachers of divine messages to the people of God; they also shared the Lord’s burden for His broken world and His deep concern for His wayward people. In this respect, Habakkuk closely resembles Jeremiah. But even more than with Jeremiah, Habakkuk’s dialogue with God and his persistent prayers (2:1, 2; 3:2, 16) take the place of prophetic preaching as the heart of the book’s message. Like Nahum, Habakkuk deals with God’s sovereign control over human affairs—not when He intervenes in judgment, but rather with the times when He does not make His control apparent. Habakkuk experienced a profound spiritual crisis because of the Lord’s seeming indifference to appalling spiritual conditions among His people (1:2–4). In particular, Habakkuk is troubled by God’s apparent inaction when society in Judah is dominated by the wicked at the expense of the righteous (1:4). The absence of covenant life and obedience was dangerous to the people of God, but even more it was a rejection of the covenant Lord and an insult to Him. Because only divine intervention could change this deadly situation, Habakkuk was persistent in his appeal to the heavenly Judge, even when it seemed to be in vain (1:2). In response, the Lord revealed that He was about to do something that no one expected (1:5): He was going to raise up the Chaldeans as His instruments of judgment (1:6). However, for Habakkuk, this cure seemed even worse than the disease and only added to the prophet’s distress (1:12–17). How could the holy God, who cannot tolerate wrong (1:13), use such wicked people to fulfill His purposes? Does God really distinguish between good and evil in His sovereignty over history? Convinced that the events of history were not determined by blind fate but by the righteous and holy God of Israel, Habakkuk expectantly waited on the Lord until he received an answer to his painful questions (2:1). The Lord’s reply came in the vision introduced in 2:2, 3, which provides a true perspective on history and gives the divine promise about its outcome. This answer does not resolve all the painful questions, but it does teach God’s people the way of covenant life in the here and now (2:3, 4). That way is to persevere in hope, waiting with confidence for the fulfillment of the Lord’s unfailing promise. Although God’s ways may be inscrutable, His purposes are consistent. They culminate in real life for the faithful, but woe and death for the self-sufficient and arrogant (2:4). The Lord’s presence in His temple affirms His Lordship over history and assures us that in the end, His legitimate claim to the whole world will be universally acknowledged (2:14, 20; Is. 45:21–25; 1 Cor. 15:24–28). The revelation of the Lord’s sovereignty over history transforms Habakkuk’s complaint into a hymn of joy (3:2–20). Instead of passively waiting for divine intervention, he now prays positively that the Lord would act in accord with the deeds and qualities He displayed in the exodus and at Sinai. Anticipating the future, Habakkuk in his prayer celebrates the Lord’s coming (3:3–7), His judgment against the nations (3:8–12), and His triumph over all opposition (3:13–15). From this perspective of faith, even the threat of severe calamity could not dampen Habakkuk’s overwhelming joy in expectation of the coming salvation, a salvation guaranteed by the Lord’s faithfulness to Himself and to His revelation (3:17–19).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Habakkuk grapples with questions and doubts regarding God’s justice and His direction over the world. Despite his puzzlement, he does not relinquish his grasp of God as a refuge in perplexity and trouble (“Rock”; 1:12), as holy (1:13) and as one who is in control (1:14). It is the divine verdict that overrules human pride and power, and God alone can resolve the conundrums of history. Habakkuk also contributes to our theology of prayer. The complaints in chapters 1 and 2 and the prayer in chapter 3 all reflect the third petition of the Lord’s Prayer, “Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matt. 6:10). Through these prayers the prophet submits and rejoices in God’s will and the temporal outworking of his eternal plans and decrees.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Paul uses Hab. 2:4 as a foundational text for his proclamation of the gospel (Rom. 1:17; Gal. 3:11; cf. Heb. 10:35–39). Like Habakkuk (ch. 1), Paul knew that sin is incompatible with God’s holiness and that the fatal tension between these opposites could only be resolved by divine intervention. The prophetic word to Habakkuk (ch. 2) reveals in principle the way God would deal with the incompatibility of sin and holiness. The cross of Christ and the final judgment are fulfillments of this revelation. Like Habakkuk, Paul also affirmed that true life is only possible in a relationship of total dependence on the Lord. Such dependence, based on the faithfulness of our God, transforms our existence in this world, filling our lives with joy in the certainty of God’s faithfulness to His promises (2:3; 3:17–19).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: There are no direct messianic prophecies in Habakkuk, but the expectations embodied in 2:14 and chapter 3 require the coming of Christ for their fulfilment. The people of God must have a faith that looks outside of them to another. Such dependence, based on the faithfulness of our God, transforms our existence in this world, filling our lives with joy in the certainty of God’s fidelity to His promises (2:3, 4; 3:17–19).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Habakkuk may be called a forefather of the Reformation. The key concepts of his preaching, as taken over by Paul, deeply influenced Luther and Calvin, and eventually became watchwords of the Reformation. Only the perspective of faith, or persevering and obedient trust in God, provides for meaningful existence in the world during the present period, between the “already” of initial fulfillment of God’s promises and the “not yet” of their final realization.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The ninth of the Minor Prophets is named after its author. Zephaniah’s lineage is traced back four generations (1:1), a presentation that is unique in the prophetic literature. This may indicate that the Hezekiah (715–686 B.C. ) mentioned is the well-known king of Judah, making the prophet a member of the extended royal family and consequently an individual of some standing in the Jerusalem community and knowledgeable about its affairs. The name Zephaniah , which means “Yahweh has hidden” or “Yahweh has treasured,” perhaps indicates the faith of his parents during the godless years of Manasseh. It is also used of a priest who was a contemporary of Jeremiah (21:1; 29:25) and of other individuals in the Old Testament (Zech. 6:10, 14). Though the prophet employs priestly vocabulary at several points (1:4, 5, 7–9; 3:4, 18), there is no conclusive evidence to indicate that he was officially associated with the temple.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Zephaniah prophesied in the southern kingdom of Judah when Josiah (640–609 B.C. ) was king. However, there is some question as to whether the prophet’s ministry preceded or followed Josiah’s great reform of the nation’s worship in 622 B.C. Zephaniah’s denunciation of continuing syncretistic worship (mixing the idolatry of the surrounding peoples with the worship of the Lord) and of Baal worship may point to a date before Josiah’s reforms, or it may point to their partial success. Since only a remnant of Baal remained (1:4), Zephaniah probably began to minister after Josiah’s initial reforms in 628 B.C. (2 Chr. 34:3 note). Certainly Nineveh had not yet been overthrown (2:13–15); therefore, the prophet’s message was spoken before its destruction in 612 B.C. Zephaniah would have been a contemporary of Jeremiah, whose call came in Josiah’s thirteenth year (627 B.C. ). If his ministry is dated in the earlier part of Josiah’s reign, then he may have been instrumental in bringing about Josiah’s reforms since the sins he attacked (1:4–6) are those targeted by the king (2 Kin. 23:4; 2 Chr. 34:1–7).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Zephaniah contains many of the features found in the Major Prophets: oracles of judgment (1:2–2:3), oracles against foreign nations (2:4–15), and oracles of hope (3:8–20).

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Zephaniah presents his material in poetic form. He uses vivid word pictures to depict the coming day of the Lord, whose sweeping judgment will encompass Judah and all humankind. The book is also marked by the contrast between the darkness of the impending day of judgment and the brightness of the future glory that awaits the people of God. At that time, the Gentiles also will come to faith in the true and living God and will “call upon the name of the Lord” (3:9; cf. Joel 2:32). Zephaniah does not extensively develop themes from the past history of the people or from contemporary events. He does, however, draw on various aspects of the law (1:13, 15, 17; 2:2; cf. Deut. 4:11; 28:15–62, 29, 30, 39). Also, his terminology is similar to that of other writing prophets (cf. 1:7 and Hab. 2:20; 1:14 and Joel 1:15; 1:7 and Is. 34:6).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Like many of the other prophets, Zephaniah begins with a message of universal judgment (1:2, 3) and ends with an oracle of salvation in which both the nations (3:9) and the revitalized remnant of Israel (3:12, 13) are brought into a saving relationship with the Lord (3:19, 20). The focal point of the prophet’s message is the day of the Lord, referred to at least eighteen times, thirteen of them in chapter 1 alone. He foresees that at that time, a foreign enemy, acting as the Lord’s sword of judgment (2:12; Is. 10:5), will inflict severe destruction upon Jerusalem (1:4, 10, 11; 2:1). Depending on when the book is dated, this enemy has been variously identified as the Scythians, the Assyrians, or the Babylonians. Zephaniah’s treatment of this subject is extensive. The day is near (1:7) and will be a day in which the wrath and anger of Israel’s sovereign Lord will be directed against the wicked (1:15, 18; 2:2, 3). It is a day of darkness and gloom (1:15). So determined is the Lord to root out evil that He conducts a thorough search to ensure that the wicked will be found and destroyed (1:12). In that day, pride will be vanquished (3:11) and the humble of the land (the remnant) will be saved (3:12, 17). Behind the day of divine intrusion into the flow of human history, which Zephaniah anticipates as imminent, he also is aware of the climactic, universal intervention of the final day of divine judgment. A less obvious point, but one that is alluded to throughout Zephaniah, is the prophet’s recognition of the importance of the Lord’s covenant with His people. Although Zephaniah never uses the word covenant , some passages echo details of previous covenantal encounters and provisions. Certainly the complaints against Judah reflect the Lord’s anger at their neglect of the covenant obligations. In the meantime, it is recognized that there is a faithful remnant whose people are encouraged to persevere in seeking the Lord (2:3) and to wait with meekness and humility for His deliverance (3:8, 12).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Zephaniah repudiates a theology that regards God as distant and uninvolved in human affairs (1:12). He asserts His hatred of violence and corruption (1:9; 3:1–5) and predicts the coming judgment of the King (3:15) who is also the Savior (3:17). Indeed, the prophet presents divine judgment as transforming the world by bringing all people’s works, both good and evil, under divine scrutiny. The restorative nature of God’s wrath is indicated by the change of tone from the warnings of 1:2, 3 (“I will utterly sweep away everything”) to the hope expressed in 3:14–20. Then the Lord will be openly in the midst of His people and deal with them tenderly as He restores their fortunes. “He will rejoice over you with gladness” (3:17) reveals the extent of divine satisfaction at the consummation of His purposes for His people.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Despite the testimony given to God’s judgment on the sin of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 B.C. , Judah refused to learn, moving God to intervene in judgment. The faithless would be purged through judgment and the faith of the godly strengthened. Zephaniah is the last of the Minor Prophets to be written before the exile. The three books that follow Zephaniah are written from the perspective that the people are back in the land following the exile. The end of Zephaniah’s book (3:9–20) prepares the way for life after the restoration of the exiled community and beyond. The prophet foresees that the Lord will preserve a remnant through whom the destiny of Abraham’s seed will be realized.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: There are no direct messianic prophecies in Zephaniah, but his focus on the day of the Lord sets out clearly the need for salvation that will only be achieved through the intervention of the Savior who loves Zion and acts on her behalf (3:15–20). This deliverance is not confined to ethnic Israel. The prophet envisions a time when Jew and Gentile will be united in enjoying the blessings of the covenant and worshiping God (3:9, 10). This occurred through the ministry of Christ.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Zephaniah has been largely neglected in the history of interpretation, perhaps because it does not seem to present anything significantly new. Indeed, past critical scholarship tended to view it as a compendium of material from a variety of sources, crediting the prophet with little more than chapter 1. This was based on the unfounded supposition that the same individual could not prophesy both judgment and blessing. In Zephaniah’s day, the need was not for new truth, but for old truth recognized as such and acted upon, particularly in regard to maintaining integrity in worship and social interaction. Unifying literary features of the book also indicate that it is the work of a single author. The message of the great day of the Lord’s wrath in 1:14–18 inspired the medieval poem Dies irae , which has played a significant role in Christian hymnology.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: We know little about the prophet Haggai, for we read about him only in the books of Haggai and Ezra, two sources that give us only a limited amount of information about the prophet’s ministry. His name might give us some biographical data. Haggai means “festal,” perhaps indicating that the prophet was born during a feast. In any case, we do know that the prophets Haggai and Zechariah cooperated to encourage the Jews to rebuild the temple at Jerusalem after they returned in the sixth century B.C. from their exile in Bab­ylon (Ezra 5:1; 6:14).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Haggai and Zechariah share a common historical background, both having begun their ministries in “the second year of Darius the king” (520 B.C. ). At that point, the Jews had returned to Palestine under the edict of the Persian king Cyrus in 538 B.C. and had begun to rebuild the temple. Opposition from the outside and discouragement from within caused them to abandon the project for about sixteen or seventeen years (Ezra 4:1–4). When Haggai and Zechariah began their work in 520 B.C. , further opposition came from Tattenai, the Persian governor of Trans-Euphrates, which included Palestine (Ezra 5). But Darius I (Hystaspes), who ruled Persia from 522 to 486 B.C. , reissued Cyrus’s edict so that the temple was rebuilt within four years (Ezra 6:13–15). The second temple was dedicated on March 12, 516 B.C. As for Haggai’s messages themselves, we learn from his book that they were delivered between August and December of 520 B.C.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The text type that Haggai represents has been called an official chronicle, since the dates of the book are historically grounded and represent the prophet’s preaching during the initial phases of the renewed temple rebuilding effort. Although the book contains several speeches, it nevertheless presents a unified picture. For many years in the modern period, scholars believed that 2:15–19 had been repositioned from its original place following 1:15b. However, support for this theory has declined significantly in recent years.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Haggai consists of four messages headed by the phrase “the word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet” or a similar phrase (1:1; 2:1, 10, 20). The four messages alternate between calls to repentance in light of God’s curses on the land (1:1–11; 2:10–19) and promises of greater blessings on the temple and of the Messiah through the Davidic line (2:1–9, 20–23). Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi use the title “Lord of hosts” more than ninety times (fourteen times in Haggai). This title has military connotations (God as the leader of Israel’s armies; cf. 1 Sam. 17:45), but it also highlights God’s glory (Ps. 24:10) and sovereign kingship over all creation (Amos 4:13). As such, it is a reminder to God’s people of His awesome power and ability to deliver His people. Although Haggai is the second-shortest book in the Old Testament, it is rich with profitable teaching for the church. Through Haggai His messenger (1:13), the Lord calls upon the unfaithful remnant of His covenant people to repent and rebuild His temple. God’s concern is based upon His own sovereign pleasure and His desire to be honored (1:8). The people’s lack of concern to build the temple showed their deeper lack of desire for God’s special presence. They were under the curses of the covenant (1:6, 9, 11, and notes) but did not realize it. In response to Haggai’s ministry, the Lord stirred up the spirit of the people (1:14), and they obeyed (1:12). Haggai reaffirms that the Lord was with His people, just as He was when He brought them out of Egypt (1:13; 2:4, 5). Haggai’s ministry was based on the expectation that God would renew His covenant promises to Israel when He brought them back into the land from captivity in Babylon. Haggai’s words draw on those of earlier prophets at a number of points (2:7, 8, and notes). The rebuilding of the temple was an important part of that renewal, and Haggai developed that hope by associating the temple with the coming era of the Messiah (2:9, 23, and notes).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Haggai’s teaching is steeped in the language of the Mosaic covenant and recognizes the significance of the Davidic dynasty within the trajectory of this covenant. Haggai is especially interested in the coming Messiah and the building of the Davidic house of God. The divine name (Yahweh, translated “the Lord”) occurs thirty-four times in the thirty-eight verses of this short work, which affirms God’s presence and activity in the lives of His people. This book expresses the comfort and challenge that comes from the presence of the living God even when His glory is not on public display (2:3). Haggai anticipates the day when the glory of God comes to earth in the person of Christ and brings about the long-promised salvation of His people (2:20–23).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Like all of the prophets, Haggai’s ministry was rooted and grounded in God’s revelation to Moses at Mount Sinai. The people’s unfaithfulness to their obligations under that covenant had led to disaster in the past and continued to haunt them in agricultural unfruitfulness. Haggai also used the provisions of the law of Moses to demonstrate that the people were defiled to such an extent that even their offerings could not save them (2:11–14). Yet the Lord had not forgotten His earlier promise to be with His people and would not leave them nor forsake them. Instead, He would act to bring about true blessing and peace for His people through the temple, and what the temple ultimately represented, which was the presence of Jesus Christ in the midst of His people. For God’s new covenant people, the message of Haggai continues to be one of encouragement. Living in between the promise and the full realization of the promise in the new heaven and earth, God’s people may know that He desires to bless them and that He will do so (2:19). Haggai sounds a message of prophetic and eschatological (last days) hope that encourages God’s people in this life.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The rebuilding of the temple was an important part of God’s plan to bless His people, especially because it was connected with the coming of the Messiah (2:9, 23, and notes). The Messiah as God’s anointed representative on earth would bring His glory, peace, and prosperity to God’s people (2:9). Indeed, in the New Testament, Jesus Christ reveals Himself as the personal embodiment of the temple (John 2:19). In Him, God took on human flesh and came to dwell among us so that we could behold His glory and receive His peace (John 1:14–17). In Him, defiled sinners are made clean and enabled with boldness to present the works of their hands to the Father in gratitude for their salvation, not as a means of attaining it (Heb. 12:18–29). The Davidic heir Zerubbabel prefigured the Messiah in Haggai’s day through his faithful work of rebuilding the temple. He was promised that because of his faithfulness, the Lord would reverse the curse upon Jehoiachin and restore to favor the cast-off line of David (2:20–23; cf. Jer. 22:24). Ultimately, Jesus fulfills the promise made to Zerubbabel to be God’s royal ruler (“signet ring”) on earth (2:23). Today, we are the recipients of these promises and look forward to the final visible enthronement of Christ as ruler, when once again the Lord will shake heaven and earth and bring all things to their rightful conclusion (Heb. 12:26). HAGGAI IN THE

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Like many OT books, the book of Haggai has remained unfamiliar to most Christians in recent years. Part of the reason for a lack of interest in this book may lie in the fact that Haggai describes events from the time after the exile, when all that was left of God’s people was a small remnant living in poverty in Judah. But Scripture is clear that God works powerfully through a faithful remnant that depends wholly on Him. If, like the apostle Paul, we are content to be broken vessels without glory in ourselves so that the glory of Christ crucified may be more plainly displayed (2 Cor. 4), we will find much blessing in this book.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The author is identified in 1:1 as “Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo.” It has traditionally been held that this man, who was a contemporary of Haggai in the sixth century B.C. , wrote the entire book. However, many critical scholars have for some time argued that there are essentially two different books contained within the canonical book of Zechariah (chs. 1–8 and chs. 9–14). The first part is considered to be from the sixth-century prophet himself, while the second part is assigned to a later time, usually the Maccabean era of the second century B.C. Various literary and historical arguments have been used to arrive at these conclusions, but all are tentative at best, and there is no consensus as to the background of each major section among those who believe that they were written by two or more different authors. Consequently, there are no compelling reasons to doubt that Zechariah was the sole author of the book.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The historical background of Zechariah is the same as that of Haggai (Introduction to Haggai), but their ministries differed in emphasis. Haggai’s work centered on the rebuilding of the temple, while Zechariah’s was largely designed to encourage God’s people about the welfare of Jerusalem and its long-term future.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Zechariah contains a variety of literary forms. The visions of the first part are similar to the visions of Ezekiel and Daniel, in part because later prophecy in Israel employed more such visions. The book is often taken to be an example of early apocalyptic literature (Introduction to Daniel: Characteristics and Primary Themes), and certainly methods and themes characteristic of such literature are present in Zechariah. In chapter 14, a description of a final war against Jerusalem is given in which God comes as a victorious warrior to save His people from their enemies. Similarly, the visions of the horsemen (1:7–11), the four chariots (6:1–8), and the woman in the basket (5:5–11) might also be viewed as apocalyptic. Our understanding of the teaching of Zechariah is greatly helped when we recognize that the prophet gives pictures of the future in a snapshot fashion that does not place the passages in any particular sequence. When we read a passage, we see only what is happening in that snapshot, not how it relates to other snapshots. Further, the prophet portrays even the present blessings that Christians enjoy in terms of the imagery and customs of Old Testament life. Zechariah’s visions combine the present and future in an interwoven fabric that is impossible to tear apart. That is why it is often difficult to ascertain what time period the prophet has in mind. The promises (e.g., 2:5, 11) relate to both the immediate audience in Zechariah’s day and also to the distant future. This telescoping, or compression of the near and distant future, is a common feature of the prophetic writings.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The welfare and future of Jerusalem as the holy city is a pervasive theme in Zechariah. Several of the visions develop this theme (1:7–17; 2:1–13; 5:1–4 and notes). Chapter 8 presents a picture of Jerusalem, with God in her midst, dwelling in beautiful tranquility. The book ends with a chapter developing this theme (ch. 14). Zechariah’s focus on Jerusalem reflects the theme of the ideal Zion longed for in the Old Testament (Pss. 46; 48; 132). This is an aspect of the Lord’s continuing care and concern for His people. In a day of small things, when the nations around them were at rest while God’s own people struggled with overwhelming challenges and difficulties, it was easy to conclude that the Lord was distant and unaware of what was going on. On the contrary, the night visions make the point that God sees everything that is happening through His angelic observers, that He cares intimately for His people, and that He is ready to act for their blessing. Yet the Lord’s favor does not isolate His people from the reality of suffering. On the contrary, the visions depict great difficulties ahead for God’s people, while assuring them nonetheless of His final victory and their final vindication.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Zechariah in its more immediate historical horizon is a call to the exilic community to repent and return to the Lord fully. The message of Zechariah also extends beyond the postexilic community to portray God’s eschatological people and rule over the nations through the Messiah. The book makes a strong case for the covenant people of God to live ethical lives in chapter 7, thus contributing to our understanding of sanctification and obedience. Note how this message of holiness stands out in the closing verses of Zechariah: at the last day, the words “Holy to the Lord” will be ubiquitous (14:20).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Zechariah addressed a people who were suffering many things as a result of their forefathers’ determined sin (1:2–6). The consequences of unfaithfulness to the Sinai covenant were real and tangible. Yet the unfaithfulness of the fathers did not condemn the present generation to a life under God’s curse. If they responded in repentance and faith, they would find God turning to them in blessing. This is a common theme in the exilic and postexilic prophets, who pointed toward the arrival of the new covenant (cf. Jer. 31:29–34; Ezek. 18). The old covenant, which had been such a curse to Israel because of their sin, would be replaced by a new covenant of blessing, in which God would pour out His Spirit on His people.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Zechariah gives many explicit pictures of the Messiah, the Lord Jesus Christ. In fact, the gospel writers quote chapters 9–14 more than any other biblical source as they seek to explain Christ’s suffering and death. A pattern established between the Old Testament and the New Testament is that of Jesus as Messiah fulfilling promises the Lord spoke about Himself in the Old Testament. God’s promises of what He will accomplish are realized through His Anointed One. This explains the frequent citations in the New Testament from this book. The Messiah is portrayed as the King who comes riding into Jerusalem in 9:9, 10, a passage quoted by Matthew at Jesus’ triumphal entry (Matt. 21:1–11). The reference to looking “on him whom they have pierced” in 12:10 points to Christ’s suffering and death on the cross (John 19:37). The Messiah’s betrayal and death are further spoken of in 13:7 as the rejection of the Good Shepherd (Matt. 26:31). Zechariah also develops the messianic figure of “the Branch,” who combines the offices of priest and king (3:8 note; 6:12 note). The era of the Messiah is touched on even in other passages where the Messiah is not explicitly mentioned. The promise in 2:5, 10 of God’s dwelling in the midst of His people, along with the Feast of Booths (or Tabernacles) celebrated in 14:16–20, will find its fullest expression in the kingdom of the Messiah when the New Jerusalem comes down from heaven (Rev. 21:1–3).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Since the book is the longest of the Minor Prophets and the one that is most quoted in the New Testament, the church fathers referred to it frequently. Among them, Theodore of Mopsuestia applied a rather strict grammatical-historical approach. Many of the other church fathers took an allegorical approach and used Zechariah to make many kinds of allegorical interpretations. In contrast to this focus in the church’s early centuries, Zechariah has received less attention from Christians in recent years (Introduction to Haggai).

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The authorship of Malachi is a subject of debate. Scholars are divided as to whether the name Malachi is a personal name or a title. Both the Aramaic Targums and the Septuagint suggest something other than a personal name. The former identifies Malachi with Ezra. The latter translates the phrase “by Malachi” as “by the hand of his angel [or ‘messenger’].” The main arguments against viewing Malachi as the personal name of the prophet are the absence of specific data concerning his father and the lack of any mention of his place of birth. In addition, the phrase “oracle of the word,” which occurs in 1:1, is alleged to be an anonymous addition to the text. Nevertheless, these are not sufficient grounds for rejecting Malachi as the personal name of an individual prophet. In the case of every other Old Testament prophetic book, a personal name is given. As with many of the prophets, we know little about the prophet’s personal circumstances. But Malachi was indeed “God’s messenger,” and the message he brought was from God (cf. Amos 3:7, 8).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Malachi is to be dated about the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. The reference to the “governor” (1:8) locates the book in the Persian period, and Malachi’s emphasis on the law (4:4) possibly indicates the time of Ezra’s ministry of restoring the prominence and authority of the law (Ezra 7:14, 25, 26; Neh. 8:18). Some date the book between the coming of Ezra (458 B.C. ) and the coming of Nehemiah (445 B.C. ). Others place Malachi in the period between Nehemiah’s two visits to Jerusalem, about 433 B.C. Also important is the recognition that the conditions and problems that confronted Ezra and Nehemiah are also found in the prophecy of Malachi. All three spoke out against marriage to foreign women (e.g., 2:11–15; Neh. 13:23–27). They condemned neglect of the tithe (e.g., 3:8–10; Neh. 13:10–14). They castigated the evils of a degenerate priesthood (e.g., 1:6–2:9; Neh. 13:7, 8), and criticized social sins (e.g., 3:5; Neh. 5:1–13).

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Malachi contains a series of prophetic disputation speeches in which the prophet cites a contemporary saying that he then goes on to refute (cf. Ezek. 11:3–12; 18:2–32). In Malachi, the pattern normally begins with the Lord’s making a statement that the people challenge and the Lord then vindicates. The people’s challenge is not necessarily a verbatim citation of their actual words, but it accurately represents the worldview of the prophet’s hearers, regardless of whether their thoughts were expressed aloud in the prophet’s hearing. The uncommonly frequent use of the first person (“I”) by the Lord in addressing the people lends an added sense of urgency and intimacy to the message of the book (1:2, 6, 14; 2:2; 3:5, 6, 10, 17; 4:5).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The theme of the covenant is prominent in Malachi. Explicit references include the covenant of Levi (2:5–9), the covenant of the fathers (2:10), the marriage covenant (2:14), and the messenger of the covenant (3:1). In addition to these direct references, the book begins with a rehearsal of God’s covenant love (1:2–5). The seriousness of priestly incompetence and unfaithfulness is seen in the resulting erosion of covenant faithfulness among the common people who broke faith in their marriages (2:10–16) and in their social and economic relationships (3:5), “profaning the covenant” (2:10). Unless they repented (3:7), they would remain under God’s curse (3:9; cf. Lev. 26:14–46; Deut. 28:15–68). Malachi spoke to a disillusioned, discouraged, and doubting people whose experience did not harmonize with their understanding of the glorious promises found in the earlier prophets. Their vision of the coming messianic age had not yet materialized. Instead, they experienced poverty, drought, and economic adversity, and they became disillusioned with God and their faith. Malachi’s word confronts a people skeptical of God’s promises and therefore indifferent in their commitment to live in the light of those promises and to worship and serve the Lord with all their hearts. Their love had grown cold and their hearts bitter toward God. The book may therefore serve as a catechism for times of doubt and disappointment, when the professing people of God are tempted to break faith with their covenant God. The prophet’s ministry is to light the lamp of faith in a disheartened people by reminding them of God’s electing love (1:2) and to set forth the continuing obligations of the covenant to those who truly know God (3:16–18).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Malachi sought to rectify the people’s wrong thinking about their covenantal relationship with their God. The people had grown discouraged during the postexilic period and were tempted to accommodate to the world around them. This book warned God’s people after the exile not to think and act like the pagan peoples that surrounded them, but instead to remember that they were God’s chosen people. God promised to send a “messenger of the covenant” who would refine the people, no one less than the Lord Jesus Christ (1–3). From the beginning verses of the book, Malachi proclaims a complex vision of God who both loves and redeems and protects His people and also hates and judges His enemies (1:2–4), leading to the conclusion of the greatness of God (1:5). This understanding of God is necessary to have a proper submission to and rejoicing in the works of God displayed as the book unfolds.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: As the last of the prophets and the final book in the English-language ordering of the Old Testament, the book of Malachi underscores the incompleteness of God’s work at this point in redemptive history. God made great promises to His people and unquestionably demonstrated His love for them, both in bringing them out of Egypt and returning them to the land after the exile. Yet the people were still poor, weak and oppressed, in bondage to the Persians even as they lived in part of the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Nor was their response one of universal faith and trust. Many had grown cold in their love for the Lord and had abandoned Him in their hearts, even if outwardly they still went through the motions of religion. Only a remnant who truly feared the Lord and kept faith alive still remained. Would this be how Israel’s story ended, not with a bang but with a whimper? This could not possibly be the case. At the right time, the Lord would return to His temple to complete His saving work for His people. The Lord would be preceded by His messenger, who would bring a message of judgment and hope like the prophet Elijah. This left God’s people waiting throughout the long years between the testaments, anticipating the coming of someone dressed in a camel’s hair coat and a leather belt, bringing a fiery message of repentance, an expectation fulfilled in the coming of John the Baptist (Mark 1:1–8; cf. 2 Kin. 1:8). He would make the way straight for God’s greatest work of redemption, turning the hearts of the Lord’s rebellious children back to their heavenly Father.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: In Malachi’s day, the people had grown tired of waiting for God to appear in Jerusalem to bring deliverance and justice to their land (2:17–3:5). They naively thought that God’s appearing would vindicate them, no matter the condition of their hearts before God. God fulfilled His promise to appear in their midst in the person of His own Son, Jesus Christ. Here was a Son who truly honored His Father, unlike many in Israel (cf. 1:6). He first appeared in the temple in great humility, as a baby in His mother’s arms, though even then it was already evident to Simeon that He had come to reveal the hearts of men and women for blessing or for cursing (Luke 2:22–35). He later returned to His Father’s house and drove out those who had turned it into a marketplace (Matt. 21:13). In His first coming, Jesus came to seek and to save those who were lost, not only from the house of Israel but from all nations as well (Matt. 28:19, 20; Luke 19:10; cf. Mal. 1:5). At His second coming, He will return in great glory, however, to bring judgment upon all those who refuse to trust in Him (Rev. 19:11–15). Mal. 4:5 prophesies of the coming of Elijah the prophet. Jesus refers to John the Baptist, His forerunner, as Elijah in Matt. 11:14 and 7:10–13. Thus, Jesus presents Himself as the One to come who not only fulfills the promises in Malachi, the twelfth and last of the Minor Prophets, but also the One to come who fulfills all the promises of redemption that may be found from Genesis to Malachi.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The church fathers recognized the announcement of the coming of Christ in this last prophet. They made broad use of the book of Malachi to discuss the nature of God’s covenants and to demonstrate the universality of the offer of the gospel. This book is one of hope and anticipation, which are of great relevance in the midst of the often harsh and difficult realities of life in this fallen world. Like Malachi’s hearers, we need to live by faith in the light of God’s profound demonstrations of His love for us in the past, while we await the consummation of His promises to His people.

sections.heading: Title
sections.content: By the middle of the second century, the ancient church referred to Matthew and the other three canonical accounts of Jesus’ life as “the gospel according to [various authors],” following the lead of the second gospel (see Introduction to Mark). Thus, the title in our English versions has ancient precedent. Its implication is that all four canonical gospels convey one message of good news through (“according to”) four inspired authors. The opening words of this document, “The book of the genealogy [ biblos geneseōs ] of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham,” are not precisely a title for either the whole document or for the first seventeen verses. Rather, they highlight this book’s connection with the first book of Moses, in Hebrew called “In the Beginning” but in Greek titled “Genesis” (generation or genealogy). Gen. 2:4 and 5:1 are the only two places in the Septuagint where the phrase biblos geneseōs occurs. Matthew’s use of this phrase appears to be an intentional allusion to these two statements in the book of Genesis. Matthew is narrating the record of the new creation, launched by the coming, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: Although many scholars believe that this gospel did not originally name its author, early manuscripts have the inscription “according to Matthew,” and Eusebius tells us that the early church father Papias spoke of Matthew as having arranged the “oracles” about Jesus. Subsequent tradition is unanimous that the disciple Matthew, also called Levi (9:9–13; Mark 2:13–17), was the author of this gospel, and not until the eighteenth century was this tradition doubted. The significance of Papias’s statement for the authorship of this gospel is debated. Papias is commonly understood to affirm that Matthew “arranged the oracles in the Hebrew dialect” (that is, in the Hebrew or Aramaic language), but our canonical gospel, which is in Greek, does not read like a translation from these languages. It is also quite similar to Mark (see Introduction to the Gospels and Acts), which was certainly written in Greek. Possibly Matthew wrote in both Hebrew (or Aramaic) and Greek, as Calvin wrote works in both Latin and French. As a tax collector operating in Galilee and interacting with Jewish subjects and Roman officials, Matthew would have been bilingual or even trilingual (Aramaic, Greek, Latin). Others have suggested that Papias meant “in a Semitic style,” referring not to the work’s language but to its literary genre and narrative approach. Some have identified Papias’s “oracles” as a source lying behind our gospels. But Eusebius appears to have understood “oracles” to mean “gospel,” and Irenaeus (writing c. A.D. 180) speaks of a “gospel” by Matthew written “for the Hebrews in their own dialect.” Other objections to Matthew’s authorship are more speculative. Some suggest that the gospel may have been the product of a group of writers (a school). Its alleged dependence on Mark and supposedly late composition (see Date and Occasion) are given as reasons to doubt Matthew’s authorship. But these objections do not disprove the tradition that Matthew was the author. Moreover, if the tradition of Matthew’s authorship is not reliable, it is hard to explain how this masterpiece of inspired apostolic witness to the Messiah came to be identified with a minor member of the Twelve, especially one whose collaboration with Rome would have cast doubt on his credentials in the minds of Jewish readers.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The earliest reference to the gospel of Matthew is probably in the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans by Ignatius of Antioch (c. A.D. 110). Almost no one dates this gospel later than A.D. 100. Some scholars have dated it as early as A.D. 50, but many critics date it after the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, usually between the years 80 and 100. Their reasons include the assumption that Jesus could not have predicted such future events as the destruction of Jerusalem; the view that the gospel’s Trinitarian theology (28:19) and exalted Christology (11:27) are late ideas that developed in a Hellenistic environment; and the assertion that the word rabbi (23:5–10) was not used as a title before A.D. 70. Some of these reasons, such as that Jesus could not have predicted the future or that a high Christology is Hellenistic and therefore late, reflect an a priori rejection of the possibility of supernatural revelation and are therefore highly dubious. Trinitarian formulas appear in such epistles as 2 Corinthians (13:14), universally acknowledged to have been written in the mid-first century. Further, evidence in the book suggests that it was addressed to the historical situation before the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70. The gospel warns against the Sadducees (16:6, 11; 22:23–32), a group that rapidly vanished after A.D. 70. The language used to describe the destruction of Jerusalem in ch. 24 reflects Old Testament prophecies of the divine judgment that Jesus foresaw as connected with the coming of His kingdom. There is no need to explain the content of ch. 24 as the author’s description of a past event. Moreover, the assertion that the title rabbi was not used before A.D. 70 presupposes that which must be proven, namely, that Matthew must be written after that date. After all, if Matthew or any of the rest of the gospels were written before the year 70, then they are sources that prove the use of that title before that time. There are also many indications that the assertion that no one used the title rabbi before that date are greatly overstated. The writer of this gospel may have used the gospel of Mark as a source. Assuming that Mark was composed to preserve the oral testimony of the apostle Peter in Rome, an appropriate date for Matthew would be between A.D. 64 and 70. Antioch in Syria is the most likely location for the writing of the gospel and for the church for which it was originally composed. Ignatius, the earliest writer to quote Matthew, was bishop of Antioch. The congregation in Antioch was of mixed Jewish and Gentile origin (Acts 11:20–26; 15:1–5). This would account for the problems of legalism and antinomianism that Matthew particularly addresses and for the fact that this very “Jewish” gospel, which stresses Jesus’ fulfillment of the Old Testament, also emphasizes the inclusion of the Gentiles in the Messiah’s kingdom of grace (2:1–12; 8:5–13; 28:18).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Each of the four canonical Gospels was written to convey authentic and authoritative teaching by and about Jesus, whose coming signaled the fulfillment of God’s promises and the arrival of God’s kingdom. Matthew stands in the biblical tradition of Moses and the Hebrew “former prophets” who authored the books of Samuel and Kings, bearing witness to God’s acts in redemptive history and drawing implications from those acts for the response of God’s people. Like the prophetic authors of the Old Testament Historical Books, Matthew makes no division between history and theology. History is the basis of theology, and theology interprets the meaning of historical events. He speaks truth about real events in history, and he does so with a spiritual, pastoral, and covenantal agenda. The authors of the four Gospels did not intend to write complete biographies that would fulfill modern expectations. Like Luke, Matthew opens his account with the narrative of the Savior’s birth from a virgin, in fulfillment of prophecy (chs. 1; 2). His account of John the Baptist’s ministry of preparation and Jesus’ baptism and temptation (chs. 3; 4) is followed by a selective record of Jesus’ ministry of authoritative teaching and miraculous deeds (chs. 5–20), leading to an extended narrative of the week of controversy and intrigue that ended in Jesus’ crucifixion and resurrection (chs. 21–28). The apparently inordinate proportion of each gospel devoted to the final week of Jesus’ earthly life in humiliation shows that this genre was designed to focus readers’ attention on the sacrifice and triumphant resurrection by which the Messiah defeated Satan and inaugurated God’s kingdom.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The opening and closing of Matthew’s gospel emphasize that Jesus is the fulfillment of God’s promises to Israel. Jesus is “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (1:1), identifications that are supported by Jesus’ genealogical descent from Abraham through David (1:2–17). Jesus’ genealogy echoes not only a repeated feature throughout Genesis but also the genealogies that open 1 Chronicles and focus attention on King David. The Great Commission at the gospel’s end echoes God’s promise to Abraham that “all nations” will be blessed in Abraham’s seed. Matthew uses two distinctive constructions to mark off significant transitional points in his narrative. First, the “seam” between the preparatory account of Jesus’ birth, baptism by John, and temptation and the launch of His public messianic ministry is shown in the formula “from that time Jesus began to preach” (4:17). Later, a transition in the focus of His teaching to His disciples is signaled by “from that time Jesus began to show” them the necessity of His impending rejection and suffering (16:21), immediately after Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the Living God. Second, a repeated formula closes each of Jesus’ five major instructional discourses: “When Jesus finished ... [sayings, instructions, parables, etc.].” The discourses concern kingdom ethics (chs. 5–7), discipleship and mission (ch. 10), parables of the kingdom (ch. 13), relationships in the church (ch. 18), and the end time (ch. 24). Although it is hard to align the content of these five discourses one to one with the five books of Moses, Matthew may have intended their number to reinforce the theme that Jesus is the promised prophet like Moses (Deut. 18:18). There may be a relationship between each discourse and the narrative preceding it. The narrative portions deal primarily with the question of the king’s identity, while the discourses focus on the king’s people. A comparison of the gospels of Matthew and Mark reveals that Matthew included much of Jesus’ teaching material that is not present in Mark, while abbreviating accounts of Jesus’ miraculous deeds and interactions with people.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Matthew makes extensive use of “fulfillment” references to the Old Testament. His citations are not presented as isolated predictions and fulfillments but as proof of the fulfillment of all the expectations of the Old Testament. This concern affects the way Matthew emphasizes certain elements in history; for example, Matthew shows the illegality of the Sanhedrin’s actions in the trial of Jesus (26:57–68), the distortion of the Old Testament by the scribes and Pharisees (15:1–9), and the covenantal nature of God’s dealing with His people (1:1; 21:33–44; 26:26–29). In addition to showing Jewish readers that God’s covenant with Israel has been fulfilled in Jesus, Matthew reminds them that this covenant had always been directed toward blessing for all nations, as the Lord had promised Abraham (Gen. 12:3). Women with Gentile associations are named in the genealogy of Jesus, “the son of Abraham” (1:1, 3, 5, 6). Magi, non-Jewish astrologers, come from the east to worship the one “born king of the Jews” (2:1–18). The risen Messiah commissions His followers to “make disciples of all nations” (28:18).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Central to Matthew’s theology is the theme that Jesus is the promised Davidic King who has come to redeem His people and establish His kingdom of righteousness. From the opening identification of Jesus as “the son of David, the son of Abraham” to the opening message of repentance in the light of the kingdom’s arrival (4:17) to the end of the gospel, Matthew argues that Jesus fulfills Old Testament prophecies, institutions, offices, landmark events, and other anticipatory patterns in Israel’s history. In this time between the first and second comings of Christ, the kingdom of God comes in a partial way—good and evil grow up side by side until the judgment; men and women looking for permanent value find it in the kingdom; the preaching of the message of the kingdom will be received by some and rejected by others (Matt 13). However, Jesus establishes His church as the fullest manifestation of the kingdom in this present age. Jesus calls His followers—His church—to deep integrity and sincere worship of the Father, who sees our hearts’ secrets; to costly discipleship; to compassion toward outcasts; and to become a community characterized by purity and peacemaking. As the church lives by the ethics of the kingdom, it serves as a witness to the world around it, salt and light in a culture that needs the King. As the church proclaims the message of the kingdom, it has the promise of Jesus’ own presence and the expectation that He will return to set the world right and usher in the final form of His kingdom.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Matthew and the other three gospels function for the NT much as the five books of Moses function for the OT. As historical prologues leading up to the inauguration of covenants, they narrate the Lord’s redemptive intervention to rescue His chosen people and then engage them through promise and command. The covenants with Abraham (Genesis) and through Moses (Exodus–Deuteronomy) established God’s bond with Israel, and Jesus inaugurates the new cov­enant with a new Israel, gathered from all the nations. As in the books of Moses, the Lord’s deeds of power and grace to initiate His covenant with His people set the context for His directions for their communal life, as we see exemplified in Jesus’ discourses in Matthew on life in the kingdom of heaven. The opening and closing words of Matthew locate the good news within the redemptive history narrated in the Old and New Testament Scriptures. In Matt. 1:1, “genealogy” recalls Genesis. In the beginning, the first man, Adam, received authority over other creatures. Through His obedience, death, and resurrection, Jesus, the Son of Man, now has all authority in heaven and earth (28:18). Jesus is “the son of Abraham” (1:1), who brings blessing to “all nations” (28:19). Jesus is “the son of David” (1:1), the king who “comes in the name of the Lord” (21:5, 9) to inaugurate the long-awaited kingdom of heaven (4:17). Fulfilling the prophetic promise of “God with us” (1:23), Jesus will be with His church “always, to the end of the age” (28:20).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The issue of Jesus’ identity is addressed repeatedly throughout Matthew. The very first verse declares Christ to be the son of David and the son of Abraham. This immediately draws the reader’s attention to Christ as the fulfillment of the covenant made with David (2 Sam. 7; cf. Ps. 110) and of the covenant made with Abraham (Gen. 12; 15). The deity of Christ is revealed as early as 1:23, where Matthew cites Isaiah’s prophecy that the virgin’s son will be called “God with us.” The Father’s voice from heaven at Jesus’ baptism and His transfiguration identify Him as God’s well-pleasing Son, demonstrating the God-given truth of Simon Peter’s confession, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (16:17). Jesus’ correction of traditional interpretations of God’s law, introduced with the striking phrase, “But I say to you,” exhibits an authority transcending anything appropriate to mere humans (7:28, 29). As Israel’s Lord constituted that people as His assembly ( ekklēsia ) at Sinai, so Jesus promises to build “my church” ( ekklēsia ; 16:18). Christ is also truly human, the perfect fulfillment of humanity’s role as covenant servant to the Lord. Though Himself sinless, He identified with sinful people by submitting to John’s baptism of repentance. After a forty-day fast in the wilderness, Jesus was hungry. His victory over the ensuing temptations show Him to be the faithful servant that Israel had failed to be. He slept in the midst of a great storm at sea—displaying His humanity—and then quelled the winds and sea with a word—displaying His divinity. Christ’s royal calling as son of David is prominent in Matthew’s portrayal of Jesus, but so also is His prophetic authority to speak God’s word, even as Moses and Elijah had done.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: For most of church history, it was assumed that Matthew’s was the first of the four Gospels to be written and that its similarities to the other Synoptic Gospels were explainable in terms of the dependence of Mark and Luke on Matthew. Many scholars today believe that both Matthew and Luke made use of the gospel of Mark in writing their own gospels (see Introduction to the Gospels and Acts). However, Matthew and Luke do not follow Mark at every point in the order of events of Jesus’ life or teachings. Matthew and Luke share some material not found in Mark, but here, too, they differ in its placement within Jesus’ ministry. To understand the chronology of the Gospels, it is important to note that Mark’s own account is not a complete diary but, like the rest of the Gospels, a God-inspired presentation of that which his original audience most needed to know. John reports that Jesus visited Jerusalem several times during a period of about three years, while in Mark a single, climactic visit to Jerusalem is recorded. Matthew and Luke similarly were led by the Spirit in their selection and presentation of events. Recording certain events and not others and arranging material thematically instead of chronologically are both consistent with the Holy Spirit’s and the Gospel authors’ purposes to preserve authentic eyewitness testimony and to show its implications for their readers’ faith and lives. The Gospels do not simply present a schedule of Jesus’ activities. Nor are they modern, technical biographies. The Synoptic Gospels are individual and complementary works; they are not three incomplete attempts to do the same task. They are, as Mark’s opening sentence shows, “good news,” namely, proclamations of God’s climactic redemptive act in history in Jesus the Christ, the Son of God, written to call people into covenant with their creator by His grace. Together with the gospel of John, they present Jesus Christ, the incarnate Word, to all generations.

content.text: Exodus and Exile of God’s Son
