sections.heading: Title
sections.content: As with his “first book,” the gospel of Luke, the author opens with a brief prologue that identifies the original recipient, Theophilus, and previews the theme. The first book reported “all that Jesus began to do and teach” (1:1), so the implication is that this second book will carry the narrative forward, showing what Jesus continued to do and teach after His ascension to heaven. He continues to act through the presence of His Holy Spirit and the ministry of His apostles (both mentioned in 1:2). Early manuscripts and patristic sources refer to this document as “Acts of the Apostles,” or “Acts of All the Apostles” (a misnomer), or “the Scripture of the Acts of the Apostles.”

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: According to early church tradition, the book of Acts was written by Luke the physician, a companion of Paul on his second and third missionary journeys and on the voyage to Rome. Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, the anonymous Muratorian Canon, and Eusebius all credit Luke as the author. Those external testimonies to the identity of the author of the book of Acts fit well with what we can determine about the individual who wrote the book from the text of Acts itself. The well-known “we” passages of the latter half of the book (16:10–17; 20:5–15; 21:1–18; 27:1–28:16) show that the narrator of Acts accompanied Paul from Troas in Asia Minor to Philippi on the Continent of Europe, returning with him to Troas. Later, he and Paul traveled from Palestine to Rome. Among those who were with Paul during his imprisonment in Rome was “Luke the beloved physician” (Col. 4:14), so Luke could well have described the travels of Paul and his companions as a fellow traveler would. The author was an educated Gentile, as attested by the style and the high level of Greek used in Luke and Acts. His Greek is sometimes fully classical (Luke 1:1–4). The author’s methodical approach to writing and his interest in research reveal an educated, highly trained man. Luke’s identity as a Gentile may be inferred from the fact that his name appears after those whom Paul calls “the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God” (Col. 4:11). That Luke was a physician means he was highly educated, making him a likely candidate as the author of the book of Acts. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, scholars drew attention to the medical terminology found in Luke and Acts and to the author’s interest in diseases (Luke 4:38; 8:43, 44; Acts 3:7; 12:23; 13:11; 20:7–11; 28:3, 8). More recently, it has been argued that medical terms were in common use among ancient writers, so that the author need not have been a physician. Still, an interest in medical matters is apparent in Luke and Acts, and that fact, coupled with the external and internal evidence listed above, make it reasonable to conclude that Luke the physician was the author. For more on the authorship of Acts, see “History of Interpretation” below.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Three dates suggested for Acts are: before A.D. 70; 80 to 85; and 105 to 130. The last range of dates is based in part on the theory that the author of Acts was probably not Luke, and obtained his information about the revolutionaries Theudas and Judas (5:36, 37) from the writings of the Jewish historian Josephus, who wrote during the latter half of the first century. But the Theudas mentioned in Acts may have been one of many revolutionaries who arose about the time Herod the Great died, not the later Theudas mentioned by Josephus. Luke’s knowledge of Judas was not necessarily derived from Josephus, any more than Josephus’s knowledge was derived from Luke. Some argue that Luke made use of Josephus’s account of the death of Herod Agrippa I in A.D. 44 (12:19–22), since both use similar words in describing the event. The two accounts, however, differ considerably. The view that Luke and Acts were written before the destruction of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 is supported by the following considerations. First, ch. 28 ends with Paul under house arrest. While waiting to appear before Caesar, he was free to preach to all who come to him. This had to occur before A.D. 64, when a great fire swept through Rome and the Emperor Nero said that Christians were to blame. Second, Acts does not mention Paul’s death, which appeared to be imminent when the apostle wrote 2 Tim. 4 and which occurred around A.D. 68. Third, near the end of Acts, Luke portrays the Roman government as benevolent toward Christianity, an attitude that changed after A.D. 64. Fourth, certain terms point to an early date. These include “disciple”; “the first day of the week” in 20:7 (later to become “the Lord’s Day”; cf. Rev. 1:10); a reference to “the peoples of Israel” in 4:27 (a term later to include both Jews and Gentiles; Titus 2:14); the early title “Son of Man” (7:56); as well as language about geographical and political details. Luke 1:3 and Acts 1:1 are both addressed to Theophilus. He may have been Luke’s patron or benefactor. Certainly, he was a Gentile who had received Christian instruction before Luke’s writing (Luke 1:4). If he was Luke’s patron, Theophilus would have provided a living for Luke to enable him to do research and write his two books, and he also would have financed the reproduction (by hand) of Luke’s works. By comparison, the historian Josephus had the Roman generals Vespasian and Titus as patrons, as well as another benefactor, a certain Epaphroditus, to whom he dedicated his book Against Apion . As he implies in Luke 1:1–4, the author collected material from his own experience and from Semitic sources inside and outside Palestine. He mentions the names of several people who may have helped him (16:11; 20:4). He could have talked to Mary, Jesus’ mother, in addition to others who were “eyewitnesses and ministers of the word” (Luke 1:2). As a traveling companion of Paul, he would have learned about the apostle’s calling and early ministry from the apostle himself.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Like Luke’s “first book” (the third gospel) and the other canonical gospels, the book of Acts belongs to the genre of biblical historical narrative, which provides a faithful (though selective) record of the events of God’s intervention for His people’s redemption, along with theological and spiritual interpretation of those events. Acts reports events associated with the establishment and growth of the church in its new covenant form in the first generation after Jesus’ ascension and His bestowal of the Holy Spirit on the Day of Pentecost. The theological and spiritual commentary on those events is provided through the author’s choice of language, often evocative of Old Testament Scriptures, through the literary structure of the book as a whole (see “Literary Features” below), and through discourses (sermons and speeches) spoken by participants in the events. Although Acts is called the “Acts of the Apostles,” the author’s selectivity is shown in the way he traces only the ministries of Peter (chs. 1–12) and Paul (chs. 13–28), and focuses attention primarily on the westward spread of the gospel and the church, reaching a terminus at Rome, the capital of the empire.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The Greek vocabulary and syntax of the books of Luke and Acts are, along with Hebrews and James, among the most polished in the New Testament, while simultaneously displaying the Semitic influence of the Septuagint and the Aramaic background of the early church in Palestine. As literature, then, this book’s style reflects the historical events that it records, bridging the roots of Christianity in the faith and Scriptures of Israel and the wider Greco-Roman world, to which God’s Word went through Paul and other apostles and witnesses. Several distinctive literary features guide readers into the message that the Holy Spirit is conveying through the account of the church’s early decades after Pentecost. 1. Phases of the Word’s Expansion. Jesus’ announcement to the apostles that, upon the Holy Spirit’s arrival, they will be empowered as His witnesses “in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (1:8), forecasts the structure of Acts as a narrative of the three phases of expansion for the apostolic church’s witness to God’s word. The focus of attention is on Jerusalem from the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost through the martyrdom of Stephen (chs. 1–7), although the church there continues to have special influence as believers carry the word to other regions (8:14; 11:1, 2; 15:1–32; 16:4; 21:17–26). The scattering of Christians after Stephen’s death “throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria” (8:1) constitutes the second phase foretold by Jesus (chs. 8–12). The third phase (chs. 13–28) focuses on the ministry of Paul and his colleagues, closing with Paul’s unhindered testimony about Jesus in Rome, the imperial capital, which represents “the end of the earth.” 2. Events and Trends Interwoven. The flow of Acts’ narrative advances as accounts of specific events alternate with summary descriptions of trends in the church’s ongoing life as a result of the events. The Spirit’s descent at Pentecost (2:1–41) is followed by believers’ daily life together, marked by devotion to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer (2:42–47). Later summaries, following or preceding noteworthy events and sermons, describe the Christians’ financial community (4:32–35), introducing Bar­nabas’ generosity and Ananias’ and Sapphira’s hypocrisy; the apostles’ miracles and the reaction they evoked (5:12–16); and the powerful growth of the word of God (6:7; 12:24; 13:49; 19:20). The numerical, geographic, and spiritual growth of the church is the growth of God’s Word in its life-changing power. 3. Sermons. The centrality of the preached word to the church’s growth is illustrated by the abundance of sermonic material included in Acts. At least thirty percent of the words in Acts are found in the speeches of apostles and other Christian witnesses. As the book outline below shows, every major section of the book contains samples (likely summaries) of the apostolic preaching of the gospel in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and in the wider Greco-Roman world. Sermons are addressed to Jews, Gentiles, and religiously mixed audiences and are delivered in the temple precincts, in synagogues, in open-air venues, and in legal proceedings. The preachers’ approach varies with their hearers’ degree of acquaintance with and respect for the Old Testament Scriptures, but their theme is consistent: God’s glory as creator, human guilt before Him, and the redemptive mission of Jesus the Messiah and the coming judge of all. 4. Parallels with the Third Gospel. Echoes of Jesus’ life and ministry in the experience of His followers recounted in Acts skillfully reinforce the theme that becoming His disciple entails following in His footsteps, particularly along the path of suffering (Luke 6:40; 9:23; 14:26, 27, 33; Mark 10:35–40). As Jesus was anointed by the Holy Spirit and began to preach good news, meeting both appreciation and opposition (Luke 3:21, 22; 4:16–30), so also His witnesses were empowered by the Spirit, preached, and encountered receptivity and resistance (Acts 2:1–41; 3:11–26; 4:1–22). As Jesus moved resolutely toward the rejection and death awaiting Him in Jerusalem (Luke 9:21–22, 44, 51; 18:31–33), so Paul would not be dissuaded from traveling to that city and the suffering there that the Spirit foretold (Acts 20:22–24; 21:4, 10–14).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Acts is a careful history of the development of the early church. Luke’s descriptions of geographical and provincial details, of governmental officials and their actions, of imperial procedure, of a sea voyage to Italy, replete with accurate nautical terms—all these come from a careful researcher who was himself an eyewitness of many of the events he records. Luke had several purposes. In 1:1, 2 he says that in his gospel he has explained the life of Jesus until the ascension. He summarizes the general theme of Acts in a statement of the risen Lord Jesus: the apostles are commissioned as His witnesses to testify in expanding circles “in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (1:8). Some have detected an interest in defending Christianity or showing that Christianity was not a threat to Rome. The abundant allusions to and citations of the Old Testament both in the third gospel and in the sermons and prayers of Acts demonstrate that the gospel of Jesus, Israel’s Messiah and God’s light to the Gentiles, fulfills the prophecies of Israel’s Scriptures, as Jesus taught His disciples before and after His resurrection (Luke 22:37; 24:25–27, 44–49). Acts is a map of the expansion of the church into the ancient Greco-Roman world, showing how the present age in the history of God’s salvation of His people began.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Acts repeats and reinforces many of the theological emphases of Luke’s gospel (see Introduction to Luke: Theology of Luke). The sovereignty of God over history and in redemption is asserted through a variety of terms and statements. Events pertaining to the suffering and resurrection of Christ were “necessary” because they were planned by God, who revealed them in advance in the Old Testament Scriptures (1:16, 20, 21; 2:23; 3:17, 18; 4:28; 13:29). God “appointed” Christ as Messiah and Judge (2:23; 10:42; 17:31), just as He appointed individuals for eternal life (13:48) and the temporal and geographical boundaries of the various nations of mankind (17:26). God’s “will” was fulfilled even by those who wickedly conspired against Jesus the Christ (2:23; 4:27, 28). God “chose” the patriarchs and Israel (13:17), but He also “chose” to send Peter to preach good news to Gentiles (15:7). God’s servant Jesus, Abraham’s offspring, blesses people by turning them from their wickedness (3:26), opening a door of faith and granting the repentance that brings life even to the Gentiles (11:18; 14:27), opening hearts to receive the gospel (16:14), and adding to His church daily those whom He saves (2:47). Salvation is a central theme in Luke’s gospel and in Acts. The terminology of salvation (“savior,” “save,” “salvation”) appears more frequently in these two books than in the other three gospels. In Acts, salvation can include relief from physical distress (4:9) and economic oppression (7:25), but it is comprehensive, including reconciliation to God and eternal life (2:21, 40; 13:26, 47; 15:1, 11; 16:30, 31; 28:28). Reconciliation to God through the work of Christ is the primary focus of the terminology of salvation in Luke and Acts, and other salvific benefits are the consequences of God’s answer to our most fundamental need—the Savior who kept God’s law in our place, died as the effectual atonement for our sin, and was raised from the dead for our justification (cf. Rom. 4:23–25; 5:12–21). Jesus is the Savior given by God (5:31; 13:23), and salvation is found in no other name than His (4:12). The bestowal of the great eschatological gift promised by the Father, the Holy Spirit, marked a new phase in Jesus’ redemptive mission and rule, and therefore in the composition of His people, His church. At Pentecost, the Spirit enabled Jesus’ followers to speak the gospel in the languages of the nations (1:5, 8; 2:1–11), and His presence was promised to those who repent and receive baptism in Jesus’ name (2:38). The Spirit ushered Samaritan believers into Christ’s church (8:14–16), and then uncircumcised Gentiles (10:44–48; 11:15–17; 15:8). The Spirit gave wisdom to Christians who ministered mercy (6:3, 5) and words to those who spoke His Word (4:8, 31; 5:32; 6:10). At times He personally directed the heralds of the gospel (10:19; 13:2; 16:6, 7). The Holy Spirit gave to Jesus’ followers both comfort and joy (9:31; 13:52). In the aftermath of the Spirit’s descent at Pentecost Jesus’ followers gathered regularly for worship, instruction, and the sharing of their lives and resources (2:42–47; 4:32–35). They are “God’s church” (20:28; cf. 5:11; 8:1; 9:31), a title that implies continuity with Israel’s congregation in the wilderness (7:38). As in the Gospels, their readiness to submit to and learn from their Master is reflected in the title “disciples” (6:1, 2; 9:1, 25, 26; 13:52). To outsiders, the church early on became known as “the Way” (9:2; 19:9, 23; 24:14), perhaps as a reflection of Jesus’ self-designation in John 14:6. However, most likely “the Way” became a name for the church because of the all-important role of the book of Isaiah (see “Acts in the Larger Story of the Bible” below). The church is established on the foundation of the apostles’ eyewitness testimony to Jesus’ resurrection (1:22; 2:32; cf. Eph. 2:20), but its growth demands the emergence of other leaders as well (6:1–7). Both in Jerusalem and elsewhere congregations are led by elders (11:30; 14:23; 15:2, 6, 22, 23), who receive ability and maturity from the Holy Spirit to shepherd and protect “the flock” (20:17–31). Although expressed in many congregations across vast distances, the church also displays its unity in submission of Gentile congregations throughout the Roman Empire to the decision of Jerusalem’s apostles and elders (16:4, 5), and in the circulation of leaders among various local churches (18:27).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Acts records the fulfillment of God’s covenant promise to impart blessing to all nations through Abraham’s offspring, Jesus of Nazareth (Gen. 22:18; Acts 3:25, 26; Gal. 3:7–9, 16), who is the Suffering Servant of the Lord (Is. 53; Acts 8:32–35) and the bestower of the promised Holy Spirit in the last days (Joel 2:28–32; Acts 2:16–21, 33). Befitting its position in the New Testament canon, Acts forms the historical bridge between the Gospels and the epistles, between Jesus’ completed ministry in humiliation on earth and His ongoing ministry in exaltation in heaven. As the Gospels open, John the Baptist is predicting the greater One who will baptize people with the Holy Spirit; but as they close, Jesus, to whom John testified, has not yet fulfilled that promise. Acts records that fulfillment, and thereby provides the context for the Epistles’ explanation of the Spirit’s transforming presence in the church. As the Gospels close, Jesus is alive, raised from the dead, and demonstrating His victory over sin and death by appearing repeatedly to a small circle of Jewish followers in Judea and Galilee. As the Epistles open, churches devoted to Jesus have been planted among Gentiles in major urban centers across the Greco-Roman world. Acts traces the course of events—the descent of the Spirit, the persecution that dispersed believers, the inclusion of Gentiles by faith, the call of Paul—that produced the churches and the issues addressed in the Epistles.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The narrative sections and the sermons of Acts reveal both the identity of Jesus as God and man and His redemptive mission. Jesus is the Lord who commissions His followers as a new, true Israel to serve as His witnesses throughout the world (1:8; cf. Is. 43:10, 12; 44:8). In His name alone is salvation to be found (4:12; Is. 45:21–25). He is the God who searches hearts (1:24; 1 Sam. 16:7; Jer. 17:10). Jesus is the Christ, the anointed king promised to Israel through the royal line of David, opposed by God’s enemies (4:25–29; Ps. 2:1, 2) but now risen from the dead and enthroned at God’s right hand, in fulfillment of Scripture (2:29–35; 13:32–37; Ps. 16:8–11; 110:1). Jesus is the righteous Suffering Servant of the Lord promised in Is. 53 (8:32–35; cf. 3:13, 26; 4:27, 30; 7:52). Raised and exalted by the Father, He is the Son of Man who now reigns in heaven (7:56; cf. 1:9; Dan. 7:13, 14). Yet the Lord Jesus continues to operate on earth, calling apostles (1:2, 24–26; 9:4–17), pouring out God’s Spirit (2:33), guiding His messengers and opening hearts to their message (16:7, 14), and saving through His name (2:21, 38; 3:6, 16; 4:10–12, 30). Looking to the future, Acts foretells the physical, visible return of Jesus from heaven (1:11). By His resurrection, Jesus has already been designated as the Judge before whom all nations will stand on the day appointed by God (10:42; 17:31). His reappearance from heaven will consummate God’s already-inaugurated redemptive reign in “times of refreshing” that will bring about the restoration of all things (3:20, 21). As the ascended Lord, Christ is exalted at the Father’s right hand in heaven and has all authority granted to Him. Acts reminds us to think of Christ’s redemptive work as encompassing His death, burial, resurrection, and ascension (2:14–36; 5:29–32).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: For most of church history, Acts has been read as a straightforward, though selective, historical rec­ord of the events in the early decades of the apostolic church, from the ascension of Christ through the gospel’s spread in the Roman Empire, until the arrival of Paul, apostle to the Gentiles, at the imperial capital in the early 60s. From at least the Reformation forward, scholars have also recognized that a pastoral-theological purpose accompanies the author’s intention to offer a reliable historical record of the birth and growth of the church in the thirty years after Christ’s resurrection and ascension. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, critical scholars raised objections to the longstanding tradition of Lukan authorship, and consequently to the historical trustworthiness of Acts. They contended that Acts could not have been written by a contemporary of Paul and the other apostles. Some claimed that Acts underplays the supposed conflict between Peter and Paul, between Jewish and Gentile Christianity, as reflected in Paul’s epistles. It was also alleged that Acts glorifies Paul as an eloquent orator and miracle-worker, whereas Paul himself, in his epistles, stresses his ineffective speech, sufferings, and weakness. The rise of form, source, and redaction criticism of the Gospels (and Acts with them) focused increasing attention on the theological agenda behind Luke–Acts, sometimes with the implication that the author compromised historical accuracy in order to convey a theological and pastoral message to his readers. More recent studies in both evangelical and historical-critical scholarship have shown the weakness of challenges to the claim that the third gospel and Acts were written by a companion of Paul, with eyewitness testimony as their source. A nuanced interpretation of Acts and Paul’s epistles show them to offer complementary, not contradictory, perspectives on the issues confronting the church in the early decades after Pentecost and on the apostle to the Gentiles himself. When Acts is viewed in its place within the trajectory of biblical prophetic history (from the Pentateuch through Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings and then to the Gospels), the allegation that theological and historiographical motives must be at cross-purposes loses its credibility.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The opening word of the letter (1:1), as well as the biographical details recorded in chs. 1; 15; and 16 show that Romans was written by the apostle Paul. The letter was already cited and listed as Paul’s during the second century. Its authenticity has been disputed only rarely and never convincingly. The title of Romans was drawn from the opening section; the book has borne that title from the earliest days of its history (1:1–7).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Paul wrote Romans shortly before his visit to Jerusalem with the gift from the Gentile congregations (15:25; cf. Acts 24:17). Internal indications suggesting that at this time he was a resident of Corinth include the reference to Phoebe, a member of the church at Cenchreae, the port of Corinth (16:1, 2), and the references to Gaius as his host (1 Cor. 1:14) and to Erastus (Acts 19:22; 2 Tim. 4:20). The time of writing was probably during his three months in Greece, described in Acts 20:2, 3. While it is not possible to fix a date with certainty, it is known that Gallio (before whom Paul appeared in Acts 18:12) was proconsul (normally a one-year appointment) in Achaia in A.D. 52. Paul was in Corinth for “many days” (Acts 18:18), presumably during the period A.D. 51–53. He then sailed to Ephesus for a brief visit, and went to Caesarea and probably Jerusalem as well as Antioch (Acts 18:22). Returning through Galatia and Phrygia (Acts 18:23) to Ephesus, he was a resident there for about three years (Acts 19:8, 10) before deciding to go to Jerusalem via Macedonia and Achaia (Acts 19:21). The earliest possible date for the writing of Romans, therefore, is toward the end of A.D. 54; but a later date leaves more leeway for Paul’s many activities, so the letter is best dated sometime between the end of A.D. 55 and the early months of A.D. 57. That the faith of the Roman Christians was well known (1:8) and that Paul had desired to visit them for some time (1:13) suggest that the Christian faith had been established in the capital of the empire for a considerable period. These facts are supported by the statement of the Roman historian Suetonius that Claudius had expelled the Jews (in A.D. 49) for rioting “at the instigation of Chrestus” (evidently a reference to Christ). Visitors from Rome were present on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:10, 11) and may have been the first to bring the good news to the city. Its strategic importance and the large number of Jews living there would have brought the gospel message to Rome as though attracted by a magnet. Though tradition stretching back to Irenaeus holds otherwise, it is certain that the church was not founded by Peter or Paul. It is clear that Paul never visited the church before writing the letter (1:8–13), and the absence of any reference to Peter or the other apostles suggests that the Roman church had not experienced direct apostolic ministry at the time Paul wrote. Both Jews and Gentiles were members of the church in Rome, and 1:13 indicates a predominance of Gentiles, as possibly does the warning to Gentile Christians not to be proud (11:13–24). The conflict between weak and strong in 14:1–15:13 may have arisen in a similar context. It is even possible that the several house churches in which the Christians met reflected these divisions (cf. 16:5, 14, 15). Paul perceived his ministry to be at a turning point when Romans was written. He believed that he had fulfilled his ministry in the eastern Mediterranean (15:17–23) and that the time was ripe to move west and evangelize and plant churches in Spain (15:24). He hoped to visit the Roman Christians on the way, fulfilling his longtime ambition, and perhaps gaining their assistance as a supporting church (15:24). In light of this, it was essential for him to pre­sent his apostolic credentials (note “my gospel” in 2:16 and 16:25), so that they might recognize the authenticity of his ministry. Paul may also have thought it necessary to defend his ministry from the false insinuations of rumor-mongers (3:8). At the time of writing his epistle to the Romans, Paul was also deeply concerned that the Christian church should be a fellowship of Jews and Gentiles together in the one body of Christ. This is clear from the importance he attaches to the Gentile love-gift to the Jerusalem church. It also surfaces throughout Romans in the theme of the unifying of Jew and Gentile—in sin because of Adam, and then in salvation through grace in Christ. The saving righteousness of the gospel is needed by both, since all have sinned; it may be received by both, since it comes by grace alone through faith alone. The accomplishment of this saving righteousness in history is the clue to God’s ultimate purposes for both; and the saving transformation accompanying this saving righteousness is to come to expression in the lives of both—personally, communally, and socially—in the body of Christ as the new people of God. The opportunity for writing while in Corinth, the pressing burden of his visit to Jerusalem, and the prospect of visiting Rome before preaching the gospel at the limits of the then-known world, all motivated him to write this letter.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: While the book of Romans is a letter and generally follows the standard epistolary conventions of the first century (See Introduction to the Epistles), it also differs in some important ways from other ancient letters and from the other NT letters. Like other letters of the first century, the epistle to the Romans contains an opening (1:1–17), a body (1:18–15:13), and a conclusion (15:14–16:27). Romans, however, unlike most other letters of Paul’s day, is an exceptionally long letter. Its length is not characteristic of most first-century letters, which were much shorter. More importantly, Romans is a distinctive type of epistle. Scholars who have examined ancient Greco-Roman epistolary conventions have distinguished several kinds of letters such as letters of friendship, letters of exhortation, and letters of recommendation. A comparison of Romans to the other Pauline epistles reveals that Romans has unique features that identify it as a specific type of letter. Romans is very similar to ancient “letter essays,” in which an author inserted a lengthy instructional “essay” within a conventional epistolary framework.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: One of the most striking features of Romans is its use of rhetorical questions (e.g. 3:8; 6:1; 7:7; 9:14). Rhetorical questions have the effect of drawing the reader into the author’s argument, articulating a mistaken conclusion from a previous assertion and thereby introducing the apostle’s clarification and correction. They are therefore an effective communicative device in engaging Paul’s readership, allowing them to “listen in,” as it were, to Paul’s presentation of the gospel in person and his interchanges with theological opponents. In 7:7–25, Paul employs another memorable rhetorical device when he speaks in the first person to describe the relationship between human beings and the law of God. Perhaps one of the most prominent literary features of Romans is its extensive citations of, references to, and allusions to the OT. The manner of Paul’s engagement of the OT in Romans is also diverse. Sometimes Paul quotes the OT in large blocks (3:10–18; 15:9–12). Sometimes Paul’s argument is driven by OT citations (chs. 9–11). Sometimes, Paul interprets an extended OT narrative (4:9–25). Both the diversity and extent of Paul’s engagement of the OT helps to show how the gospel “uphold[s] the law” (3:31), and how the old covenant prophets promised the saving mission of God’s Son that is now proclaimed in the gospel (1:1–4; 3:21–26; 16:25, 26).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Romans is Paul’s fullest, grandest, most comprehensive statement of the gospel. Its compressed declarations of vast truths are like coiled springs—once loosed, they leap through the mind and heart to fill one’s horizon and shape one’s life. John Chrysostom, the fourth century’s greatest preacher, had Romans read aloud to him once a week. Augustine, Martin Luther, and John Wesley, three supremely significant contributors to the Christian heritage, all came to assured faith through the impact of Romans. All of the Reformers saw Romans as the God-given key to understanding all Scripture, since here Paul brings together all the Bible’s greatest themes—sin, law, judgment, human destiny, faith, works, grace, justification, sanctification, election, the plan of salvation, the work of Christ, the work of the Spirit, the Christian hope, the nature and life of the church, the place of Jew and non-Jew in the purposes of God, the philosophy of church and world history, the meaning and message of the OT, the duties of Christian citizenship, the nature and purpose of Christian liberty, and the principles of personal godliness and morality. From the vantage point given by Romans, the whole landscape of the Bible is open to view, and the relation of the parts to the whole becomes plain. The study of Romans is vitally necessary for the spiritual health and insight of the Christian.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Romans gives us not only the most comprehensive statement of Paul’s gospel in the NT, but also a compendium of the Bible’s leading themes. In his “dedicatory epistle” to his commentary on the book of Romans, John Calvin says, “When any one understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture.” Of all the books in the NT, Romans comes the closest to offering a systematic theology. It is Paul’s most comprehensive outline of Christian doctrine. Romans is concerned to set forth the righteousness of God in the gospel (1:16, 17). It is a righteousness that we lack (1:18–3:20), but it is a righteousness that God is pleased to accomplish and to give in Christ (3:21–26.). This righteousness of God accomplishes the singular need of humanity, to move from being under the wrath of God (1:18) to having peace with God (5:1). Only justification by faith alone in Christ alone accomplishes this. Throughout the epistle, Paul explains this gospel in which the righteousness of God is revealed. Central to the gospel are the doctrines of justification by faith alone and substitutionary atonement. We are justified “by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (3:24, 25). This propitiation is necessary because “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all unrighteousness” (1:18), and if man is to be reconciled to God this wrath must be removed. Jesus is the substitutionary sacrifice who bears this wrath in our place and removes it from us. God put forward Christ as an atonement “to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (3:26). To the one who has faith in Jesus, God imputes the righteousness of Christ, and on the grounds of this imputed righteousness, the believer is declared righteous; he is justified by faith alone (3:21–4:25). Having been justified by faith alone in Christ alone, the believer has peace with God and is reconciled to Him. The righteousness that God is pleased to impute to us is ours in union with the crucified and risen second Adam, Christ (5:12–20). Believers are not only justified by faith alone; they are also sanctified, and Paul elaborates carefully on this theological theme. It is in union with Christ and by the power of the Holy Spirit that we put sin to death and strive for holy living in soul and body (chs. 6; 8). We are now “dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus” (6:11). Nothing in heaven or earth can “separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (8:39). The place of Israel in the purpose and plan of God is a significant theological theme addressed by Paul in chs. 9–11. Because Israel has rejected Christ, some have concluded that perhaps God’s promises to Israel have failed. Paul proceeds to defend God’s integrity, explaining that even under the old covenant, not all who were descended from Israel belonged to Israel (9:6). God is sovereign and has mercy on whom He will have mercy (9:15). Yet Paul continues to pray for Israel’s salvation (10:1). In ch. 11, he explains that God has not rejected His people, for even at the present time, a remnant of Jews is being saved (11:1–10). He also teaches that the current state of Israel in which the nation as a whole has stumbled while only a remnant is being saved, will be reversed by a future work of grace in which God will turn the heart of Israel to their Messiah (11:11–32). In chs. 12–15, Paul addresses the implications of the gospel for the life of Christians in the world and in the church. Because what Paul has said in chs. 1–11 is true, Christians are to present their bodies “as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (12:1). We are not to be conformed to this world but to be transformed by the renewing of our minds (12:2). Those who are believers in Christ are to behave in a way that is distinct from the behavior of the world, abhorring what is evil, blessing those who persecute them, and living in harmony with one another (12:9–21). Christians are to submit to governing authorities (13:1–7). We are to make no provision for the flesh (13:14). We are not to pass judgment on one another (14:1–12), and we are to remove all stumbling blocks from our brother’s path (14:13). With one voice, believers are to “glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (15:6).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Romans is replete with OT quotations, references, and allusions. It also provides something of a survey of the promise of the gospel revealed in the OT (16:25–27). Though we all fell in Adam and were reckoned sinners in him (5:12–21), God promised to crush Satan under the feet of Eve’s offspring, and—in Him—of believers (16:20, cf. Gen 3:15). God proclaimed and Abraham believed the message of justification by faith alone (ch. 4). Paul insists that the gospel does not destroy but establishes the Mosaic law (3:31). Jesus is the promised descendant of David (1:4, cf. 2 Sam. 7). Jesus is the One to whom all the prophets look (1:2; 15:12). Romans documents the fulfillment, in Christ, of all that God had been promising His people Israel for centuries and that in Christ, Gentiles receive the blessing that was to come through the line of Abraham (ch. 4; cf. Gen. 12:1–3).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Romans offers a full presentation of the person and work of Christ. He is both divine (9:5) and human (1:3, 4). He died and rose again for His people (3:21–26; 4:25). The Spirit of the exalted Christ indwells each believer (8:9–11) and applies the benefits that Christ secured for His people through His obedience and death. Christ’s example shapes the way that the church should order its life together (15:1–7). We eagerly await the outcome of our redemption wherein we will be fully conformed to the image of Christ, in order that He may be the firstborn among many brothers (8:29).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: As noted in “Characteristics and Themes,” Romans has figured significantly in the lives and ministries of some of the church’s greatest preachers and theologians. It was particularly important at the time of the Reformation. Against the church of Rome’s insistence that the believer needed a sacramental system and good works in order to be justified, the Reformers proclaimed, with Paul, that the sinner is justified by faith alone. They further insisted, with Paul, that justification by faith alone is never a license to sin, but mandates a holy life. Reformed believers in particular have pointed to ch. 9 as a passage that is important for our understanding of divine sovereignty, election and reprobation, and human responsibility.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: This letter bears the name of Paul as the author. No one has seriously questioned that Paul was the author of the Corinthian letters. These epistles are widely acknowledged as fundamental for our understanding of the apostle Paul, his ministry, and his message.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Paul makes it clear in 16:8 that he wrote this letter from Ephesus during the third missionary journey ( A.D. 53–57). Since the apostle stayed in Ephesus more than two years (Acts 19:8, 10), 1 Corinthians can be dated around A.D. 55. Although Luke says nothing about this correspondence in the book of Acts, he does provide some important information about the founding of the church in Corinth during Paul’s second missionary journey ( A.D. 50–52; Acts 18:1–11). First, Paul arrived in Corinth after his visit to Athens (Acts 17:16–34), an experience that had impressed on his mind afresh the foolishness of worldly wisdom. Evidently, this incident with the Athenian philosophers had further confirmed Paul’s determination to preach the simple message of the cross, however offensive it might appear to some (2:1–5). Second, with the support of an influential Christian couple, Aquila and Priscilla (16:19), Paul preached in the synagogue until Jewish opposition forced him to focus his ministry on Gentiles. Third, the Christian congregation in Corinth, composed of both Jews and Gentiles, flourished dramatically (Acts 18:8–10). Finally, Paul’s ministry in Corinth lasted a fairly long time (more than eighteen months; cf. Acts 18:11, 18). Since he had taught them the gospel and its implications at length and in depth, Paul had reason to expect some spiritual maturity from the Corinthian Christians. This letter reveals that the Corinthian church, instead of maturing in the intervening period between Paul’s departure from Corinth and his writing of the letter, had developed a remarkable number of serious problems, including division; abuse of the sacraments; disorder during worship services; theological confusion over such doctrines as the resurrection and the proper exercise of the Christian’s liberty in the gospel; and the extremes of moral laxity and unhealthy asceticism. What had happened? First, Corinth was one of the largest cities in the Roman world and one of the most corrupt (Acts 18:1 note). A strategic commercial center, the city sought to provide a wide variety of pleasures to international visitors and to those who settled there. In that setting, the Christians polarized, some insisting that association with sinners was permissible and necessary, others arguing that a measure of isolation was essential to preserve holiness. These opposing tendencies grew out of control in Corinth and endangered the future of the congregation. Second, the Corin­thians appear to have suffered from what has been called an “overrealized eschatology.” They overemphasized the spiritual attainments that they believed they possessed. They failed to appreciate the incompleteness of our present spiritual experience in Christ and the fullness of what we have yet to experience in Christ. This distorted understanding of the Christian life was manifested practically in the Corinthians’ spiritual overconfidence and in their failure to grasp the reach and influence of indwelling sin in their own lives. In other words, many Corinthians believed that the fullness of salvation had arrived and did not reckon with the remaining presence of sin with which Christians must deal until their glorification. We may infer from 5:9 that Paul had sent the church an earlier letter (which has not survived) exhorting the Corinthian believers to separate from immoral Christians. That letter must also have contained a request for an offering for needy believers in Judea (16:1–4; cf. 2 Cor. 8; 9; Rom. 15:25–27) and probably other instructions related to problems in the congregation. The troubles did not subside. Eventually, the apostle received reports that the church in Corinth was being torn apart by internal divisions, especially as a result of some in the congregation who viewed themselves as more spiritual and knowledgeable than their fellow believers (1:11, 12; 3:1–4; 8:1–3). Paul also learned about other matters: criticisms hurled at him, gross immorality, and lawsuits between Christians (4:1–4; 5:1; 6:1–6). Moreover, the church itself had written to Paul requesting instruction about such matters as marriage and divorce, food offered to idols, spiritual gifts, and the method Paul was using for his collection (7:1, 25; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1). They also asked for a visit from Apollos (16:12). The apostle was confronted with a massive task, and this long letter to the Corinthians the means by which he could deal with the problem.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of 1 Corinthians is a letter written by the apostle Paul, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see “Introduction to the Epistles”). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1–9), body (1:10–16:12), and conclusion (16:13–24).

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: One of the characteristic features of this letter is that Paul sequentially takes up concerns that have been brought to his attention. Given that the letter addresses so many topics, some have suggested that 1 Corinthians is a composite collection of various Pauline writings. A closer examination of the letter reveals a better explanation. The letter was written in response to a variety of specific issues and questions that were put to the apostle. Paul’s discussion of division and unity in the church was prompted by a report from Chloe’s people (1:11). His discussion of sexual immorality was also prompted by a report that made its way to Paul (5:11). In 5:9–13, Paul responds to a misunderstanding occasioned by an earlier and lost letter that he had sent to Corinth. In 6:12, Paul likely quotes statements made to him in a lost letter that the Corinthians had sent him. In ch. 7, Paul takes up “the matters about which you wrote” (7:1). The recurring phrase “now concerning” (cf. 7:1, 25; 8:1; 12:1) likely marks out the various issues raised in that correspondence. Scholars have long debated the degree to which 1 Corinthians is indebted to ancient rhetorical conventions. It is doubtful that this epistle can be comprehensively classified according to precise rhetorical categories. However, it would be a mistake to conclude that there is no trace of rhetorical forms in this letter. While Paul tells the Corinthians that he eschewed “lofty speech or wisdom” when he preached to them (2:1), it is clear from the letter that he was distancing himself from the misuse of rhetoric rather than its proper use. Some scholars, for example, see Paul’s “defense” in ch. 9 as a well-crafted legal argument.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The contents of the letter are determined by the kinds of problems that had surfaced in Corinth. Many scholars have suggested that the letter is roughly organized on the basis of a distinction between matters that had been reported to Paul (chs. 1–6) and problems that the Corinthians had raised in their letter (chs. 7–16). Such an outline provides a valuable overview. Behind the great diversity of issues treated in this letter there lie some deep and recurring problems. Challenges to Paul’s authority, pride in personal spirituality, and especially a lack of love were fundamental questions that the apostle needed to address. In the course of dealing with these issues, the apostle sets forth his teaching on important doctrines including God’s sovereignty, the nature of the church, sanctification, and the bodily resurrection. THEOLOGY OF 1 CORINTHIANS First Corinthians is one of Paul’s most occasional letters. That is to say, Paul addresses a wide variety of topics and circumstances that had arisen specifically in the lives of the Corinthian believers and that have come to his attention. First Corinthians helps us to see how wide-reaching the gospel (defined at 15:1–8) is in its applicability to the lives of Christians. The gospel not only teaches us to forsake division and disunity, but it gives us the resources to pursue true Christian unity (chs. 1–4). The gospel instructs us how and why to be sexually pure and to relate peaceably with our fellow believers (chs. 5; 6). The gospel instructs us how to think about singleness, marriage, divorce, and widowhood (ch. 7). The gospel helps us think through how to live our lives in the cultures of which we are part—without either wholesale withdrawal or ungodly compromise (chs. 8–10). The gospel also teaches us how to use our Christian freedom for the glory of Christ and for the edification and well-being of His people (chs. 8–10). The gospel teaches us how to order our lives together—as husbands and wives (11:2–16), in observing the Lord’s Supper (11:17–34), and other occasions of public worship (chs. 12–14). The gospel gives us a sure hope of life beyond the grave (ch. 15). 1

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: First Corinthians begins by addressing the people of God as those who are “sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints” or “holy ones” (1:2). Believers in every age are set apart from the world and set apart for God. Under the old covenant, God gave His people Israel an elaborate system of ceremonies and observances that served to distinguish them from the world and to point them to Christ the Savior for the forgiveness and the cleansing of their sins. In the new covenant, the old covenant system has been set aside because it has been fulfilled in Christ. However, God continues to call His people to be morally holy and, in that respect, distinct from the world, and Paul’s ethical teaching assumes the abiding validity of the moral law of the OT as a guide for the life of the believer (e.g., 1 Cor. 6:9–11). First Corinthians helps us to understand more fully what God’s pattern of holiness for His people looks like, and how that pattern is tied to the saving work of the Holy One, the Lord Jesus Christ. CHRIST IN 1 CORINTHIANS Crisp summaries of our redemption occur in such places as 1:30 and 6:11. Chapter 15 then offers an extensive discussion of Christ and is critical to a proper understanding of Christ’s work. The gospel is Christ’s death for sinners and His resurrection, all in accordance with the OT Scriptures (15:3, 4). The remainder of the chapter is one of Paul’s fullest statements about the resurrection. He stresses the importance to Christian belief of the bodily resurrection from the dead—to deny the believer’s resurrection from the dead is to deny that Christ has been raised from the dead. He also gives us a glimpse into the glory that will characterize the resurrection body. Throughout the chapter, he emphasizes that our resurrection hope is a hope in Christ—He is the firstfruits of the resurrection harvest (15:23), and the One through whom God has given us victory over death (15:57). In this chapter, Paul also expounds on the contrast between the first man, Adam, and the last man, Christ. In Adam, we are children of dust. In Christ, we are made new and will bear His image (15:45–49).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: One of the most discussed portions of 1 Corinthians is chs. 11–14, the chapters addressing public worship in the church of Jesus Christ. Along with the parallel passages in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, 11:17–34 has figured prominently in discussions throughout the church’s history concerning the presence of Christ in the Lord’s Supper. Chapters 12–14 have been central to recent discussions concerning spiritual gifts, specifically whether tongues and prophecy are continuing gifts in the church, or whether those particular gifts ceased with the passing of the apostolic age. Throughout the history of the church, the teaching regarding singleness, marriage and divorce in ch. 7 has also been a significant matter of discussion.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The apostle Paul is universally acknowledged as the author of this letter (1:1). It is an intensely personal letter in which Paul gives many details of his movements and associations. The title draws from the information in the salutation (1:1, 2).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The most likely date for the epistle is A.D. 55. Paul wrote it after he left Ephesus (Acts 20:1) but before he arrived again in Corinth (Acts 20:2). After founding the church at Corinth in A.D. 51–52 (Acts 18:1–18), Paul returned to Antioch, ending his second missionary journey (Acts 18:22). On his third missionary journey, Paul traveled to Ephesus and stayed there three years (Acts 19:1–41; 20:31). During his stay at Ephesus, messengers came from Corinth with the questions that Paul would answer by writing 1 Corinthians (1 Cor. 16:17, 18). Sometime later, Paul apparently heard of difficulties at Corinth and made a quick voyage by sea from Ephesus to Corinth and back. This visit did not go well, and Paul later referred to it as a visit made “in sorrow” (2:1). Though it is not recorded in Acts, this visit is indirectly attested by Paul’s statement in 2 Corinthians that he would be coming to them for the “third time” (12:14; 13:1). We do not know many details about what made this visit sorrowful, but apparently someone at Corinth had opposed or seriously offended Paul (2:5, 10). Most commentators think that after the sorrowful visit, Paul wrote the Corinthians a strong letter, commonly called the “severe letter,” rebuking them and encouraging them to repent (2:3, 4; 7:8). It seems most likely that the letter referred to in these verses has not been preserved. But some hold that the letter referred to is 1 Corinthians. Others think that the originally separate letter has been preserved as 2 Cor. 10–13. In any case, Paul sent Titus ahead by sea to Corinth, carrying the strong letter, while Paul took the longer land route around through Troas and Macedonia (2:12, 13; 7:5–9, 13–15; Acts 20:1, 2). Paul did not know how the Corinthians would receive Titus and the strong letter. When he left Ephesus and traveled to Troas, he experienced considerable anxiety because of his concern for the Corinthian church (2:13; 7:5). Though there was an opportunity for effective ministry when he reached Troas (2:12), Paul’s spirit was still deeply troubled. He left Troas and went on to Philippi in Macedonia, hoping to meet Titus there. When Titus finally arrived (probably at Philippi but perhaps at Thessalonica), Paul was overwhelmed with joy as he heard about the genuine repentance of the Corinthians and their deep affection for and loyalty to him (7:6–15). Paul then wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia to express thanksgiving for the repentance and renewed obedience of some members of the Corinthian church (7:5–16). Yet further reconciliation and healing were needed between Paul and other members of the Corinthian congregation. Consequently, he appealed for the opening of their hearts to an even fuller restoration of their relationship (6:11–13). This lingering tension may underlie the sober tone of chs. 10–13. He also wrote to encourage them to complete their collection for the poor Christians in Jerusalem (chs. 8; 9). Moreover, Paul shows concern throughout the epistle to defend his ministry against the accusations of “false apostles” (11:13) at Corinth who were challenging his authority and the integrity of his ministry (chs. 10–13; also 3:1–6; 7:2). Scholars debate the precise identity of these opponents. They appear to have been Jewish Christians (11:22) whose teachings constituted a denial of the biblical gospel (11:1–5). It is not certain that their teachings were identical to those of Paul’s opponents in Galatia. From the criticisms of Paul’s personal presence and speaking proficiency (to which he responds in 10:1, 10) and the way he emphasizes the sufferings that authenticate his apostolic calling (1:8–11; 4:7–12; 6:3–10; 11:21–32; 12:1–10), it is reasonable to infer that the false apostles (“super-apostles”; 11:5 ; 12:11) were projecting an image of Christian leadership and Christian living characterized by power and personal proficiency, rather than the weakness and dependence on Christ’s strength that were the hallmarks of Paul’s ministry, in the image of his Savior (13:4). Finally, Paul arrived in Corinth and stayed for three months (Acts 20:2, 3) before departing for Jerusalem with the collection that had been sent from many churches for the Christians there (Acts 20:3–21:17).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of 2 Corinthians is a letter written by the apostle Paul, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1,2), body (1:3–13:10), and conclusion (13:11–14). Like Paul’s first epistle to the Corinthians, his second epistle is an occasional letter written to address specific concerns. Given the number of issues he addresses and the changes in tone, the letter was likely written over a period of days or even weeks.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Over the last two centuries, critical scholars have suggested that 2 Corinthians is a composite of several Pauline letters or letter fragments. These hypothesized portions include 2:14–7:14 (and within this section, 6:14–7:1) and chs. 10–13. There is no compelling reason, however, to doubt the unity and integrity of this letter. For example, scholars have long noted the difference in tone between chs. 1–9 and chs. 10–13 . This difference, however, poses no necessary difficulty for accepting the letter’s unity and integrity (see Special Issues below). What are said to be preexisting letters or fragments within 2 Corinthians are better seen as segments or sections of a single letter. As a personal letter, 2 Corinthians includes significant biographical information regarding Paul, especially the discussion of his thorn in the flesh (12:2–10). The letter also includes a range of personal expression and idiom from very affectionate remarks to sarcasm.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Second Corinthians is a personal letter, filled with expressions of deep emotion. As such, it affords us extraordinary insight into the gospel ministry as carried out by Paul. Two chief themes reveal the nature of Paul’s apostolic ministry. In chs. 1–7, it is a service of divine comfort and encouragement in the midst of suffering and troubles (1:3–7; 7:4, 7, 13), and in chs. 10–13, it is an experience of God’s strength manifested in human weakness (12:9, 10). Supporting themes include the blameless nature of Paul’s conduct (1:12, 17, 18; 6:3–10; 7:2, 3); his frequent suffering for the sake of the church and for God’s glory (1:5–11; 4:8–12; 6:4–10; 11:23–12:9); his strong love for all his churches, especially the Corinthian church (2:4; 11:2, 7–11; 12:14, 15); his apostolic authority to build them up and defeat any opposition (2:9; 10:8; 13:8–10); and the frequent emphasis that Paul judges not according to worldly standards but according to the invisible spiritual realm known to the eyes of faith (1:12). Other distinctive emphases are the glory of the ministry of the new covenant (ch. 3) and the principles of Christian stewardship (chs. 8; 9). CORINTHIANS Second Corinthians is best understood as Paul’s defense of his own apostolic ministry. This is not the only time in his letters that he defends his ministry against opponents’ attacks (cf. Galatians), but this is the fullest defense that the apostle has left on record. It is not because Paul is unduly sensitive to criticism that he defends himself. It is because there are false apostles at work in Corinth who are peddling “another Jesus” and “a different gospel from the one you accepted” (11:4). He wants the Corinthians to know that his apostleship is authentic (12:12), precisely to confirm their confidence in the gospel (3:1–3; cf. 13:3). One of the major differences between Paul and his opponents concerns their understanding of suffering. For his opponents, Paul’s outward weakness and suffering disqualified him from the apostleship. For Paul, it was precisely these matters that qualified him to be an apostle of Christ (12:9, 13:4). This fact occasions Paul’s reflections on the Christian life generally in chs. 4; 5 that “though our outer nature is wasting away, our inner nature is being renewed day by day” (4:16). Even our “affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” as we gaze upon things unseen (4:17, cf. 4:1–6, 18). By undergoing suffering in a Christ-honoring way, the Christian shares in both the sufferings and the glory of Jesus Christ (cf. 4:10– 12). Paul points us to gospel realities that help us in suffering to persevere by faith. Believers in any and all circumstances stand confident in the righteousness of Christ, imputed to them and received by faith alone (5:11–21). The indwelling Holy Spirit (5:5), by whom each believer has been sealed (1:22), assures us of our ultimate hope—the hope of the resurrection body (5:1–10). For these reasons and more, “we walk by faith and not by sight” (5:7). 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: God in every age of redemptive history calls His people to trust the promises of His Word and not to put their confidence in human flesh or strength. This latter point was a temptation that Abraham and his sons faced, as Hebrews reminds us (Heb. 11:13–16). God was frequently admonishing Israel and her leadership not to put their trust in kings and horses but in the Lord. Many Jews in Jesus’ day rejected Him and His ministry because He did not offer them a kingdom of worldly glory and splendor. In Paul’s day and in our own, the temptation remains to put our confidence in what we can see, not in what God has said in his Word. 2 Corinthians helps us to understand how and why the gospel, though despised by the world, has a genuine and lasting glory all its own (4:1–6). Consequently, we must believe in and walk by God’s promises, all of which find their fulfillment in Christ (1:20). CHRIST IN 2 CORINTHIANS Although the leading concern of 2 Corinthians is Paul’s apostolic ministry, Paul never loses his focus on Jesus Christ, through whom God is reconciling the world to Himself, and in light of whom Paul has been entrusted with what he calls the “ministry of reconciliation” (5:18). Paul offers a concise statement of the doctrine of imputation, declaring that Christ took upon Himself our sin, so that those in Christ might become righteous (5:21). Paul’s ministry finds its definition and meaning from this full exposition of the person and work of Christ (4:7–18; 13:4). Paul’s goal in ministry is to lead God’s people in paths of righteousness (chs. 6; 7) that he may present them “as a pure virgin to Christ” (11:2). Second Corinthians presents a fully Christ-centered view of ministry.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Second Corinthians 3:1–4:6 has figured importantly in the history of interpretation. In these verses, Paul contrasts his ministry with that of Moses, and he also contrasts the new covenant with the old covenant. These verses provide us one of the fullest statements in the New Testament about the nature and purpose of the old (Mosaic) covenant; the nature and purpose of the new covenant in Jesus Christ; and the relationship between the two.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Even though the authorship of 2 Corinthians is not disputed, many question the unity of the letter, most frequently proposing that chs. 10–13 should be considered a separate letter written on a different occasion and only later appended to chs. 1–9. The basic support for this argument is that Paul’s tone and attitude toward the church at Corinth seems so positive and encouraging in chs. 1–9, but so severe and threatening in chs. 10–13. Given this difference, many wonder how both sections could have been written on the same occasion to the same church. Certainly there is a change in tone at 10:1. But this can be accounted for by the change of subject matter. Furthermore, it is not as if chs. 1–9 contain no hints that some problems remained between Paul and at least some members of the Corinthian church at the time the apostle wrote the letter. True enough, Paul is primarily concerned in the first part of the letter to share his joy and thanksgiving at the repentance of the Corinthians. Yet even in chs. 1–9 Paul alludes to a further need for their reconciliation with him (6:11–13). There is clearly tension in Paul’s tone in ch. 3. Nevertheless, chs. 1–7 are largely positive, and therein the apostle gives an extensive and confident description of his own ministry. Having done that, he then appeals to them to complete the collection for the Jerusalem Christians (chs. 8 ; 9). Finally, leaving the most distasteful task until last, he takes up the problem of the false apostles and their accusations against him (chs. 10–13). From the earliest years in the history of the church there has been no indication of division in this letter, either in the manuscript tradition or in the early historical writings of the church. It has always been read and understood as one letter. This remains the best explanation for the canonical form of the letter.
