sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The apostle Paul wrote Galatians (1:1). He mentions a group of his coworkers who had some role in sending the letter (1:2), but the letter’s style and theology demonstrate that Paul was the immediate author. Since the eighteenth century, a few scholars have considered the letter pseudonymous (that is, that the name “Paul” was used by another, unknown author) but their arguments are generally regarded as having no foundation. The title is taken from the information found in the salutation (1:1, 2).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The question of the letter’s date is intertwined with the problem of its destination. Paul names his addressees as “Galatians” (3:1; cf. 1:2), but to which “Galatians” was he writing? Galatia was a Roman province that encompassed roughly the eastern portion of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). He may have been writing specifically to the Celtic people who lived in northern Galatia and who were widely known as “Galatians,” or he might have been addressing the people who lived in southern Galatia in central Asia Minor. When we follow the course of Paul’s first and second missionary journeys (Acts 13; 14; 15:36–18:22), we discover that this question has implications for the epistle’s date and for its relationship to Paul’s other letters. Paul visited Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe (all cities in southern Galatia) on his first and second missionary journeys. If Paul wrote to southern Galatia, he probably wrote to those churches early in his career, shortly after the first missionary journey, or about the time of the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15; cf. Gal. 2:11–14). The date most often given by those who hold this view is A.D. 49. If this is correct, Galatians may be Paul’s earliest epistle in existence today. Many scholars, however, think that Galatians was written to the ethnic Galatians in the north. If this view is correct, Paul may have planted the Galatian churches on his second missionary journey (Acts 16:6), and probably wrote the letter after passing through “Galatia and Phrygia” (Acts 18:23) on his third missionary journey. Many who follow the “northern Galatian theory” believe that Paul wrote the letter either during his two-year stay in Ephesus (Acts 19) or as he was traveling through Macedonia on his way to Greece at the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:1–6; cf. 2 Cor. 2:13). If this is correct, Galatians was probably written in A.D. 54 or 55. Theories that date the letter later in Paul’s career have the merit of placing Galatians in the same period as 2 Corinthians, Romans, and perhaps Philippians—letters that share with Galatians some matters of common concern. The earlier (southern Galatian) dating, on the other hand, is more easily reconciled with the account of Paul’s movements in the book of Acts. In Galatians, he reports two visits to Jerusalem, the first coming three years after his conversion (1:18–20; Acts 9:26–30) and the second “after fourteen years” (perhaps from his conversion, rather than from the first visit; 2:1–10; Acts 11:29, 30). Paul’s description of the second visit involving his meeting “privately” (2:2) with James, Cephas, and John seems not to fit the description of the apostolic council that, according to Acts, took place on Paul’s third visit to Jerusalem after his conversion (Acts 15). Yet, if Galatians was written after that council, it is hard to explain why Paul omitted mention of that visit—and failed to cite the council’s decision defending the Gentiles’ freedom from the obligation to be circumcised (Acts 15:1, 5, 10, 11, 19, 20, 24–29, 31; 16:4). Galatians was written to answer specific problems in particular churches. In order to understand the epistle, some knowledge of the situation that provoked Paul to write is essential. Not long after the Galatians had accepted the gospel, agitators came among them who attacked Paul personally (4:17) and preached a distorted form of Christianity, a false gospel (1:6, 7). Their “gospel” required circumcision for justification (6:12). Since the Galatians were uncircumcised Gentiles, the agitators insisted that the Galatians not only believe in Christ for justification but also accept circumcision (2:3–5; 5:2, 6, 11; 6:12, 13, 15). The zeal of these agitators likely reflects Jewish pressure as well as their own pride. Perhaps they were attempting to convert the Gentile Galatians to Judaism under pressure from nationalistic Jewish groups in Judea who, according to the Jewish historian Josephus, were becoming increasingly intolerant of contact between Jews and Gentiles during the last half of the first century. The agitators were not content merely to preach their brand of the gospel. They also attempted to discredit Paul, who had founded the Galatian churches (4:13). Their attacks took three forms: (1) They claimed that Paul was a renegade who had defied his superiors, the Jerusalem apostles. Paul responds to this attack in 1:11–2:10. (2) They said that Paul had recently argued with Peter over whether the gospel required Gentiles to become Jews in order to become Christians. Paul gives his account of the encounter with Peter in 2:11–14. (3) The agitators spread the notion that Paul had originally preached circumcision for salvation (5:11) but had recently changed his gospel so that he might more easily accommodate the Gentiles (1:10). The Galatians, for their part, were showing interest both in the rumors about Paul and in the agitators’ new form of the gospel. By the time Paul wrote, they were in the process of deserting the true gospel and, consequently, God Himself (1:6, 7). They now wanted to be “under the law” (4:21; cf. 5:1) and, specifically, to become circumcised (5:2). This attraction to “a different gospel” (1:6) bore bitter fruit. Dissension appears to have broken out within the community (5:15; 6:3–5). Paul’s purpose in writing was to persuade the Galatians that no Gentile needs to accept circumcision in order to be justified and to belong to God’s covenant people. The “truth of the gospel” (2:5, 14) is that justification and entrance into communion with the people of God comes by faith in Jesus Christ. Anyone who seeks to violate that sacred sphere of faith by adding other requirements corrupts the gospel and must be resisted at all costs (1:8, 9). In order for his argument to be persuasive, Paul had to demonstrate that the rumors about him were false, and that both his gospel and his authority to preach it came from God Himself (1:11–2:14; cf. 5:11; 6:17).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of Galatians is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1–5), body (1:6–6:10), and conclusion (6:11–18). It is important to note, however, that while Paul uses the standard conventions of first-century letter writing, he does not do so slavishly. He feels free to adapt the form when it suits his specific needs. For example, in his letter to the Galatians, he does not include a thanksgiving immediately after his opening salutation, as he does in his other letters. Instead, he moves immediately into a rebuke of the Galatian believers. This subtle alteration to the standard epistolary form is another piece of evidence indicating the true seriousness of the Galatian error.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Many scholars believe that Galatians has an outline indebted to ancient rhetorical forms. After offering the salutation in 1:1–5, he proceeds to introduce the main concerns of the letter in 1:6–10. In antiquity, this portion of the letter was called the exordium . In 1:11–2:14, Paul gives an extended historical narrative (the narratio ), the goal of which is to defend the authenticity of his apostleship and to respond to criticisms that it had originated from men. In 2:15–21, Paul presents the thesis, or main proposition (the propositio ), of the letter. The argument defending that proposition follows in 3:1–4:11 (the argumentum ). After an expression of personal concern (4:12–20) and an illustration drawn from the biblical account of Hagar and Sarah (4:21–31), Paul proceeds to exhort the Galatians to holy living in Gal 5:1–6:10 (the exhortatio ). The letter’s conclusion comes in Gal 6:11–18 (including the peroratio , which recaps the main points and makes a final appeal to the Galatians, in 6:11–17). Scholars differ over the precise outline of the letter, but one thing is clear: as impassioned as Paul is in this letter, his passion is fully in the service of clear thinking and sound argument. The rhetorical shape of the letter also accounts for two features that are absent from this letter but are normally present in Paul’s letters. Galatians lacks an opening prayer of thanksgiving, as well as closing greetings and prayer requests. The absence of these customary epistolary features undoubtedly helps to call attention to the urgency of Paul’s overarching concern in Galatians: the defense of the gospel.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The letter to the Galatians stands like a sentinel over the truth that justification is the gift of God’s grace, unearned and undeserved, to be received by faith alone (2:15, 16). Indeed, faith itself is God’s free gift (1:3, 6, 15; 2:19, 21; 6:18; cf. Eph. 2:8, 9). Quite simply, this is “the truth of the gospel” (2:5, 14). Paul shows deep anger over the agitators’ denial of it (3:1; 5:12), warning that those who reject it cannot expect to be saved (1:8; 5:4). Faith alone is critical because Christ alone is the Savior. He bore the curse of the law in our place on the cross (3:13; 6:14). Made one with Him, we are clothed with His righteousness (3:26, 27), which is our sure hope (5:5). Because we are united to Christ, we receive the rights of His sonship (4:4, 5) and the Spirit of the Son becomes ours, enabling us to live in the Spirit, in fellowship with our Lord (2:20; 4:6, 7; 5:16–18, 25). The gift of the Spirit is the full blessing promised long ago to Abraham (3:6–9, 14). References to the Holy Spirit actually outnumber the terminology of justification (“justify,” “righteousness,” etc.) in this epistle. Paul appeals to the Galatians’ experience of the Spirit’s life-giving power—apart from circumcision and law-keeping—as evidence supporting his argument that faith in Christ alone is the means by which they have become children of Abraham and heirs of God (3:2, 3). Their new life must be lived in keeping with the Spirit’s lead and in dependence on the Spirit’s power (5:13–26). Against the proud imagination of sinners that they can earn their own salvation by keeping God’s law, Paul boasts only in the cross, in faith receiving and resting on the promise of God in Christ Jesus (6:14).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: This epistle is one of Paul’s earliest and most powerful statements of justification by faith alone (2:16–21). Paul stresses that our works, however good they may appear to be, in no way justify us. By faith alone we receive the righteousness of Christ—His perfect obedience and His full satisfaction for sin—and it is on the basis of Christ’s righteousness alone that we are declared righteous before God. It is through this same faith that we are the adopted sons of God (3:26, 4:5), and this justifying faith, far from being a dead faith, works by love (5:6), even as by this faith and through the Holy Spirit we eagerly await for the fullness of the gospel hope that accompanies our righteousness in Christ (5:6).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Paul emphasizes that every saving benefit that the believer enjoys comes to him by the merits of Christ and through the Holy Spirit. In fact, Christ died precisely in order that “the blessing of Abraham,” that is the “promised Spirit through faith” might “come to the Gentiles” (3:13, 14). Paul stresses that the gospel that he preached and the gospel that we have received through faith alone is the same gospel that was preached to Abraham (3:8). All believers in Christ, who is the promised offspring of Abraham (3:16), are thereby “Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (3:29). This is another way of saying that Jesus is true Israel (“Abraham’s seed”) and all those who trust in and are in union with Christ are true Israel (“Abraham’s seed”). Paul goes to great lengths to demonstrate that the Mosaic law was not contrary to God’s promises (3:21). The law was never meant to be and has never been an independent source of justification and life. It was training Israel to look to Christ; in fact, it was driving them to Christ, in whom alone life is found through faith (3:19–29). Believers, then and now, have always been saved by the work of Christ alone, set forth in the Scriptures of both the OT and the NT. Galatians helps us to understand that throughout redemptive history, God has always had one way of salvation, one gospel for all kinds of people. It expresses passionately and pointedly the Pauline gospel that is elaborated more fully in the epistle to the Romans and articulated more concisely elsewhere in Paul’s correspondence (Eph. 2:1–10; Phil. 3:2–11; Titus 3:4–7)

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Because of his concern to address justification by faith alone in this letter, Paul reflects upon the cross of Christ. Not only is Christ’s death on the cross decisive for justification (3:10–14), but it is also decisive for sanctification (1:4; 2:20; 5:1, 13; 6:14, 15). As elsewhere in his letters, Paul is concerned to emphasize that Jesus Christ was raised from the dead (1:1). Paul assumes that no sinner can be saved apart from Christ and His work for sinners, and he asserts that corrupting the gospel by the addition of human works subjects oneself to God’s curse (1:8, 9).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The interpretive framework known as the New Perspective on Paul has dominated the study of this letter since the last quarter of the twentieth century. The New Perspective on Paul stands in contrast to the traditional view of Paul since the Reformation. The traditional view understands Paul’s use of the expression “works of the law” as referring ultimately to a system of works righteousness—wrongheaded attempts to earn God’s favor through human effort and merit in keeping the law. The Protestant Reformers drew a parallel between this view among first-century Jews in Paul’s day and later medieval Roman Catholicism in the sixteenth century because of the emphasis in both of those groups on the role of the believer’s good works in meriting a right standing before the Lord. Justification by faith alone through grace alone in Christ alone was the Reformation’s answer to this futile attempt to achieve righteousness through human “works of the law.” Martin Luther and the other Reformers saw this view heralded by Paul in Galatians. The New Perspective, on the other hand, argues that Paul’s main concern in Galatians is not fundamentally how a sinner is saved but rather how one may be identified as a member of the people of God and how one remains part of this covenant community. The New Perspective suggests that Paul’s opponents were claiming that circumcision, dietary laws, and feast days (“works of the law”) were required for inclusion in the covenant community; in Galatians, Paul answers by positing justification by faith as the badge of entrance into the covenant community. Justification, according to the New Perspective, is not about how one gets saved, but rather about how one identifies the church. In other words, for the New Perspective, Galatians is about ecclesiology (the nature of the church), not soteriology (the nature of salvation). While Paul undoubtedly has Jew/Gentile relations in the church in view in Galatians (as he does in Romans and Ephesians), the New Perspective reverses Paul’s approach in this letter. He focuses on “the works of the law” not as badges of covenant inclusion but as badges of righteousness before God. For instance, in Gal. 3:10–14 the apostle clearly understands “works of the law” not as sociological or ecclesiological identifiers, but as deeds that one does in order to secure acceptance before God. And he says quite plainly that “by the works of the law” as deeds that must be done, “no one will be justified” or declared right with God (2:16). How then is one in the right with God? “Through faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16). Justifying “faith” in Christ, therefore, consists in renouncing our own efforts for justification, and receiving and trusting only in Christ and his work for justification. As individuals trust in Jesus Christ, they are declared right with God—they are justified—based only on what Christ has done and not in any way on what they have done. In fact, all that is true of Christ is true of them: they are crucified with Him and they are raised with Him (2:20). That is the basis, then, of the justification that is required for inclusion in the true covenant community, whether one is Jew or a Gentile (3:28). All those who trust in Jesus Christ alone are united to Him, declared righteous, and are now part of a new humanity. They are heirs to Abraham’s promises, and they have received the Holy Spirit. Individuals reveal that they are part of the true covenant community by walking in step with the Spirit and living lives of faith-filled love (5:6, 13, 14, 16–26). Such love and holiness are outward evidences of saving faith, and demonstrate that one is in Christ and has received the imputation of His righteousness by faith in Him alone; therefore, one is also a part of the true church of God that will celebrate the marriage supper of the Lamb on that last day (Rev. 19:6–10) Soteriology, then, is the basis for ecclesiology.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The title of the book comes from the salutation (1:1). The author is Paul, as evidenced by the letter itself (1:1; 3:1). Themes and language common in Paul’s earlier letters appear frequently in Ephesians, and the verbal similarities with Colossians are especially striking. However, modern scholarship has challenged both the traditional view on the authorship and recipients of this letter. In the modern era, Pauline authorship of Ephesians has been questioned. Some scholars say Ephesians appears to be too dependent on Colossians. Although the letter seems like Paul’s writing, its phrases tend to build and multiply more than in his earlier letters. The letter strikes some as less instructional and more prayerful. Ideas that are only implicit in his earlier letters (e.g., that beyond local churches there is one worldwide church) become explicit here. The author describes “hearing” of his readers’ faith rather than having witnessed its evidence in person, although Paul had ministered for several years in Ephesus (cf. Gal. 4:13, 14; Col. 1:9; 2:1). Such considerations lead many to say that Ephesians was written by one of Paul’s students who was attempting to develop some of Paul’s ideas, especially those in Colossians. The language and style of Ephesians differ in some respects from Paul’s other letters. Still, they are so similar to Paul’s that even if the letter did not bear his name, it is difficult to imagine the church crediting it to anyone else. Furthermore, it seems unlikely that a student of Paul would be so eager to imitate his teacher that he would transcribe verses from Colossians word for word, and yet be so daring as to move dramatically beyond Paul’s theology of the exalted and reigning Christ to one of a universal church. The verbal similarities with Colossians are most easily explained by assuming that Paul wrote Ephesians shortly after completing Colossians. Paul’s devotional and prayerful tone reaches its height as he contemplates the eternal and universal significance of Christ’s church. In this way, he continues his reflections on the subject that dominated his correspondence with the Colossians—the eternal and universal significance of Christ. Because some early manuscripts lack “in Ephesus” at 1:1 (see Date and Occasion below and ESV text note on 1:1), some have proposed that this epistle was a circular letter addressed not only to Ephesus but also to other churches in Asia (cf. 1 Pet. 1:1; Rev. 1:4, 11). This wider audience could explain not only Paul’s mention of “hearing” of his readers’ faith but also the fact that his tone is more meditative and less directed to specific local crises.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The identity of the letter’s original audience has also been questioned. This letter may have had a broader audience than the church at Ephesus alone. Some of the oldest Gk. manuscripts do not include “in Ephesus” in the address of the letter (1:1), reading instead: “to the saints who are also faithful in Christ Jesus.” Several early Christian writers seem unaware of a specifically Ephesian address. The letter lacks the personal references and greetings Paul almost always included in his correspondence, and there are other details about which Paul writes that seem to conflict with what we know about his ministry in Ephesus (e.g., 3:1–13). At the same time, no manuscripts name any other city as the address of the epistle. Many scholars believe Ephesians was written as a general letter to a number of churches in the region, which would be in keeping with the sweeping contents of the letter as a whole. It is possible that Paul originally sent the letter to Ephesus, but as the letter was sent from church to church the address was omitted because the contents had little to do with Ephesus in particular. Or, it may be that the letter was originally in two forms, one for the Ephesians that contained “in Ephesus” and one for general circulation that did not. Questions about to whom Paul wrote this letter also lead to questions about when he wrote the letter. The imprisonment mentioned in 3:1 and 6:20 is the same as that in Colossians 4:3, 10, 18, and is probably Paul’s two-year house arrest in Rome ( A.D. 60–62), recounted in Acts 28. Ephesus was the capital of the Roman province of Asia on the west coast of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). It lay between the eastern and western halves of the Roman Empire and was among the five most prominent cities in the empire during the first century. During Paul’s unusually long stay in Ephesus, it became the center for evangelizing the western part of Asia Minor (Acts 19:10). Paul’s affectionate ties with this church are evident in his farewell speech to its elders (Acts 20:16–38). Ephesus’s most prominent civic monument, the temple of the goddess Diana, was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The city is described in one inscription as the “nurturer” of the goddess, and the goddess in turn makes Ephesus the “most glorious” of the Asian cities. People from the area would have appreciated the irony of Paul’s words about Christ’s nourishing His own body, the church (5:29). They would have appreciated the point of contrast when Paul describes Christ’s church as a glorious or radiant bride (5:27). It was also in Ephesus that Paul’s preaching of Christ came into dramatic conflict with an important trade dependent on pagan worship (Acts 19:23–41) and that the gospel inspired a great turning away from the occult (Acts 19:17–20). Paul’s call to expose the deeds of darkness (5:8–14) and prepare for war against “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (6:12; cf. 1:20, 21; 3:10) would have struck the original readers with special force.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: Because of its style, some have suggested that the book of Ephesians should be classified as a written sermon or a theological essay. The book, however, generally follows the standard epistolary conventions of the first century (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1, 2), body (1:3–6:20), and conclusion (6:21–24). It should, therefore, be classified as an epistle. As he does in his other epistles, Paul adapts the standard conventions to his own purposes in his letter to the Ephesians. For example, instead of moving immediately from his opening greeting to thanksgiving and prayer as he does elsewhere, he introduces in Ephesians an extended rhapsody (1:3–14) immediately after the greeting and before the thanksgiving. This has resulted in some disagreement concerning whether the body of the text begins with 1:3 or with 2:1. However, because 1:3–3:21 is a coherent unit, it is preferable to identify the beginning of the body of the letter at 1:3.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: The most striking feature of this book is how it reflects a deeply and thoroughly Pauline approach to thinking about the Christian life. Chapters 1–3 build up the “indicatives,” the glorious statements of fact that undergird Christianity. Here Paul lays out the riches that are ours in Christ Jesus through His work of redemption. Chapters 4–6 then offer the “imperatives,” the commands regarding how we are live in light of our calling and the riches that are already ours in Christ. Another important structural feature of this letter is the repetition of the verb “walk.” Believers formerly “walked” in trespasses and sins (2:1) but now have been “created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them” (2:10). Chapters 4–6, the applicatory section of this epistle, are structured around the Christian’s “walk,” or way of thinking and living. Paul begins this section by urging us to “walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called” (4:1). He later summons us “no longer [to] walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their minds” (4:17). We are to be “imitators of God, as beloved children. And [to] walk in love” (5:1, 2a). We are to “walk as children of light” (5:8) and “look carefully then how [we] walk, not as unwise but as wise” (5:15). Paul picked up “walking” as a metaphor for one’s pattern of conduct from OT precedents (e.g., Deut. 5:32; 10:12; Ps. 1:1; 119:1). Although the letter does not frequently quote the OT in a formal manner (see Eph. 4:8), it alludes to it and engages it in other ways. Terms such as “redemption,” “forgiveness,” “adoption,” and “inheritance” evoke specific covenant blessings mentioned in the OT (1:5, 6, 11). Paul invokes such familiar old covenant realities as “circumcision,” “the commonwealth of Israel,” “the covenants of promise,” and “temple” in order to help believers understand the nature and identity of the new covenant people of God (2:11, 12, 21). Furthermore, the phrase “the helmet of salvation” directly picks up terminology from the OT (6:17; cf. Is. 59:17). Other pieces of the “armor of God” allude to weaponry wielded by the Lord, His Messiah, or His messengers in the OT (Ps. 144:1–2; Is. 11:5; 49:2; 52:7). No small part of the literary craft of this epistle is the way in which Paul has seamlessly incorporated OT motifs.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: One of the key words in this letter is “mystery,” which appears seven times (1:9; 3:3, 4, 6, 9; 5:32; 6:19). The first statement is the most important: Paul tells us that God is now revealing the “mystery of his will,” which is the uniting of all things in heaven and on earth in Christ. The great evidence that this cosmic redemption is happening is the church, the body of Christ, His new humanity (1:23, 2:15). In the church, God is uniting Jew and Gentile, reconciling them and tearing down the “wall of hostility” between them through the cross (2:14). This “mystery of Christ” was hidden in past times (i.e., before the coming of Christ), but is now seen clearly: “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ through the gospel” (3:6). That means, then, that the church is central to God’s purpose in the world because it is a sign of the final reconciliation of all things in Christ. The church is God’s precious possession, a colony in which the Lord of history has begun to fashion the renewed humanity after His own image (1:10–14; 2:11–22; 3:6, 9–11; 4:1–6:9). The church is a community where God’s power to reconcile people to Himself is experienced and shared in transformed relationships (2:1–10; 4:1–16; 4:32–5:2; 5:22–6:9). It is a new temple, a building of people, grounded in the sure revelation of what God has done in history (2:19–22; 3:17–19). The church is an organism in which power and authority are exercised after the pattern of Christ (1:22; 5:25–27), and its stewardship is a means of serving Him (4:11–16; 5:22–6:9). The church is an outpost in a dark world (5:3–17), looking for the day of final redemption. Above all, the church is the bride preparing for the approach of her lover and husband (5:22–32).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Ephesians is a summary of Paul’s gospel. In ch. 1, Paul reflects on the triune God’s accomplishment of our salvation: God the Father chose His people before the foundation of the world (1:3–6); God the Son accomplished redemption for His people (1:7–10); and God the Spirit applies redemption to us and assures us that the inheritance is ours (1:11–14). Throughout this epistle, Paul reflects on salvation in personal and individual terms (2:1–10), in corporate terms (2:11–22), in cosmic terms (1:9-10; 6:10–20), and in historical terms (3:1–6). Redemption is both individual and cosmic; as such, it has profound implications for the way in which God’s people understand themselves and live together (4:1–5:21). In particular, Paul uses the plural pronouns “we” and “you” (1:12, 13; 2:1–3, 11–22) to emphasize God’s dismantling of the dividing wall between Israel (His ancient covenant people) and the Gentiles through the sacrificial death of Christ, by which the two have been made one and given access to God the Father by the Spirit (2:14, 16–18). In summary, this letter impresses upon us how comprehensive and far-reaching the gospel is. The gospel also transforms the way we conduct ourselves in marriage, in parenting, and in the workplace (5:22–6:9). Paul prefaces these commands regarding our relationships and roles with two significant points: (1) We are to walk in love as Christ loved and as He gave Himself for us in His atoning death and in His active obedience (5:1). (2) We are to submit to one another out of reverence for Christ (5:21). Love and submission then serve as the foundation to our roles as spouses, parents, children, employers, and employees. We are also kept from moralism by remembering the cross and our redemption as that which enables to live the lives to which Paul calls us in 5:22–6:9.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In 1:9, 10, Paul tells us that God’s purpose, “set forth in Christ,” is “a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Him, things in heaven and things on earth.” All of history, including the history recorded throughout the OT (4:8, quoting Ps. 68:18), moves toward this goal and destination—the bringing together of all things under the sovereign rule of the crucified and exalted Christ (1:19–22). Christ’s mediatorial reign is most visible in the church (1:22; 4:7–14), through whom “the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places ... according to the eternal purpose that [God] has realized in Christ Jesus” (3:10, 11). Even so, under the new covenant, “the mystery of Christ” was first made known by the Spirit and through Christ’s “holy apostles and prophets” (3:5). This mystery, whose fulfillment was not yet visible during the era of the OT, was that Jews and Gentiles would be fellow members of the people of God, on equal terms and without distinction (3:6; cf. 2:14, 15). (Although “hidden” in the sense of “not exhibited in history,” the inclusion of the Gentiles by faith in a coming Messiah was also foretold in the OT, as Paul argues elsewhere; cf. Rom. 3:21, 22; 4:1–17; 15:8–12; Gal. 3:5–14.) Christ’s universal reign is now on particular display in His church, drawn from all people and nations who stand alongside one another as spiritual equals in Jesus Christ.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: This epistle helps us to understand the critical biblical doctrine of union with Christ. The importance of this doctrine is evident from the opening verses of the book. It is “in Christ” that the Father “has blessed us ... with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (1:3) and that in whom He “chose us before the foundation of the world” and “predestined us for adoption” (1:4, 5). It is “in the Beloved” that we have been “blessed” by the Father’s “glorious grace,” and in Christ that we have “redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (1:6, 7). In Christ “we have obtained an inheritance” (1:11), and “in him ... you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (1:13). Furthermore, it was by being united to Jesus Christ in His death and resurrection that we were saved by the grace of God (2:1–10). In Christ, the whole church is “being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (2:22) and is the bride of Christ (5:25–33). We are joined to Christ, as the body is to the head, and thus grow into maturity (4:15, 16). In this letter, Paul particularly emphasizes Christ as raised from the dead as well as our union with Christ in His resurrection. The very same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead made us alive together with Christ (2:5), presently indwells us (3:16, 17), and is at work in us presently “according to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead” (1:19, 20a). Paul’s point is plain—in Christ and by the Spirit of the risen Christ, believers have all the resources they need to walk with God in this age.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Paul’s teaching on slavery (6:5–9) has been the occasion of both discussion and controversy, particularly within the last two centuries. For further discussion of this issue, see Introduction to Philemon: History of Interpretation. Ephesians 1:3–14 has played a long and crucial role in the Reformed tradition’s understanding of the gospel. This passage is a concise and at the same time comprehensive statement of the gospel that gives expression to the distinctively Reformed approach to the doctrines of grace. Furthermore, Eph. 2:8–10 is one of the most concise and complete presentation of the doctrine of justification by grace alone through faith alone that can be found in all of Scripture. Ephesians 6:10–20 has often been emphasized in discussions of spiritual warfare.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The author identifies himself as Paul (1:1), and the early church unanimously attributed this letter to him. It has many personal references, and is similar to the other Pauline writings. These facts together leave no doubt that Paul is the author. The beginning of Paul’s involvement with the church at Philippi is recorded in Acts 16. Prompted by a vision (Acts 16:6–10), Paul and his colleagues traveled to Philippi (Acts 16:12). During their brief visit, God did mighty works and a church was established (Acts 16:40), Paul’s first on European soil. Paul himself returned on at least two more occasions to strengthen the believers (Acts 20:1–6; 2 Cor. 2:13).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Paul writes from prison (1:12–30), but the location of the imprisonment is a matter of discussion. Some think he wrote from Ephesus, though Acts 19 says nothing of his being imprisoned during his lengthy Ephesian ministry. A stronger case can be made for his having written the letter during his imprisonment in Caesarea (Acts 23:23–26:32). But it is most likely, in keeping with longstanding tradition, that Paul wrote Philippians during the Roman imprisonment described in Acts 28 and that he did so toward the end of this period, around A.D. 61. His references to the “imperial guard” (1:13) and “Caesar’s household” (4:22) accord best with a Roman setting, and the language of 1:7–26 (with the possibility of execution) suggests legal proceedings at the highest level. Finally, the continuing success of Paul’s ministry during his imprisonment (1:12–14) is in keeping with his freedom to preach during his confinement in Rome (Acts 28:16–31). The city of Philippi was named for Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great. Its location on the main road between the eastern provinces and Rome contributed to its importance. A Roman colony populated in part by retired Roman soldiers, the city afforded its inhabitants the privileges of Roman citizenship (including exemption from taxation and right to due process in Roman courts). Paul’s references to “citizenship” in 1:27 (see note) and 3:20 would be particularly meaningful to residents of a city that was a colony of the imperial capital. The absence of OT quotations (though allusions appear at 2:5–11, 15, and perhaps elsewhere) and absence of Jewish names in the letter indicate that the church of Philippi was largely Gentile. The fact that Paul and Bar­nabas first preached at a place of prayer outside the city suggests that they found no synagogue at Philippi, an inference that seems to be confirmed by archaeological evidence. The book of Philippians rings with joy and gratitude for the way God was carrying forward His saving work among the Philippians and for the special bond that existed between Paul and his readers. At the same time, there is a gravity to the letter. The Philippians faced persecution (1:27–30) and felt the pressures exerted on them by false teachings (3:2–21). Conflicts in the church jeopardized the believers’ witness to the world and their ability to withstand its assaults (1:27–2:18; 4:2, 3).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of Philippians has been classified by many as a “friendship letter.” The book generally follows the standard epistolary conventions of the first century (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1, 2), body (1:3–4:20), and conclusion (4:21–23). Some have suggested that although Philippians is clearly an epistle, to classify it more narrowly as a “friendship epistle” is to oversimplify the complex nature of the book. Paul adapts ancient epistolary conventions to meet his own needs, and Philippians is therefore more complex than many other ancient friendship letters; however, characteristics of such letters are prominent in many places in this book (e.g., 1:8, 27; 2:1, 2; 4:15). Paul does not merely repeat ancient Greco-Roman ideas of friendship, however. He redefines friendship in terms of the believer’s communion with Christ and his communion with other believers.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Many scholars recognize the theme or main proposition of this letter to be found in 1:27: “Only let your manner of life be worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that whether I come and see you or am absent, I may hear of you that you are standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel.” Several concerns surface in this verse: the unity of the church, the integrity of the gospel, and steadfastness in the face of opposition. At several points in the letter, Paul urges the Philippians to pursue the unity that is theirs in Christ and to which Christ calls them (2:1–18; 4:2, 3). Paul also urges the Philippians to preserve the integrity of the gospel against false teachers and false teaching (3:1–11). There can never be true Christian unity when the gospel is not clearly proclaimed and maintained. Neither can one genuinely embrace the gospel while being indifferent to the claims of Christian unity. Paul himself sets an example for steadfastness in the face of suffering, joyfully assessing his present imprisonment and its possible outcomes in terms of the advance of the gospel (1:12–26, 28, 29). Some scholars consider 2:5–11 to be an early Christian hymn, either adapted by Paul or an original composition of Paul. Whether it is a hymn or not, the poetry of this section is noteworthy. The elegance of Paul’s writing in the passage reflects its lofty content. Some critical scholars have argued that ch. 3 was an independent fragment that was joined to chs. 1; 2 in the formation of this epistle. They particularly appeal to the change in tone beginning at 3:2 (“Look out for the dogs”). Given the seriousness of the issues to which Paul turns in this chapter, however, this change of tone is not unexpected. Furthermore, Paul stresses two matters in this chapter that have dominated his argument in the first two chapters of this letter—suffering for Christ (3:10) and genuine humility (3:3). Scholars have also noted numerous verbal connections between ch. 3 and earlier portions of the letter. There is no compelling reason to doubt and every reason to accept the unity and integrity of the epistle.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Despite its short length, Philippians incorporates a number of themes that enrich our understanding of the person and work of Christ as well as the nature of faithful Christian service. Some of the most important of these include: 1. Paul’s Affection for His Readers. This epistle amply attests to the special bond of love Paul felt for the Philippians (1:3–8; 4:10–19). The church at Philippi had faithfully supported Paul’s ministry, and their willingness to suffer with him for Christ was a source of encouragement for Paul. 2. Joy. Even though he was in jail, Paul’s letter resounds with the theme of joy. Forms of the word “joy” occur sixteen times in the letter. Paul’s joy is grounded in the peace of God, the antidote to all anxiety (4:4–7). 3. The Triune God. Paul uses the word “God” to refer to the Father (1:2; 2:11; 4:20). Paul’s favorite designation for Jesus Christ is “the Lord” ( kyrios in Gk.; see 1:2; 2:11, 19; 3:8, 20; 4:23). On the one hand, Paul affirms in this letter that the Father and the Son are one God. Both are divine and worship is due to both (2:5–11). In calling Jesus Christ “the Lord,” Paul identifies Him with Yahweh, the God of Israel. Yet by calling the Father “God” and Jesus “the Lord,” Paul shows that there is a distinction of persons within the Godhead. Finally, God the Holy Spirit stands alongside God the Father (3:3) and Jesus Christ (1:19). Paul’s theology is Trinitarian, confessing one God in three persons. 4. The Example of Christ’s Humility. The majestic “hymn to Christ” (2:5–11) offers a model for believers. Before He was incarnated (“became flesh”; John 1:14), Christ Jesus was truly God. Nevertheless, He humbled Himself and took the form of a slave by taking on human nature for the sake of going obediently to the very depth of humiliation and anguish—“death on a cross” (2:8). Yet in adopting a true and complete human nature, He did not cease to be God. Rather, Christ manifested His divine character by becoming a human servant; and He therefore was exalted by the Father as Lord over all, to be worshiped by every creature everywhere, in fulfillment of Is. 45:23. See History of Interpretation below. 5. Justification by Grace Alone through Faith Alone. Against those who require obedience to the OT law as a way of meriting salvation, Paul stresses God’s will that His people should be justified by receiving His righteousness as a gift and not by striving to establish their own. Although Paul had been scrupulous in his obedience to the law, he came to realize that his obedience could not merit a righteous standing before God, and that his confidence in such obedience was a great sin, for it kept him from trusting God. Paul views his former boasting with disgust (3:7, 8), and Christ alone is now his confidence (3:3, 9). 6. The Christian Life. The letter is filled with instruction on practical Christianity. Just as Christ became a slave, so also the Christian becomes the slave of Christ (1:1). Only the person enslaved to Christ is free to love and serve others (2:3–5). 7. Christian Giving. Paul ends his letter with a significant barometer of the Christian life, namely, a view of material resources and giving to meet the needs of others. Paul likens financial gifts to the OT offerings and sacrifices of tabernacle and temple worship in 4:18. Paul also teaches by example of the beauty of contentment in life (4:11–13). Only the person enslaved to Christ and empowered by Christ can take this view of personal resources. 8. Identification with Christ. Paul emphasizes the importance of identification with Christ in His death and resurrection. As it was for Christ, suffering for the believer is the prelude to resurrection and is a way in which the believer presently comes to experience the resurrection power of Christ (3:10, 11). For the present, it is in the midst of ongoing struggle that the Christian experiences joy and power (3:10; 4:13). 9. Perseverance. The importance of striving toward the goal of full salvation is highlighted. Confident of God’s calling, Paul pushes forward toward the heavenly prize (3:13, 14). As Christians work, they realize that God is working in them (2:12, 13). Human effort is precisely the area where the power of God is manifested, and perseverance unto glory is the God-given gift to everyone who has rested in Christ alone for salvation. When God begins a good work in a person, He always completes it (1:6), and our pressing forward in repentance, faith, and obedience is evidence that we are in Christ by faith alone and heirs of the Lord’s promises.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Paul not only calls Christians to unity, but he also demonstrates how to pursue unity in the church. Unity is a command of God (1:27, 2:2, 4:2, 3). Unity is possible only when believers commit themselves to putting away “rivalry” and “conceit”; they are instead to “in humility count [others] more significant than [themselves]” and to “look … to the interests of others” (2:3, 4). Christ has provided the greatest example of this life (2:5–11), and such ministers as Timothy and Epaphroditus exemplify this Christlike pattern of living as well (2:12–30). The gospel promotes unity. Justification is by faith alone and on the basis of Christ’s merits alone, and not on anything that believers have done (3:9). One’s ongoing Christian life, imperfect as it is (3:12, 13), finds its focus and power in Christ’s death and resurrection (3:10–16). All that believers do is owed to the grace and strength of God (2:12, 13). Knowing these realities helps to prevent boasting in the flesh and promotes glorying in God alone (3:3). It is precisely this attitude that is conducive to unity in the body of Christ. Joy and thanksgiving, which permeate this letter (see “Characteristics and Themes”; 4:10–20), find their ground in the gospel. Those who were once part of a “crooked and twisted generation” (2:15) and have been delivered from the destruction to which their sins subjected them (3:19) have reason to be thankful and joyful. Those who have been given “the righteousness from God that depends on faith” (3:9), who share in Jesus’ death and resurrection (3:10), and who now have their “citizenship in heaven” and the sure hope of a resurrection body “like his glorious body” (3:21) ought to respond in thanksgiving and joy.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: In every age, God has called His people to lives of thanksgiving and joy, and to celebrate and to pursue the unity that uniquely belongs to the people of God. The Psalms, for instance, are filled with such calls, and those calls come in light of the mercies and bounty of Israel’s redeeming Lord. It is in Philippians, however, that we see the deepest and fullest grounds for such a call: the finished redemptive death and resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ. Philippians helps Christians not only grasp the saving plan and work of the triune God (see “Characteristics and Primary Themes”), but also see that there is one God and one plan of redemption throughout redemptive history.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The hymn of Christ in 2:6–11 is one of the richest statements of the person and work of Christ in the NT (cf. John 1:1–14, Heb. 1:1–4, Col. 1:15–20). We learn of the deity of Jesus (2:6), His sinless humanity (2:7, 8), His humiliation in suffering (2:8), and His resultant exaltation by the Father in glory (2:9–11). In the incarnation, the divine Son of God took on true and sinless humanity. He became, and continues to be, God and man in two entire distinct natures and one person, forever (Westminster Larger Catechism Q&A 36). We speak of the two states of Christ—His humiliation and His exaltation. His humiliation began at His conception and birth and continued through His death and burial. He was obedient to God, all the way to His death on the cross (2:8). But God exalted Him at His resurrection and ascension, and has given Him “the name that is above every name” (2:9). All creation will acknowledge His Lordship, to the glory of God the Father (2:10, 11).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Paul’s words in 3:1–11 have been crucial in the church’s understanding of the Bible’s teaching on justification by faith alone. For this reason, it has become a central passage in discussions relating to the New Perspective on Paul (see Introduction to Galatians: History of Interpretation). The so-called “Kenotic Hymn” or “Kenosis Passage” of 2:5–11 has been the subject of intense debate in recent decades. At issue is the assertion by some scholars that the hymn teaches Christ’s divestment of certain divine attributes in the incarnation, that the Son of God set aside or gave up aspects of deity when He came in the flesh. This position is untenable. The passage describes the incarnation not as a subtraction but as an addition: the Son of God took on “the form of a servant” (v. 7). Without ceasing to be God or surrendering any of the attributes who make God who He is, the Son of God added to Himself a true human nature. Other passages in the NT make it clear that Son did not give up any of His divine attributes; rather, for the sake of our salvation, He chose not to exercise some of His prerogatives at certain points in His ministry even though He very well could have. By virtue of His divine authority, for example, Christ could have called down twelve legions of angels to rescue Him from the Roman soldiers in Gethsemane (Matt. 26:53), but He did not exercise His rightful authority to do that because the cross was His mission. When the Son of God “emptied Himself” in the incarnation (2:7), He veiled but did not surrender His refulgent glory. At particular points in His ministry, He allowed this glory to be seen by His disciples—most notably in His transfiguration (Matt. 17:1–8)—and at His return, every eye will behold this glory and confess that He is Lord of all (2:9–11).

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: Colossians was written by Paul the apostle (1:1; 4:18). Though many modern scholars have doubts about Paul’s authorship of this letter, compelling grounds for questioning its authenticity are lacking. The language and style are well within the range Paul displays elsewhere and, while aspects of the vocabulary of Colossians are distinctive (e.g., terms such as “fullness,” “mystery,” “elemental spirits,” and “asceticism”), these stem largely from Paul’s use of the language of his opponents in order to refute them.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Paul never visited Colossae (2:1). The church there was founded by a Colossian named Epaphras, apparently in the wake of Paul’s ministry in Ephesus ( A.D. 53–55), where “all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks” because of Paul’s daily teaching visitors in the “hall of Tyrannus” (Acts 19:1–10). Some five to seven years later, the founder of the Colossian church joined Paul in prison at Rome (Col. 4:12, 13; cf. Acts 28) to tell the apostle of a strange teaching threatening the health of his home church and to remain with Paul to pray for the churches of the Lycus Valley. In earlier days, Colossae, a city on the Lycus River in southeastern Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), had been a prosperous and large city, enjoying a thriving wool industry and a strategic location on a main overland trade route between Ephesus one hundred miles (160 km) to the west and the Euphrates some four hundred miles (650 km) to the east. In Roman times, however, Colossae had declined in the face of the growth of two sister cities in the Lycus Valley: Laodicea, the district capital ten miles (16 km) to the west, and Hierapolis, famous for its healing springs, some twelve miles (19 km) to the northwest. In Paul’s day, Colossae was a fairly unimportant market town, easily the least significant city to which any of Paul’s surviving letters were addressed. As noted in “Characteristics and Primary Themes” below, at least one occasion for the epistle was Paul’s concern to counteract a false approach to spiritual experience that focused on visions (2:18) and ascetic self-denial (2:23), apparently undermining the gospel’s declaration that the fullness of God’s nature and glory dwells in the incarnate Christ (1:19; 2:9), who has accomplished both human and cosmic reconciliation through His cross (1:19–22).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of Colossians is a letter written by the apostle Paul, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1–14), body (1:15–4:6), and conclusion (4:7–18). As he does in all of his letters, Paul uses the standard epistolary conventions, but he does not do so in a mechanical way. He feels free to adapt the form when it suits his specific needs, and he varies the wording of his salutations, his prayers, and his closing greetings accordingly.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Like many of Paul’s letters, the first half of Colossians (1:1–2:23) consists of doctrinal teaching (Some see the transition from theological instruction to ethical application as early as 2:6, with its “Therefore ... walk.”). Specifically, Paul dwells on the person and work of Christ. The second half of the letter (3:1–4:18) consists of application. The application flows directly from the earlier doctrinal teaching (“If ... then”; 3:1; cf. 2:20). This pattern reinforces not only the fact that Christian living is grounded in Christian doctrine, but also that the Christian finds his motives and resources for living the Christian life not in himself, but in the triune God who has saved him. The hymn of 1:15–20 is a particularly striking example of Paul’s literary craft. The repetition of the Gk. word translated “all” in 1:15–20 (v. 16 [2x], v. 17 [2x], v. 18, v. 19, v. 20) serves to underscore Paul’s message of the sufficiency of Christ for the believer’s salvation. One way of outlining the hymn is to see it in two main parts (vv. 15–17, 18–20), highlighting Christ as the Creator and the Redeemer, respectively. Each part contains the word “firstborn” and some form of the phrase “things in heaven and on earth.” The first part ends in the same way that the second part begins (“and he is”). This literary symmetry highlights the majesty and glory of Jesus Christ in creation and new creation.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The Christians Paul addresses in this letter were likely struggling with a Greek-influenced form of Jewish philosophy or “spirituality” that viewed Christians as still vulnerable to spiritual forces. It was thought that these forces needed to be placated through veneration, through some sort of asceticism of food and drink, and by honoring certain days prescribed in OT ceremonial law. The epistle is designed to help Christians understand that in order for them to gain acceptance before God, they need Christ only . God has already accepted them by virtue of the crucified and risen Christ to whom they are united. While there is a perfection, or maturity, that still stands before them as a goal (1:22, 23, 28), they are already “filled in him,” the perfect One (2:10).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: In this letter, Paul is combating a heresy that scholars have found very difficult to identify (see Special Issues below). Apparently, this heresy did not categorically deny that the work of Jesus Christ is necessary for the sinner’s salvation. It did, however, deny the sufficiency of that work for salvation. The Colossians were being told that by means of observing a cycle of feasts and festivals (2:16), and particularly through an ascetic lifestyle of abstention from food and drink (2:21–23), they could usher themselves into ecstatic, visionary states in the present (2:18) and, with Christ’s help, make it to heaven one day. Paul overwhelmingly emphasizes the sole sufficiency of Christ for salvation. This theme surfaces at many points in his opening thanksgiving and prayer (1:3–14) and becomes the subject of the rich meditation of 1:15–20—the supremacy of Christ in creation, providence, and redemption (cf. 1:21–23). In 2:6, 7, we find one of the most important points of the letter—“as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.” It is Christ alone who can deliver the sinner from the guilt and dominion of sin (2:6–15). The Christian life begins with the realization that we are united to Jesus Christ in His death and resurrection. Thus united to the Savior, we are enabled to take up the work of putting sin to death (3:5), of “putting away” sin and of “putting on” the graces of the Christian life (3:5, 12). Having “put off the old self” (or “man”), and having “put on the new self” (or “man”), each Christian is “being renewed after the image of its creator,” that is, Jesus Christ (3:9, 10, cf. 1:15–17). This pattern of living works itself out across the whole of the Christian’s life—marriage and child-rearing (3:17–21), the workplace (3:22–4:1), prayer (4:2–4), and our conduct toward unbelievers (4:5, 6).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Throughout the OT, Israel was frequently tempted to engage in idolatry. Very often this temptation entailed serving idols alongside the living and true God. Throughout the OT Scriptures, God told His people that He allows no rivals. He not only warned them against idolatry but He also wooed them to Himself (cf. Hos. 2:14–23). Colossians provides a reminder that idolatry—setting up anything instead of or alongside God to rival Him in one’s thoughts, service, or affections—is an ongoing temptation in the life of God’s people. The attraction of rivals to Christ wanes and the bonds of devotion to Him strengthen only when believers truly grasp the beauty and the glory of their all-sufficient Savior.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Col. 1:15–20 gives one of the fullest statements of the person and work of Christ in the NT (cf. John 1:1–14, Phil. 2:5–11, Heb. 1:1–4). Paul states in no uncertain terms that Jesus is God (1:15). As God, He created the world and all things in it—“by him all things were created” and that Jesus is the very purpose or goal of the creation (1:16). Furthermore, “by him all things hold together”—that is, moment by moment, He upholds the creation that He spoke into existence (1:17). He also is the “firstborn from the dead,” the beginning and author of the new creation (1:18). In Christ is all that the sinner could need for redemption (1:19), and it is in Christ alone that God has purposed to reconcile sinners to Himself (1:20). Throughout this passage, Paul stresses that Jesus’ work as the Creator, Sustainer, and Redeemer means that He has supremacy over the works of His hands, and particularly over the church (1:15, 18). He therefore deserves the worship, adoration, and service of every human being, not least the people of God. Colossians 2 reiterates many of these same themes, including the deity of Christ, “for in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (2:9). Paul also provides important insight into the work of Christ in His atonement, reminding readers that the death of the Savior satisfied the legal debt His people owe to God; thus, there is no further temporal or eternal payment that believers must make for their sin (2:14). The apostle also presents the cross as the point at which the Savior achieved His decisive defeat of Satan and his minions (2:15).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Colossians was an important book at the time of the Reformation. The Roman church, the Reformers argued, was detracting from the sufficiency of Christ for salvation, especially through its elaborate sacramental system. Colossians helps the church in every age to see that Christ’s work is fully sufficient to save sinners. Furthermore, adding to what the Bible has revealed about Christ detracts from His lordship and supremacy. To cling to Christ alone for salvation is the only proper way to honor the person and work of Christ.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Paul addresses the false teaching at Colossae. Phryg­ia, the region in south central Asia Minor where Colossae was located, is an area with a peculiar religious history. In ancient times, the region gave birth to the worship of the goddess Cybele, whose cult (renewed during the Roman era) was characterized by ritual cleansing in the blood of a bull, ecstatic states, prophetic rapture, and inspired dancing. In the latter half of the second century A.D. , Phrygia became the center of a distorted version of Christianity known as Montanism, a teaching that prized ecstatic and apocalyptic prophecy, freedom from the responsibilities of daily life, and rigorous fasts and penances for ritual purity. Within a few years of the inception of Christianity among these Phrygians, Epaphras and Paul found that an appetite had emerged for something more than the crucified and risen Christ. It is notoriously difficult to reconstruct the false teaching to which Paul responds in the book of Colossians because the letter is less a critique of error than a positive statement of the sufficiency of the person and work of Christ. However, certain features of the false teaching do surface: (1) It claimed to be a “philosophy” (2:8), a term that in the Hellenistic age often referred not to rational inquiry, but to occultic speculations and practices based on a body of tradition. (2) The teaching appears to have reflected Jewish influences, as evidenced by the value placed on legal ordinances, food regulations, Sabbath and new moon observance, and other prescriptions of the Jewish calendar (2:16). Though circumcision is mentioned, it was not necessarily seen as one of the requirements imposed by the false teaching in Colossae (2:11). (3) The role of angelic spirits was also an important element in this teaching. Two factors point to this. First, there is stress on Christ’s superiority to and victory over “rulers” and “authorities” (1:16; 2:10, 15). Second, the role of angels in the Colossian error is evident in the phrase “worship of angels” (2:18). Early Christians knew that there were angels who served agents at creation and in the giving of the law (Acts 7:53; Gal. 3:19; Heb. 2:2). The false teaching in Colossae had confused the limited and legitimate role of angels as “ministering spirits” (cf. Heb. 1:14) with the larger role attributed to angels in some parts of Judaism, not to mention the astral powers of the Gentiles. As a means of overcoming fear of these astral or cosmic powers, and under the guise of revelations that so-called “philosophers” received in ecstatic states, the Colossians were being urged to become ascetics and to worship angels. Scholarly opinion is divided as to whether the term “elemental spirits of the world” (2:8, 20) also refers to superhuman spiritual beings, thought to control various aspects of human experience (see 2:8 text note and the same expression in Gal. 4:3, 9). Phrygia was well known for preoccupation with the need to placate various spiritual forces associated with stars and planets. The Colossians appear to have come under the influence of a combination of Jewish and pagan piety presenting itself as a philosophical system (2:8) and insisting on submission to various astral or cosmic powers.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The author of this epistle identifies himself as the apostle Paul (1:1; 2:18). The authenticity of 1 Thessalonians has occasionally been challenged but with little success. The contributions of Silas (Silvanus) and Timothy, named by Paul as coauthors (1 Thess. 1:1; 2 Thess. 1:1) in some sense, to the substance of the Thessalonian letters cannot be detected with any certainty. It remains possible that certain peculiarities of these letters, in comparison with the rest of Paul’s writings, are due to the influence of either of these close associates of Paul.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The city of Thessalonica was named for Alexander the Great’s half-sister, Thessalonike. It was founded about 315 B.C. by her husband, King Cassander of Macedonia. In Roman times, Thessalonica was a provincial capital with more than two hundred thousand inhabitants. On his second missionary tour, Paul and his companions Silas and Timothy came to Thessalonica by road from Philippi, where they had been “shamefully treated” (2:2). Acts 17:2 records that Paul preached and debated in the synagogue of Thessalonica for three successive Sabbaths. Eventually, members of the Jewish community enlisted unscrupulous men to stir up animosity against the Christians. A riot ensued, and a number of Christians, including a Jewish convert named Jason, were dragged before the authorities. Jason and the others were forced to post security money to guarantee that the church would not cause trouble. Paul, Silas, and Timothy were whisked away by the believers under cover of night and soon found themselves in Berea to the west, where the gospel received a more open-minded hearing from the Jewish community (Acts 17:5–12). Although the existence of the synagogue shows a larger Jewish presence in Thessalonica than in Philippi, the Christian congregation was predominantly Gentile. This indicates that a successful ministry among Gentiles continued after Paul’s access to the synagogue was cut off. During their stay in Thessalonica, which cannot have lasted more than a few months, the missionaries apparently received more than one contribution for their support from the congregation at Philippi (Phil. 4:15, 16). This, combined with earnings from their own labors (2:9; 2 Thess. 3:6–12, 8), meant that they were able to support themselves without depending on the Thessalonian believers, who were young in the faith. The missionaries’ example of humble, industrious behavior was a rebuke to the minority in the church who wanted to refrain from working for a living (5:14; 2 Thess. 3:11). Paul wrote 1 Thessalonians after receiving a report from Timothy regarding the state of the Thessalonian congregation (3:6, 7). The letter expresses the apostle’s joy and relief that the Thessalonians were continuing firm in the faith despite the premature departure of Paul and his coworkers, and the harassment they still suffered from hostile factions. Paul’s discussion of matters related to Christ’s second coming and the bodily resurrection (see Characteristics and Primary Themes below) in both epistles to Thessalonica may offer a clue to the occasion for his writing: apparently the brevity of his initial ministry in planting this church did not permit sufficient instruction on God’s plan for the consummation of history and its implications for Christians as they wait for the end. Furthermore, Paul’s brief stay did not permit much time for teaching on what happens to Christians who die before Jesus returns to consummate His kingdom. As a result some confusion about these matters was present in the Thessalonian church when the apostle wrote (see Characteristics and Primary Themes below). It is almost certain that Paul wrote the first letter to the Thessalonians in Corinth, where Silas and Timothy were reunited with him during his second missionary journey, which reached Macedonia and Achaia (Acts 18:5; 2 Cor. 1:19). The letter was most likely written in A.D. 50 or 51, with 2 Thessalonians following shortly thereafter. Therefore, 1 and 2 Thessalonians are among the earliest letters we have from the hand of Paul, with only Galatians having any reasonable claim to be earlier (see Introduction to Galatians: Date and Occasion).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of 1 Thessalonians is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1), body (1:2–5:22), and conclusion (5:23–28). The letter, however, does not fit neatly into any of the various types of first-century epistles that have been identified. It has characteristics of several kinds of letters. Although Paul identifies himself as the author in 1:1 and 2:18 (see Title and Author above), his first epistle to the Thessalonians differs from his other epistles in that the first-person plural is used throughout the letter (“we,” “us,” “our”). This reflects the opening of the letter, in which the senders are identified as “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy.” It does not, however, mean that Paul is not the primary author, since he does revert to the first person singular on occasion (2:18; 3:5; 5:27). Second Thessalonians shares with 1 Thessalonians many of these features that set the latter book apart from the rest of Paul’s epistles. See Introduction to 2 Thessalonians: Genre.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: First Thessalonians affords us a close look into the relationship between a pastor and a young congregation. Paul speaks in very pointed and intimate terms of his pastoral ministry among them (2:1–12, 2:17–3:5). He helps these new believers to understand the circumstances and nature of their conversion (1:3–10), and what it means to stand firm in the faith and to persevere in the life that the gospel calls believers to live (3:6–13). Like 1 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians addresses a series of pastoral issues that have arisen in the young Thessalonian church. Paul helps the Thessalonians to persevere through persecution (2:13–16). He must press upon them the importance of pursuing sexual purity (4:1–8), as well as of ordering their lives in a way that commends the gospel before all people (4:9–12). Much of his letter is devoted to addressing mistaken understandings of the return of Christ and its implication for believers who have already died (4:13–18), and then helping the Thessalonians to understand what the return of Christ means for the Christian life presently (5:1–11). First Thessalonians is an especially personal letter. Not only does Paul frequently address the Thessalonians as “brothers” at important points in his argument (2:1, 17; 3:7; 4:1, 9, 13; 5:1, 12), but he also speaks of himself both as their “father” (2:11) and “mother” (2:7). This incidence of familial language serves to express and to emphasize the deep affection that Paul had for this young church. As he would in his later letter to another Macedonian city, Philippi, Paul calls the believers in Thessalonica his “joy” and his “crown” (2:19; cf. Phil. 4:1).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: A rich vein of teaching about the last days runs through 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Paul’s preaching at Athens, recorded in Acts 17, confirms that his strategy among non-Jewish audiences at the time he wrote these letters was to stress the coming judgment (4:6) that God has placed in the hands of the risen Christ. The return of Christ will occur on what Paul calls the “day of the Lord” (5:2; 2 Thess. 2:1 note). On this day, there will be a resurrection of the just to inherit salvation in the Lord’s presence (4:16; 5:10), and of the unjust (presupposed by Paul though never explicitly stated) to be eternally separated from Christ (2 Thess. 1:9). The end will be preceded by a widespread apostasy and the appearance of a diabolical “man of lawlessness” (2 Thess. 2:3). Since this person had not yet appeared, those in the congregation who were saying that the “day of the Lord” had already arrived were wrong and should be silenced. Another notable characteristic of the letters is Paul’s affirmation that Christ is divine, the more striking because of the early date of the letters and the spontaneous nature of the references. Several times Christ and God the Father are linked together as the common source of divine blessings and as the divine addressee of prayer (1:1; 3:11; 2 Thess. 1:1, 2, 12; 2:16; 3:5). In Paul’s use of the OT expression “day of the Lord,” in which “the Lord” is now revealed to be the Lord Jesus Christ (5:2; 2 Thess. 2:2), there is a similar assignment of the prerogatives of deity to Jesus Christ (5:2 note). The united work of the three persons of the Trinity is mentioned in 2 Thess. 2:13, 14. THEOLOGY OF 1 THESSALONIANS First Thessalonians is concerned to help believers understand the gospel and its implications for daily living. Paul reminds them that, before Christ, they were idolaters (1:9). By the grace of Christ, which was purposed before time (5:9), they “turned to God ... to serve the living and true God” (1:9). Jesus their Savior has both died for their sins (5:9, 10) and has been raised from the dead for them (1:10). For this reason, they will not receive “wrath” but “salvation” from God (5:9). They share in Jesus’ death and resurrection, and not even death can sever their union with Christ (4:14). Therefore, they have a sure hope that when Christ returns they will be with him forever (4:17), fully sanctified and blameless (5:23). Paul is also concerned to remind the Thessalonians of the ministry of the Spirit. It was the Spirit who made the “gospel,” the “word,” come home with “power” and “full conviction” (1:5). As those rescued by God and given salvation in Christ, believers must “live and please God . . . more and more” (4:1). He has called them not “for impurity, but in holiness” (4:7). That call entails keeping His commands. The commands of God come to them “through the Lord Jesus” (4:2, 3), and Paul warns them against “quench[ing] the Holy Spirit” (5:19). Christian obedience, therefore, has a distinctly Trinitarian shape. The Christian must live the entirety of his life confident in and looking towards Christ’s return at the end of the age (5:1–11). Both the accomplished work of Christ and his future return, then, give form and direction to the Christian’s life in the present. 1

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: God has always called His people to holiness. After He redeemed His old covenant people, the Israelites, from bondage in Egypt, the Lord told them that they were to be holy as He is holy, and that He was the One who sanctified them (Lev. 11:44, 20:8, 26). The same pattern is present in this letter. God has redeemed His people through the death and resurrection of His Son. He has redeemed them precisely so that they may pursue holy lives (4:1, 2). They pursue this biblical pattern of holiness knowing that God Himself will complete and perfect that work on the day of Christ’s return (5:23, 24). CHRIST IN 1 THESSALONIANS Paul leaves the reader in no doubt about the deity of Jesus Christ (see Characteristics and Themes above). Furthermore, he is clear that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, and that this salvation was accomplished through His death and resurrection (4:14), and is being applied to His people by the Holy Spirit (1:5). The final and great hope of the believer is the event that will bring history to a close—the glorious return of the Lord Jesus Christ “from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God” (4:16).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: One passage that has garnered considerable attention within the evangelical church is 4:13–18. Some Christians have argued that Paul teaches here a secret rapture of believers before the return of Christ at the end of the age (see notes). This secret rapture is thought to inaugurate a series of catastrophic global events that will find their focus in the city of Jerusalem and among the people of the Jews. What Paul describes in these verses, however, is not secret or private but public. Furthermore, Paul is concerned to describe what happens when Christ returns at the end of the age (cf. 4:15 with 3:13). Paul and the other biblical writers look for only one great and final event in redemptive history—the return of Jesus Christ in glory at the end of the age, when the final bodily resurrection will occur (1 Cor. 15:23–26; Titus 2:13).
