sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: Second Thessalonians opens with Paul’s identifying himself as the author (1:1; 3:17), and the earliest Christian writers outside of the New Testament, including early second-century figures, such as Ignatius of Antioch, Polycarp, and Justin Martyr, all viewed the epistle as genuinely Pauline. Despite this early attestation, 2 Thessalonians has suffered more frequent attacks on its authenticity than has 1 Thessalonians. Those who deny that Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians base their claim on several lines of supposed evidence. Some critical scholars, for example, have viewed the similarities between the two letters in subject matter and phrasing as an indication that 2 Thessalonians was not written by Paul but by someone who was self-consciously attempting to imitate the apostle. Of course, such an argument overlooks the simplest and most likely explanation for the similarities between 1 and 2 Thessalonians—the same author, Paul, wrote both epistles. Some critical scholars have said that the two letters teach contradictory eschatologies (doctrines of the end time and eternal future) and therefore cannot be from the same author. According to these individuals, the first letter teaches an imminent return of Christ, whereas 2 Thessalonians insists that certain intervening events must occur before Christ returns. However, the conflict is illusory and overstated. Nothing definite about the imminence of the second coming of Christ is stated in 1 Thessalonians, which stresses the suddenness and unexpectedness with which the day of the Lord will overtake the unwary. The second letter specifies an order of events so as to counteract a misunderstanding at Thessalonica that the day of the Lord had already arrived, a misunderstanding that became more common among the Thessalonian believers after Paul wrote the first letter. Furthermore, the same two points (suddenness, an order of events) find parallel in Jesus’ own teaching about the future (Matt. 24:14, 42–44). If Jesus could teach that the end will come suddenly and that it will be preceded by a certain series of events, surely Paul could have done so as well. In 2:5 and 3:10, Paul reminds the Thessalonians of what he had taught while he was with them. If these statements were written by someone else using Paul’s name, they could have been exposed without difficulty at any time during the first generation after the events reported. Also, it is difficult to explain why anyone using Paul’s name falsely as a means of gaining influence would include such a sharp attack on some of the readers as is found in 3:10, 11. On such counts, the traditional affirmation that Paul wrote 2 Thessalonians continues to stand firm.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Second Thessalonians mentions an earlier letter from Paul (2:15). In all likelihood, this earlier letter was 1 Thessalonians; thus, 2 Thessalonians is to be dated shortly after it, about A.D. 51. Both letters were written from Corinth. As indicated in the Title and Author section above, the occasion for 2 Thessalonians was Paul’s need to further clarify doctrinal matters related to the future and the second coming of Christ, especially in response to rumors—even some attributed to Paul by word of mouth or forged correspondence (2:1, 2; 3:17)—that “the day of the Lord” had already occurred.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of 2 Thessalonians is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see “Introduction to the Epistles”). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1, 2), body (1:3–3:15), and conclusion (3:16–18). Like 1 Thessalonians, this letter does not fit neatly into any of the various types of first-century epistles that have been identified. It is a mixed type letter in that it has characteristics of several kinds of letters. Although Paul identifies himself as the author (see Title and Author above), his second epistle to the Thessalonians differs from his other epistles in that the first-person plural is used throughout the letter (“we,” “us,” “our”). This reflects the opening of the letter, in which the senders are identified as “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy.” It does not, however, mean that Paul is not the primary author since he does revert to the first-person singular on occasion, and he specifically identifies himself as the author in the close of the letter (2:5; 3:17). This prevalent use of the first-person plural is also characteristic of 1 Thessalonians. See Introduction to 1 Thessalonians: Genre.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Paul likely authored 2 Thessalonians shortly after 1 Thessalonians (see Date and Occasion above). It therefore shares some of the literary features of 1 Thessalonians. Paul has less to say about his pastoral ministry in 2 Thessalonians than he does in 1 Thessalonians, but he does speak to it (3:1–5). Paul also gives the Thessalonians guidance in pursuing sanctification (1:11, 12, 2:13–17) and in facing persecution (1:4–10). Two pastoral concerns that Paul addressed in 1 Thessalonians resurface in this letter: instruction about the return of Christ (2:1–11) and the importance of diligence in the callings that the Lord has assigned to each Christian (3:6–15). Second Thessalonians continues Paul’s pattern in 1 Thessalonians of addressing these Christians in familial terms. He addresses them as “brothers” seven times in this short epistle (1:3; 2:1, 13, 15; 3:1, 6, 13). Although Paul addresses some difficult pastoral issues in this letter, he does so with the same kind of familial affection that he demonstrated in 1 Thessalonians.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: After he sent his first letter to the church at Thessalonica, Paul received further reports concerning the congregation. There was cause for rejoicing in their continued growth in faith, love, and patience (1:3, 4) as well as cause for concern in certain doctrinal and behavioral matters. Second Thessalonians was written mainly to supplement Paul’s earlier teaching by correcting a premature and unsettling announcement that the day of the Lord had already arrived (2:1–11). This misguided claim may have been due in part to wrong inferences drawn from Paul’s own teaching, coupled with the congregation’s painful experience of persecutions thought to be indicative of end-time disturbances. A second motive for writing was to deal with the chronic idleness of some members (3:6–15). Their behavior had continued uncorrected since the last letter (1 Thess. 4:11, 12; 5:14) and, indeed, ever since the missionaries had been present (3:10, 11). Exhortations were made even then in an attempt to rectify the situation but, according to fresh reports (3:11), matters had only grown worse. Many scholars believe the cause of idleness was the erroneous expectation that the Lord’s return might happen so soon (2:1–3) that working for a living amounted to a lack of faith. Some connection between a faulty eschatology and faulty conduct of this sort likely occurred in the Thessalonian context. Yet it must be said that Paul never draws the connection himself. Since 3:10 shows that the problem had surfaced while the missionaries were still in Thessalonica, it is unlikely that eschatological errors gave birth to the problem, though they may have provided a convenient excuse for continuing in it. THEOLOGY OF 2 THESSALONIANS Second Thessalonians is rich in instruction about the return of Christ. It serves to complement and also to advance his earlier teaching in 1 Thessalonians (see Characteristics and Themes above). In particular, Paul stresses the implications of Christ’s return for both unbelievers and believers. Jesus will appear “with his mighty angels in flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and on those who do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:7, 8). Paul speaks of this just judgment in two respects. First, unbelievers will be cast “away from the presence of the Lord,” that is, the favorable presence of the Lord with His people (1:9). Second, they will “suffer the punishment of eternal destruction” in hell (1:9). For believers, the day of judgment will be a day when Jesus is “glorified in his saints and ... marveled at among all who have believed” (1:10; cf. 2:14). Paul puts this teaching to practical use: the return of Christ should stir believers up to good works in the present as they cling fast to the Word of God (1:11, 12; cf. 2:15; 3:6–15). We should not “grow weary in doing good,” knowing that “the Lord is faithful [and] will establish [us] and guard [us] against the evil one” (3:3, 13). In addition to this rich teaching on the return of Christ, 2 Thessalonians shares with 1 Thessalonians an important emphasis on the deity of Christ. In fact, Christ’s deity is more assumed than it is defined, showing how natural it was for the earliest Christians to think in Trinitarian terms and to hold to a high Christology that sees Jesus as the incarnation of God Himself, specifically the Son of God. See Introduction to 1 Thessalonians: Characteristics and Primary Themes. 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The Old Testament prophets speak frequently and powerfully about the “day of the Lord.” On this day, the Lord comes to earth and brings salvation and judgment, not only for Israel or her enemies, but for the whole world. The Psalms often celebrate the coming of the Lord to judge the world in righteousness. The New Testament tells us that in Jesus Christ the day of the Lord has already been inaugurated. Christ has accomplished salvation for all kinds of people, Jew and Gentile. He did so by becoming obedient unto death on the cross, where He bore judgment for the sins of His people; and by rising gloriously from the dead. However, the New Testament goes on to tell us that the day of the Lord has not yet come in its final and full form. Jesus Christ will one day return in glory, not to bear judgment but to bring judgment on all people. For the ungodly, the prospect of this return should be a great terror and should stir them to repentance and faith in Christ. For the godly, however, Christ’s coming is something for which we eagerly hope, and this hope transforms our lives in the present. CHRIST IN 2 THESSALONIANS In speaking so fully and graphically about the judgment of Christ, Paul reminds us that Jesus Christ is just. Now is the day of mercy, when the gospel goes forth (cf. 1:8) and God’s chosen are brought to faith in Christ through the Word of God and by the power of the Spirit (2:13, 14). All are invited to come to Christ in the way of faith and repentance. When Christ returns, however, that day of mercy will come to a close. The impenitent will face Jesus as their just judge. Paul presents this reality to believers to help them persevere through affliction. We need to know that our God is just and that the afflictions of His people will not go unanswered on the final day of judgment (1:5–7).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: One of the most difficult passages in this letter—and in all of Paul’s writings—is 2 Thess. 2:1–12. This passage concerns the rise and activity of the “man of lawlessness” (“man of sin” in older translations, following poorer manuscripts). Christians have long speculated about the identity of the man of lawlessness. First John 2:18 refers to a report known to John’s hearers “that antichrist is coming” and goes on to assert that many antichrists, who deny Jesus’ identity as the Christ, were already at large in the first century. Paul does not apply the title “antichrist” to the man of lawlessness, although later generations of believers have identified the two. The beast of Rev. 13 has been identified as the antichrist/man of lawlessness, although the imagery in which the beast of Revelation is presented, drawn as it is from Dan. 7:2–8, suggests that the beast symbolizes a “kingdom,” a political-military-religious system or regime, represented by one individual. Many Protestants in the Reformed tradition have argued that the man of lawlessness is the pope of the Roman Catholic Church. We cannot, however, be certain about the identity of the man of lawlessness, especially since 1 John 2:18 speaks of many antichrists. We do, however, know with certainty a few things about the revelation man of lawlessness, who seems to be the ultimate embodiment of the spirit of antichrist. First, what Paul calls the “mystery of lawlessness” is “already at work,” and it is under restraint in the providence of God (2:7). Second, the man of lawlessness will bring this activity to a head, leading rebellion against God (2:3). Third, his coming will be “by the activity of Satan with all power and false signs and wonders” (2:9). Those who follow him will do so as a divine judgment on their unbelief (2:10–12). Finally, he will be brought to an end, suddenly and effortlessly, by the return of Christ (2:8). In our uncertainties, it is reassuring to know that God will protect His people (3:3) and that Jesus Christ will bring the man of lawlessness and all His other enemies to naught at His return. Moreover, Paul’s calming of the Thessalonians’ eschatological excitement should caution succeeding generations, including ours, against becoming preoccupied with date-setting, in contradiction to our Lord’s specific statements (Mark 13:32; Acts 1:7)

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: According to the salutations of the letters, the author of the three Pastoral Epistles (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) was the apostle Paul. The tradition of the early church is in agreement. Nevertheless, some NT scholars have questioned the Pauline authorship of these letters, citing alleged differences in vocabulary, style, and theology, as well as what are believed to be inconsistencies between Paul’s travels in the Pastoral Epistles and his travels recorded in the book of Acts. Such arguments are unconvincing, as noted below, and there is no persuasive reason to deny that Paul wrote these letters.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The apparent inconsistencies between Paul’s travels as reflected in the Pastoral Letters and his three missionary journeys as recorded in Acts have led to the suggestion that the Pastorals were written during what might be called Paul’s “fourth” missionary journey, either a single uninterrupted journey or, more likely, a cluster of travels to various destinations in the Mediterranean basin. Acts ends not with Paul’s death but with his house arrest in Rome (Acts 28:16, 30, 31). While the late-first-century document 1 Clement suggests that Paul was martyred in Rome, it does not link his martyrdom with the imprisonment recorded in Acts 28. The fourth-century church historian Eusebius preserves a tradition that Paul was released from that imprisonment, continued his missionary labors, and was martyred by Nero on his second visit to Rome. This tradition is supported not only by the Pastoral Letters but by Philippians and Philemon as well, which, if they were written during the Roman imprisonment recorded in Acts 28, provide evidence that Paul expected to be released (Phil. 1:25, 26; Philem. 22). By contrast, 2 Timothy, also written during an imprisonment (1:8, 16, 17; 2:9), expresses the apostle’s sense that the time of his “departure” had arrived, since he had “finished the race” (4:6–8). A fourth missionary journey (1 Timothy, Titus) and a second imprisonment (2 Timothy) that took place after the imprisonment recorded in Acts 28, is the most probable setting for the Pastorals. If there were two imprisonments, Paul was released from his first around A.D. 62. According to later tradition, he was martyred by Nero, who died in A.D. 68. Paul composed 1 Timothy while he was still in the midst of his fourth missionary journey, probably during the earlier part of this period, between A.D. 62 and 64. Timothy was a native of Lystra, a Roman colony in the province of Galatia. The son of a mixed marriage, his father was a Gentile and his mother was a Jew (Acts 16:1). Little is known about his father, who seems not to have become a Christian, but his mother and grandmother were sincere believers (2 Tim. 1:5). From his childhood, they had instructed Timothy in the Jewish Scriptures (2 Tim. 3:14, 15), and they were undoubtedly influential in Timothy’s own conversion to Christianity. When Paul returned to Lystra on his second missionary journey, some of the Christians called his attention to this young believer and Paul decided to take him along on his journey (Acts 16:2, 3). Two specific actions seem to have taken place at this time. First, since Paul would be evangelizing Jews, he circumcised Timothy according to Jewish custom, apparently to clarify and “regularize” Timothy’s religious identity in Jewish eyes (Acts 16:3). Paul had no problem circumcising Timothy even though he did not circumcise Titus because Timothy was of Jewish heritage, while Titus was a full-blooded Gentile (Gal. 2:1–10). Second, Paul and the elders of the church laid their hands upon Timothy to set him apart and equip him for ministry (1:18; 4:14; 2 Tim. 1:6; 2:2). Timothy traveled with Paul throughout most of his second and third missionary journeys (Acts 17:14, 15; 18:5; 19:22; 20:4) and for part of the fourth missionary journey that is reflected in the Pastoral Epistles. He seems to have become Paul’s protégé, and Paul speaks figuratively of himself as Timothy’s “father” (Phil. 2:22) and of Timothy as his “son” (1:2, 18; 1 Cor. 4:17; 2 Tim. 1:2; 2:1). As Paul’s coworker, Timothy served as Paul’s representative in the churches of Thessalonica (1 Thess. 3:2, 6), Corinth (1 Cor. 4:17; 16:10), Philippi (Phil. 2:19, 23), and Ephesus (1 Tim. 1:3). Paul himself seems to characterize Timothy as having a “spirit ... of fear” (2 Tim. 1:7). Paul felt it necessary to ask the church at Corinth to receive Timothy in a manner that would set him at ease (1 Cor. 16:10, 11). In the Pastorals, Paul exhorts Timothy not to let anyone despise him on account of his youth (1 Tim. 4:12), not to neglect the spiritual gift that he had received (1 Tim. 4:14), and not to be ashamed to speak out boldly for the gospel (2 Tim. 1:8). Apart from the statement in Heb. 13:23 that Timothy had been “released” (presumably from prison), little is known about what happened to Timothy after the writing of 2 Timothy. Paul wrote 1 Timothy while he was in Macedonia (1:3). He thought it necessary to leave Timothy behind in Ephesus (in Asia) because of the presence of false teachers in that city (1:3). Paul had established the Ephesian church early on his third missionary journey, spending about three years there (Acts 19; 20:31). At the close of that journey, he warned the Ephesian elders that false teachers, some coming from the leadership itself, would plague the church (Acts 20:29, 30), and this letter indicates that his prediction apparently came true (1:6, 19; 4:1, 2; 6:3–5, 10, 21). There is evidence that some of the false teachers either came from or moved into positions of leadership in the church (1:7, 20; 2:12; 3:6; 5:19, 20; 6:3–5, 10), and the false teachers seem especially to have made inroads among some of the women in the church (2:9–15; 3:11; 5:11–15).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: First Timothy is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see “Introduction to the Epistles”). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1, 2), body (1:3–6:19), and conclusion (6:20, 21). It is a personal letter, written from Paul to a single individual, although there are indications that the apostle intended for the teaching and content of these letters to be shared with the entire church under Timothy’s charge. For instance, while all three of the Pastoral Epistles are addressed to individuals, it must be observed that each of the three 1etters, including 1 Timothy, also concludes with a plural benediction indicating that these letters have a public relevance as well (the Gk. word translated “you” in 1 Tim. 6:21 is plural). Some scholars have noted that 1 Timothy shares fewer features of ancient personal letters than 2 Timothy or Titus do; nevertheless, it does share those features that are necessary to distinguish personal letters from non-personal letters. The Pastoral Epistles also have some similarities with certain types of ancient Greek government documents that consisted of directives from rulers to delegated individuals who were expected to carry out whatever directives or mandates the rulers included in the document. This is another example of Paul’s adapting ancient epistolary conventions to fit his particular needs.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Although this is a personal letter to Timothy, it is also a letter written to the church (note the Gk. plural “you” at 6:21). He writes Timothy “so that . . . you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, a pillar and buttress of truth” (3:14, 15). This letter therefore has much to say about the doctrine, government, and worship of the church. Regarding doctrine, Paul begins by warning Timothy against the instruction and influence of false teachers (1:3–11) and reminds him of the glorious gospel of grace (1:12–20). The end of the letter gives specific instructions to groups within the church: masters and slaves (6:1, 2) and the wealthy (6:17–19). It also returns to the subject of false teaching and how Timothy must handle that false teaching in the church in Ephesus (6:3–16). With respect to the church’s government, Paul spells out the qualifications for and duties of the offices of elder (or “overseer”; 3:1–7) and deacon (3:8–13). He also handles issues relating to the discipline and ordination of elders (5:19–25), as well as to diaconal care of widows within the church (5:1–16). Much of the letter is devoted to spelling out the responsibilities of the elder who is entrusted with the ministry of the Word (4:6–16; cf. 5:17), responsibilities that include responding to false teaching within the church. As to the church’s worship, Paul addresses these issues in ch. 2. After addressing the matter of prayer in the church (2:1–7), Paul gives distinct instructions to men (2:8) and to women (2:9–15). Paul wants the worship of the church to be orderly and therefore glorifying to God. One significant literary feature of this epistle (as well as of 2 Timothy and Titus) is the recurrence of the phrase “the saying is trustworthy” (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; cf. 2 Tim. 2:11; Titus 3:8). The purpose of this phrase is to call attention to the importance of the truth that Paul references. These phrases often serve as crisp summaries of the gospel and its implications for the life of the Christian. In this way, Paul helps Timothy grasp the central or core truths of the message that he is called to proclaim (cf. 4:13, 16). Another significant literary feature is 3:16. Some scholars think Paul is quoting a creed that was circulating in the early church. Or, it could be that Paul is giving the church a creed. Paul introduces the successive and rhythmic phrases with the expression “we confess.” The phrases then offer a summary of the earthly life of Christ from the incarnation to the ascension. Finally with respect to literary style, a brief word must be said about the vocabulary and syntax of the Pastoral Epistles. Those who deny that Paul wrote 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, and Titus frequently point out that there are significant differences between the vocabulary of these three letters and the vocabulary of the rest of the Pauline corpus. The most basic form of the vocabulary-based argument against Pauline authorship of the Pastorals says that since these three letters contain many words not found in the other letters attributed to Paul, the Pastoral Epistles must be from a different author. This argument is flawed for several reasons. First, it assumes that a well-educated individual such as Paul had a limited vocabulary and was bound to use only a select set of words every time he wrote. This is not tenable. It would be quite easy to point to several modern books that are known to be written by the same author and find differences in vocabulary between them, but we would not then deny the common authorship of those books. The vocabulary Paul does use in the Pastoral Epistles was common in his era, so there is no reason to think he would not have known it. Furthermore, the vocabulary-based argument against Pauline authorship of the Pastoral Epistles is quite circular. Critical scholars who hold this position first assume—without really proving—that only a handful of letters are authentically Pauline and then attempt to disprove the Pauline authorship of the Pastorals based on that. Effectively, what happens is that critical scholars presuppose that Paul did not write the Pastorals and then conclude, based almost exclusively on that presupposition, that Paul did not write the Pastoral Epistles. The vocabulary-based argument against Pauline authorship of the Pastoral Epistles is overstated and circular. Any differences between the Pastorals and the rest of Paul’s epistles are more easily explained by the fact that the addressees and circumstances of the Pastoral Epistles are different than the addressees and circumstances of Paul’s other epistles. The same applies in the case of syntactical differences between the Pastoral Epistles and Paul’s other letters. Moreover, Paul also likely used an amanuensis (secretary) to help him write the Pastorals who was not the same amanuensis that helped him write his other epistles. This would also explain some of the differences between the Pastoral Epistles and the rest of the Pauline letters.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The letter is noteworthy for its interest in church organization. It provides the longest description in the NT on the qualifications for “overseer” or elder (3:2–7; cf. Titus 1:5–9), along with evidence for two kinds of elders, ruling and teaching (5:17); comments about supporting and rebuking elders (5:17–20); and the only explicit description in the NT of the qualifications for deacons (3:8–10, 12, 13). Paul’s specific directives to Timothy also contain much practical advice on how a church leader is to function. This letter is also noteworthy for its emphasis on sound doctrine (1:10; 3:9; 4:6; 6:3) and for its two theological meditations on the salvation God extends in Jesus Christ (1:13–16; 2:3–6). These include affirmations of salvation by grace (1:13–16), Christ as the one mediator between God and humanity (2:5), and the substitutionary atonement of Christ (2:6). First Timothy also includes the poetic meditation mentioned above on the work of Christ, which contains affirmations of His incarnation, resurrection, and ascension (3:16); an expectation of the second coming of Christ (6:14); a marvelous doxology (6:15, 16); and evidence of the expansion of the “Scripture” beyond the OT to include = the NT books (5:18, where the words of Christ as recorded in Luke 10:7 are cited as “Scripture”). Also distinctive about 1 Timothy are its comments about the role of women in the church (2:9–15) and the proper care for widows in the church (5:3–16). THEOLOGY OF 1 TIMOTHY This letter is full of practical counsel for the work of the ministry. It provides, with Titus and 2 Timothy, a biblical model for elders and deacons. It is not, however, simply for the benefit of church officers. Paul wanted the whole church to read this letter also. This letter shows how to better support biblical ministry in the church, and to pray for those who are called to serve as officers. It provides criteria to help determine what kind of men may be candidates for church office. Above all, it helps believers to see the character of God as a God of order and peace, and of Jesus the Savior as the king and head of His church. In regard to the theology of 1 Timothy and the rest of the Pastoral Epistles, it should be noted that many critical scholars argue that these letters possess a distinct, non-Pauline theology that indicates that Paul did not write these letters. For example, it is often argued that the church presented in the Pastoral Epistles is far more organized than Paul would have ever intended, and that the strict prescriptions for church officers would be foreign to the apostle as one who supposedly favored more spontaneous and less structured forms of church governance. This contrast is largely based on a certain reading of what Paul means when he says Christians are to be “led by the Spirit” (Rom. 8:14; Gal. 5:18) and his description of what these scholars believe to be relatively unstructured early Christian worship (1 Cor. 14). As is true of arguments against Pauline authorship of the Pastorals based on vocabulary and syntax, the case for the Pastoral Epistles as affirming a theology different from the rest of the Pauline Epistles is weak and will not withstand careful scrutiny. Acts 14:23 reveals that it was Paul’s practice to appoint elders in the churches he planted, so there is nothing inconsistent about him giving instructions for choosing elders in the Pastorals (1 Tim. 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). Furthermore, the belief that being led by the Spirit is somehow contrary to a structured church goes against what we know about the earliest Christians. Acts 15:1–35 shows us that the early Christians understood the Spirit’s leading of the church to include decisions made by elders in submission to the apostolic gospel. In 1 Corinthians 14:40, the apostle also puts great stress on orderliness in the church. Paul’s teaching in the Pastorals is entirely consonant with what we know of apostolic doctrine and practice. Finally, just as the vocabulary- and syntax-based arguments against Pauline authorship of the Pastorals are circular, so is the theology-based argument against Pauline authorship of these letters. Critical scholars who employ these arguments assume that Paul did not write the Pastorals and then use the theological themes of the Pastorals that may not be as strongly emphasized in the other Pauline letters as proof that he did not write the Pastoral Epistles. They end up concluding that Paul did not write the Pastoral Epistles based mostly on their presupposition that he did not write the Pastoral Epistles. 1

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: God has always been concerned with the order and welfare of his people. This is one reason why He appointed circumcision to Abraham and his offspring—to distinguish them from the world around them. This is why He legislated so many details relating to the government and worship of His people under the old covenant and prescribed the spiritual maturity to be sought in Israel’s leaders (Deut. 1:13; cf. Num. 27:15–20). The new covenant is no departure from this principle. We are God’s church (3:15) and He therefore has much to say about how our life together should look. Epistles like 1 Timothy reflect, then, God’s care for His people. CHRIST IN 1 TIMOTHY Christ is powerfully present in this epistle in at least two ways. First, Paul reminds Timothy that it is the grace of Christ that redeemed Paul and set him apart for service in the church (1:12–17). Jesus is the Savior not just of Paul, Timothy, or the church at Ephesus, but of all kinds of people throughout the world (4:10). Paul’s words in 3:16 provide a profound meditation on the saving work of Jesus Christ, now made known to the nations (see notes). Second, the government of the church is given by Christ as her head and king (cf. Eph. 4:7–16). To the degree that the letter speaks of the church’s government, it testifies to the reign of Christ as head over His body.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Paul’s words in 2:8–15 and 3:11 have bearing on the question whether women may serve as officers in the church, and these texts have been debated quite a bit in recent decades (see notes on these passages). Furthermore, Paul’s teaching on slavery (6:1, 2) has sparked discussion and controversy, particularly in the last two centuries. For further discussion, see Introduction to Philemon: History of Interpretation.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The details of Paul’s fourth missionary journey are sketchy, since the journey must be reconstructed largely from hints in the Pastoral Letters. It is possible that Paul fulfilled his earlier wish to go to Spain (Rom. 15:24, 28). Either on his return from Spain or, if the contemplated journey to Spain never took place, upon his departure from Rome, he seems to have returned to the east, sailing to Crete (Titus 1:5) and visiting Ephesus (1 Tim. 1:3) and Macedonia (1 Tim. 1:3; cf. Phil. 1:25, 26). From that point on, things become less clear. Paul seems to have planned (possibly at two different times) to leave Macedonia for both Ephesus (1 Tim. 3:14, 15; 4:13) and Nicopolis (Titus 3:12). The last we hear is that he is back in Rome awaiting execution (2 Tim. 1:8, 12; 2:9; 4:6, 7, 16), having visited Troas (2 Tim. 4:13), Miletus, and perhaps Corinth (2 Tim. 4:20). On the false teaching that was being promulgated at Ephesus at the time Paul wrote the Pastoral Epistles, see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The second letter to Timothy was written by Paul. As is true of the other Pastoral Epistles (1 Timothy, Titus), many scholars have questioned whether the apostle actually wrote 2 Timothy. For details on why the arguments against Pauline authorship should be rejected, see Introduction to 1 Timothy, esp. the sections Date and Occasion, Literary Features, and Theology of 1 Timothy.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Although it does not appear last in the arrangement of Paul’s letters in the NT canon, 2 Timothy is the last NT letter that Paul wrote. He prepared it after his fourth missionary journey, probably between A.D. 64 and 68 (see Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion and Introduction to 1 Timothy: Special Issues). Paul wrote 2 Timothy during his second Roman imprisonment (1:8; 2:9). Why he was under arrest is unknown, but it is possible that he was arrested in Troas (4:13). Paul had received no support at his preliminary hearing (4:16). His trial still awaited him, but he knew that it would end in his execution (4:6; note the contrast with his expectation of release when he wrote Philippians [Phil. 1:24–26; 2:24]). Most of his friends found it convenient to be elsewhere (4:10, 11). Before Paul wrote, Phyge­lus and Hermogenes had turned away from him (1:15, 16) and Alexander the coppersmith had done him great harm (4:14), although a Christian named Onesiphorus had been an encouragement to him (1:16, 17). Timothy was still in Ephesus (4:19), where Paul had left him previously (1 Tim. 1:3), and where the false teaching that Paul had addressed in his first letter to Timothy continued to be a problem (2:17, 18; 3:1–8). Remembering their longstanding friendship, Paul desired to see Timothy one last time before his death (1:4). Paul seems to have written 2 Timothy with two purposes in mind. First, he directs Timothy to come to Rome (4:9, 21), providing instructions on who and what (4:11–13) to bring with him. Second, he wants to provide Timothy with a final letter of personal encouragement in his ministry (1:5–14; 2:1–16, 22–26; 3:10–4:5).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of 2 Timothy is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see “Introduction to the Epistles”). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1, 2), body (1:3–6:19), and conclusion (6:20, 21). It is a personal letter, written from Paul to a single individual. Of the three Pastoral Epistles, 2 Timothy most closely resembles first century Greco-Roman examples of personal letters, particularly in the closing remarks (4:19–22). Although 2 Timothy is addressed to an individual, like 1 Timothy and Titus there is evidence that the apostle intended his words in this final letter to Timothy to be shared with the Christians at Ephesus. For instance, the Gk. word translated “you” in 4:22 is plural. In addition to serving as a personal letter, 2 Timothy is similar in some ways to certain ancient Greek government documents. See Introduction to 1 Timothy: Genre.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Although this is a personal letter to Timothy, it is also a letter written to the church (note the Gk. plural “you” at 4:22). It bears many similarities to 1 Timothy, but is distinct from it in some important respects. First, Paul in 2 Timothy does not dwell on the false teaching in Ephesus as much as he does in 1 Timothy (cf. 2 Tim. 2:16–18; 3:1–9). Second, Paul in 2 Timothy is not concerned to detail the principles of government and worship found in 1 Timothy. Third, Paul’s overwhelming concern in this epistle is to set forth the minister’s work in preaching the Word of God. One significant literary feature of this epistle (as well as of 1 Timothy and of Titus) is the appearance of the phrase “the saying is trustworthy” (2:11; cf. 1 Tim 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; Titus 3:8), which calls attention to the importance of the truth that Paul references. Often, the phrase also serves as a concise summary of the gospel and its implications for the Christian life. In this way, Paul helps Timothy grasp the central or core truths of the message that he is called to proclaim and to entrust to others (cf. 2:2).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Both of Paul’s letters to Timothy provide important background information about the apostle’s young protégé. This second letter names his mother (Eunice) and his grandmother (Lois), identifying them both as Christians (1:5). It speaks of Timothy’s early training in the Scriptures (3:15) and includes a probable reference to his ordination to ministry (1:6; cf. 2:2). Like 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy exhibits a strong concern for sound doctrine (1:13, 14; 2:2; 4:3) and contains marvelous meditations on the grace of God (1:9–11), the faithfulness of Christ (2:11–13), and the nature and function of Scripture (3:15–17). There are affirmations of salvation by grace (1:9), election (1:9; 2:10, 19), and the divine inspiration of Scripture (3:16). Second Timothy also affirms the resurrection (2:8) and the second coming (4:1, 8) of Christ. As the last of Paul’s letters, 2 Timothy provides an important final picture of Paul. His situation was bleak. No longer could he look forward to fruitful ministry (cf. Phil. 1:22–26), and most of his friends had left him (4:10, 11). Yet Paul remained confident. He was not ashamed to suffer for the gospel (1:12) and he was willing to endure everything for the sake of the elect (2:10). He knew that he had been faithful to Christ (4:7) and that Christ Himself is faithful (1:12; 2:13). Paul had confidence that the One who in the past had rescued him from death (3:11; 4:17) would rescue him through death for eternal life (4:8, 18). Paul was one of the most influential figures in human history. Yet, in 4:13, we see that his earthly possessions at the end of his life consisted of little more than a cloak, his books (his writing materials and/or letters), and his beloved parchments (copies of OT books). This verse paints for us an intensely earnest and personal portrait of the apostle. THEOLOGY OF 2 TIMOTHY Paul in this letter takes up matters relating to the work of the minister. In light of the fact that Paul expected to die soon after finishing this epistle (4:6–8), this letter has poignancy and urgency—Timothy needs to know what ministry will look like in the postapostolic age. Paul sets forth the contents of the message that Timothy is to preach: nothing less than Jesus Christ as he is revealed in the God-breathed Scriptures (3:16, 17). Paul also sets forth the nature of the work to which Timothy is called. Preeminently, it is to “preach the word” (4:2), that is, the message that he received from the apostle Paul and that he must pass on to “faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2:2; cf. 1:13). Faithful preaching particularly involves “rightly handling the word of truth” (2:15), as well as patient reproof, rebuke, and exhortation (2:14; 4:2). The ministry will involve suffering (1:8; 2:3; 4:5), persecution (3:10–13), opposition (3:8), and abandonment (1:15–18; 4:3). But the minister of God has the surpassing resources of God’s Word and God’s Spirit (1:14; 2:1, 9), and he rests in God’s good purposes toward His people (2:19). Second Tim. 3:16, along with 2 Peter 1:21, helps to establish the foundation for the doctrine of inspiration of Scripture. Scripture is not a human construct, or the human sense of the divine. Rather, Scripture is the Word of God. Because it is the Word of God, it is both fully authoritative and wholly true. 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Christ appointed the apostles to lay the foundation of the church (Matt. 16:18; Eph. 2:20; Rev. 21:14). That foundation consists preeminently of the NT, which along with the OT comprises the church’s Scripture, the Word of God. As Paul looks ahead, beyond the apostolic age into the coming generations of new covenant believers, he charges Timothy both to preserve the deposit of God’s Word as a sacred trust (1:14) and to ensure that this priceless treasure is entrusted to faithful future custodians, who will pass it along unchanged to the next generation (2:1, 2). Second Timothy helps us to see the church’s task and mission until Christ returns. The church’s ministers must be faithful in proclaiming the Word God, that the “elect ... may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory” (2:10). CHRIST IN 2 TIMOTHY Paul reminds Timothy at important points in this letter of major themes in his own teaching about Jesus Christ. There is the person and work of Christ: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel” (2:8); “our Savior Christ ... abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (1:10). There is the doctrine of salvation by grace alone: “[God] who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began” (1:9). And there is the doctrine of the believer’s union with Christ: “If we have died with him, we will also live with him” (2:11). These reminders serve to underscore Paul’s charge to Timothy that he must faithfully preach the apostolic word that has been entrusted to him.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The early church used the expression depositum fide , the “deposit of faith,” to refer to the essence of Paul’s teaching and the apostolic witness to the gospel. In 1:13, Paul exhorts Timothy “follow the pattern of sound words” that Timothy had heard from Paul (cf. 2:2). This is the origin of the notion of orthodoxy, a “straight teaching” by which all teaching and views must be judged. Over the centuries, church traditions were added to the depositum fide and regarded as part of the deposit of faith itself even when they could not be reasonably traced back to the actual writings of the apostles. This led Martin Luther to declare in one of his Ninety-Five Theses, “The church’s true treasure is the gospel of Jesus Christ.” The gospel is the deposit entrusted to the apostles and handed down from one generation to another via the faithful teaching and preaching of the apostolic witness, namely, sacred Scripture. In 2 Timothy, Paul establishes the pattern by which the church is to entrust God’s Word to faithful teachers who will entrust it to those who follow them (2:1, 2). Paul’s words in 2 Tim. 3:16, 17 have figured importantly in discussions about the Bible’s doctrine of Scripture. Verse 16 teaches the doctrine of plenary, verbal inspiration. That is, the Bible is the God-breathed (or inspired) Word of God. Inspiration is plenary, extending from the beginning to the end of the Bible. Inspiration is also verbal, extending down to the very words of the Bible. The Bible, therefore, is inerrant, without error in all that it affirms.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: There was false teaching at Ephesus that Paul describes as coming from within the church (2 Tim. 2:18; 4:4; 1 Tim. 1:6, 19; 4:1; 6:10, 21). It was characterized by a concern with what Paul terms “myths” (4:4; 1 Tim. 1:4; 4:7), “endless genealogies” (1 Tim. 1:4), “quarrels about words” (1 Tim. 6:4; cf. 2 Tim. 2:14, 23), “speculations” (1 Tim. 1:4), “controversy” (1 Tim. 6:4), “what is falsely called ‘knowledge’” (1 Tim. 6:20), “vain discussion” (1 Tim. 1:6), and “irreverent babble” (2:16; 1 Tim. 6:20). The false doctrines included the prohibition of marriage and of certain foods (1 Tim. 4:3) and the belief that the resurrection had already taken place (2:18). Those who taught these false doctrines also sought to ground their instruction in the Jewish law, but they ended up greatly misinterpreting it (1 Tim. 1:7). Specific leaders of the movement included Hymenaeus (2:17; 1 Tim. 1:20), Alexander (1 Tim. 1:20), and Philetus (2:17). Some who sought leadership positions in the movement did so for financial gain (1 Tim. 6:5, 10). The false teachers had been divisive (1 Tim. 6:4, 5) and seem to have been particularly effective in deceiving some female members of the church (3:6, 7; cf. 1 Tim. 2:11–15; 5:11–15), perhaps by offering them positions of leadership (1 Tim. 2:11, 12). A number of these features—the specific doctrinal teachings, the interest in myths and genealogies, and the concern for “knowledge” (Gk. gnōsis )—suggest that the false teaching at Ephesus might have been an early form or precursor of Gnosticism, a heretical movement that became a strong competitor to the developing church in the second and third centuries. However, some of the more characteristic aspects of later Gnosticism are lacking, and some assert that the movement can be explained simply in terms of Jewish and Hellenistic influences. These two suggestions need not be seen as contradictory, for Gnosticism itself was a product of both Jewish and Hellenistic ideas. Gnosticism’s dualistic worldview, which devalued material reality and virtually deified the immaterial (cf. 1 Tim. 4:1–5), had pagan roots, since it strongly repudiated the Bible’s doctrine of creation. Other features of at least some forms of the Gnostic heresy, however, can well be traced to Jewish sources. The precise nature of the false teaching at Ephesus remains elusive.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: According to the letter itself and early Christian tradition, the book of Titus was written by Paul. Some critical scholars have attempted to prove that someone other than the apostle wrote the letter, but as is true of their attempts to do so with the other Pastoral Epistles (1 Timothy, and 2 Timothy), they have been unable to make a convincing case. See Introduction to 1 Timothy, esp. the sections Date and Occasion, Literary Features, and Theology of 1 Timothy.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Titus, like 1 Timothy, was composed while Paul was in the midst of his fourth missionary journey and probably dates to between A.D. 62 and 64 (see Introduction to 1 Timothy: Date and Occasion and Introduction to 1 Timothy: Special Issues). Titus was a Gentile Christian who was probably converted under the ministry of Paul (1:4). The NT provides little information about him, and he is not mentioned in Acts. Paul took him to Jerusalem early in his missionary labors, where he refused to have Titus circumcised (Gal. 2:1–3), and Titus apparently traveled with Paul on his second and third missionary journeys, as well as for part of his fourth missionary journey. He was a trusted associate of Paul, upon whom Paul could count in delicate situations, such as the situation at Corinth (2 Cor. 2:13; 7:6, 13, 14; 8:6, 16, 23; 12:18). Titus later served as Paul’s representative on the island of Crete (1:5) and in the province of Dalmatia (2 Tim. 4:10). Paul wrote to Titus from Macedonia (3:12). On an earlier leg of the journey, he and Titus had been involved in missionary activity on the island of Crete. When Paul departed, he left Titus behind to continue the work (1:5). Paul wrote this letter to Titus to encourage him to bring his ministry on the island to a close. Specifically, Paul wanted Titus to complete the organization of the churches via the appointment of mature and godly elders (overseers; 1:5–9) to deal with the false teachers who were present (1:10–14; 3:9–11), and to give instructions on proper conduct to the churches and to various subgroups in them (2:1–3:8). Sound leadership was particularly needed not only because deceivers “especially of the circumcision party” were unsettling the faith of individuals and families (1:10, 11), but also because the ethically unhealthy cultural atmosphere on the island, diagnosed even by an indigenous “prophet,” made Cretans particularly vulnerable to religious exploitation (1:12–16). When his replacement arrived, Titus was to meet Paul in Nicopolis (3:12).

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of Titus is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see “Introduction to the Epistles”). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1–4), body (1:5–3:11), and conclusion (3:12–15). It is a personal letter, written from Paul to a single individual. Like 1 and 2 Timothy, the epistle to Titus closely resembles first-century Greco-Roman examples of personal letters. As is true of the other Pastoral Epistles, Titus concludes with a plural “you” in its benediction (3:15), thereby indicating that Paul intended this letter to have a public relevance as well. Like 1 and 2 Timothy, there are also similarities between the letter to Titus and other ancient Greek government documents. See Introduction to 1 Timothy: Genre.

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: Like 1 and 2 Timothy, Titus is a private letter from Paul to Titus, but it is intended to be read by the whole church (“Grace be with you [plural] all”; 3:15). Although Titus and Timothy were ministering in different locations (Crete and Ephesus, respectively), the principles of ministry that Paul gives to each are the same. For this reason, there are certain similarities between Titus and 1 Timothy especially. Paul sets forth qualifications for elders (1:5–9). He points Titus to the gospel that he must preach and emphasizes that God’s grace, revealed in that gospel, produces transformed lives of self-control and purity (2:11–14; 3:1–6; cf. 1:1–3). Furthermore, the apostle reminds Titus that his work is to “teach what accords with sound doctrine” (2:1) which entails bringing the Word of God to bear on people in various circumstances in life (2:2–3:2) and admonishing false teachers (1:10–16; 2:15; 3:9, 10; cf. 1:9). One significant literary feature of this epistle (as well as of 1 and 2 Timothy) is the appearance of the phrase “the saying is trustworthy” (3:8; cf. 1 Tim. 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim. 2:11). This phrase serves the same purpose in the letter to Titus as it does in the other Pastoral Epistles, namely, to provide a concise presentation of the essential truths of the gospel and their application to the believer. By this phrase, Paul assists Titus in grasping the central truths of the message that he is to proclaim (cf. 2:1).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Like 1 Timothy, Titus is noteworthy for its information on church organization. It provides a lengthy description of the qualifications for the office of overseer and elder (1:6–9; cf. 1 Tim. 3:1–7), as well as important evidence that the terms “overseer” (1:7; rendered “bishop” in KJV) and “elder” (1:5) refer to one office, not two separate ones (cf. Acts 20:17, 28). Titus exhibits a strong concern for sound doctrine (1:9, 13; 2:1, 2) and contains two marvelous theological meditations on the grace that God has extended in Jesus Christ (2:11–14; 3:4–7). These include affirmations of the second coming of Christ (2:13), the substitutionary atonement of Christ (2:14), regeneration by the Holy Spirit (3:5), and justification by grace (3:5, 7). Titus also affirms the deity of Christ in a striking manner—the title “Savior” is applied freely, and in the same contexts, to both God (1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and Christ (1:4; 2:13; 3:6). Paul’s concern in this letter for sound doctrine is balanced by an emphasis on proper Christian conduct. For Paul, the two clearly go hand in hand, since the display of God’s grace in Christ’s saving work (3:4–7) is designed to produce grateful believers who “devote themselves to good works” (3:8). In particular, he emphasizes the quality of sober-mindedness (1:8; 2:2, 4–6, 12) and the importance of doing what is good, specifically in generosity toward those in need (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14). Specific instruction is to be given to various subgroups within the church—older men (2:2), older women (2:3), younger women (2:4, 5), younger men (2:6–8), and slaves (2:9, 10). Character and conduct that evidence sober-mindedness and self-control are essential because unbelievers are watching the members of the Christian community, looking for opportunities to revile God’s Word (2:5) and speak evil of the church and its leaders (2:8). Submission and integrity even in the adverse conditions of slavery, on the other hand, will “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (2:10).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: This brief epistle helps us to see the close and necessary connection between the “knowledge of the truth” and “godliness” (1:1)—“those who have believed” must be “careful to devote themselves to good works” (3:8). The reason why “the grace of God has appeared” is to “bring salvation for all people” and “train us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,” even as we wait for Christ to return at the end of the age (2:11, 12, cf. 2:13). After all, the very reason that Christ died was to “redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works” (2:14). Paul insists that this salvation is a salvation by grace alone. We were morally unattractive to God and gave Him no reason to prompt Him to save us (3:3). Our salvation stems from “the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior” (3:4). And so “he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (3:5). It is through Jesus our Savior that we have received the Spirit, that we are justified by grace, and that we are heirs according to the hope of eternal life (3:5–7). The sure sign that we have rightly grasped these truths is a life of obedience that springs from faith in Jesus Christ.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: God declares throughout the Scriptures that His purpose in saving His people is to set them apart from the world and for Himself. This setting apart entails a moral separation from the world and a moral conformity to God. We are to be holy because God is holy, a motif that finds early expression in the books of Moses (Lev. 11:44, 45; 19:2; 20:26; cf. 1 Pet. 1:16). The NT helps us to see this same principle even more clearly. God has redeemed His people in Christ. Part of that redemption is being delivered from sin’s dominion and being enabled to live holy lives that are pleasing to God. The pattern after which we are being conformed as believers is the image of God in Christ, the second Adam (Rom 8:29; 1 Cor. 15:49; Eph. 4:24; Col. 3:10). Paul’s concern in Titus to show that the knowledge of the truth accords with godliness (1:1) is therefore part of a broader biblical concern to emphasize that the doctrines of the grace of God, when rightly embraced, always to lead to holy living.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: In 2:13, Paul speaks of Jesus as “our great God and Savior,” a testimony to His deity (see notes). Christ took on our nature and “gave himself for us to redeem us,” that is, to die on the cross for sinners (2:14). Having been exalted to glory through His resurrection and ascension, Jesus Christ is the One through whom God “pour[s] out” the Holy Spirit “richly” upon us (3:6). Because Jesus has died and has been raised for us, we may be “justified by his grace” and “become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (3:7). It is by the Spirit of Jesus that we receive the “washing of regeneration and renewal” (3:5). What makes salvation a matter of God’s “own mercy,” is that in His “goodness and loving kindness,” God sent Jesus Christ to secure, by His death and life, all the saving blessings and benefits that we enjoy in Him (3:4). He did not make it possible for us to save ourselves. He “saved us” by His grace (3:5).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Paul’s teaching on slavery (2:9, 10) has sparked discussion and controversy, particularly within the last two centuries. For further discussion, see Philemon: History of Interpretation.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Paul describes the false teaching on Crete as something that had come from within the church (1:10, 16). It was characterized by a concern with Jewish myths (1:14), genealogies and quarrels about the law (3:9), and human commandments (1:14). The false teachers reflected a narrowly Jewish-Christian perspective (1:10) and sought leadership positions for financial gain (1:11). They had been effective in leading people astray and were divisive (1:10; 3:10). Nearly everything that Paul says in Titus about the false teaching on Crete has parallels with what he says in 1 and 2 Timothy about it in Ephesus (see Introduction to 2 Timothy: Special Issues). It is not clear why this should be the case. There is no reason to believe that there was any direct link between the two false teachings, or that everything being taught in one place was being taught in the other. On the other hand, the false teachings in the two areas may have been similar manifestations of a more general syncretistic movement in the Roman Empire at this time (compare the problems Paul addresses in Titus with those he addresses in Colossians and Ephesians). Placing Titus in the chronology of Paul’s life given in the book of Acts is difficult, but there is evidence in the Pastoral Epistles that Paul was released at the end of the imprisonment recorded in Acts 28 and then embarked on a fourth missionary journey. On the evidence for this fourth missionary journey, see Introduction to 1 Timothy: Special Issues.
