sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The apostle Paul wrote the letter to Philemon. Its authenticity as a Pauline epistle has not been seriously challenged.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: The letter was written while Paul was in prison in Rome (c. A.D. 60) and was probably sent to Philemon together with the letter to the Colossians. Philemon was a Christian brother and slaveholder in Colossae. His slave Onesimus had run away and had somehow met Paul in Rome. Through Paul’s teaching, Onesimus had become a Christian. Paul’s purpose in writing was to ask Philemon to spare Onesimus’s life and to receive Onesimus back not as merely a slave but also as a Christian brother. Paul even hints that he would be pleased if Philemon were to voluntarily return Onesimus to render valuable assistance to Paul (vv. 12, 13, 20, 21). In pursuit of this goal, Paul barely restrains himself from demanding the favor. He writes as powerful an appeal as he can, even offering to repay Onesimus’s debts, if any, to the master whom he had wronged.

sections.heading: Genre
sections.content: The book of Philemon is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see “Introduction to the Epistles”). It contains a standard letter opening (vv. 1–7), body (vv. 8–22), and conclusion (vv. 23–25). It is the shortest of Paul’s epistles, with only 335 words in the Greek text. Like the Pastoral Epistles (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus), Paul’s letter to Philemon is a personal letter. Also like those letters, Philemon is not only a personal letter. Paul addresses it also to “the church in your [Philemon’s] house” (v. 2).

sections.heading: Literary Features
sections.content: This letter is a model of understated persuasion, a tacit appeal to apply the grace of the gospel to an interpersonal relationship in which serious wrong has been committed by Onesimus. Paul is seeking from Philemon, at the very least, clemency for Ones­imus, whom he is sending back to Philemon (see “Date and Occasion” above). He does not expressly command Philemon to do anything (v. 8), but he appeals to Philemon “for love’s sake” (v. 9). Much of this letter consists of that appeal. Paul reminds Philemon of the spiritual benefit that he and the church have received from Philemon’s faith and love (vv. 4–7), of Paul’s own old age and imprisonment (v. 9), of his own affection for and confidence in Onesimus (vv.10–16), of his own willingness to rectify any past wrongs committed by Onesimus (vv. 17–19), and his role in Philemon’s salvation (v. 19)—a debt that Philemon could acknowledge by “refreshing” Paul’s “heart” (that is, Onesimus; v. 12) in Christ (v. 20). He concludes with a note of confidence that Philemon will act in accordance with Paul’s counsel (vv. 21, 22). Paul carefully selects his words to help advance or to underscore his argument in the letter. The Gk. words translated “sharing” (v. 6) and “partner” (v. 17) come from the same root. This form of repetition helps to underscore an important concern of Paul in this letter: the communion or fellowship that believers have with one another. Paul also capitalizes on the meaning of Onesimus’s name (“useful”). At v. 11, he informs Philemon that “formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.”

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Philemon shows the apostle using all his personal force to bring about a Christian answer to a very serious problem. Paul’s judgment appears to be that Philemon should show mercy to the offending slave, for the sake of Christian love toward a fellow Christian. Paul’s letter is passionate but carefully composed to achieve the desired end. The document was written in his own hand (v. 19), and is much more than an example of rhetoric. It brings us close to Paul’s ministry, so that we can practically feel his profound desire to make Christian love the first rule of human action.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Philemon makes two important theological points. First, Paul makes a gracious offer in v. 18: “if he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account.” He is willing to assume the consequences for Onesimus’s actions and to make satisfaction to Philemon. This offer is a picture of the way in which God has reconciled sinners to Himself in Christ. Although we offended God by our sins against Him and His law, He in mercy sent His beloved Son to bear the penalty for our sins in order that we might be restored to fellowship with Him. Our relationship with one another should reflect God’s mercy in Christ to us. Second, in v. 16, Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave but more than a slave, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.” Paul is not suggesting that Onesimus will no longer be a slave upon his return, but that to Philemon he will be “more than a slave,” that is, a “beloved brother ... in the Lord.” When we become Christians, we do not cease being parents, spouses, employees, etc. But the gospel radically transforms our relationships with the people in our lives. Paul makes essentially the same nuanced point when he reminds slave owners that they answer to the same heavenly Master as do their believing slaves (Eph. 6:9; Col. 4:1). But in vv. 15, 16, Paul says that Onesimus’s Christian identity is greater than his slave identity, which appears to suggest a notion of emancipation (cf. the note on vv. 15, 16 and “History of Interpretation” below).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: When man fell into sin, that fall had profound consequences for human relationships (Gen. 3:16–19). But the grace of God bears upon and transforms relationships among fellow believers, a fact that both the OT and the NT teach. Philemon’s life had been one that had “refreshed ... the hearts of the saints,” and this fact brought “joy and comfort” to the heart of Paul (v. 7). In this letter, Paul invites Philemon to seek restoration with a Christian brother who had offended him. In so doing, Paul says, he will “refresh [Paul’s] heart in Christ” (v. 20) and undoubtedly those of the church that met in his house (v. 2).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Paul makes clear throughout this letter that what distinguishes and characterizes the fellowship of believers is the “grace” and “peace” that come from “God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (v. 3, cf. v. 25). Paul’s appeals to Philemon are grounded on the saving mercies of Christ in which they both share (vv. 16, 20). What makes Onesimus, formerly useless, now useful (v. 12) is the intervention of Christ’s grace (v. 10). While the objective work of Christ for believers is not in the foreground in Philemon, its application by the Spirit to the lives of believers is.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Over the last two centuries, the Bible’s teaching on slavery has come under particular scrutiny, especially as the Western world has witnessed the welcome abolition of the chattel slavery of its recent past. Some have appealed to Philemon as indication that the New Testament commands the abolition of slavery. Care needs to be taken in assessing this claim. Scripture is clear that slavery was not instituted at creation, and will not be part of life in the new heavens and the new earth. Slavery only entered into human experience after the fall. Both the OT and the NT regulate slavery in order to ameliorate its effects, not unlike the way that the Scripture regulates divorce to the same purpose. In doing so, it regards neither slavery nor divorce to be a positive good. Paul, at many points in his letters, gives instructions to both Christian slave owners and Christian slaves (1 Cor. 7:17–24; Eph. 6:5–9; Col. 3:22–4:1; 1 Tim 6:1, 2; Titus 2:9, 10). He does not insist upon immediate abolition, but he does indicate that the gospel must thoroughly transform the relationship between a Christian slave owner and a Christian slave. Emancipation would certainly be a legitimate option for the slave owner and one that Paul implicitly commends to Philemon, and Christians have taken leadership over the centuries in seeking not only to ameliorate the effects of slavery but also to abolish the institution itself.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The fact that Paul does not directly call for Philemon to release Onesimus has troubled many people, and many individuals have criticized the Bible for allowing slavery. However, as noted in the History of Interpretation section above, it is clear that slavery was not a part of the original created order, so it would be impossible to argue that slavery was ever an inherently good thing. Furthermore, it is also important to keep in mind that slavery as practiced in biblical times was very different than the chattel slavery practiced in the Western world until the nineteenth century. As an example, in both ancient Israel during the OT period and the Roman Empire during the NT period, slavery was not based on one’s race and slaves in both systems had the opportunity to purchase their freedom. While it would be a mistake to glorify ancient slavery, it is also necessary to remember that slavery in the ancient world was almost the only way to deal with impoverishment. When one could not take care of oneself and one’s family, selling oneself into slavery could mean the difference between life and death. In other words, ancient slavery enabled people to escape starvation in the absence of charitable or government assistance. God revealed Himself to people trapped in personal sin as well as the sinful structures that exist in a fallen world. Slavery was key to the ancient economic system and kept many people from going hungry. Had the apostles and prophets called for its immediate abolition, things would have been made much worse not only for the slaves but also for the entire society. People would have starved and economic collapse and chaos would have ensued. The most loving thing that could have been done was the regulation of slavery and the revelation of principles that over time would lead to its abolishment without making life much worse for those who had no other option for survival except slavery . That is exactly what we find in Scripture—a transformation of the master-slave relationship that leads inevitably to the end of slavery wherever the gospel is truly embraced and its implications for all of society are lived out.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The author of Hebrews was skilled in Greek and Hellenistic literary style, immersed in the OT (specifically, the Septuagint), sensitive to the history of redemption culminating in Jesus, and pastorally concerned for the original readers, who knew him personally (13:22, 23) and whose background he knew (10:32–34). Like his readers, he came to faith not through direct contact with Jesus but rather through the apostles’ preaching (2:3, 4). In addition, he was acquainted with Timothy (13:23). But the epistle does not tell us his name, leaving a tantalizing mystery. In the Eastern church, by the time of Clement of Alexandria and Origen, the epistle was attributed to Paul, although both early church fathers recognized the stylistic differences between Hebrews and the Pauline epistles. In the West, Tertullian proposed Barnabas, a Levite of the Jewish Dispersion who was noted for his encouragement of others (Acts 4:36). Other early suggestions were Luke and Clement of Rome. From the fifth to the sixteenth centuries Paul’s authorship was accepted in East and West. During the Reformation, Luther proposed Apollos, a Jewish Christian from Alexandria who was skilled in speech and powerful in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). Suggestions in the modern period have included Priscilla (but cf. 11:32, where the author refers to himself with a masculine gender participle), Epaphras (Col. 1:7), and Silas (Acts 15:22, 32, 40; 1 Pet. 5:12). A few have suggested that Hebrews is a Pauline speech or sermon composed by Luke (see the Pauline speeches in Acts 13:16–41; 14:15–17; 17:22–31; 20:18–35; 22:1–21; 24:10–21; 26:2–23, 25–27; 27:21–26; 28:17–20). While it is difficult to rule out many of these candidates, it is equally hard to make a convincing case for any one of them. From the standpoint of early tradition, Paul has the strongest claim, but as Calvin observed, Hebrews differs from Paul in style, teaching method, and in the author’s inclusion of himself among the disciples of the apostles (2:3)—a statement at odds with Paul’s characteristic claim to have received his appointment and revelation of the gospel directly from Christ (Gal. 1:1, 11, 12). If the author is not Paul (or someone such as Luke whose other writings we have), knowing the author’s name would add little to our understanding of the epistle in any case. The epistle does have theological affinities with Paul. On the other hand, John’s lofty doctrine of Christ as the divine “Word” is detectable. But these combined characteristics, along with the portrayal of Jesus’ suffering as described in the first three (Synoptic) Gospels, are to be expected in view of the Holy Spirit’s unifying authorship of all of Scripture. While the human author of this book remains unknown, the important thing is that this writing, like the OT before it, is what “the Holy Spirit says” (3:7).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Hebrews offers a fair amount of information about the original recipients and their situation, while leaving questions of date and destination without certain answers. The original readers spoke Greek and used the Septuagint. They could follow arguments drawn from the OT and were interested in the OT sanctuary, sacrificial system, and priesthood. They had not heard the gospel directly from Jesus, but from the apostles (2:3), had faced previous persecution (10:32–34) and were facing present persecution, including expulsion from Jewish institutions (13:12, 13). They were in danger of falling away, perhaps fearing death (2:14–18), although their faith had not yet led to martyrdom (12:4). In addition, they may have been undergoing a transition in church leadership (13:7, 17), and were therefore concerned about security and permanence (6:19; 11:10; 13:8, 14). Finally, they receive greeting through the author “from Italy” (13:24). Drawing these features together, we conclude that the recipients were Jewish Christians of the Dispersion (the scattering of Jews outside Palestine), probably in Italy. Although some propose that the recipients were in Spain or Jerusalem, Rome remains the best choice, albeit any proposal is speculative. This would take 13:24 to be a greeting sent “home” by expatriates, though 13:24 may also be a greeting sent from Italian Christians with no such relationship to the letter’s readership. Further evidence of an Italian setting of the original audience lies in the fact that the earliest evidence of acquaintance with the epistle is from Rome, in 1 Clement, a work dating from about A.D. 96. Apparently, the temple was still standing and its sacrificial rituals were being performed when Hebrews was written (10:2, 3, 11). Perhaps the situation is that of the persecutions under Nero (c. A.D. 64). In that case, the suffering mentioned in 10:32–34 could have been caused by the edict of Claudius, which expelled the Jews from Rome in A.D. 49 (Acts 18:2). The effect of this expulsion would have been felt into the 50s and early 60s. Subject to suffering and shame for their confession of Jesus, stripped of the familiar and visible institutions of organized Jewish religion, and confused by the hidden character of Jesus’ glory (veiled in suffering when He was on earth and now hidden in heaven), the original readers were tempted to turn away from the faith (10:38, 39), to fall into unbelief, and thus to give up their pilgrimage toward God’s rest and God’s city (4:1, 2, 11; 11:10, 14–16; 13:14). Thus, a date of composition between 50 and 90 is viable, but the lack of mention of the destruction of the temple, which was a confirmation of the author’s message and thus would almost have certainly been included if it had happened before he wrote, as well as the references to persecution (as noted above) point strongly to a pre-70 date. Perhaps better is a date between A.D. 60 and 70.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: It has been generally observed that Hebrews begins as a theological treatise (esp. signaled by ch. 1), continues in the main body like an oral sermon (cf. 13:22), and concludes like an epistle (13:22–25). Thus, as some commentators have observed, the book is to be understood as a theological document, heard as a sermon, and read as an epistle. On the other hand, the author refers to his work as a “word of exhortation” (13:22). Since the same Gk. expression in Acts 13:15 refers to a synagogue speech, the term may identify this “epistle” as an expository sermon in written form. Viewing Hebrews as primarily sermonic is consistent with its emphasis on God’s speaking and the recipients’ hearing the Word (1:1, 2; 2:1–3; 3:1, 15; 12:25; etc.). The emphasis on exhortation in 13:22 shows that the sections of direct application and admonition to hearers (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; etc.) are not interruptions of the theological discussion, but rather show the author’s purpose for his rich argument for the mediatorial superiority of Christ.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Hebrews’ high literary style and special focus on Christ’s high priesthood set it apart from other NT books. It is aptly described as a “word of exhortation,” for exhortation or encouragement is the heart of the book’s purpose (3:13; 6:18; 10:25; 12:5). The author repeatedly calls his readers to an active and courageous response (4:11, 14, 16; 6:1; 10:19–25). The exhortation to persevere in the pilgrimage of faith is grounded in the author’s proof that the OT itself testified to the imperfection of the covenant at Sinai, the temple (or tabernacle), and its sacrificial system, thereby pointing ahead to a new High Priest—Jesus Christ. Jesus is better than the mediators, sanctuary, and sacrifices of the old order. He is worthy of “more glory” than Moses (3:3). The arguments from lesser to greater of 2:2, 3; 9:13, 14; 10:28, 29; and 12:25 (“if ... much less”) underscore the greater grace and glory, and the greater accountability, which have now arrived in the new covenant mediated by Jesus. Unlike the earthly and external aspects of the OT sanctuary, Jesus sanctifies us for the true worship of God, so that we draw near to heaven itself with clean consciences. He is the guarantee of this better covenant bond, for He links us inseparably with the God of grace.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Jesus Christ is central to the theology of Hebrews. The book opens with an assertion that Christ stands as the better prophet who reveals God and His way of salvation: “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world” (Heb. 1:1, 2). The reason Christ is the better prophet is because He is God’s “Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things,” a reference to Ps. 2:7, 8 wherein God promises that His “Son” would have an “inheritance” that would extend to “the very ends of the earth.” This end-time prophecy has begun to be fulfilled in Christ. This “inaugurated eschatology” is an important theological key to the book. Heb. 9:26, for example, affirms that Christ “has appeared once for all at the end of the ages [i.e., at His first coming] to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.” Yet, only two verses later there is reference to Christ concluding history: “so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him” (9:28). Jesus Christ is able to put away sin by the sacrifice of Himself because He is our great High Priest. Jesus, the typological fulfillment of the OT priest Melchizedek, is a priest forever in contrast to all human priests, including Melchizedek (7:3 note). All priests, whether Melchizedek or the Levitical priests, point to Jesus, who has eschatologically (finally, ultimately, in the last days) “completed” the incomplete and faulty former priestly ministers who pointed to Him (cf. 5:9). The “new covenant” prophesied in Jer. 31:31–34 is another key theological theme in the epistle. It is discussed at length in 8:8–13 and 10:16, 17. Heb. 8:10–12 recites the essential content of the new covenant that is contained in Jer. 31:33, 34: “I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.” The main point of the new covenant fulfillment in Jesus is that He has entered into the true heavenly Most Holy Place in God’s presence, and has enabled others to achieve that position in God’s very special presence to which only OT high priests formerly had access (8:11 note). This begins its fulfillment at Jesus’ first coming and is consummated at His last coming.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Within the book of Hebrews, the OT relates to the NT in several ways. This epistle’s unique contribution to the NT revelation of Jesus Christ is its comprehensive disclosure of Jesus’ fulfillment of the old covenant—the sanctuary, sacrifices, and priesthood established in the law of Moses. Also, Christian believers are seen to recapitulate Israel’s wilderness journeying and the achievement of rest in the Promised Land. In order to establish Christ as the high priest, the writer to the Hebrews focuses on how Christ fulfills OT types and prophecies. What the OT foresees happening in the end times has been inaugurated in Christ’s first coming and will be consummated at His final coming.

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Hebrews makes a distinctive contribution to the NT’s revelation of the both the person and the redemptive work in Christ. This epistle affirms in the strongest terms both Christ’s full deity and His complete humanity. The prologue introduces Jesus as God’s Son, the agent of creation, the radiance of God’s glory, and the “exact imprint of God’s nature,” and the sovereign preserver of the universe (1:2, 3). The OT quotations are applied to the Son, addressing Him as “God” (1:8, citing Ps. 45:6) and “Lord,” describing Him as the unchanging creator of the earth and the heavens (1:10–12, citing Ps. 102:25–27). Yet this divine Son, exalted above his angels, “became for a little while lower than the angels” (2:6–8, citing Ps. 8:4–6) by partaking of humanity’s flesh and blood, and thus our vulnerability to death, “made like his brothers in every respect” (2:14–17). In terms of Christ’s redemptive work, Hebrews shows Jesus as fulfilling all three mediatorial offices known to Israel—prophet, priest, and king. As fulfillment of the prophetic mission to convey revelation from God to humanity, Jesus is the Son in whom God has spoken in “these last days” (1:2), who has announced the arrival of “such a great salvation” (2:3), and whose voice now warns us from heaven (12:25–27). At greater length and depth, Hebrews explores Jesus’ priestly ministry in His atoning sacrifice, which cleanses believers’ consciences to approach God in worship, and in His constant intercession on their behalf at the right hand of God in heaven (2:17, 18; 4:14–5:10; 7:1–10:25). Since Christ is in the order of Melchizedek, He is both a priest and a king (7:1), addressed by God not only as the royal-messianic “Son” (5:5) but also as a priest forever (5:6). As king, Christ wields a righteous scepter (1:8, 9), conquers His people’s arch-foe, the devil (2:14, 15), and confers on them an unshakable kingdom (12:28).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The assertion in Heb. 7 that Christ is a priest after the order of Melchizedek affected the way in which some early church fathers understood the sacrament of the Lord’s Supper. For example, Ambrose, the fourth-century bishop of Milan, observed in Gen. 14:18, that Melchizedek offered a sacrifice of bread and wine. Because Jesus used bread and wine at the institution of the Lord’s Supper, and because Jesus is a priest after the order of Melchizedek, Ambrose and others began to speak of the Lord’s Supper as a sacrifice. Over the centuries, this idea developed into the Roman Catholic doctrine of the Mass, in which the sacrament is seen as a meritorious work, a propitiatory sacrifice that repeats or re-presents the sacrifice of Christ each time it is offered. Such a doctrine, however, is clearly at odds with the stress in Hebrews on the once-for-all nature of Christ’s atonement (10:11–14). The warning passages of Hebrews (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:12; 10:19–39; 12:14–29) have also been the source of much debate in the history of the church. In the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, they became one of the focal points of debate between traditionally Reformed theologians and their Arminian opponents. The Arminians argued that several of these passages prove that true Christians could fall away from Christ. The Reformed churches rejected this interpretation at the Synod of Dort held in 1618–19.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Despite the Reformed tradition’s rejection of Arminian theology, the warning passages in Hebrews continue to trouble many believers and are often cited by opponents of Reformed theology as proof that true believers can lose their salvation. The issues raised by these warning passages need to be addressed, and the study notes on these texts deal with many of these issues in great detail. It is worth noting at the outset, however, that many have failed to appreciate the ways in which the book of Hebrews affirms the security of the believer’s salvation. The extended presentation of the full sufficiency of Christ’s sacrifice in 9:1–10:18, for example, makes it inconceivable that Jesus could lose any of those for whom He died. This is a key part of the doctrine of definite or limited atonement, which states that God intended the death of Christ to pay only for the sins of the elect; therefore, those for whom He died will most certainly be saved (cf. John 10:14–16, 22–30; theological note “Definite Atonement” on p. 1875). In other passages, the author of Hebrews affirms that those who have true faith will persevere to the end. Heb. 3:14 is a key text: “We have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end.” This verse reveals a clear connection between the reality of one’s sharing in Christ and perseverance in faith. Professing believers have come to share in Christ only if they persevere in faith until the end, and the failure to persevere—to hold their “original confidence firm to the end”—proves that they never shared in Christ to begin with. All those who have true faith will persevere and only those who persevere have true faith. This is in keeping with other biblical texts on perseverance, including Paul’s emphasis in Phil. 2:12, 13 that believers work out their salvation in fear and trembling as God works in them, as well as John’s teaching that those who forsake the faith and never return were never actually part of the family of God to begin with (1 John 2:19). See theological note “Perseverance of the Saints” on p. 1994. Finally, the emphasis in Hebrews on Christ’s work of intercession also gives readers confidence that those who truly believe in Him will persevere in faith. Christ can save to the uttermost all who draw near to Him in faith because He always lives to intercede for them (Heb. 7:25). Under the old covenant, not everyone for whom the high priest prayed actually persevered in faith. If they had, there would have been no exile, for the entire nation would have been made up of men and women of faith. If, as the book of Hebrews argues, the High Priest of the new covenant is greater than the high priests of the old covenant, then it is impossible for Him to lose anyone for whom He prays. There is a great example of this in the case of Peter and Judas. Both Peter and Judas denied Christ, but only Peter was restored. What was the difference between the two men? Jesus prayed for Peter but not Judas (Luke 22:31, 32, 54–62; John 21:15–19; cf. Matt. 27:3–10). If Jesus ever lives to make intercession for those who draw near to Him in faith, then He is not going to stop praying for anyone who is truly converted. Once a person trusts truly in Christ, Christ will not stop praying for that person, and the Father will not deny His Son, for such would put them at odds in their joint work of saving the people whom God has chosen. Why, then, these warning passages if true believers cannot finally fall away from the faith? The key here is to understand the role of the believer in perseverance as well as the limitations of the biblical writers. First, believers have a role to play in their perseverance; while God’s monergistic work of regeneration undergirds the whole enterprise of salvation from start to finish, guaranteeing the redemption of the elect, those who have been regenerated do press forward in faith, paying attention to the teaching of Scripture and examining themselves to make sure they are in the faith. Warnings such as we find in the book of Hebrews are used by the Spirit of God to encourage believers to persevere. Second, it is important to remember that though the biblical writers were inspired by God to give us the very Word of God, this act of inspiration did not thereby make them omniscient. The gift of inspiration did not carry with it the granting of the ability to see into the hearts of others. Paul, Peter, the author of Hebrews, and the rest of the biblical authors did not have the kind of knowledge that the Lord has about the state of others’ souls. However, they did know that their audiences likely included both those who possessed faith as well as those who only professed faith, and they understood that God would use their words to save His elect; thus, they issued warnings to the entire church, confident that the Lord would use them to preserve His people. God cannot fail to save His people. All those who have been justified will also be glorified (Rom. 8:28–30), and the Lord’s work in people such as Paul—who before His conversion did all that he could to oppose God’s kingdom—proves that if God really wants to save a person, He will not fail to save that person. But He does not save us and then remove us immediately from the planet; rather, He has His people work out their salvation in fear and trembling, paying heed to His warnings as they grow in faith and cling daily to Christ.

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The author of this letter identifies himself as James. Though several different people named “James” are mentioned in the NT church, it is almost certain that the author of this book is James the brother of Jesus. The author assumes a position of authority in the church, which certainly was accorded to James the Lord’s brother, who was a leader of the Jerusalem church (Gal. 1:19) and who presided at the council of Jerusalem (Acts 15). He was considered one of the pillars of the church, along with Peter and John (Gal. 2:9). The NT lists James as one of the sons of Mary, Jesus’ mother (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3). James, along with his brothers, was skeptical of Jesus during His earthly ministry (John 7:5), but was converted when he became an eyewitness of the resurrection (1 Cor. 15:7). The early church historian Hegesippus identified him as “James the Just,” testifying to his extraordinary godliness, his zeal for obedience to the law of God, and his singular devotion to prayer. It was said that James’s knees became so calloused from prayer that they resembled the knees of camels. Josephus records that James was martyred in A.D. 62. Eusebius says he was beaten to death with a club after being thrown from the temple parapet; Hegesippus also records that he was thrown from the pinnacle of the temple.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: James was written between A.D. 44, the beginning of the persecution that spread to Jewish Christians living in the Diaspora as well as to Gentile believers (Acts 12), and A.D. 62, the year of James’s death. Since no mention is made of the controversy leading to the council of Jerusalem (Acts 15), it is possible that James was written before A.D. 49. Thus, James may be the earliest NT writing. The letter is addressed to “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion,” which likely refers to churches spread throughout Asia Minor (on the meaning of “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” as a way of referring to the churches, see note on 1:1). Since this is the case, the letter was probably intended to be a circular letter that would be read by many congregations in many places, and as such, it treats issues and problems that would have been common to all of the recipients, problems that impacted Christian congregations wherever they were located.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: James has been variously considered an epistle, a sermon (to be read aloud in the churches), a form of wisdom literature, a diatribe, and a moral exhortation. These categories are not mutually exclusive, and there are elements of all these forms in James. It most closely resembles Jewish “diaspora letters,” such as the letters of Gamaliel to Jews living outside of Israel. The literary structure of parallelism is used (1:9, 10), along with aphorisms, concrete images drawn from nature, and groups of sayings that have a clear similarity to the style of Jesus.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: The epistle has a markedly Jewish flavor and refers frequently to the OT. It shares a number of characteristics, for example, with OT Wisdom Literature. These similarities have led many to refer to James as the “NT book of Proverbs.” As such, James is characterized by its focus on practical Christian living. James does not settle for right doctrine if that right doctrine is not resulting in godly character in which faith bears fruit. We are not merely to be hearers of the word according to James, but doers (1:22–24). The nature of true faith as bearing the fruit of loving service to others, therefore, is central to this epistle (2:14–26). James is clear that although we are not justified—declared righteous before God—by our works, good works are the necessary and inevitable demonstration that the faith we profess is genuine. Among the most important themes in the book of James is perseverance in the midst of trials. The faith of Christians is under constant attack, and James encourages believers to stand firm, to not be double-minded (1:6, 7). He calls believers to patiently persevere in faith (5:7–11). One aspect of godly perseverance involves the way in which we use our speech, another major theme of the epistle. Again and again, James confronts believers who use their tongues to lie, gossip, and tear down others (1:19–21, 26; 3:1–12; 4:11, 12; 5:12; cf. Luke 6:45). The final judgment is another of the major themes found in James’s epistle. He repeatedly refers to future judgment and uses it as a motivation for ethical exhortation (1:11; 2:10–13; 3:1; 4:12; 5:3, 9).

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: Though one may say the same of every book of Scripture, it is important to observe that James is a God-centered book. God is the One who is the giver of wisdom (1:5). He is holy and cannot be tempted with evil (1:13). Every good gift comes from God, whom James describes as “the Father of lights with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (1:17). God has chosen the poor of the world to be rich in faith (2:5). He is also the One who has given the moral law, summarized in the Ten Commandments, and He is the great Judge (2:11, 12; 4:12). He is “one” (2:19), and He is worthy of our faith (2:23). He is our Lord and Father (3:9), and He is gracious, merciful, and compassionate (4:6–8; 5:11). James opens his epistle with a statement that sheds much light on his understanding of Christ: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). This simple opening places God and Jesus Christ in parallel, indicating that they share the same authority. If there are any doubts among his readers about the identity and status of Jesus Christ, James removes them in ch. 2, when he refers to Jesus as “the Lord of glory” (2:1). If this translation of 2:1 is correct (see study note on the other possible translation of the Gk. phrase), it is reminiscent of David’s description of God as the “King of glory” (Ps. 24:7–10). In any case James speaks of Jesus as “Lord” in 2:1, and this is important because God is “Lord” (3:9). The eschatology of James is centered on the expectation of the coming judgment of God. This coming judgment forms the background to James’s ethical admonitions. The coming judgment is closely associated with the coming of the Lord (5:7, 8). Those who persevere through the trials will be rewarded and receive the crown of life (1:12) because perseverance is the fruit of saving faith, the faith by which alone we are granted entrance into God’s kingdom. The faithless and merciless will be condemned (2:13; 5:1).

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: James addresses his readers as “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” (1:1). The language immediately evokes the OT story of Israel. The “twelve tribes” originally referred to the twelve tribes of Israel. The “Dispersion” (or Diaspora) originally referred to those Jews who had been scattered at the time of the exile throughout the Near East and then later into Europe and Africa. Here, James is using this language to refer to Christians (whether ethnically Jewish or Gentile). By doing so, James places the church in the context of the story of Israel. Because Israel has now been redefined in terms of Jesus Christ, the true Israel is the church comprising Jewish and Gentile believers in Christ. Some have suggested that by speaking of the church as “the Dispersion,” James is reversing the connotation of that word. Whereas the first “dispersion” was an act of judgment, this second “dispersion” is the means by which God is blessing the nations with the gospel (cf. Acts 8:1, 4).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: The epistle teaches a high Christology and stresses the importance of dealing with affliction from the standpoint of faith. The name of “Jesus” or “Christ” occurs rarely (1:1; 2:1), though sometimes “Lord” refers to Christ (1:1; 2:1; probably also 5:7, 8) and other times it refers generally to “God” or the “Father” (3:9; 4:10, 15; 5:4, 10, 11, 14, 15). James’s interchangeable use of the title “Lord” interchangeably for both Jesus and God the Father indicates Jesus’ identification with the Father as “Lord,” and thus shows the deity of Jesus (note also that the Gk. word for “Lord” refers very often in the Septuagint to Yahweh). Though “Jesus Christ” is not mentioned explicitly very often, His first and second comings are assumed at key points throughout the book. James 1:1 speaks explicitly about James’s being a “servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ,” and 2:1 refers to those who “hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.” The last reference refers to Jesus’ exalted state, most likely as a result of His ascension and session at God’s right hand (cf. Matt. 26:64; Mark 14:62; Luke 22:69; Eph. 1:20; Col. 3:1; Heb. 8:1).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: The most debated issue in the history of the interpretation of James is the relationship between James and Paul. Specifically, do Paul and James (esp. 2:14–26) teach contradictory views of justification and the relationship between faith and works? If not, how are their views to be reconciled? Orthodox interpreters of James in the early church assumed that Scripture could not contradict itself. They resolved the issue by noting that works are a result of true faith; true faith is demonstrated by good works. The same subject arose at the time of the Reformation as some appealed to James to support the Roman Catholic doctrine of justification, which states that good works are more than just a demonstration of true faith—they merit heaven when done in cooperation with God’s grace. Protestants rightly returned to the distinction made in the early church, for they recognized that even the best of our works are “splendid vices” and cannot meet the standard of perfection that God requires if we seek to be justified by our own doing of the law (Matt. 5:48; Gal. 5:3).

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: The motif of the future judgment is very important in understanding the highly contested section in 2:14–26 on the relationship of faith, good works, and justification. One key for understanding the passage is noticing how 2:14–26 relates to its surrounding context. James 1:10, 11 makes an apparent reference to the last judgment, while 2:9–13 focuses on being a “transgressor of the law” for which final judgment will come. The next verse then asks whether a person with faith but no works can be saved from this final judgment (2:14). After the contested text is another reference to future judgment: those “who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (3:1). The reference in 3:6 to the “tongue ... set on fire by hell” likely also refers to this judgment. The theme of judgment is continued later in the epistle: God “is able to save and destroy” (4:12), and 5:1–9 warns those who oppress others that “the coming of the Lord is at hand” (v. 8) and “the Judge is standing at the door” (v. 9), a reference respectively to the imminent expectation of the end and the judgment to come at the end; 5:12 also warns people not to “fall under condemnation.” In light of the surrounding context and its emphasis upon future judgment, it seems that 2:14–26 mainly addresses the issue of how faith and works relate to the final judgment at the very end of one’s life. Genuine faith will produce and be accompanied by good works; such good works will be evidence at the last day of a genuine faith. False faith, or “dead faith,” is empty belief, like that of the “demons” (2:19; purely cognitive recognition of who God is without a desire to trust and to obey Him). Therefore, the reference to being “justified” by works together with faith in vv. 21–24 probably has this final judgment in view. The Gk. word dikaioō in Paul has the sense of “vindicate.” Sometimes Paul uses it in the sense of (1) “vindicating” a person from the guilty verdict of their sin by which a relationship with God is established through Christ during the present age, and sometimes in the sense of (2) “vindicating” such people before God’s judgment seat at the end of the age against the unjust verdict of the world. James has this second meaning in mind, namely, that good works demonstrate that the verdict of the world against God’s people—that God’s people are foolish and enemies of the common good—is false and unjust. Good works will vindicate others at the last day because they will demonstrate the reality of faith in the only wise God, whose plan and purpose is for His creation is wholly good. They will show that we are united to Christ by faith alone and therefore share in His goodness and wisdom (cf. 1 Cor. 1:30, 31). James 2:24 offers an axiom based on the example of Abraham: “You see that a man is justified by works and not by faith alone.” Notice the plural “works” here that indicates that the many good works of Abraham’s whole life vindicated the true nature of his faith. Thus, the works of a person’s entire life are displayed at the final judgment , not in order to receive God’s verdict that we are righteous in our sight, but to prove that we possess the kind of faith by which we lay hold of the righteousness of Christ, which is the only basis for God’s justifying verdict (cf. Rom. 3:21–4:25; 5:12–21; 2 Cor. 5:21). For James, good works done throughout a person’s life serve as evidence of genuine faith (2:14, 18).

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The author identifies himself as “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). That he is the well-known apostle of the Gospels and Acts is confirmed by both internal and external evidence. The author describes himself as “a witness of the sufferings of Christ” (5:1), and there are numerous echoes of Jesus’ teaching and deeds in the epistle (e.g., 5:2, 3; cf. John 21:15–17). Parallels of thought and phrasing between 1 Peter and Peter’s speeches in Acts lend further support to Peter’s authorship (e.g., 2:7, 8; cf. Acts 4:10, 11). The external attestation of 1 Peter as a genuine epistle of Peter is widespread, early, and clear, and there is no evidence that it was ever attributed to anyone else. Apart from the possible witness of 2 Pet. 3:1 (note), second- and third-century church fathers including Irenaeus, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen all attributed the epistle to Peter. By the time of Eusebius in the early fourth century, there was no question of its authenticity. Although the case for Peter being the author of this epistle is strong, linguistic and historical objections have been raised to the traditional view of Petrine authorship in the last two centuries. The Greek of 1 Peter is said to be too polished and too influenced by the Septuagint to have come from an uneducated Galilean fisherman like Peter (Acts 4:13). The persecutions alluded to in the epistle (4:12–19; 5:6–9) are alleged to reflect a situation later than that of Peter’s lifetime. None of these objections is decisive against Pe­trine authorship. In response to the linguistic objection, several points can be made. First-century Galilee was bilingual (Aramaic and Greek were both spoken in the region), and it is not unlikely that a commercial fisherman would have known the language of commerce, namely, Greek. The description of Peter and John as “uneducated, common men” in Acts 4:13 may refer only to their lack of formal training in the Scriptures. The thirty years that elapsed between Peter’s days as a fisherman and the time the epistle was written would have provided ample opportunity for him to improve his proficiency in Greek. Finally, Silvanus’s possible role as secretary (5:12) could account for the smoother style of 1 Peter as compared to 2 Peter. With regard to the historical objections, the sufferings alluded to by Peter can just as well be accounted for by local, sporadic harassment—which was the routine experience of early Christians from the days of the apostles on—as by official persecution in the days of Nero (c. 64 A.D. ).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: According to 5:13, Peter was in “Babylon” when he wrote the epistle. Various identifications of the location have been suggested, among them (1) a military outpost in Egypt, (2) the ancient Mesopotamian city itself, and (3) Rome. Several lines of evidence favor the last proposal. Mark, who was with Peter when he wrote (5:13), is known to have been with Paul in Rome (Col. 4:10; Philem. 24). Rome is often referred to as “Babylon” in the book of Revelation (Rev. 17:5, 9). In Peter’s day, Rome was the pagan power under which God’s “exiles” in the provinces of Asia Minor lived as their inheritance awaited them in heaven (1:1, 4), just as in the days of Jeremiah and Daniel, pagan Babylon had conquered Judah and carried captives far from the Promised Land. This interpretation has been generally accepted since the second century. The uniform testimony of early church history is that Peter was in Rome at the end of his life. If Rome is the place of origin, the epistle must have been composed between A.D. 60 and 68. The first limit is established by Peter’s familiarity with Ephesians and Colossians (cf. 2:18 with Col. 3:22; and 3:1–6 with Eph. 5:22–24) and the second limit by the tradition that Peter was crucified upside down in Rome in A.D. 68 at the latest. While the introduction (“the Dispersion”; 1:1 and note) and the frequent OT quotations and allusions in the epistle might imply Jewish Christian recipients (so Calvin), there are stronger indications that most were from a pagan background. The reference in 1:18, for example, to “the futile ways inherited from your forefathers” hardly seems fitting for Jews. Furthermore, the sins listed in 4:3 were more typical of Gentile pagans than the Jewish people. The reason believers are addressed as “exiles of the Dispersion” may be that they voluntarily or under compulsion helped to colonize Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). But even if that is not the case, the reference to the hearers’ being “exiles of the Dispersion” reflects the past notion of Jews’ living in exile and in the “Dispersion” as a result of and since the Babylonian exile. By attributing the status of “exiles” to the letter’s recipients, whatever their specific situation, Peter shows that Jewish and Gentile Christians are to be regarded as exiled Israel—the true fulfillment of Israel—as it continues in Christ and those who identify with Him (cf. 2:4–10). Peter also reminds them that other churches in other parts of the world are likewise in the same exile (cf. “she who is in Babylon greets you”; 5:13). It is apparent from the letter that the readers were suffering persecution for their faith (1:6, 7; 3:13–17; 4:12–19; 5:8, 9). But nothing in the letter indicates official, legislative persecution or requires a date of composition later than the 60s. Their sufferings were the trials common to first-century Christians, and included insults (4:4, 14) and slanderous accusations of wrongdoing (2:12; 3:16). Beatings (2:20), social ostracism, sporadic mob violence, and local police action may have been involved as well. Yet the epistle is addressed to Christians scattered across six Roman provinces in Asia Minor, and churches and individual believers may have been encountering different degrees of reception or resistance in different places. Peter’s qualification “if it should be God’s will” (3:17) implies that his original audience may have been persecuted in some regions and not in others. The purpose of the letter was for the hearers to “stand firm” in faith in the midst of trials and persecutions (5:12; cf. 1:7–9; 2:18–23; 3:13–17; 4:12–19).

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The literary form of 1 Peter is that of an epistle, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see “Introduction to the Epistles”). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1, 2), body (1:3–5:10), and conclusion (5:12–14). Unlike the typical Pauline epistle, however, the structure of the body does not move from a foundational doctrinal discussion (what is called the “indicative”) to a section in which the gospel’s ethical implications for Christian living and relationships are spelled out (the “imperative”). Rather, in 1 Peter, indicative instruction (particularly the church’s identity as the house, temple, and family of God) and the outworking of the truth are interwoven.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Peter wrote to encourage persecuted and bewildered Christians and to exhort them to stand fast in their faith (5:12). In its encouragement and exhortation, the letter stresses several themes: 1. Already and not yet. The OT predicts a number of events to occur in the end times. First Peter portrays some of these events as being fulfilled in Christ’s first coming and others as awaiting consummation at His second coming. Peter sees that Jesus’ sacrificial death (1:18, 19, alluding partly to the end-time prophecy of Is. 52:3) has occurred “in these last times for the sake of” his readers (1:20). There is a sense in which the final judgment is already beginning (4:17). Yet there will be a conclusion to history. This is referred to as “the last time,” when there will be a final completion of the “salvation” of God’s people (1:5) in that they will receive an incorruptible “inheritance,” which includes their bodily resurrection (1:3–9). But there will also be a final judgment for the ungodly (4:18). This consummation of all things could happen at any moment, so believers must be alert to be faithful and godly (cf. 4:7). 2. Living in exile. As noted earlier, the reference to Peter’s readers’ being “exiles of the Dispersion” reflects the past idea of many Israelites’ existing in exile and in the “Dispersion” since the Babylonian exile. Thus, the letter’s recipients, as Jewish and Gentile Christians, are viewed as exiled Israel—the true Israel—as it continues in Christ and those who identify with Him (cf. 2:4–10). Peter also brings to their recollection the fact that other churches in other parts of the world also live in the same exile (cf. 5:13). Accordingly, he reminds them that that they are true Israel living in the exile of the world (1:1; 2:11; cf. 5:13), and as such, their lives are to be characterized by the reality of God’s lordship rather than the ungodly values of the world. 3. The suffering of believers. Peter repeatedly turns the thoughts of his readers to the joys and glories of their eternal inheritance (1:3–13; 4:13; 5:1, 4) and instructs them about proper Christian behavior in the midst of unjust suffering (4:1, 19). Christ is held up as the model to follow in persevering through suffering (2:21–23; 4:1, 2). While addressed primarily to persecuted Christians, these principles apply to all suffering, regardless of the cause, provided it is not occasioned by one’s own sin. On the basis of this epistle, Peter has been called “the apostle of hope” (cf. 1:3, 13, 21; 3:15). The central exhortation of the entire epistle can be summed up in the phrase “trust and obey” (cf. 4:19), especially in the face of suffering. THEOLOGY OF 1 PETER Peter fortifies his readers in order that they might endure suffering for Jesus’ sake by grounding their assurance in Christ’s redemptive work and by invoking their exalted identity as God’s church. Christ’s redemptive sacrifice has cleansed believers and set them free from sin’s condemnation as well as its destructive domination. They have been chosen by God for “sprinkling with [Christ’s] blood,” cleansed from defilement and consecrated to serve freely in God’s presence (1:1, 2). The precious blood of Christ, worth more than the most precious metals, has redeemed them from the futile patterns of conduct that marked their pagan past and those of previous generations (1:19). The Suffering Servant was innocent of sin and deceit, but He “bore our sins in his own body on the tree” in order to free us from sin’s control, that we might “live to righteousness” (2:22–25). His substitutionary suffering sets the pattern for believers to follow in their own response to suffering (2:21). By suffering in our place, the Righteous One brings us to God (3:18). Christ’s resurrection gives us new birth to a living hope and expectation of an imperishable heavenly inheritance (1:3, 4, 21). He is the living stone who imparts life to others, gathering a spiritual house composed of living stones—the precious cornerstone of God’s temple, even though unbelievers dismiss Him as a stone of stumbling (2:4–8). When the prophets foretold His sufferings and the subsequent glories, the Spirit of Christ used them to serve those who now hear His good news of salvation in Him (1:10–12). The church’s identity as newborn children of God, the exiled people of God, and the holy house and priesthood of God connects Christians to the heritage of ancient Israel and reinforces the summons to unity and patient endurance under suffering. Since God gave them birth (1:3) and they can call Him Father (1:17), believers must obey Him as children (1:14) and love each other as brothers (1:22, 23; 3:8). Like newborn babies, they must thirst for the spiritual milk that fosters their growth (2:2). Despite their pagan past and previous exclusion as “not a people” (1:18; 2:10; 4:3, 4), Peter’s readers are now heirs to Israel’s exalted titles, high privilege, and glorious mission to “declare the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (2:9, 10). Yet like Israel in exile, these believers are scattered far from their inheritance (1:1, 4), are strangers and aliens (1:1, 17; 2:11) living among “Gentiles” (non-Christians; 2:12; 4:3) and regarded as “strange” by those with whom they once indulged in sensuality (4:4). As Israel was once a kingdom of priests with God’s temple in its midst, so now those throughout the Christian Dispersion are under construction as the spiritual house of God (2:5; 4:17) on which His glory rests (4:14). Their sufferings are His refining fire to purify and prove their faith (1:7; 4:12). These sufferings are not symptomatic of God’s rejection, neglect, or absence; rather, they signify His approval and strong presence by His Spirit. It is a tribute to God’s grace that the apostle who once dared to rebuke his Master over the prospect of the Messiah’s sufferings (Matt. 16:22, 23) and who flinched in fear when identification with Jesus became risky (Matt. 26:69–75) is in this epistle the Holy Spirit’s spokesman to declare the necessity both of Christ’s unique sacrificial suffering and of Christians’ suffering for His name. 1

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The Christian audience is closely linked to Jesus in His suffering, since He serves as the model for their faithful suffering (2:21–23; 4:1). Yet His suffering is greater than theirs, especially since it was a vicarious and penal substitutionary sacrifice for their sake, which “healed” them (2:24). This was in fulfillment of Is. 53:4–7, which records Isaiah’s vision of the substitutionary suffering of the messianic Servant on behalf of His people. His death is what enables His people to “return” to God, since the penalty of their sin has been paid. This is language used in the OT of God’s causing Israel to “return” to their land and to Him. Thus, Christians are no longer alienated from God but have been restored through Christ’s death as authentic Israel from spiritual exile, even though they continue to live in physical exile in the world until the eternal new world comes (cf. 2 Pet. 3:13). CHRIST IN 1 PETER The Christians who are addressed in this letter are regarded as true Israelites who are in the exile in the world, and they are considered true Israelites because of Peter’s presupposition that their identification and union with Christ—the true Israel of God (John 15:1–17; cf. Is. 5:1–7)—makes them the true Israel of God. This presupposition especially comes to the surface in 2:4–10. There, Jesus is the “living stone” and “chosen” stone of the new end-time temple, and consequently, Christians are “living stones” of that temple, “being built up as a spiritual house ... through Jesus Christ” (2:4, 5). And because Christ is a “chosen stone” (2:6), so His people who are identified with Him were “chosen” before the foundation of the world (2:9). So also, the salvation of these believers can be described in 2:10 as the fulfillment of the prophecy in Hos. 1:6, 9, and 2:23, where, for example, God will say to Israel, “[You were] not my people, [but now] you are my people” (Hos. 2:23). Thus, both Jewish and Gentile Christians are seen to be fulfilling a prophecy about Israel, since they are identified with Jesus who is true Israel. Christ has not only died on behalf of believers to restore them to God, but in His resurrection, when He was “made alive by the Spirit” (3:18, 22), He caused them to be made “living” people (2:5) and to be restored as true Israelites to God (3:18).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Over the centuries, the most controversial text in 1 Peter has been the discussion of Christ’s preaching to the spirits in prison and the typological connection between the flood in Noah’s time and Christian baptism (3:18–22). Since the patristic age, this passage has been cited, along with two Pauline texts (Rom. 10:6–8; Eph. 4:8–10), in support of the doctrine of Christ’s “descent into hell” between His death and resurrection, and thus of this article in the Western church’s version of the Apostles’ Creed. Among ancient and modern interpreters who identify the time frame with the interim between Jesus’ death on Good Friday and His resurrection on Easter Sunday, significant differences exist regarding the content of Christ’s preaching and the audience He addressed. The following are among the views proposed: (1) Christ announced His victory over sin and death to the spirits of human beings who persisted in unbelieving rebellion while Noah built the ark (Gen. 6:5). (2) Christ announced His victory on the cross to the demons (“sons of God”; Gen. 6:1–4) who drew humanity into wickedness in Noah’s day. (3) Christ preached good news to the spirits of the deceased rebels of Noah’s day, giving them a second opportunity to repent (viewing 1 Pet. 4:6 as commentary on 3:19). This view should be rejected because it conflicts with Heb. 9:27. (4) Christ announced to OT believers the good news that His death had accomplished their redemption. In this view, Noah’s contemporaries are presumed to have repented as the floodwaters rose and are to be taken as representing believers in all generations before Christ’s coming. Both presumptions are unlikely in view of the text’s actual description of these imprisoned spirits. Another view, held by Augustine, Aquinas, and more recent interpreters, argues that the proclamation took place in Noah’s time and through Noah, a “herald of righteousness” (2 Pet. 2:5), as the “Spirit of Christ” spoke through him (1 Pet. 1:11). The content of the message was a summons of repentance and promise of salvation (good news; 4:6), but Noah’s contemporaries rebelled. Consequently, they are now “spirits in prison,” reserved for final judgment. This view poses fewer interpretive and theological problems than the various interpretations that “date” the proclamation during the time that Jesus’ body was in the grave. But a reference to a preaching that took place centuries before Christ’s suffering and being “made alive in the Spirit” (see below) does not easily fit the flow of the text. Finally, several recent interpreters have argued that “made alive in the Spirit” refers to Christ’s resurrection, as it typically does in the NT (John 5:21; Rom. 4:17; 8:11; 1 Cor. 15:22, 36). The journey mentioned next (“he went”; 3:19) as preceding Christ’s proclamation to the spirits in prison is to be interpreted by the later “has gone” (3:22), which refers to Christ’s ascension when He had subjected angels, authorities, and powers (“he went” and “has gone” represent the same Gk. participle). The content of Christ’s proclamation to rebellious spirits (whether human or demonic) is therefore His announcement of victory over both sin (the cross) and death (the resurrection), which vindicates the faith of His suffering followers on earth (as Noah’s faith was vindicated by God’s flood). Biblical cosmology is flexible enough that “spirits in prison” need not be envisioned as “under the earth,” but may rather refer to “spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: This epistle claims to have been written by Simon (Hb. Simeon ) Peter (1:1), and there is evidence in the epistle to support this claim. The author refers to his own imminent death in terms that recall Jesus’ words to Peter (1:14; cf. John 21:18, 19); he says that he was an eyewitness of the transfiguration (1:16–18; cf. Matt. 17:1–8 and parallels); and he seems to imply a connection between this epistle and 1 Peter (3:1). Although there are possible allusions to 2 Peter in Christian literature of the late first and early second centuries A.D. , it is not as well attested as 1 Peter or other NT books. Origen, in the third century, was the first writer outside of the Bible to attribute the epistle explicitly to Peter, but he said that others doubted Peter’s authorship. Eusebius listed it among the disputed NT books, and Jerome, while noting some disagreement regarding its authenticity, suggested that stylistic differences with 1 Peter were due to Peter’s use of different secretaries. The epistle was accepted as authentic and canonical by influential fourth-century church fathers such as Athanasius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Ambrose, and Augustine, as well as by the late-fourth-century church councils of Hippo and Carthage, and its subsequent place in the NT canon was assured. Notwithstanding the epistle’s own claims, a number of objections have been raised to Petrine authorship. Among the more common ones are the lack of early attestation, slow recognition by the church, stylistic differences with 1 Peter, and the apparent use of Hellenistic religious and philosophical language. The usual alternative to Petrine authorship is pseudonymity, i.e., it was written by an unknown author who attributed the work to a well-known writer as a literary device to commend his message. While several of the objections must be taken seriously (especially attestation and style), their force should not be exaggerated, and none conclusively disproves Peter’s authorship. On the one hand, there is stylistic diversity between 1 and 2 Peter. Many of the favorite words and expressions of 1 Peter, for example, are absent in 2 Peter. On the other hand, the differences are not absolute, and several striking similarities do exist between the two epistles. There are also a number of parallels between 2 Peter and Peter’s speeches in Acts (e.g., the use of the Gk. word eusebeia , “godliness,” in 2 Pet. 1:3, 6, 7; 3:11; and in Acts 3:12, a word occurring elsewhere in the NT only in the Pastoral Epistles). Furthermore, stylistic differences between 1 and 2 Peter can be easily explained by the apostle’s use of different amanuenses (secretaries) without having to resort to the unlikely conclusion that a different author wrote each letter. The claim that 2 Peter is pseudonymous is weak. Genuine examples of pseudepigraphy (writings by authors who are pretending to be someone else of greater authority) in early Christian literature are almost all heretical, an indication that the device was used to commend works of questionable and false content. There is strong evidence that the church did not tolerate the practice, but in fact strictly rejected pseudepigrapha. The author introduces himself as “Simeon Peter,” rather than simply “Peter” (1 Pet. 1:1) or “Simon Peter,” the most frequent combination of his given name and the one bestowed on him by Jesus. Peter is called “Simeon,” a form that more closely reflects the Hb. original than “Simon,” only once elsewhere in the NT (Acts 15:14), so it is unlikely that a pseudepigraphist, especially one of a later generation, would employ this lesser-known form of his name in a ruse to claim apostolic authority for his work. In sum, the case against Peter’s authorship fails, and the epistle’s own claim to have been written by Peter can be taken at face value.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Assuming Peter’s authorship, 2 Peter must have been written before the apostle’s death around A.D. 67–68. The reference to his imminent death in 1:14 suggests a time near the end of his life. If 3:1 refers to 1 Peter, the date of composition must be sometime after 63–64 (Introduction to 1 Peter: Date and Occasion). A date between 65 and 67 is therefore plausible. The place of origin of 2 Peter is uncertain. Rome is a likely suggestion, given that Peter wrote his first epistle from that city (1 Pet. 5:13 note) and the tradition that he was martyred in Rome under Nero. The letter was written because of false teaching that threatened the recipients. Unlike 1 Peter, this epistle contains little information about the identity of its recipients. If 3:1 refers to 1 Peter, the recipients, Christians in Asia Minor, are the same in both epistles. If 3:1 is not a reference to 1 Peter but rather to a lost epistle, there is no firm information from which the recipients can be determined.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Second Peter is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (1:1, 2), body (1:3–18a), and conclusion (3:18b). Some have proposed that the letter form of 2 Peter has been combined with a so-called “last testament” or “farewell speech,” which was a literary type found in early Judaism. Accordingly, this would mean that the letter is also a last testament of the apostle Peter. Some commentators, however, have noticed that there is no deathbed narrative or any narrative of the author’s burial, which was typical for the testament genre. Thus, it is unlikely that 2 Peter should be categorized as a last testament or farewell speech. Furthermore, most who hold that 2 Peter was a testament also believe that Peter did not write the book, since the other Jewish writings that conform to this literary type are pseudonymous. Considering the weakness of the case for pseu­donymous authorship, it is best to see 2 Peter as a classic letter and the apostle Peter as its author.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: As an antidote to the threat of false teaching from within (2:1), Peter emphasizes the truth and ethical implications of the gospel against the false teachers. Although the false teaching is difficult to define precisely, it appears to be an early precursor of Gnosticism. This term designates any of a variety of heretical movements in the early Christian centuries (esp. the second century) that combined ideas from Greek philosophy, oriental mysticism, Judaism, and Christianity, and emphasized salvation through intuitive, esoteric knowledge (the Gk. word for “knowledge” is gnōsis ) rather than through faith in Christ. In the Gnostic system the physical body was regarded as evil, so second-century Gnostics were usually characterized by either blatant immorality (because they believed the evil body would be discarded anyway and so it does not matter what one does with it), or rigorous asceticism (because they believed physical pleasures were inherently evil and should be denied). Asceticism is not addressed as a problem in 2 Peter, but immorality is (2:13–19). The false teachers seem to have been using Christian liberty as a license to sin, especially to commit sexual immorality (2:14). In addition, they were guilty of denying the Lord (2:1), despising authority, slandering celestial beings (2:10), and scoffing at the second coming of Christ (3:3, 4). THEOLOGY OF 2 PETER The theology of 2 Peter is presented in the context of addressing false doctrine. Peter describes God as One who has power, glory, and excellence (1:3). He is the almighty Creator (3:5). And although He is patient (3:8, 9), He will render judgment (2:4–10; 3:7). The epistle also addresses Christology. It contains one of the most direct statements of the deity of Christ found in the NT. In the opening of the letter, Peter refers to “the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ (1:1). Both “God” and “Savior” are applied to Jesus in this verse. Peter also speaks of having been a witness of the “majesty” of Christ at His transfiguration (1:16–18). The One who is both God and Savior is also a King who reigns over an eternal kingdom (1:11). Christ’s final coming and judgment serve as another important theological theme in 2 Peter (3:3–13). Before the final judgment, there will be a time of tribulation in which there will be false teaching. This time of trouble that will come “in the last days” was prophesied by the OT prophets, the apostles, and Jesus Himself (3:2, 3; cf. Dan. 8:17–26; 11:30–45). These “last days” had already begun when Peter wrote. For example, throughout 2:1–3:7, the descriptions of the false teachers should not all be viewed merely as referring to future events but as describing what was already going on. It is also likely that “the ignorant and unstable” who “distort” Paul’s letters (3:15, 16) included false teachers already present in the community. Peter probably wrote this letter to address false teaching that had already begun and would continue to arise in the future (cf. 3:17). 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The turning point in redemptive history has arrived with the coming of the Messiah, Jesus of Nazareth (1:1). Peter was a witness of the majesty of Christ on the “holy mountain” (1:18). This language is reminiscent of OT references to Mount Zion/Jerusalem (cf. Pss. 48:1; 99:9; Isa. 11:9; 27:13; 65:25; Joel 3:17; Zech. 8:3), and perhaps even to Eden (Ezek. 28:14). The revelation of Christ’s majesty on the “holy mountain” indicates that He is the promised Messiah who is fulfilling and will fulfill these OT promises and prophecies. Although the coming of Christ has inaugurated the end times, the final judgment is still future; yet God’s past judgments reveal something about His future judgment. Peter recalls the judgment of angels, the judgment of Noah’s generation, and the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of how He rescues the righteous and judges the wicked (2:4–10). The past judgments of Scripture are a foreshadowing of the great final judgment to come. This judgment will involve the bringing of all creation full circle. The present heavens and earth are being kept for this judgment (3:7), and believers await a new heavens and a new earth (3:13). Even the physical creation, which was defiled by sin at the fall, will itself be redeemed and renewed (cf. Rom. 8:19–23). CHRIST IN 2 PETER Christ is equal to God (1:1–3 notes). It is Christ’s divine power that enables believers to be able to reflect divine attributes (1:3–9; cf. 3:18) and to be able to “enter into the eternal kingdom” (1:11). The historical truth of Christ’s first coming is underscored by Peter as foundational to his readers’ ability to reflect God by Christ’s power and to enter the consummated kingdom of God (1:3–11). What Christ taught during His first coming is foundational to understanding the error of the false teachers in contending that there will be no coming of Christ in the future (3:1–15a). That the historical veracity of Christ’s first coming is crucial is apparent from 3:2, where Christ’s prophecy that false teachers would come confirms the OT prophecy of the same thing (cf. Dan. 8; 11).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: As discussed above, questions concerning the authorship of 2 Peter arose during the patristic period. Challenges to Petrine authorship have multiplied with the rise of historical criticism, fueled in large part by the perceived stylistic differences between 1 Peter and 2 Peter. The relationship between 2 Peter and Jude is another point of contention (see “Special Issues” below). Given the similarities between the books, the scholarly consensus is that material in 2 Peter reflects dependence on Jude, which is held to contravene Petrine authorship. The conclusion is made on the assumption that an apostle (Peter) would not have derived material from one who was not formally appointed to the office of apostle (Jude). This view assumes that an apostle would regard a document by a prophet (and half-brother of Jesus) as necessarily less inspired by the Holy Spirit and therefore less authoritative than the writing of an apostle. That assumption needs to be supported, not merely asserted. Several passages have been addressed in depth by interpreters because a superficial reading seems to contradict orthodoxy or the consensus of Reformed theology: (1) That God promises to make believers “partakers of the divine nature” (1:4) has been thought to teach theosis, the deification or divinization of believers in a manner that violates the essential and eternal distinction between the Creator and the creature. (2) That false teachers “deny the Master who bought them” (2:1) has been construed to teach either that genuine believers can apostatize (cf. 2:20) or that the divine intention of Christ’s atoning death was to redeem all humanity and not His elect specifically, or both. (3) The timing of God’s consignment of rebellious angels to Tartarus in antiquity has been debated (2:4). (4) There has been and is disagreement whether 3:10–13 predicts an utter destruction of the present universe through incineration or allows for a recasting of its elements after their purification from all pollution. Each of these interpretive issues is addressed briefly in the notes on these passages.

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Some relationship between 2 Peter and Jude is virtually certain. Although verbatim agreement is rare (2:17; cf. Jude 13), they have similar ideas, words, OT illustrations, and order of text (2:1–18; cf. Jude 4–16). Several explanations are possible. Either 2 Peter used Jude (the scholarly consensus), or Jude used 2 Peter, or there was a common source unknown to us. None of these possibilities regarding the direction of dependence between 2 Peter and Jude (or even a lost shared source) is problematic for the apostolic authority of this epistle. There is no reason why an apostle could not choose to make use of other documents in his writing as long as these documents teach the truth.
