sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: In style, diction, and content, 1 John follows the fourth gospel closely. It is almost certainly by the same author (see Introduction to John: Author). Despite the fact that 1 John does not identify its author explicitly and the fact that many scholars believe the gospel of John does not identify its author either, the traditional assignment of these books to John the son of Zebedee cannot be disproved. It rests on firmer evidence than more speculative proposals of other authors, such as John the Elder or John Mark. The emphasis in 1:1 on authoritative proclamation and eyewitness testimony is most naturally seen as a reflection of John’s apostolic calling (cf. John 19:35; 20:3–8; 21:24).

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: First John was written to warn and instruct the readers about false teaching (2:26; 3:7) that denied Jesus Christ had come in the flesh (4:2, 3). This teaching held that Christ only appeared to be human, so that there was no real incarnation and no divine Savior who was able to die as an atonement for sinners. Christ only seemed to die. There is much speculation about precisely who these false teachers were, but the letter does not offer much information about them. The false teaching of 1 John is generally known from early Christian history and is called “Docetism” (from the Gk. dokeō , “to seem” or “to appear”). Some scholars think that the false teaching was a variety of Gnosticism, a religious movement that connected salvation with an experience of individual, esoteric revelation (from the Gk. gnōsis , “knowledge”). An example would be the teaching of the late-first-century teacher Cerinthus. Later writers regarded Cerinthus as both Gnostic and Docetic, but there is little in 1 John to connect the false teaching opposed there with the specific ideas attributed to Cerinthus, or even to Gnosticism more generally. Several considerations indicate that 1 John was written after the gospel of John. First, it refers very briefly to ideas that the gospel unfolds much more clearly and fully. Apparently the original audience is presumed to have knowledge of the gospel. Second, the conflict with Docetism is absent from the gospel and appears to be a later development. Third, there is no hint in 1 John of the ideological conflict with “the Jews” that pervades the first half of the gospel. The gospel shows the Christian community painfully distinguishing itself from the Jewish people, while 1 John reflects a later time, when Christian self-identification was well established and could be presupposed. Another indication for the date of 1 John comes from comparison with the letters of Ignatius and Polycarp that are to be dated no earlier than c. 110 A.D. These writings criticize false teachings similar to but more developed than those addressed in 1 John. To accommodate this development, 1 John should be dated some years earlier than 110 and likely at some point in the 90s.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Although 1 John has traditionally been regarded as a letter, it lacks key distinguishing features of a letter (salutation, introductory greeting, final greeting; see “Introduction to the Epistles”). On the other hand, John addresses his readers as “my little children” (2:1). He seems to be writing to a specific group of people with whom he has a close relationship. In its basic purposes of admonition and instruction, 1 John is similar to most of the NT letters, though it is not a typical letter. Since there is no specific beginning address to a particular church or final farewell to particular people in a church, some scholars believe that 1 John may be a circular epistle that was intended for several churches. The letter is notoriously difficult to outline, since unlike the structure of Paul’s letters, there appears to be no linear argument. There is a repetition of discussions or arguments to which the author returns. The only semblance of structure appears to be a circular or conical kind of movement throughout. It may be a type of rhetoric known in the ancient world that repeatedly amplified themes laid out in the beginning of the writing. Another interesting feature of 1 John is its use of John’s gospel, which likely had been written earlier in the 80s or early 90s A.D. , or perhaps even earlier. In fact, John’s gospel can be a key to understanding some of the issues in 1 John. For example, there is some debate about whether John makes a distinction throughout the letter between true spiritual believers (close to God) and true believers who are misguided (and not so close to God) or between true believers and pseudo-believers. First John uses terms such as light and darkness , truth and lie , and love and hate to make the distinction, terms that the gospel of John uses to distinguish true believers in the God of Israel (Jesus’ followers) from pseudo-believers in the God of Israel (the unbelieving Jewish leaders). There is also a relationship between 1 John and 2 and 3 John. There are some common themes, though each letter has its own unique features. If, as is most likely, the same author is responsible for all three letters, it seems plausible that 1 John was written first, followed by 2 John and then 3 John.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: One of the recurring themes of 1 John is assurance. John seeks to reassure his readers that they are Christians, and he provides them with a number of ways in which they can know that they are believers. His method of assurance involves proceeding through a variety of contrasts. He contrasts those who walk in the light with those who walk in the darkness (1:6, 7), those who say they have no sin with those who confess their sin (1:8–10). He contrasts those who keep God’s commandments with those who do not (2:3–6), and those who love their brother with those who hate their brother (2:9–11; 3:11–15). He contrasts those who love the world with those who do not (2:15–17). He contrasts those who practice righteousness with those who practice sin (3:1–10). John contrasts those who love with those who do not love (4:7–12). Finally, he contrasts those who believe God and those who do not believe, those who have the Son and those who do not (5:10–12). By means of contrast, John also explains how believers will be able to discern false teachers, or “antichrists.” Antichrists are those who “went out from us” in contrast to those who did not (2:18, 19). They went out “that it might become plain that they are not of us” (v. 19). The “antichrists” are those who deny “that Jesus is the Christ” (v. 22) in contrast with those who “confess” the Son (v. 23). The antichrists are also identified as those who do not confess that Jesus Christ “has come in the flesh” in contrast with those who do (4:2, 3). Interspersed throughout this series of contrasts by means of which John both assures his readers and enables them to exercise discernment is the repeated phrase “by this we know” (2:3; 3:16; 3:24; 4:6, 13; 5:2). His intent is to provide his readers with the doctrinal knowledge they need in order to judge rightly regarding their own faith and the faith of others. The common theme is an echo of Jesus’ words in the Sermon on the Mount: “You will recognize them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16, 20). His purpose is to encourage them to flee from sin (2:1) Another primary theme in 1 John is love. It is a particular emphasis in chs. 3 and 4, but it occurs throughout the epistle. In those who keep God’s Word, John says, God’s love is perfected (2:5). Those who abide in the light love their brother (2:10). John insists that love of the Father is inconsistent with love of the world (2:15). Furthermore, we are children of God as a result of His love for us (3:1). Love for one another characterizes Christians and is evidence of the indwelling love of God (3:11–24). We are to love one another because love is from God (4:7). John tells his readers that their love is founded on God’s love. God demonstrated His love for us by sending His Son to be the propitiation for our sins (4:8–10). Because He so loved us, we are to love one another (4:11–12). To abide in love is to abide in God for “God is love” (4:16). Finally, John explains, love of God is inconsistent with hatred of one another. Whoever loves God must also love his brother (4:20, 21). THEOLOGY OF 1 JOHN Several theological emphases are to be found in John’s first epistle. Among the most significant of these include: 1. Eschatology. As do the other books of the NT, 1 John robustly espouses the idea that the latter days prophesied by the OT have begun to be fulfilled with the coming of Christ, are ongoing throughout the church age, and will be consummated at Christ’s second coming. These aspects of eschatology, as well as John’s other theological themes, are elaborated in the study notes. 2. God. God is light (1:5, 7), truth (implied in 4:6), and love (4:8, 9, 16), and the Father of Jesus Christ (1:3; 4:15) and of His people (2:13; cf. 3:10). God has expressed His love to His people through sending His Son (4:9–11, 19), and His love is the source for Christians’ love for one another (3:16; 4:7, 9–12). Each of these characteristics is the subject of some meditation, but always in connection with the development of corresponding virtues in the believers. The ideals of purity and love that are held out to the reader are gifts from God, communicated from His self-revelation. At the same time, they are made real in the believer’s experience through the believer’s practice of them . This reality is possible through being born again and through the forgiveness of sins. 3. End-time Eternal Life for God’s People. Christ is called “the eternal life” (1:2). The reason for this most likely is that He not only possesses eternal life because of His deity, but because of His resurrection. People who trust in Jesus come into union with Him as the resurrected Christ, so that they partake of “eternal life” (5:11–13, 20), which is eternal resurrection life, which begins spiritually in this age and is completed later in physical resurrection. Thus, believers have “passed out of death into life” (3:14), which is “eternal life” (5:13) and which is a clear allusion to John 5:24, where the same language is used together with “eternal life.” John 5:25 says this is a spiritual resurrection happening “now” at the present “hour,” and that will be completed in physical resurrection (5:28, 29). 4. The Holy Spirit. Believers have been given the Spirit, which assures them that God “abides” in them (3:24; 4:13). The Spirit enables believers to accept the apostolic testimony to Jesus (4:6) and to maintain the truth of Christ’s incarnation (4:2). The “Spirit is the truth” (5:6b). Therefore, the Spirit’s testimony can be trusted (5:6a), for example, with respect to His witness that the divine Christ has come in the flesh (5:6, 8). John refers to the Spirit’s work through speaking of their “anointing” by the Spirit, which enables them to know the crucial truths of the gospel (“you all have knowledge”; 2:20) in contrast to the competing false teaching (2:19–21; 2:26, 27). 5. The Latter-Day Tribulation and Coming of Antichrists and False Teachers. The spirit of antichrist (4:3), a latter-day enemy of the gospel, attacks at every point. He impugns the self-revelation of God by trying to deny that the Son of God truly came in the flesh, that is, was incarnated. In this way, he threatens to undermine the believer’s confidence before God. Moreover, the adversary tries to make the case that someone can believe in God without taking part in the love and kindness that is God’s nature. This would make salvation also a mere appearance. To the light and truth of the gospel, the spirit of antichrist, which may appear in several individuals who can rightly be called antichrists, opposes by darkness, lies, and the rule of hatred and mental confusion. The only defense against this end-time enemy is to hold to the truth of God’s Word (cf. 2:14), especially the revelation that the divine Son has come in the flesh and, as a man, died for His people, who can rely on His commandments and follow them by the power of His Spirit. 1

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: John writes as one who was an eyewitness of the turning point of redemptive history. All of the promises and prophecies of the OT began to be fulfilled with the incarnation of the Son of God, and John was a witness to this incarnation (1:1–3). John’s contrasts between light and darkness recall the creation narrative of Gen. 1. His reference to the children of God (3:1) and the children of the devil (3:10) recall the distinction God makes between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent (Gen. 3:15). John presents the entire Christian life as a continuation of the cosmic spiritual battle that began at the fall and continues until the final judgment. Our enemies in this battle are represented as “antichrists” who deny the incarnation of the Son in the flesh (2:18, 22; 4:3). Although the cosmic battle continues, there is no question about who will win: “The darkness is passing away and the true light is already shining” (2:8, 17). In fact, the decisive victory in the cosmic battle has already been won because the Son of God came “to destroy the works of the devil” (3:8; cf. Heb. 2:14). Christians, then, live between the decisive victory won at the cross and the consummation of that victory, when sin, death, and the devil will be cast away (cf. Rev. 20:10, 14). The consummation has not yet come, but when it does, not only will our external enemies be vanquished, but our internal enemies will be a thing of the past as well. John tells us that on that day, “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (3:2). CHRIST IN 1 JOHN John declares that God has been revealed in Christ in order to communicate eternal life to those who believe. The letter opens with a focus on the incarnate Christ as the “Word,” whom the apostles had heard, seen, and touched, and whom they proclaimed (1:1–3). This emphasis here and elsewhere in the letter (4:2; 5:1, 5–7; cf. 4:15) is an attempt to counter the false teachers’ claim that the divine Christ did not truly take on human form (2:22, 23; 4:3). There is also emphasis on Christ’s dying for His people as a penal substitute (e.g., 2:2; 3:16; 4:10), cleansing them from sin by His blood (1:7), and coming to “destroy the works of the devil” (3:8). Christ’s giving of Himself is the epitome of love (3:16). Christ’s vicarious death is also related to the false teaching that the divine Christ did not truly take on human form but perhaps only appeared to do so. If this false teaching were true, then Christ’s death for human sinners would not be effective, since He would not have been a real human representative, bearing human sin in behalf of other human beings. Christ is also called “the word of life” and “the eternal life” (1:1, 2).

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: While 1 John is simple to read in both Greek and its English translation, its concepts are profound and sometimes hard to understand. Some of the more difficult of these to understand, at least upon first reading, are such concepts as: 1. “Not sinning” (3:6, 9; 5:18). First John 3:6 affirms that the genuine believers do not “keep on sinning.” Verse 9 states, “No one born of God makes a practice of sinning ... and he cannot keep on sinning because he has been born of God” (cf. 5:18). On the surface, these verses appear to say that true Christians should not sin at all. That John is not making perfectionistic claims in 3:6, 9 is clear from 1:8–10. First, 1:8 says that if people claim not to be in a condition of sin, then they are liars; 1:10 says that if people claim not to have committed actual acts of sin, then they make God a liar. God has said that all are sinners, including Christians, who will not be completely without sin until their final glorification at the end of history. Thus, Christians should “confess their sins” throughout the course of their life (1:9). In stating that believers do not “keep on sinning” and that they do not “make a practice of sinning” (3:6, 9), John is talking about the general course of a believer’s life. While believers will sin until they are glorified, the bent of their lives is not toward sin; rather, their primary orientation and direction is away from sin and toward God. This is evident in their confession of the true faith, their ongoing life of repentance, their love for other believers, and their progress in personal holiness as they put sin to death in their lives (1:8–10; 4:7, 8; 5:1–12). 2. “Sin that leads to death” (5:16). First John 5:16 says, “there is sin that leads to death.” Some think this refers to a particular sin that true believers can commit, which will lead to their physical but not spiritual death. But commentators do not agree on what type of sin this would be. Furthermore, the first part of 5:16 speaks of praying that God would “give” true believers “life,” which refers either to continuing to maintain the eternal spiritual resurrection life that had begun in them or to give them final, physical resurrection life at the very end of history. The opposite of “eternal life” is eternal “death,” which is likely what is in mind with the “sin that leads to death.” Thus, the sin that leads to death is not a sin that produces physical death but a sin that produces spiritual death—cuts one off from God’s blessed presence. That the sin that leads to death is one that produces spiritual death is the view of those who believe that the “sin that leads to death” refers to the sin of apostasy (unbelief in the gospel), upon which a true believer would lose his salvation, i.e., spiritually suffer death. Similarly, it could refer to a sin of apostasy that reveals that a professing Christian was never really a Christian at all (2:19). The second option—apostasy that only false professors of faith commit—best fits the teaching of this epistle, since 3:6, 9 affirm that genuine Christians “cannot keep on sinning.” Those who have truly been born of God cannot live a life that is oriented away from the Lord; rather, they will continue to seek Him in faith and repentance. They will not be perfect, but they will keep coming to the Lord such that He will raise them up on the last day (cf. John 6:39, 40, 44). They will not commit the sin of final apostasy. John does not teach that true believers can lose their salvation, and he does clearly affirm that apostatizing false teachers who profess to believe never had true faith to begin with (cf. 2:19). First John 5:16 speaks of this end-time sin of apostasy, which the elect will not commit but only those who profess faith falsely.

content.text: PROLOGUE: THE ORIGINAL APOSTOLIC MESSAGE CONCERNING ETERNAL LIFE
THE FIRST EXPOSITION OF TRUE SALVIFIC COMMUNION WITH GOD
Communion with God is demonstrated by acknowledging sin and Christ as the provision for sin
Genuine faith is discerned by the end-time tests of righteousness and love
Genuine faith is discerned by the end-time test of correct belief in Christ in contrast with the world and the antichrists’ view of Christ
THE SECOND EXPOSITION OF TRUE SALVIFIC COMMUNION WITH GOD
Divine sonship of believers is discerned by the test of righteousness
Divine sonship of believers is discerned by the test of love
Divine sonship of believers is discerned by the test of correct belief
THE THIRD EXPOSITION OF TRUE SALVIFIC COMMUNION WITH GOD
Genuine faith is discerned by a love that comes from God and is rooted in faith
Genuine faith is discerned by the test of correct belief, which is the basis of love
EPILOGUE: TO GIVE ASSURANCE TO CHRISTIANS ABOUT THEIR SALVATION
To give assurance to true Christians that eternal life is through Christ
To give assurance that they have access to the Father through prayer, especially with respect to prayer for others in the Christian community
To give assurance that genuine believers are characterized by righteousness and that they really have a relationship with God and Jesus

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The style, diction, and content of 2 John mark it as written by the same author as 1 John and the gospel of John. This author has been traditionally identified as the apostle John, son of Zebedee, and no more plausible ascription has been proposed. See Introduction to 1 John: Title and Author.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Second John was written to warn against the same strain of false teaching that 1 John opposes, namely, Docetism (see Introduction to 1 John: Date and Occasion). It must have been written at about the same time, in the last two decades of the first century, likely in the late nineties A.D. While it repeats ideas from 1 John, it does not presuppose knowledge of 1 John on the part of the reader. It provides theological criteria for extending hospitality—and implicit endorsement—for traveling teachers (vv. 9, 11). Third John also addresses the motif of encouraging hospitality to orthodox teachers (3 John 5, 10). It is plausible that 2 John was written after 1 John. But 2 John’s identified audience (v. 1) is more specific, and the original readers of this epistle may or may not have been familiar with 1 John. Therefore the epistles’ order of composition does not affect our interpretation.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Second John is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (vv. 1–3), body (vv. 4–11), and conclusion (vv. 12, 13). It is also a very brief epistle, unlike most of Paul’s epistles, but much like the shorter letters written in the Greco-Roman world.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Some scholars understand 2 John to be written to a Christian woman and her family, either her natural family or the fellowship of believers associated with her. It is also possible that “the elect lady” is the church to whom John is writing and “her children” are the members of the church. Like the early letters of Paul, it is a letter of encouragement and warning written to a specific fellowship for which the author has pastoral responsibility. As in 1 John, there is a focus in the letter on the false teaching of those who have the spirit of antichrist and their followers who “deceive.” THEOLOGY OF 2 JOHN Truth is indispensable to “the elder” who wrote 2 John. He loves the letter’s recipients “in truth,” as do “all who know the truth” (v. 1). This truth “abides in us and will be with us forever” (v. 2). This language may suggest that, as “eternal life” functions as a name for Christ in 1 John 1:2, so here “truth” stands for the Son of God, who described Himself as “the truth” (John 14:6) and promised to abide in and be with those who follow Him (John 15:5; 14:8). Or the reference may be to the Spirit of truth, who, Jesus promised, will be in believers and “with you forever” (John 14:16, 17). As personal as “the truth” is, it also has specific doctrinal content. To “walk in the truth” (v. 4) is to confess that Jesus is the Christ who has come in the flesh (v. 7), which is “to abide in the teaching of Christ” that secures communion with God the Father and the Son (v. 9). “Walking in the truth” is also walking “according to his commandments,” by which Christians obey God’s preeminent commandment to “love one another” (vv. 5, 6). The command to love is not new, but has been delivered to us “from the beginning” (1 John 2:7–11 note). Since love is defined as walking according to the Father’s commandments (v. 6), it has more to do with concrete, compassionate actions than with merely affectionate emotion (1 John 3:16–19). Though John in this letter does not discuss the motif of God’s sovereign election, he affirms it in addressing his readers as “elect” and conveying greetings from “your elect sister” (vv. 1, 13). John’s gospel speaks of the Father’s giving people to Jesus as the sheep for whom He lays down His life (John 10:15, 29; 17:6) and of Jesus’ choice of His disciples (John 15:16, 19). 2

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: The confession that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh (v. 7), which distinguishes believers who walk in the truth from the many deceivers in circulation, affirms the incarnation of “the Father’s Son” (v. 3) as the indispensable bedrock of revealed truth and, implicitly, of God’s redemptive plan for history. Unlike 1 John (1:7; 2:2; 3:16; 4:10), this brief letter does not elaborate the atoning purpose for which the Son assumed human nature, but the confession that Christ came “in the flesh” implies the purpose (vicarious obedience and suffering) for which He embraced the frailty of humanity. CHRIST IN 2 JOHN Second John affirms both the deity of Christ and His true humanity. “Jesus Christ the Father’s Son” is joined with God the Father as the divine persons who confer the blessings (grace, mercy, peace) pronounced in the opening benediction (v. 3). The unique authority of Christ to reveal God the Father is implied in the statement that those who abandon “the teaching of Christ” have no access to God; however, remaining in that teaching brings saving communion with “both the Father and the Son” (v. 9). Remaining in this teaching entails maintaining the reality of the Son’s incarnation and humanity: anyone who fails to confess that Jesus is the Christ who has come in the flesh is a deceiver and an antichrist (v. 7).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Due to its short length, 2 John has not had the same influence on the history of the church as many of the other books in the New Testament. However, its testimony to the centrality of the incarnation has reminded generation after generation of Christians that orthodox Christology is indispensable to a saving relationship with Jesus Christ.

content.text: The Danger of False Teaching and Response to False Teachers

sections.heading: Title and Author
sections.content: The third letter of John was written by the author of 2 John, as indicated by key similarities of style and structure. As with the gospel of John and 1 and 2 John, the traditional ascription to the apostle John cannot be disproved and is more likely than any alternative. See Introduction to 1 John: Title and Author.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: While 1 and 2 John celebrate truths that unite all Christians, 3 John laments the petty rivalry that sets Christians against one another. In particular, the letter was occasioned by a sharp conflict between Diotrephes (apparently an elder in a congregation under John’s care) and others in the congregation over hospitality shown to traveling missionaries. It is likely that Demetrius, who is commended to Gaius by the letter, was himself such a traveling missionary in need of temporary lodging; and clearly Gaius, the letter’s recipient, had distinguished himself for hospitality to traveling teachers of “the truth” (vv. 3–8). There is no trace in 3 John of the christological conflict that looms large in 1 and 2 John, and it may be that 3 John was written earlier than either 1 or 2 John, possibly in the 80s of the first century A.D. , before the christological conflict became most heated. It is also just as plausible that 3 John was written after 1 and 2 John, perhaps in the late 90s.

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: Like 2 John, 3 John is patterned after a classic short Greco-Roman letter. It generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles); it contains a standard letter opening (vv. 1, 2), body (vv. 3–12), and conclusion (vv. 13, 14).

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Third John is marked by its salutation, introductory greeting, and final greeting as a letter. More specifically, it is a letter of commendation introducing Demetrius to the recipient, Gaius. THEOLOGY OF 3 JOHN As in 1 and 2 John, the elder emphasizes love and truth and their close interconnection. John loves Gaius in truth (v. 1). Brothers who had enjoyed Gaius’s generous hospitality, though they were strangers to him, bore witness both that he was “walking in the truth” (vv. 3, 4) and that he had shown love by providing for them (vv. 6, 7). By contrast, the prideful Diotrephes expressed his defiance of the apostle’s authority both by “talking wicked nonsense” (instead of truth) and by punishing (instead of loving; vv. 9, 10) believers such as Gaius who welcomed the brothers. Although John does not accuse Diotrephes of denying the confession of Jesus as Christ come in the flesh, as deceivers do (2 John 7), refusing or opposing hospitality to those who faithfully bear “the name” is nonetheless a failure to “walk in the truth.” Whatever one’s church office or professed beliefs, the principle announced by Jesus holds: “You will recognize them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:15–20). As John expresses it, “Whoever does good is from God; whoever does evil has not seen God” (v. 11; cf. 1 John 2:4; 4:8). 3

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: This short letter beautifully illustrates a theme that runs through redemptive history: that believers who have received God’s gracious welcome through the gospel gladly share in the spread of the good news by welcoming and providing for its messengers. The letter’s recipient, Gaius, belonged to the blessed company of those who became “fellow workers for [God’s] truth” (v. 8) by housing, feeding, and funding the bearers of God’s Word. This company includes a Gentile widow in Zarephath who fed the prophet Elijah at the risk, she expected, of her own and her son’s starvation (1 Kin. 17:8–16), and the woman of Shunem who persuaded her husband to remodel their home to accommodate the visits of the prophet Elisha (2 Kin. 4:8–10). Obadiah risked his life and proved true to his name (“Yahweh’s servant”) by hiding a hundred true prophets in a cave and bringing them bread and water (1 Kin. 18:12, 13). When Jesus sent out the Twelve and the seventy-two, He promised that as they traveled to spread the good news of God’s kingdom, they would be provided for by people of peace (Luke 9:3–5; 10:4–9). In receiving Jesus’ messengers, these hosts were welcoming Jesus Himself, so they would share in the messengers’ reward (Matt. 10:40–42). In Philippi, Lydia’s first instinct upon coming to faith was to open her home to welcome the missionary team of Paul and Silas (Acts 16:15). When Paul wrote his letter to the Romans, he expected to be “helped on my journey” (same Gk. verb as in 3 John 7) to Spain by their financial support after a spiritually refreshing sojourn among them (Rom. 15:24). Hebrews urges its hearers not to neglect “hospitality to strangers,” subtly reminding them that when Abraham welcomed unknown guests he was entertaining angels (Heb. 13:2, alluding to Gen. 18:1–15). Such assistance not only shows love for one’s fellow believers, but it will also be repaid by the Lord Himself. At the last judgment, the Son of Man will commend and reward those who fed, welcomed, clothed, and cared for the least of Jesus’ brothers (Matt. 25:34–40). CHRIST IN 3 JOHN There is no explicit mention of the divine-human Savior in 3 John. This is not surprising in view of the brevity of the letter and its specific focus on hospitality to traveling gospel emissaries. However, 3 John seems to contain two allusions to Christ that would have been easily recognizable to early Christians. First, John says that faithful teachers “have gone out for the sake of the name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (v. 7). That “name” almost certainly belongs to Jesus. The apostles rejoiced to suffer for the sake of “the name” (Acts 5:41; cf. 9:16), having declared that this is the only name under heaven in which salvation is found (Acts 4:10–12; John 3:18; 1 John 5:13). Christians are baptized in “the name” of Jesus (Acts 2:38) and call on His name (Acts 9:14). His is the “honorable name” by which they are called (James 2:7). The brothers whom John commends do not accept support from non-Christians (“Gentiles”) as they carry Jesus’ name and convey without charge the good news of God’s gift of grace in Him (1 Cor. 9:18; 2 Cor. 11:7–11). Second, John endorses Demetrius, probably the letter’s carrier and a brother in need of shelter and supply, as one whose faithfulness is testified to by everyone, by “the truth itself,” and by John (v. 12). It is possible that the testimony of “the truth itself” on Demetrius’s behalf simply means his fidelity to the apostolic gospel. But it is perhaps equally likely that John, who reported Jesus’ self-identification as “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), intends readers to think of Jesus, who is the truth in person (see note on 2 John 2).

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: As is the case with 2 John, the brevity of 3 John explains why Christians throughout history have referred to it infrequently and have not paid it the same kind of attention as a book such as the gospel of John or Paul’s epistle to the Romans. Nevertheless, its exhortation to support those who labor for the truth of the gospel remains an important call to the church to provide for the needs of those who work in full-time gospel ministry as preachers and teachers of God’s Word.

sections.heading: Author
sections.content: The author of this epistle identifies himself as “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (v. 1). The name Judah (Gk. Judas ; English Jude ) was common among first-century Jews, and at least eight different individuals of that name are mentioned in the NT, including two of Jesus’ disciples (Luke 6:16). The author cannot, therefore, be identified on the basis of name alone. The best clue to his identity is the description “brother of James” (v. 1). The only James known well enough in the early church to be referred to in this unqualified way is James the prominent church leader (Acts 12:17; 15:13), author of the epistle that bears his name, and half-brother of Jesus (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3; Gal. 1:19). If this identification of James is correct, the author of the present epistle is Jude the half-brother of Jesus (Matt. 13:55; Mark 6:3), who, along with his other brothers, did not believe in Jesus until after the resurrection (Mark 3:21, 31; John 7:5; Acts 1:14). Jude might be one of those to whom Paul refers in his mention of the itinerant ministry of the Lord’s brothers and their wives (1 Cor. 9:5). If Jude was in fact the brother of Jesus, it is likely his humility that motivates him not to tell his readers that explicitly (note the similar reserve in James 1:1). Several objections to the authenticity of Jude have been raised, but all rest on questionable assumptions or exegesis. Most are linked with proposing a date too late for Jude’s lifetime (“Date and Occasion” below). Some argue that the quality of the Greek used in this epistle is better than one could expect of a Galilean, but Galilee was no doubt bilingual (Greek and Aramaic) in the first century, and too little is known about Jude’s knowledge of the Gk. language to conclude that he could not have written this letter. Furthermore, it is quite possible that Jude used a secretary to whom he dictated the letter and who could write in a more refined Gk. style than Jude himself (as was possibly the case for Peter as well; cf. 1 Pet. 5:12). In light of the aforementioned evidence, we may safely conclude that the author of this epistle is Jude the brother of Jesus.

sections.heading: Date and Occasion
sections.content: Practically the only evidence for the date of Jude is what can be inferred about the lifetime of its author and the heresy he combats. If Jude was younger than Jesus and James, as his position in the lists of brothers in Matt. 13:55 and Mark 6:3 suggests, he could have survived well into the last quarter of the first century. If we assume that Peter wrote 2 Peter, and, with most scholars, that 2 Peter used Jude (see Introduction to 2 Peter: Special Issues), then Jude would have been written before A.D. 65–67, the likely date for 2 Peter. Perhaps Jude was written as early as the mid-50s. Some argue for a second-century date on the grounds that Jude is combatting Gnosticism. While the teachings Jude opposes may well have been precursors of Gnosticism, they cannot be identified with the fully developed Gnostic heresies of the second century (see Introduction to 2 Peter: Characteristics and Themes). There is no indication in the letter of its place of writing or its destination. While some believe Jude’s use of the OT and Jewish apocryphal literature points to a Jewish Christian audience, this material may reveal more about his own background than that of his readers. Perhaps Jude wrote his epistle as a circular letter to a number of churches whose conditions he knew from having conducted an itinerant ministry among them (cf. 1 Cor. 9:5).

sections.heading: Genre and Literary Features
sections.content: The book of Jude is a letter, and it generally follows standard first-century epistolary conventions (see Introduction to the Epistles). It contains a standard letter opening (vv. 1, 2), body (vv. 3–23), and conclusion (vv. 24, 25). This letter strongly reflects the context of first-century Jewish Christianity, as one would expect from a Jewish-Christian author like Jude. Evidence for the author’s Jewish background includes his many allusions to the OT (though he does not quote the OT directly), his familiarity with Jewish apocryphal tradition, and his strong ethical concerns.

sections.heading: Characteristics and Primary Themes
sections.content: Jude confronts a threat similar to that opposed in 2 Peter: false teachers who were using Christian liberty and the free grace of God as a license for immorality (v. 4; cf. 2 Pet. 2:1–3). Most of the epistle (vv. 4–19) is devoted to stern denunciation of the false teachers in order to impress upon his readers the seriousness of the threat. But Jude’s strategy is more than mere negative opposition. He urges his readers to grow in their knowledge of Christian truth (v. 20), to bear a firm witness for the truth (v. 3), and to seek to reclaim those whose faith was wavering (vv. 22, 23). This prescription for confronting spiritual error is as effective today as when it was first written.

sections.heading: Theology
sections.content: As does 2 Peter, Jude contains the idea of a time of tribulation in which there will be false teaching (cf. Dan. 8:17–26; 11:30–45). Verses 17, 18 introduce and quote a prophecy from Christ and the apostles (also referred to in 2 Pet. 3:2, 3, with minor differences): “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly passions.” Much of the letter is dedicated to describing this false teaching and those who spread it (vv. 4–18). The “last time” mentioned in v. 18 is not likely only future, but had already begun in their midst. This is clear from v. 4, where the false teachers are described as those who had already “crept in unnoticed” (v. 4; cf. the present tense description of the false teachers in vv. 9–13, 16). Indeed, most commentators agree that the reason that Jude wrote this letter was to address the problem of false teaching that had already started and that the church would continue to face in the future (cf. 2 Pet. 3:17). Jude encourages the church with his reminder that the impenitent false teachers of his era would undergo a terrible judgment at the very end of the church age (v. 14, 15). Believers can be assured that this end awaits all those who pervert the gospel and never repent, regardless of the generation in which they live.

sections.heading: In the Larger Story of the Bible
sections.content: Like Peter, Jude recalls past judgments of God in order to warn his readers of the greater judgment to come upon false teachers and other wicked people. Jude reminds his readers of the judgment of unbelievers at the exodus (v. 5) and the judgment of angels (v. 6). He points to the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of how God will punish with eternal fire (v. 7). He compares the false teachers to those who perished in Korah’s rebellion (v. 11). In short, Jude applies the principle of 1 Cor. 10:11 to show how the judgments of the OT happened “as an example” and “for our instruction.” Jude understands that he is living before the final judgment and that God’s former judgments are but a shadow of this greater judgment to come. Because there is a final judgment yet to come, believers are to persevere (vv. 20–23), knowing that it is Jesus Christ who is able to keep them from stumbling and to present them blameless before God (vv. 24, 25).

sections.heading: Christ in This Book
sections.content: Although his epistle is among the shortest books of the NT, Jude contributes much to our understanding of the person and work of Christ. In regard to the person of the Savior, the ESV translation of v. 5 states that “Jesus” delivered Israel from Egypt and destroyed unfaithful Israel in the wilderness. Normally, it would be expected that “the Lord” would be credited (as other manuscripts and translations read), but the ESV translation here reflects the best ancient manuscripts, which have the name “Jesus” instead of “the Lord.” Thus, Jude is identifying Jesus with Yahweh, the One who described in Exodus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy as delivering Israel from Egypt and judging the unbelieving Israelites in the wilderness. This apostolic understanding of the activity of the preincarnate Jesus is comparable to 1 Cor. 10:4, where Paul says that Israel was “drinking from a spiritual rock which followed them [in the wilderness], and the rock was Christ.” In any case, Jude’s description of Jesus’ work in the exodus is a strong affirmation of the deity of Christ and proof that this belief goes all the way back to the earliest Christians. Other indications of Jude’s belief in the deity of Christ include the fact that he calls Jesus “Master and Lord” (v. 4). His omniscience, or at least His ability to foresee the future, is seen in his prediction of the coming of false teaching in the church community to whom Jude writes (vv. 17, 18), which had already begun. The end times that have been inaugurated by Christ will be consummated at His final coming, when He shows “mercy” to those who believed (v. 21; cf. v. 24). The epistle ends on a christological note: “to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen.” Jude also gives us insight into the work of Christ, particularly His work in preserving us in the faith. Believers’ salvation is “kept for Jesus Christ,” presumably by the reality of their effective “calling” and the “loving” power of God (v. 1). Christ “is able to keep you from stumbling, and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (v. 24). Jude’s short epistle, therefore, reminds us that from start to finish, salvation is granted, sustained, and consummated by Christ alone, according to the sovereign purposes of the Father and outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: History of Interpretation
sections.content: Despite its brevity, the epistle was widely used in the early church because of its obvious orthodoxy and value. Questions about its canonical status arose largely because of its use of apocryphal literature (vv. 9, 14, 15 and notes; “Special Issues” below). In addition to possible allusions in the apostolic fathers, Jude is listed in the Muratorian Canon (second century A.D. ) and was accepted as authentic by Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, Origen (second–third centuries), and Athanasius (fourth century).

sections.heading: Special Issues
sections.content: Any discussion of the book of Jude must take into account several issues regarding its composition and sources. The most important of these include: 1. The Relationship of Jude to 2 Peter. Because Jude and 2 Peter have several concepts in common and seem to be combatting a similar heresy, many have suggested that Peter actually used Jude as a source for his second canonical epistle. A number of scholars conclude the opposite, namely that Jude used 2 Peter. For more information on the relationship between Jude and 2 Peter, see Introduction to 2 Peter: Special Issues. 2. Jude’s Use of Nonbiblical and Apocryphal Materials. As noted above, Jude’s use of apocryphal Jewish materials was the chief obstacle to the epistle’s acceptance in the NT canon. Specifically, Jude 9 seems to refer to the Assumption of Moses and Jude 14, 15 seems to incorporate material from 1 Enoch either through direct quotation or allusion. However, it is also possible that Jude does not refer to these works directly but to common traditions that were used by the authors of those works. Judaism, Protestantism, Roman Catholicism, and Eastern Orthodoxy have rejected first Enoch as canonical Scripture, although some in the Oriental Orthodox tradition consider it inspired. The Assumption of Moses is rejected by all the aforementioned ecclesiastical traditions. Allusion to or citation of extrabiblical materials is rare in the NT. But given the currency of apocryphal religious works during the period, and the desire of the NT writers to communicate the gospel in terms familiar to their readers, it is not surprising to find some occasional use. Examples include 2 Tim. 3:8, which uses Jewish traditions about Ex. 7:11; and the quotation of pagan poets in Acts 17:28; 1 Cor. 15:33; and Titus 1:12. Certainly, Paul never would have believed that the original statements of pagan prophets were divinely inspired, but when he quoted them as part of his own speech at Athens (Acts 17:28), his use of them was inspired by God. Since all truth is God’s truth, Paul could discern where these pagans said true things and therefore use them in his defense of the gospel. The same is true of Jude and his use of extrabiblical sources. Whether Jude quotes the Assumption of Moses and 1 Enoch directly, merely alludes to those works, or cites common traditions incorporated by the writers of those books, he was able under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit to discern what was true in those works from what was false or legendary, and therefore he could appropriately use the material in his epistle. The inclusion of such quotations in the inspired canon, whether for illustrative purposes or as an appeal to conventional wisdom, does not imply that the apocryphal and nonbiblical documents were themselves inspired or that everything in them is being endorsed by the Bible. It is the use of the particular reference that is inspired, not the source of that reference. The apostolic use of extrabiblical traditions and documents is not contrary to the inspiration of the NT, for the authors of the NT were enabled by the Lord to incorporate only that which is truth into their writings.
